title: ‘I’ve hit my midlife sexpot era!’ Romola Garai on marital misery, cheating … and sex scenes in cars | Television | The Guardian
description: Layby hookups are all in a day’s work for Romola Garai in her steamy new drama Adultery. She talks faking orgasms, keeping secrets – and making audiences pass out
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: Layby hookups are all in a day’s work for Romola Garai in her steamy new drama Adultery. She talks faking orgasms, keeping secrets – and making audiences pass out
Content: Tryst issues … Romola Garai in Adultery.Photograph: Nick Eagle/ITVView image in fullscreenTryst issues … Romola Garai in Adultery.Photograph: Nick Eagle/ITVTelevisionInterview‘I’ve hit my midlife sexpot era!’ Romola Garai on marital misery, cheating … and sex scenes in carsMichael HoganLayby hookups are all in a day’s work for Romola Garai in her steamy new drama Adultery. She talks faking orgasms, keeping secrets – and making audiences pass outFri 9 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a raging storm in the Peak District last winter, a blue Toyota Yaris was parked in a remote roadside spot with a sex scene being filmed inside it. “It can pose challenges, depending on the size of the car,” chucklesRomola Garai. “Me and Dominic [Cooper] got in this hatchback and asked: ‘How far do these seats go back?’ Soon there was a gale blowing outside. We were in the car, ready to shoot, but outside the entire film crew were being buffeted by high winds. They said: ‘You guys stay in there, don’t get out!’ while all the lights were getting blown away.”What did the co-stars do while the camera crew battled the elements? “What actors always do in these situations – have a long, gossipy conversation about people in the industry. While everyone else was trying to save the show, we were sitting in the car, like: ‘Well, I’ve heard he’s a total nightmare!’”The in-car tryst is a pivotal moment in new drama Adultery, created by Bafta-winning writer Danny Brocklehurst (Shameless, Fool Me Once, Brassic). The six-parter is billed as a “steamy, scandalous romance” about a whirlwind fling that threatens to unravel two families. Personal trainer Beth (Garai) and GP Tom (Cooper), both married, are thrown together when their teenage children start dating. Insatiably drawn to one another, the pair embark on an intense illicit affair.Can they keep it secret? Will the guilt get too much? Might they even leave their respective spouses? There are shades of Doctor Foster, Cold Feet and The Affair as the story unfolds. The 44-year-old actor – who helpfully explains that her name is pronounced “Romola with the emphasis on ‘Rom’, not ‘ola’, andGary as in Neville or Barlow” – admits the premise gave her pause.View image in fullscreenContents may be hot … Dominic Cooper and Romola Garai in Adultery.Photograph: Thomas Wood/ITV“I picked up a script about a cheating wife, written by a man, with a little bit of hesitation,” she admits. “In our cultural imagination, unfaithful women haven’t always been well served and can often be a projection of male insecurity – from Eve onwards. But some of my favourite books, like Madame Bovary, are so much more than that. Happily, Danny’s scripts were brilliant. They go into the complex area of marital disappointment. Beth’s dissatisfaction isn’t based on anything big. Her husband is a good guy but she’s had to suppress herself. By the time Beth realises she’s given up too much for her marriage, it’s too late. When you have an extreme physical connection with someone else, growing in the fertile ground of marital disappointment, disaster ensues.”Garai immediately connected to the character of Beth. “I just knew her. There are so many versions of that woman in my life. Somebody who’s exhausted from doing all the right things. Ferrying the kids around, washing the team’s football kit, contributing financially to the home in two different jobs. She’s part of the sandwich generation and she’s overwhelmed. I was like: hard-relate. No acting required. She’s also had to give up her own business. I know so many women who had high-powered jobs which went on the back-burner in service of the family. It gave them meaning in their life and value in society. Losing that can be destructive. Resentment sits inside you like a little gremlin.”Extramarital liaisons take place in cars, kitchens and toilets – not to mention the storeroom of a city farm. “I’ll never look at a city farm the same way,” says Garai. “As a mother of two [she’s married to actor-director Sam Hoare and they have two children, aged 10 and 13], I’ve spent many a day at those places but certainly never had anything like that happen. I just had a juice box and bought a squirrel keyring.”Sex scenes have transformed since Garai started out. “They never used to be properly directed,” she says. “It was a case of ‘Do what you want. As long as she gets her tits out, it doesn’t matter.’ Which was awful for 90% of people and great for 10% of people. It’s so much better now with intimacy coordinators. There are respectful, technical conversations. You’re doing it like a stunt, basically, with the equivalent of a fight director telling everyone exactly what to do. You have a very strong line of communication with someone whose responsibility, apart from getting the footage, is to ensure you feel comfortable. It’s a shame it had to get so bad before change came.”Humour helps, too. “Sex scenes are still weird and a bit embarrassing. Physical intimacy with another person releases all sorts of chemicals. Your body is responding and your brain sometimes doesn’t know how to process that. So it’s useful to have a scene partner you can laugh with. It releases the tension.”View image in fullscreen‘I just knew her. There are so many versions of that woman in my life’ … Romola Garai on Adultery.Photograph: PRGarai gets a Meg Ryan moment as the camera lingers on her orgasmic face. “Our intimacy director asked: ‘What’s the storytelling here?’ And I was like: ‘Well, I think she comes.’ Beth is sexually unfulfilled in her marriage. It was important to see her get the specific thing she’s lacking in her life: sexual pleasure.” She laughs. “All it’s missing is a woman in a diner saying: ‘I’ll have what she’s having.’ Hopefully the audience will fill in that gap!”She realises adultery is a hot-button topic. “I’ve already had some pretty punchy conversations, just by telling people what the show’s about. At the hairdresser’s or school gates, I’ll say it’s two ordinary married people who have an affair and people are angry already. Cheating is an issue that’s affected or wounded everyone.” Will there be whispering in the street? “Hope so,” she grins. “I have such a boring life, I love the idea of causing scandalous chat. Maybe I’ll become a figurehead for adulterers. Women might come up and say: ‘Now you understand why I was serially unfaithful to Jasper!’ I’ll be like: ‘I really don’t! Poor Jasper!’”Adultery doesn’t flinch from the fallout from the affair. “It doesn’t pull its punches,” says Garai. “I’m like a prefect on set and thought it was important to show the impact on their spouses and children.” How is she a prefect? “You know in Celebrity Traitors where Professor Hannah Fry says she’s dripping with prefect energy? I’ve got a similar vibe, albeit for less academic reasons. I like to talk about the moral aspects of scenes more than other actors. I don’t mean that as a boast. It’s probably deeply annoying. I bet Danny would be delighted if he never saw my face looming at him again!”She also points out the double standard of how men and women are judged for affairs: “Women get called ‘whores’. There’s no slur word for sexual incontinence in men. You’d never call a dude a ‘home-wrecker’ either.” Even the show’s title caused misunderstandings. “People would ask my kids: ‘Where’s Mummy? She’s not been around for ages.’ They’d reply, ‘She in Manchester doing Adultery. She’s busy with Adultery.”Could Garai’s husband and Cooper’s partner, Gemma Chan, start looking at them askance? “I knew you’d ask that!” she says. “Thankfully not, because there’s nothing more helpful for the stresses and strains of a marriage in midlife than doing a show like this. It really makes you discuss the pitfalls. I hope it provokes conversations between couples at home. Beth and Tom are both the hands-on parent. They’re the carers. But it’s them that have the forbidden relationship. They’re good people doing something bad.”Garai had to master a Manchester accent for the part. “That was terrifying,” she says. “I tried to stay in it on set, which makes everyone call you a twat. People took the piss but I went through fire to make it as accurate as I could. When the show airs, I’ll stay away from Mancunians because I’m sure they’ll tell me exactly what they think!”View image in fullscreenDangerous waters … Beth (Romola Garai) and Tom (Dominic Cooper).Photograph: Thomas Wood/ITVEqually challenging was leading a zumba class. “What got me through the embarrassment was the sense of a woman who loves being in her body. Beth relishes being sweaty and having that endorphin release. It relates to her quest for passion. There’s a well-spring of physical energy within her which needs to be run off. She wants to feel alive and feel joy.” She also croons loudly along to the car stereo. “That was another moment with heavy cringe factor. I figured that Beth married too young. Singing and dancing shows her longing for lost youth. For freedom, for fun, for sex. But belting out Rhythm Is a Dancer without a backing track? God! Dominic and I were both like: ‘Let’s never speak of this again.’”Much of Adultery’s intrigue is played out via technology. Sexy selfies are sent, phone-tracking apps are deployed, Insta accounts are stalked. Teens are regularly told off for being glued to their devices. “Of course, it’s all bullshit,” says Garai. “Kids would be perfectly within their rights to say: ‘No, fuck off, older people. You’re all on email for work, you’re meeting people on Hinge, you’ve got Ring doorbells for your parcels.’ The show attacks that hypocrisy. Technology is ingrained in all their lives. Personally, I’m a complete technophobe with very mixed feelings about social media but it’s a huge part of modern relationships.”Garai was among the 80-plus women who accused Harvey Weinstein of sexual misconduct in 2017, allegations that sparked the #MeToo movement. Has enough progress been made? “It’s much harder for women to get sexually assaulted at work now, which can only be a good thing. Social media played a huge role. It gave women the power to push back against systemic abuse. They could call it out anonymously and en masse. I’m happy but also sad it wouldn’t have happened without social media. The tech itself is something I’m still conflicted about.”Garai has been a reliably excellent presence on stage and screen for two decades. Her TV breakthrough came in 2011 when she was Bafta-nominated for playing a polymath sex worker in The Crimson Petal and the White. She got a Golden Globe nod the following year for period newsroom drama The Hour. Other TV roles include Emma, Born to Kill, The Miniaturist, Just Act Normal, Scoop, Betrayal and Vigil. Such roles have been punctuated by acclaimed theatre work.She won an Olivier award last year for her blistering performance in the stage adaptation of Annie Ernaux’s memoir The Years. Garai was actually nominated twice, for her back-to-back performances in The Years and Giant, the play about the antisemitism row that engulfed Roald Dahl. This double honour led to the strange sight of Garai competing with herself, simultaneously appearing in two closeups as the winner was announced. “That was so surreal,” she smiles. When her Giant co-star John Lithgow collected the best actor gong, he began his acceptance speech with “Romola, I think I’m going to faint!” – a reference to The Years’ graphic backstreet abortion scene, which infamously made theatregoers pass out.“It was so intense,” says Garai. “It didn’t totally blindside me because the piece was originally staged at the National Theatre in Holland and the director warned me that people had fainted. I was like: ‘That won’t happen here. We’re British, we’re not fainters! We do Coriolanus and Sarah Kane plays. I’ve been in shows where people’s hands have been chopped off.’ But the first time I said the word ‘foetus’, it was bang, bang, bang. People were just hitting the deck. It happened almost every night. Out of 53 performances, I’d say it happened 51 times. Extraordinary. I doubt I’ll experience anything like that again as an actor.”With Adultery, she’s about to shock a whole new audience. “I’m hoping I’ll get lots more cheating wife roles,” she says. “I was in my nun era, playing a lot of buttoned-up characters. A sort of a professional cross lady. Now I’m hoping to be a sexy untrustworthy wife. Entering my midlife sexpot era. That would be great.”Adultery starts this October on ITV1 and ITVX.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionRomola GaraiDramafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 11 questions to ask yourself before going no contact with a family member | Family | The Guardian
description: In the UK, one in five families are affected by permanent estrangement – it’s not a decision to be taken lightly. These are the questions experts suggest you ask yourself before cutting a relative out of your life
Author: Laura Potter
Headline: In the UK, one in five families are affected by permanent estrangement – it’s not a decision to be taken lightly. These are the questions experts suggest you ask yourself before cutting a relative out of your life
Content: Illustration: Pete Gamlen/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Pete Gamlen/The GuardianFamily11 questions to ask yourself before going no contact with a family memberIn the UK, one in five families are affected by permanent estrangement – it’s not a decision to be taken lightly. These are the questions experts suggest you ask yourself before cutting a relative out of your lifeLaura PotterFri 9 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTShareAm I avoiding difficult feelings?It’s important to be certain you aren’t walking away because it feels more manageable than addressing challenging issues. “Sometimes estrangement is exactly what’s needed for safety and healing. Other times it functions as an attempt to avoid grief, conflict, disappointment or the painful acceptance that a parent cannot become the person one longs for,” says Joshua Coleman, a clinical psychologist and the author ofRules of Estrangement.“Distance alone doesn’t resolve those emotions.”Fern Schumer Chapman, the author ofBrothers, Sisters, Strangers, says people can become estranged due to poor communication skills, learned through family dynamics: “When parents are unable to express feelings and negotiate differences, they don’t model the necessary skills – listening, apologising, cooling off. As a result, small disagreements can explode into nasty rifts. Those with poor communication skills may handle stress by simply shutting down and cutting off.”Ultimately, though, says Terri Apter, a psychologist and the author ofGrandparenting, “people who decide to be estranged make the decision that the extent of discomfort from contact is unbearable”.What doIneed from this relationship?This is about double-checking your expectations. “One of the hardest psychological tasks is distinguishing between what someoneshouldbe and what they’recapableof being,” says Coleman. “Many adults understandably long for parents who can become emotionally attuned, validating or apologetic. The healthiest outcome isn’t always getting the relationship you wanted; sometimes it’s grieving the relationship you never had while deciding what level of contact is sustainable.”double quotation markIt’s useful to understand pressures our parents were facing – illness, financial hardship, divorce, trauma – that were invisible to us as childrenPhil Lane, a clinical social worker and psychotherapistwho has been estranged from his father for eight years, adds that it’s “important to consider if the other person is willing and/or able to provide what you need. This is not to suggest that we should cut someone off if they don’t meet our expectations, but rather it can help us determine if our expectations are reasonable and ifwe, not the other person, need to adjust.”ShouldIre-examinemychildhood?As Coleman says: “Most families are neither entirely loving nor entirely harmful.” Therefore, it’s useful to take a second look through adult eyes, which allows us to “understand pressures our parents were facing – mental illness, financial hardship, divorce, trauma, cultural expectations – that were invisible to us as children”. Crucially, though, Coleman adds: “Context doesn’t excuse harmful behaviour.”Becca Bland, a researcher and counsellor in estrangement who has been estranged from her parents for 18 years, agrees: “It’s important to appreciate context, but not to explain away harm. Harm is harm. Seeing people in their context doesn’t take away the impact on you.”HaveI considered the collateral damage?Cutting ties can also mean losing other relationships. It’s something Schumer Chapman,who was estranged from her brother for decades, experienced. With the loss of her role as sister, she also lost that of her sister-in-law and aunt, and her children lost their cousins. “I felt like a whole branch of our small family had been sawed off, and all the responsibilities for our parents fell on me,” she says. She describes this estrangement as “a grief state that produces ongoing distress and deep insecurity and longing that can go on for decades”. For Apter, ultimately, “there are always trade-offs. In most cases you decide that you cannot take the pain, humiliation or chaos that comes with the relationship and have to accept the collateral.”Lane echoes this: “While I stand by my decision, there is grief attached to the fact my son does not have a relationship with his grandfather. Factors like this should be considered deeply.”View image in fullscreenIllustration: Pete Gamlen/The GuardianAre they rigid in theirviews?Mismatched values are often a factor in estrangement – families not accepting someone’s religion, sexuality or life partner, for example – and the rigidity of those views matters. “Differences in morals, values and beliefs can be well dealt with in families if everyone is adaptable and respectful. It’s when family members need values reaffirmed rigidly that it all falls apart,” says Bland. Coleman agrees: “If both people can accept differences without constant attempts to convert, shame or control one another, many relationships can adapt. If every interaction becomes psychologically unsafe, greater distance may be healthier.”Am I being pressured?Going no contact is a deeply personal decision, so it needs to be one that you make without outside influence. Pressure can come from romantic partners, online communities, friends, siblings, other relatives and therapists, says Coleman, who wants to distinguish between helpful and unhelpful interactions. “Support can be invaluable. Pressure is different,” he says. “The decision should ultimately reflect your own considered judgment.” Specifically, when it comes to social media and “therapy speak”, exercise caution. “Terms such as ‘toxic’, ‘narcissist’, ‘gaslighting’ and ‘boundaries’ can be useful when applied carefully, but social media often rewards certainty over complexity. Good therapy increases curiosity. Poor advice encourages premature certainty,” says Coleman.Apter warns that “unreliable therapists make judgments about a family member’s personality when they have never met them, which can influence the client’s views”.CanI still repair the relationship?This is about feeling sure you have tried everything, so the decision can be as comfortable as possible. It took Lane five years “and much excruciating consideration” to arrive at his choice to estrange. “I felt I had exhausted all options. I was nearly 40, so it was certainly not a youthful or impulsive response. Sometimes it’s important to trust your instincts, even if they are telling you to do something that goes against the grain.”Bland recommends involving a professional, who “can see a broader picture and help identify blind spots in a less confrontational way. In attempting to repair a relationship, we can get angry with people because they’ve hurt, neglected or harmed us. It helps to include a professional who understands when to say ‘stop’.”double quotation markIt’s not a case of they’re out of my life, they’re out of my head – they will be in your head more. People reconsider their decision almost every couple of daysYou may be able to heal after some time away. Schumer Chapman finally managed to reconcile with her brother over the course of a year. “We met every week. Sometimes we went for a bike ride to become reacquainted with each other. Sometimes we discussed the estrangement, what had happened and why. Other times we recalled memories and laughed about our childhood, which was bonding.” She says the most important change was the way they communicated: “When we did have disagreements, which are inevitable, we talked our differences out.”How willI cope with ‘what ifs’?You won’t know if your relative hits hard times, becomes ill or even dies. You will need to consider whether you can live with that level of uncertainty. “Many people imagine estrangement will provide relief. What they’re less prepared for is ambiguous loss – the uncertainty of not knowing whether they will ever reconcile, whether they will hear about illness second-hand, or whether a death will occur before anything is resolved. Those are burdens worth considering,” says Coleman. Bland cautions: “It’s an unresolved attachment, and our brain wants to resolve it. It’s not a case of they’re out of my life, they’re out of my head – they will be in your headmore.My research has foundthat people reconsider their decision almost every couple of days.” Lane, meanwhile, describes this uncertainty as something you ultimately have to “accept as part of the process, with the belief that the larger outcome will be positive and healthy for you”.DoI have an emotional support base?This is crucial for you to be able to cope with the emotional after-effects. “I don’t think people can do it without social support, because the sense of isolation is crippling,” says Bland. “It’s about having people around you who understand you’re breaking free of a heavily abusive pattern.” Bland’s other family members were instrumental in her decision and her ability to stick with it: “They gave me validation that my parents weren’t safe, which reinforced I had made the right choice.”Lane describes the emotional fallout as producing “grief, very similar to that associated with the death of a family member. It’s psychologically unhealthy to go through grief and loss in isolation.” It may also be associated with stigma and shame. Bland describes how she often sees “the perpetrators of abuse getting sympathy from the rest of the family because they present themselves as the victim. People will potentially judge your decision because they don’t understand the relationship you’ve had from the inside.” In those instances, support is critical.Would limiting contact work?Bland recommends that you “consider what your window of tolerance is. Can you tolerate one meeting in a park every few months? Would that cost you more than having no relationship at all?” She describes it as cost/benefit analysis, but adds: “If people are in a very harmful situation where there’s abuse, I wouldn’t recommend going low contact because that doesn’t help them get out of the cycle.”double quotation markEstrangement is sometimes the healthiest option, particularly when there is ongoing abuse, coercion or repeated violation of boundariesLane has seen “many clients change the nature of a relationship, implement boundaries and recalibrate expectations to improve negative relationships”. Coleman says estrangement “exists on a spectrum”, and that many people could benefit from “limited contact, shorter visits, communicating primarily by text or email, avoiding volatile topics, seeing relatives only in group settings and having clear expectations about frequency and duration of contact. Sometimes these arrangements preserve enough connection while protecting emotional wellbeing.”Apter adds: “Most people try going low contact before they decide to cut themselves off from a family member, but many discover it is not possible to set boundaries or avoid painful interactions”.DoI feel safe?This is potentially the most salient question you can ask. Coleman says: “Estrangement is sometimes the healthiest option, particularly when there is ongoing abuse, coercion or repeated violation of boundaries.” Lane agrees, saying: “If a person consistently causes you to feel unsafe – physically or emotionally – you will live in a persistent state of feeling at risk. Over a long period of time, this can become unsustainable, and removing the abusive or harmful element may be necessary.”

title: ‘Infinite genius’: Yiyun Li on Anne Carson | Nobel prize in literature | The Guardian
description: When her sons died, the Book of Goose author turned to Grief Lessons, Carson’s translation of four plays by Euripides. She reflects on the ‘life sustaining’ work of an extraordinary writer
Author: Yiyun Li
Headline: When her sons died, the Book of Goose author turned to Grief Lessons, Carson’s translation of four plays by Euripides. She reflects on the ‘life sustaining’ work of an extraordinary writer
Content: ‘She does not subjugate or manipulate her words. She lets them be’ … Anne Carson.Photograph: TT News Agency/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreen‘She does not subjugate or manipulate her words. She lets them be’ … Anne Carson.Photograph: TT News Agency/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Nobel prize in literature‘Infinite genius’: Yiyun Li on Anne CarsonWhen her sons died the Book of Goose author turned to Grief Lessons, Carson’s translation of four plays by Euripides. She reflects on the ‘life sustaining’ work of an extraordinary writerWhere to start with: Anne Carson‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Anne CarsonYiyun LiFri 9 Oct 2026 07.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is preposterous to agree to write a short piece on Anne Carson’s work. The task is impossible, akin to that of solving the mathematical problem of dividing zero by zero. If one had the power to solve it, perhaps one would have some confidence in attempting to write about Anne Carson’s work. Attempting, I say, not succeeding. In attempting to do so, I shall emphasise that all words fall short in extreme situations, which not only include unfathomable losses (of children, in my case) but also include articulating anything about Anne Carson’s work.One could start with Carson’s words. “Words, if you let them, will do what they want to do and what they have to do.” (Autobiography of Red) But to let the words exist in their own desires and yearnings and frustrations and confusions, to let the words scream with inarticulable pain or tell a riddle with a twinkling smile or make love to one another – how many of us have achieved that kind of mastery of words? But, oh no, mastery is the wrong word here. Only the minor and the greedy and the power-thirsty writers want to be the masters of the words. Carson does not subjugate or manipulate her words. She lets them be; and lets herself be led by the words – hers, and the ancients’ translated into unforgettable English by her.And what extraordinary words they are! Say, let’s suppose every person in the world could be viewed as a formation of some words – a poem, a story, a play, a novel, an earnest and muddle-minded op-ed, a loud slogan, or a much repeated and tired cliche, or, simply, a line of ellipses, or some white space (if we include words in this game, we must also include punctuations and silences).In a gathering of a vast number of word formations, those written byAnne Carsonwould surely be easily recognisable. The fact that they exist at all is a miracle, because many rules have been bent or broken to make them possible. Nevertheless, they are not anarchists or revolutionaries. They are both mortal and immortal because they know their priorities (“Love is not conditional. / Living is very conditional.”– The Beauty of the Husband). They are compelling because they are compelled (“I know / you find me extreme / in my grief. / I bear it hard. / But I tell you I have no choice. / It compels. I act because it compels” – Elektra, translated by Carson). They, beings unto themselves, are defiant (“That which is known, attained, possessed, cannot be an object of desire.” – Eros, the Bittersweet). Their concerns are vast and undefinable; one blunders if one uses words like philosophical or metaphysical, tragical or dramatic.For those who were less fortunate, written by a lesser mind, there is no worry because any encounter with Anne Carson’s creations expands, deepens, mystifies and clarifies our minds; a paragraph from her is enough for a long meandering in a less visited landscape, a line is enough for one to understand oneself better.I teach Anne Carson from time to time, but to say one can teach Anne Carson is also preposterous. One hands her work to the next generation, trusting that there are bound to be kindred spirits among them. I have done this for the past 20 years, and like to watch the first encounter of young, inquisitive minds with Anne Carson. Some of them, like me, will remain her lifelong readers. Some will find her work the only words to read in life’s extremities.This morning, when the news came out that Anne Carson is the newest Nobel Laureate, I immediately moved all of Anne Carson’s books from my bookcase to my desk, intending to spend a morning with them. Then I realised that the most important book of hers for me – Grief Lessons, her translation of four Euripides plays – was missing. It was likely misplaced because I taught it in a recent semester. After our older son Vincent died in 2017, I spent a winter reading that book. Then I read it again after our younger son James died. To say Carson’s words are life-sustaining is an understatement. What is infinity divided by infinity? Or, infinity subtracted by infinity? Or, zero multiplied by infinity? Reading Carson gives one the perspective and the courage to live in an often inexplicable life.It is joyful news to see Anne Carson recognised with the Nobel prize. Sometimes there comes the good news that is rightandjust. But that is only as simple as knowing one plus one makes two. The recognition underlines the infiniteness of Anne Carson’s genius, but to get a better sense of that genius, one only needs to turn to any page of any one of her books.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: ‘Nobody is listening to us’: on the school protest frontline, I heard why France’s students feel disowned | Alexander Hurst | The Guardian
description: Fixing the broken education system will be just the start. The biggest challenge for an aloof political class is to finally pay attention to an abandoned generation, says Guardian Europe columnist Alexander Hurst
Author: Alexander Hurst
Headline: Fixing the broken education system will be just the start. The biggest challenge for an aloof political class is to finally pay attention to an abandoned generation, says Guardian Europe columnist Alexander Hurst
Content: Student protesters in Place de la République, Paris, on Monday.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAView image in fullscreenStudent protesters in Place de la République, Paris, on Monday.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAOpinionFrance‘Nobody is listening to us’: on the school protest frontline, I heard why France’s students feel disownedAlexander HurstFixing the broken education system will be just the start. The biggest challenge for an aloof political class is to finally pay attention to an abandoned generationFri 9 Oct 2026 07.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTShareWhen adolescents protest that the government is failing to uphold their right to an education, and the government’s response is to send in riot police, the government has lost the plot. People outsideFrancemay have spent the past week watching the student protests in Paris and other cities, and thought, “Well, France has a long tradition of insurrection” or, “That’s just the French being French.”But the situation that has provoked the high-schoolwalkouts and teenage angeris most likely not one they would immediately associate with the France of their imaginations. In place of its lost plot, the French government has a collection of anecdotes and statistics that it should be ashamed of: 27th place in the most recent OECDeducation rankings, schools with ceilings collapsing and rats in classrooms and, in a school in Bagnolet,no drinkable water; an increase in the average number of students per class from 27 in 2010 toover 30 today; half of primary and high schoolsmissing teachers at the start of the school year– many of them with no substitutes or replacements.Julie, a 34-year-old teacher who joined the demonstrations, told me that staff shortages were the fault of “low salaries and poor treatment.” She has to commute for an hour and 45 minuteseach waybetween Paris and the school on the city’s outskirts where she accepted a post last year after switching careers. All for €2100 (£1,780) a month, plus some overtime pay. Teachers’ salaries in France are only56% of what they are in Germany– even as over €200bn inpublic subsidiesfinds its way annually to businesses.So it could easily have been a teacher-led revolt – instead, the high-schoolers themselves cracked first.They paid a high price for refusing to accept a failing education system: a 16-year-old has lost the use of an eye, a 15-year-old has lost a hand, a 14-year-old has a broken jaw – all from police munitions. Hundreds morehave been injuredin some way. In total, 4,400 people, the vast majority minors, have been arrested in a little over a week,almost halfthe number of arrests made during the months ofgilets jauneschaos. It might be incoherent that protesting students shoot fireworks at high school buildings, while at the same time denouncing the poor facilities they have to study in. But the far greater incoherence belongs to a government that has disinvested in its youth, and has chosen to answer bin fires with police charges.“Sure some people were burning trash cans,” Fatoumata Sylla Wague, a 17-year-old in her final year at the Lycée Paul Éluard in Seine-Saint-Denis, where pupils were among the first to set up blockades outside their campus, told me. “But trash cans can’t feel anything.” She and her fellow students, on the other hand, certainly felt the teargas that the police launched in response.Despite “unlivable” temperatures in the school buildings, extreme heat and extreme cold, walls covered in mould, electricity cuts and often not enough tables or chairs for everyone, Fatoumata would rather have been in class than out braving the riot police. But she wants to teach history some day and felt compelled, in a moment in history, comparable to May 1968, to take part. “If I’m fighting for our rights today, it’s because I really want to teach, but in good conditions. And so this is for the next generation of students and teachers.”View image in fullscreenStudents gather during a blockade at the Lycee Paul-Eluard high school in the northern Paris suburb of Saint-DenisPhotograph: Luc Auffret/Anadolu/Getty ImagesI can’t imagine how hard it must be to be a teenager in general today. In 2021 The Lancetfound that75% of French 16-25-year-olds exhibited signs of eco-anxiety, telling researchers they were “frightened” about the future. In France and beyond, students and young workersactively dislike AIand feel pessimistic about the future it portends. As for Fatoumata, she worries about the rise of far-right political movements, both in France and elsewhere.For years, successive French governments have dealt with problems in some of France’s most troubled urban areas by unleashing heavy-handed policing that all too frequently targets young people with random checks that can be personally degrading. Centralised policymaking has also produced a national education system that often sends its least experienced teachers to these same areas, while granting more senior teachers priority in requesting transfers to other, less difficult, schools.A future far-right government, the kind Fatoumata says she worries about, would almost certainly ramp up these kinds of tensions. Already, in response to the protests, rightwing politicians have called for harsher sentences andmore law and order.But this is not a problem that will be solved with more police and more batons, any more than it already has been.Because none of it signals a government that truly wants to listen – it signals that society at large does not really claim these places, or these teenagers, as its own.On n’est pas mal éduqué, on n’est pas écouté(“We’re not poorly educated, we’re just not being listened to”), read one sign I saw brandished at Paris’s Place de la République on Tuesday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionResponding to the crisis is going to require some tangible acts, such as upgrading dilapidated facilities. Arnaud Richards, 50, head of student services at Iqbal Masih middle school in Saint-Denis, offered me the example of how thoughtful architecture can have more impact than one might expect. The technical high school he previously worked in – Gabriel Péri, in an extremely poor area –reopened in 2022 after a total reconstruction, which, according to Richards, led to a calmer climate for both students and teachers. “Having the school itself be a beautiful place made the community feel more respected,” he told me. That in turn “created a calmer environment” for both students and staff.But a real answer doesn’t stop with better facilities. Showing up to cut ribbons on new construction, or renovations, isn’t enough. During Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power, his government has, on any number of issues, successively failed to listen in a way that makes people feel deeply seen and heard.As Fatoumata said: “Honestly, I don’t think the government cares, they just want to shut us up with false promises. We know nothing will change, because the government doesn’t listen to us.” Of all the things going wrong for France at the moment, this underlying lack of a feeling of “togetherness”, the feeling that nobody is really listening, is going to be the most difficult to deal with.Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. title: The Filter is two! 31 things we loved this year, from cloud-like duvets to the perfect running shoe | Life and style | The Guardian

Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Whether it’s a super-glowy serum or a cult gardening tool, here are our writers’ favourite buys from the past year
Content: Illustration: Cynthia KittlerGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterLife and styleThe Filter is two! 31 things we loved this year, from cloud-like duvets to the perfect running shoeWhether it’s a super-glowy serum or a cult gardening tool, here are our writers’ favourite buys from the past yearDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereGuardian writersFri 9 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Filter is turning two! To celebrate, we asked our contributors for their favourite products from the past year, and rounded up the team’s picks too.From handbag-sized umbrellas and stylish yet practical wellies to reading lights and luxurious duvets, these are the products that stood out.The Filter products we love the mostBrush with greatnessView image in fullscreenRevamp Straight & Go cordless hot brush£89.99 at Currys£90 at ArgosOne of the best tools I’ve tested this year is Revamp’s Straight & Go cordless for my review of thebest hot brushes. It’s compact, so easily fits into hand luggage, a work backpack or even a decent-size handbag. It’s my hot brush of choice when I’m away from home (and at home: it’s cordless so I can use it in the bathroom without trailing cables all over the hallway).Lise SmithCream of the cropView image in fullscreenIlliyoon ceramide ato concentrate cream, 75ml£9.99 at Boots£9.99 at AmazonThe best product I’ve bought on another writer’s recommendation is the Illiyoon ceramide ato concentrate cream, whichSarah Matthewswrote about in herbest facial moisturisers roundup. It’s rich but gentle and leaves my rather dry skin soft, smooth and plump.LSScreen saverView image in fullscreenBrick£44.75 at BrickI wrote about Brick, a device that helps reduce screen time,for myphone addiction piece. I didn’t view myself as having a problem,but after finding that Brick really improved my wellbeing, I became the first person in history for whom admitting you have a problem is the last step on the road to recovery.Alan MartinA pizza the actionView image in fullscreenGozney Arc Lite£349.99 at Gozney£349.99 at John LewisI’m continuing to cook with the Gozney Arc Lite, which I reviewed for our guide to thebest pizza ovens, and starting to relax more and enjoy it. Slowly, my hand-stretched bases are getting better, though I think I would still be laughed out of any self-respecting pizzeria: “Don’t quit the day job.”Rachel OgdenA good foundationView image in fullscreenSaie the Base Brush£26 at Cult Beauty£26 at SephoraI trust all beauty recommendations from my beloved colleagueSali Hughesimplicitly, so after reading herguide to makeup brushes, I thought it was perhaps time I stopped slapping foundation on by hand and invested in this Saie brush. It makes foundation sit more lightly on your skin and makes blending at the neck and hairline foolproof.Jess Cartner-MorleyTub thumpingView image in fullscreenTown & Country square flexi-tub, 25l£10.95 at Tooled Up£13.93 at AmazonFor my rundown ofitems that make camping with kids easier, I tested a pair of square flexi-tubs during a trip with my six-year-old. They were a godsend then – helping keep everything organised and tidy – but they’ve since found a place in home life as indispensable declutterers. Kids’ toys everywhere? Throw them in the flexi-tub. Doing some DIY? Tools in the tub! Too many tubs? Stack them! You get the picture.Matt CollinsBest foot forwardView image in fullscreenBarbourBedewellington bootsMen’s£55 at John Lewis£79.95 at BarbourWomen’sFrom £55 at Frasers£79.95 at BarbourIn the past I’ve opted for more fashion-led wellies, but these days I use them more for dog walking than festivals. So I tookDanielle Wilkins’ recommendation in her roundup of thebest welliesand bought her top pick of Barbour boots. With a classic look and excellent grip (even across muddy fields), I get to balance style and practicality.Sabine WieselRain checkView image in fullscreenDavek mini umbrella£65 at DavekWhen I needed an umbrella this year, I turned toPete Wise’sumbrella test. I’m terrible for not carrying a brolly and getting caught out by rain, so I wanted something small I could leave in my handbag. I picked the Davek Mini. It has saved my veggie bacon many times already and its lifetime guarantee is reassuring.Caramel QuinWalk this wayView image in fullscreenUrevo SpaceWalk 5L walking pad£399.99 at Urevo£349.99 at AmazonHaving tested lots ofwalking pads and under-desk treadmillsfor the Filter, I have become quite attached to the Urevo SpaceWalk 5L model (a review for which is on the way). I walk on it most days in an attempt to rack up at least 10,000 steps. It’s an easy way to burn extra calories when I’d otherwise be glued to my desktop, and I’ve found this model exceptionally quiet, while the automatic incline is great for varying the terrain without lifting a finger.Leon PoultneyLight my fireView image in fullscreenPrimus Lite Plus stoveFrom £98.99 at Mountain Warehouse£130 at PrimusI tested the Primus Lite Plus for our guide tobest camping stoves. I recently took it on a three-day trek in the Lake District and found it simple to use and clean, and great for boiling water.Sian LewisCashmere crushView image in fullscreenMicro bandana£55 at Rise&FallJess Cartner-Morleyalsoinspired meto buy a jazzy cashmere bandana from Rise&Fall.SLUnder coverView image in fullscreenPanda the Cloud duvet, double£129.95 at Panda£129.95 at AmazonMy Panda duvet from my test of thebest duvetshas been a real bedding upgrade. When you go from a cheap polyester duvet (which was perfectly fine, I thought) to this cloud-like breathable bamboo hug, there’s no going back. I always look forward to wrapping myself in it at night. I now have two versions – thewinter 10.5-togone I tested for best duvets, and the4.5-tog summer version.Jane HoskynFace valueView image in fullscreenBeauty of Joseon relief sun rice + Probiotics SPF50+, 50ml£15.50 at Cult Beauty£11.62 at AmazonI bought a double pack ofBeauty of Joseon’s Relief Sun Rice + Probiotics SPF50+, which not only took the top spot in Sarah Matthews’best face SPFguide but was also raved about by Sali Hughes in herhero skincare 2025 roundup. I’ve got fair skin, so I need a good daily SPF, ideally one I can slap on without looking like I’ve fallen face-first into my cereal, but my skin is also greasy and spotty, so the light texture of this is such a lovely relief after the thick sun creams I’ve been used to.JHFry highView image in fullscreenNinja Double Stack XL SL400UK air fryer£269 at John Lewis£269.99 at NinjaI’ve been tempted to buy an air fryer for ages but didn’t think I had the counter space. So, whenRachel Ogdenhighlighted the Ninja Double Stack as the best compact air fryer (with a smaller footprint than most) inher roundup, I decided to go for it. As someone who mainly cooks for one, I’ve found it makes mealtimes far more convenient (and saves energy because I no longer need to heat up a whole oven for just me). It also produces the crispest, most delicious jacket potato skin I’ve ever had.Lily Smith, researcherLeaf it to meView image in fullscreenStihl SHA 56garden vacuum£231.79 at Farol MowersThe Stihl SHA 56 leaf blower and garden vacuum, which I tested for our guide to thebest leaf blowers and vacuums, has been an absolute hit in my garden this year, not just for collecting leaves but for doing any of the work I’d normally use a broom for. Its added superpower of collecting whatever it’s been blowing about at the end of the job is the icing on the cake.Andy ShawHands downView image in fullscreenE45 repairing hand cream, 50ml£6.60 at Sainsbury’s£5.65 at AmazonI’ve taken up pottery this year, and my hands have paid the price. There’s nothing like handling wet clay to extract all the moisture from your skin. So, as soon as I’m done wiping down my station and labelling my wonky creations, I’m in need of urgent relief. I opted for the E45 repairing hand cream fromSarah Matthews’best hand cream guidefor two reasons: it’s cheap enough to share around the studio, and (as promised) it has a thick, nourishing texture. Sarah described it as a “refreshing drink of water for the hands”, and I couldn’t agree more – my mitts absolutely slurp the stuff up.Millie Fender, commissioning editorCase closedView image in fullscreenJuly packing cellsskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion£40 for four at July£86 for eight at RevolveThe best thing I’ve tested is this set of July packing cubes, which came out on top in myroundup. For a disorganised person like me, packing cubes are a revelation. The July set did a particularly good job of preserving the crispness of shirts and trousers during a chaotic cross-country journey this summer.Pete WiseGlow getterView image in fullscreenCeraVe skin renewing vitamin C serum, 30ml£22.50 at Lookfantastic£22.50 at BootsI bought the CeraVe vitamin C serum onDanielle Wilkins’recommendation. I was astounded when, after a week of using it, people started commenting on how “glowy” my face looked. I’m hoping it keeps me looking alive all the way through the grey winter months!Zoë PhillimoreTake a seatView image in fullscreenThunderX3 Solo 360 gaming chair£169.99 at OverclockersWe were switching my son’s and daughter’s rooms over and we needed extra incentive for him (Iggy) to accept the deal – he was moving into the smaller bedroom – and this chair from ourbest gaming chairsguide swung it. Iggy now has his own “gaming nook” (doubling up as my workspace), and the chair is saving my working-from-home slouching.Alex Jones, picture editorMiles betterView image in fullscreenSaucony Endorphin Azura running shoesMen’sFrom £96.89 at Cotswold OutdoorFrom £112 at SauconyWomen’sFrom £97.89 at Runners Need£112 at SauconyI’ve logged thousands of miles this year searching for thebest running shoes. One of the standout all-rounders that can cope with almost anything is the Saucony Endorphin Azura. Go fast, go slow. No trouble. The perfect suitcase shoe at a pretty competitive price.Kieran AlgerDress rehearsalView image in fullscreenNobody’s Childfloral starlight midi dress£51 at Nobody’s ChildThis isn’t so much something I’ve bought as something I’ve bought into. The vast majority of the clothing I’ve bought this year has been secondhand, thanks toJane Hoskyn’smoney-saving tips. My favourite find is along cream dress (with pockets!) from Nobody’s Child, which I snagged for £15, down from a usual £85.Sarah MatthewsDry runView image in fullscreenVonHaus Smart dehumidifier with laundry mode£144.99 at VonHaus£144.99 at ArgosAfter readingCaramel Quin’s roundup of thebest dehumidifiers, I was convinced the budget VonHaus Smart dehumidifier was exactly what our damp house was crying out for. Not only is it incredibly satisfying to see so much water sucked out of the air, but it’s also become my new favourite (and fastest) way to dry laundry.Ella Jinadu, audience editorLight readingView image in fullscreenGritin rechargeable book light£13.95 at Fruugo£8.59 at AmazonMy partner and I each have a clip-on reading light, recommended in our guide to theeveryday items that could improve your life, and can fully vouch for how the disturbance-free glow has transformed our reading routines – both at bedtime and in the dark early mornings. They also came in handy on a recent camping trip when the wind made it impossible to sleep.EJCool customerView image in fullscreenGreenPan Frost ice-cream maker and slushie machine£399 at Debenhams£399.90 at BootsI love a kitchen gadget and became obsessed with the GreenPan soft-serve and slushie maker while I was testing it forbest ice-cream makers. While I enjoyed the ice-cream, I loved making frozen cocktails even more – it was a real crowd-pleaser at parties too.Danielle AmatoSpirited awayView image in fullscreenJo Vodka101 the Purist, 70cl£48.95 at Master of Malt£50 at John LewisView image in fullscreenChopinpotato vodka, 70cl£37.38 at Master of Malt£39.75 at the Whisky ExchangeWhen I am tasked with testing a specific category, it ends up reigniting my love and interest in it. So, sincetesting vodka, I’m still fully into mixing myself ice-cold martinis (dry, with a twist, please) and variations on the theme. The top vodkas I’m still reaching for are the Jo Vodka and the Chopin, though I also made a fab lychee martini recently usingSapling raspberry.Joanne GouldBlooming lovelyView image in fullscreenScilly FlowersFrom £17 at Scilly FlowersI’m also a new customer of Scilly Flowers after readingZoë Phillimore’s piece on thebest flower delivery services. I like that it tends to do arrangements of just one type of flower, which I find elegant, and it has varieties you don’t usually find with online florists; plus it can be amazing value. I sent someone40 narcissus, which looked stunning, and sent my friend a sweet arrangement of scented pinks for a post-op cheer-up.JGBear essentialsView image in fullscreenMerz b Schwanen 215 classic fit T-shirt£85 at Stuarts£95 at Merz b SchwanenTesting white T-shirtswas my highlight, particularly Merz b Schwanen’s – the one Carmy wears in The Bear. After all, whodoesn’twant to channel Jeremy Allen White sweating it out in a hot kitchen? At the risk of sounding like a true fashion nerd, there’s something fascinating about trying a dozen pieces that look identical but wear completely differently – and then deciding which takes the top spot. My partner now gets to hear all about 150gsm versus 220gsm and whySupimais the gold standard. Riveting stuff, I’m told.Peter BevanCutting edgeView image in fullscreenNiwaki hori hori pro£42 at Niwaki£42.99 at CrocusNiwaki’s hori hori tool has quite a cult following among professional gardeners (intools pros can’t live without), but I could never see why I’d have much need for a knife in the garden. Now I realise it’s more of a sharp trowel – a very nifty garden tool – which has quickly replaced the old butter knife I previously used for all the same jobs.Kate JacobsSoy goodView image in fullscreenPoon’s premium first extract soy sauce, 250ml£13 at Ocado£18.99 at SelfridgesI’ve tasted so many good things this year, but it’s the simplest one-ingredient products that have stood out for their incredible quality. The best thing I tried was Poon’s premium first-extract soy sauce (best overall from mysoy sauce taste test). It’s wildly complex and fruity, made from non-GMO soya beans grown in Kaohsiung, southern Taiwan, pressed only once and naturally fermented in earthenware jars.Tom HuntDaily grindView image in fullscreenKitchenAidKF3£749 at KitchenAid£749 at John LewisThere are times when I wish the steady flow of big, brown boxes entering my home would slow to a drip, but KitchenAid’s recent deliveries have earned their keep. The standouts were from its new trio of slightly – just slightly, mind you – more affordable coffee machines.The range-topping £899KF4(featured in our guide to thebest coffee machines) is a delight, but it’s the fully automatic £749 KF3 that I think is the best value of the bunch. The coffee quality is superb, the milk froth is a delightfully dense, creamy microfoam, and given the performance, the price is fair. The slimline build is perfect for cramped kitchen worktops, too. A full review is on the way.Sasha MullerView image in fullscreenTwinkle Tongue saliva enhancer gel£34 at Twinkle TongueOne of the most original and unexpectedly fun products I’ve tested this year was for mysexy gifts for Valentine’s Day guide. Twinkle Tongue is an all-natural, sour cherry-flavoured liquid that instantly provokes your salivary glands.What’s the point of a product that makes you slaver and slobber? If you suffer from dry mouth caused by smoking, menopause, or as a side-effect of certain medications, then Twinkle Tongue can help make all sorts of intimate oral activities easier and more comfortable.Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox?
