title: Labour hails byelection win as return of leftwing voters after Starmer era | Holborn and St Pancras byelection | The Guardian
description: Party now polling 15 points above Greens, who had been ahead of Labour before Keir Starmer resigned as PM
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Party now polling 15 points above Greens, who had been ahead of Labour before Keir Starmer resigned as PM
Content: The education secretary, Lucy Powell (left), with the newly elected MP Sagal Abdi-Wali, who won the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenThe education secretary, Lucy Powell (left), with the newly elected MP Sagal Abdi-Wali, who won the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAHolborn and St Pancras byelectionLabour hails byelection win as return of leftwing voters after Starmer eraParty now polling 15 points above Greens, who had been ahead of Labour before Keir Starmer resigned as PMSammy GecsoylerandPeter WalkerFri 9 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour is starting to win back voters on the left who became disillusioned under Keir Starmer’s leadership, the party’s deputy leader has claimed after it saw off Zack Polanski and the Greens to win theHolborn and St Pancras byelection.Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali took 45% of a relatively low turnout to keep Starmer’s old north London seat for the party, pushing Polanski, who had stood for the party he leads, into second place on 33%.While the result was broadly as predicted, Labour strategists were buoyed up by the party’s relatively straightforward route to victory in a diverse inner-city area of the sort the Greens have been targeting with recent success.The result “sends a clear message to those voters who lost faith in Labour in recent years”, said Lucy Powell, whocalled last monthfor the party to unite progressive voters under Andy Burnham if it wants to win the next election.After the byelection win, she told the Guardian: “We hear you, we’ve listened and we know we needed to be clearer about what we stand for and what type of country we want to see, proudly putting our values centre stage. We’re delighted so many of you are backing us once again.”The byelection came after the Green party voted at their conference last weekend to adopta hugely controversial policy equating Zionism with racism, and saying Israel should be replaced with a single Palestinian state.Polanski has been criticised for showing minimal leadership on the most toxic internal debate the Greens have faced in living memory, with the chair of Jewish Greens saying he should resign.The byelection, called after Starmerresigned his Commons seatshortly after he was ousted by Burnham, saw a low turnout of 38.7%, possibly due to the widespread predictions that Labour was set to win, despite a major campaigning effort from the Greens.The turnout also suggests Burnham could still face a battle to engage some voters in urban areas, particularly London, where the Greens took control of three councils in May’s local elections.In an emotional victory speech, Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, hit out at “those who seek to divide us”, in what appeared to be a response to Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, who suggested she was not British shortly after the byelection was called.“I hope this moment says something about who gets to belong,” she said. “For people who look like me, I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden, and this is Britain.”Responding to the defeat, Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, said that while the result showed his party remained a major threat to Labour, many voters had told him they wanted to “give Andy Burnham a chance”.It was the Greens’ second best-ever byelection result, more evidence of the party’s increased prominence and campaigning power since Polanski became leader 13 months ago.The best came in February, when the Greenstook an equally safe Labour seat, Gorton and Denton in Greater Manchester, in a major upset that weakened Starmer’s position. Around the same time, the Greens peaked at 21% in national polling, above Labour. They are now about 11%, more than 15 points behind Burnham’s party.Polanski’s position has come under scrutiny since the Zionism motion was passed, with critics accusing him of abdicating leadership after he missed the debate to campaign in the byelection, giving no clear message about whether or not he backed it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn interviews after the byelection loss, Polanski said he would have voted against the motion had he attended, given that two amendments he supported, both saying any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians rather than a one-state system being imposed, were voted down.On Friday, Vivien Lichtenstein, chair of Jewish Greens, said Polanski, who is Jewish, made a “big mistake” by avoiding the vote. Asked if he should continue in his role, she told Times Radio: “No, I think he should resign.”However, other members of Jewish Greens said Lichtenstein’s comments did not reflect the majority view in the group, and that a vote of no confidence in her had been tabled.Speaking shortly before the byelection result was announced, Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ former leader and first MP, said Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”.Speaking to Newsnight, she said: “I would have hoped that he would have really been a very strong critic of this motion, because the motion was flawed from top to bottom in my view. It’s dangerous, it’s divisive, it tries to have a singular definition of Zionism when we know that there are many.”Asked if Polanski should stand down, Lucas did not definitively say he should remain as leader: “I think let’s just see what happens in the … coming days and weeks.”There is no formal mechanism for ejecting a leader of the Greens. However, they are re-elected every two years, meaning Polanski, who took over in September 2025, will have to go before party members again in less than a year.Explore more on these topicsHolborn and St Pancras byelectionLabourGreen partynewsShareReuse this content

title: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President says deal essential to lower US fuel prices but move set to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: President says deal essential to lower US fuel prices but move set to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies
Content: Trump in Washington on Wednesday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump in Washington on Wednesday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpZelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian dieselPresident says deal essential to lower US fuel prices but move set to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato alliesUS politics – live updatesRobert Taitin WashingtonFri 9 Oct 2026 19.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 20.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump was on a fresh collision course with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and European allies on Friday after a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine.Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with President Vladimir Putin of Russia,calling it“absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’sNatoallies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran.“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trumpwrote.“Based on the condition of their diesel refineries,Russiawill then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 tons of diesel fuel.”He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”Fuel prices have rocketed due to Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of the global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – with a gallon of fuel now averaging $4.20 – it is the soaring price of diesel, which last month rose to a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most political damage to Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm approach.Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need to operate machinery.The agreement was criticized by Democrats, who said it undercut a lawTrump signed last monthallowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions.“This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries,” the Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, joined by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, said in a statement. “Failure to follow the law and the bipartisan will of Congress that only weeks ago passed legislation aimed at cutting off revenue for Russia’s war machine and curbing purchases of Russian oil and gas.”Some Republicans were also critical of the agreement.“Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican,wrote on X. “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.”Perhaps the fiercest response came from Zelenskyy, whotold Axiosthat it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 earlier this week.In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump,saidthe deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.Trump announced the oil deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia accepted a reciprocal de-escalation plan that would stop Moscow attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.The agreement also comes on the heels of rising tensions between Russia and Washington’s Nato allies in Europe, amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.The latest development is likely to lead to a further deterioration of Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment in his failure to reach a deal.Trump’s willingness to reach an agreement with Putin that will lower fuel costs comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of American forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS politicsRussiaEuropeNatoUkrainenewsShareReuse this content

title: Parties prepare for byelection in Farage seat amid speculation over £5m gift inquiry  | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Tories said to be ready to fight in Clacton, with standards investigation rumoured to be nearing its end
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Tories said to be ready to fight in Clacton, with standards investigation rumoured to be nearing its end
Content: Conservatives are hopeful Nigel Farage will decide not to fight, but Reform sources insisted he would.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersView image in fullscreenConservatives are hopeful Nigel Farage will decide not to fight, but Reform sources insisted he would.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersNigel FarageParties prepare for byelection in Farage seat amid speculation over £5m gift inquiryTories said to be ready to fight in Clacton, with standards investigation rumoured to be nearing its endRowena MasonWhitehall editorFri 9 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 17.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage’s rivals are gearing up for a byelection in Clacton in the months ahead, amid speculation that the standards inquiry into his £5m gift is nearing a conclusion.Conservative sources said the party was ready to fight in Farage’s seat, although senior figures in the shadow cabinet are divided about whether it would be winnable, given Farage’s victory in abyelection over the summer.Other parties, including the hard-right Restore Britain, are also expected to put up candidates in the seat this time, after boycotting the August poll.Westminster is poised for a battle over the future of Reform if the sanction from the standards inquiry is a heavy one.The process could theoretically take place before Christmas if a decision is imminent, but the timelines of previous cases suggest it is more likely to be next year – if a serious sanction is imposed.In the cases of Margaret Ferrier, the SNP MP who broke lockdown rules, and Peter Bone, the Tory MP found to have bullied staff, it took well over six months from the conclusion of the commissioner’s report for a byelection to take place.The investigation into Farage’s gift began afterthe Guardian revealed in Maythat the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024.The Reform leader has said itwas a personal matter, not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.Under the process, if a serious breach is found, the commissioner will pass a memorandum to the standards committee of MPs and lay members.They would then have further discussions and call a further hearing or invite evidence from the MP before deciding on a penalty. That process can take weeks. The MP also has a right of appeal to the independent expert panel, which can take a further month or more.If parliament agrees with a penalty of more than 10 days of suspension from theHouse of Commons, a recall petition could be held, requiring signatures from 10% of voters in the MP’s constituency over a period of six weeks.In the cases of Bone and Ferrier, neither contested their seats, andConservativesare hopeful that Farage could decide not to fight. “There’s a question of whether he will stand again,” said one shadow cabinet minister.But Reform sources insisted Farage would fight for his seat again, having won the byelection against independent candidates including Count Binface by more than 11,000 votes.He has also recently embarked on a tour of the country, in an attempt to shore up his core support, and a reorganisation of his party HQ. This includes launching a new Reform TV channel to pump out the party’s message direct to voters, hiring a team of 12 “journalists” headed by the former GB News producer Aaron Lobo, who had been director of operations.Farage won a majority of 8,000 at the last general election, when he beat the sitting Tory MP, Giles Watling. The Conservative had previously won the seat with a majority of more than 25,000 in 2019, when there was no Brexit party candidate in the seat.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKConservativesHouse of CommonsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Medieval’ and ‘disturbing’: US plan to livestream execution elicits global condemnation  | US justice system | The Guardian
description: Pentagon said execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, would be broadcast live
Author: David Smith
Headline: Pentagon said execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, would be broadcast live
Content: Army soldiers after the memorial service for the 13 victims of the shooting rampage by Nidal Malik Hasan, on 10 November 2009 in Fort Hood, Texas.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArmy soldiers after the memorial service for the 13 victims of the shooting rampage by Nidal Malik Hasan, on 10 November 2009 in Fort Hood, Texas.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesUS justice system‘Medieval’ and ‘disturbing’: US plan to livestream execution elicits global condemnationPentagon said execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, would be broadcast liveUS politics live – latest updatesDavid Smithin Washington andAriana Baioin New YorkFri 9 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 14.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US is facing worldwide condemnation over a “barbaric” plan to execute a disabled man by firing squad and livestream it to the public, with critics comparing theTrump administrationto dictatorships inIranandAfghanistan.The Pentagonconfirmed on Thursdaythat the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood inTexasin 2009, would be livestreamed on 3 December.The United Nations’office of the high commissioner for human rightswarned on Friday that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”.Pentagon says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamedRead moreThe plan also drew opprobrium from politicians, religious leaders and human rights advocates in the US and abroad. Hillary Clinton, the former US secretary of state,wrote on social media: “A barbaric idea, beneath our dignity as a country. Push back on this.”Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress,posted: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”11:14‘Barbaric’: firing squad livestream ordered by Pete Hegseth - The LatestBritain, which abolished the death penalty in the 1960s, moved to distance itself from the execution. Bridget Phillipson, the UK’s equalities minister and Labour party chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that she found the concept “rather disturbing”.Phillipson stressed that the decision was a matter for the US government, adding: “They are a close ally. Does that mean that we support everything the US government does? No.”Under US military law, a president must approve an execution by firing squad. Trump did so on the recommendation of his defence secretary,Pete Hegseth, according to the Pentagon.JD Vance – a practicing Catholic – told reporters on Friday he wouldn’t watch the livestreamed execution of Hasan, but stopped short of criticizing the administration’s decision.When asked how his Christian beliefs influence his view of the public execution, Vance dismissed controversy about the manner of execution and appeared to question whether the livestream will happen.“Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope the people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” the US vice-president told reporters. “That said, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”Hegseth gleefully confirmed the livestream plan after previously saying that the execution would be public. Speaking to the conservative broadcaster Real America’s Voice, he said people should be able to watch because they need to understand that there were “serious consequences” for such crimes.Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”Now 56, Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 after being convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. Twelve of those killed and 30 of the wounded were soldiers.The former army psychiatrist opened fire with a handgun at a medical facility at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009 as soldiers waited for medical checks before deployment. He was shot by a police officer during his arrest and left partly paralysed, and now uses a wheelchair.0:45Pete Hegseth says execution of Fort Hood mass killer will be livestreamed – videoThe execution is expected to be the first by firing squad carried out by theUS militarysince 1945, when army private Eddie Slovik was executed for desertion during the second world war. The last US military execution of any kind took place in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged.Hasan’s case comes amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US following thebotched lethal injection of Tennessee death-row prisoner Christa Pikelast week. Her lawyers said she awoke in hospital “angry and confused” and remained seriously ill and shackled to her hospital bed.Media have sought to televise US executions ⁠in the past, but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream legal executions, experts said.Indeed, public executions have largely disappeared around the world. Amnesty International recorded at least 17 in 2025, including 11 in Iran and six in Taliban-run Afghanistan.In the US, executions have been conducted privately for about nine decades. The hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky in 1936, witnessed by thousands, is generally regarded as the country’s last public execution, although another hanging took place in Missouri the following year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExperts said there was no known precedent for livestreaming a legal execution. The execution of the Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001 was made available to victims’ relatives through closed-circuit television, but was not broadcast publicly.The proposed live stream has prompted criticism from religious leaders. Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.Politicians from both sides of the aisle also spoke out. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives armed services committee, said the plan was “disturbing and makes a mockery of our legal system”. The Democratic senator Chris Murphy described public executions as “medieval”.View image in fullscreenNidal Hasan.Photograph: Bell County Sheriff’s Department/APThe Republican senator Thom Tillis said Hasan should face the death penalty but that broadcasting his execution was “beyond disgusting”, arguing that public executions were associated with oppressive regimes.Others warned that the spectacle would be counterproductive and act as a recruiting sergeant for US enemies seeking fresh propaganda.Ned Price, a former deputy to the US representative to the United Nations,posted on X: “You can take it from those of us who’ve spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause.“Or take it from [al-Qaida] and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth’s proposal. Either way, it’s hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America’s image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable.”Some experts have raised questions about whether the live stream could be challenged in court. Eugene Fidell, a military law specialist at Yale Law School, said Hasan could seek legal action to block the public display of his death.Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at the University of California, Berkeley, said the announcement raised serious questions about the dignity of the condemned prisoner and the government’s motivation for staging such an unusual spectacle.“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,”she told the Associated Press.Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said: “Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end.“This announcement adds to the display of cruelty that we have just witnessed in the senselesspursuit of the execution of Christa Pikein Tennessee. The US death penalty is irredeemably broken. It is high time that the US authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all.”Other experts argued that public access could increase transparency around capital punishment. Deborah Denno, a death penalty specialist at Fordham University, told the AP that a live stream could make the process more transparent at a time when the botched execution in Tennessee had renewed questions about how the state puts prisoners to death.It remains unclear whether Hasan will seek to challenge his execution in civilian court, a move that could significantly delay the proceedings.Explore more on these topicsUS justice systemCapital punishmentTrump administrationPete HegsethGun crimeUS crimeUS militarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant bans Drumcree parade | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Prospect of contentious Orange Order march through Garvaghy Road in Portadown has led to a nearly two-week standoff
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Prospect of contentious Orange Order march through Garvaghy Road in Portadown has led to a nearly two-week standoff
Content: A PSNI vehicle near Drumcree church in Portadown, where the parade would have begun.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenA PSNI vehicle near Drumcree church in Portadown, where the parade would have begun.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PANorthern IrelandNorthern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant bans Drumcree paradeProspect of contentious Orange Order march through Garvaghy Road in Portadown has led to a nearly two-week standoffRory CarrollIreland correspondentFri 9 Oct 2026 16.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNorthern Irelandsecretary of state has banned the Drumcree parade after a 13-day impasse between the Orange Order and nationalists.Chris Bryant announced on Friday night that it was “not in the public interest” for Orangemen to march the contested route through Garvaghy Road in Portadown, which Catholic residents had blocked.He said he took the decision after advice from Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of theNorthern IrelandPolice Service, that the parade “would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect” across Northern Ireland.The Parades Commission ruled two weeks ago that a small, circumscribed march could pass along Garvaghy Road – a reversal of 28 years of successive bans. But police prevented the Orangemen from marching after thousands of residents and supporters, including Sinn Féin leaders,blocked the road.Garvaghy Road residents welcomed the secretary of state’s decision, saying it brought relief and certainty after a tense standoff that revived memories of the 1990s, when Orangemen fought pitched battles with police in an attempt to march the route.It was the only “sensible, reasonable and logical outcome”, said Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition.TheSinn Féinleader, Mary Lou McDonald, and the party’s Northern Ireland first minister, Michelle O’Neill, said in a statement that residents had endured fear and anxiety. “There will be an enormous sense of relief within the community this evening.”The Irish government welcomed the decision and appealed to both sides to seek common ground. “This isn’t a time for triumphalism or claiming victories or anything like that,” said the taoiseach, Micheál Martin. “Those on the unionist, loyalist side will look at this through a different prism. We need to be conscious of that. We need to acknowledge that.”Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, accused Boutcher and Bryant of bowing to republican agitation and threats of potential violence. “These decisions are a mistake, and send profound signals that the country should be run on force of numbers and who shouts the loudest. The framework for both parading and protests now lies in tatters, and the rule of law has been fundamentally undermined.”Robinson asked the secretary to state to explain what the government will do to “restore confidence in the rule of law”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArtists including Noel Gallagher show support for Garvaghy Road residents in Drumcree disputeRead moreEarlier on Friday the chief constable asked Bryant to review the Parade Commission’s determination, made last month, that conditions in Portadown enabled the parade to go ahead.“I’ve looked at the changing situation in Portadown, the fact that it’s very difficult for that procession to proceed, and I’ve decided that it’s not in the public interest for it to proceed, and I’ve therefore banned the procession,” said Bryant.He thanked Portadown’s Orange Lodge for its “peaceful and law-abiding approach” and regretted that both sides could not reach a compromise, leading to a standoff. “With this in mind, I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions.”Boutcher said the dispute had affected relationships within and between communities and the police. “It is in everyone’s interest that time and space is now created for conversations about finding long-term solutions to this complex and sensitive issue.”The dispute has fuelled angry exchanges at the Stormont assembly and destabilised the executive, with unionists demanding O’Neill step down as first minister for allegedly breaking the law at aGarvaghy Road protest.Earlier on Friday, the PSNI sent the Sinn Féin deputy leader a letter probing alleged criminal offences relating to her involvement in the protest. O’Neill said she will cooperate with the investigation.Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandNorthern Irish politicsChris BryantnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor faced £1.8m repair bill after leaving Royal Lodge | Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor | The Guardian
description: Ex-prince was granted £302,000 in compensation for early end of lease and king has reportedly contributed to costs
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Ex-prince was granted £302,000 in compensation for early end of lease and king has reportedly contributed to costs
Content: Mountbatten-Windsor moved out of the Windsor mansion this year.Photograph: Invicta Kent Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMountbatten-Windsor moved out of the Windsor mansion this year.Photograph: Invicta Kent Media/ShutterstockAndrew Mountbatten-WindsorAndrew Mountbatten-Windsor faced £1.8m repair bill after leaving Royal LodgeEx-prince was granted £302,000 in compensation for early end of lease and king has reportedly contributed to costsJamie GriersonFri 9 Oct 2026 09.09 EDTFirst published on Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndrew Mountbatten-Windsor faced a £1.8m bill to cover repair and restoration of his former Royal Lodge home in Windsor after the lease was officially surrendered.But the former prince was granted £302,000 in compensation for giving up the lease early on the 98-acre property, meaning his total costs came to £1.5m.Recouping costs for dilapidations is a standard process when exiting a lease, and the Guardian understands the repairs covered the entire estate, which includes several properties, gardens and large outbuildings.Andrew was entitled to compensation because, as per the terms of his lease, he surrendered it within the first 25 years.The Times reported that King Charles had contributed to the repair costs.The crown estate spokesperson said: “The lease for Royal Lodge has ended and our focus now is firmly on its future use and the opportunities to generate additional financial value for the nation from its early return.”The former Duke of York moved out of the Windsor mansion this year as the US Department of Justice released files related to the child sex offenderJeffrey Epstein.He was forced to move into Marsh Farm on the king’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk amid public outcry about the rent he paid on the Royal Lodge.In June, a National Audit Office investigation revealed that the late queen’s second son received an unknown amount of private income from subletting three cottages on the Royal Lodge estate while paying a peppercorn rent – a small, symbolic payment – for more than two decades.The crown estate spokesperson said the property would now be marketed by two nationally recognised agents for its proposed future use.On Thursday, Mountbatten-Windsorwon a legal challengeagainst Thames Valley police over search warrants used to raid his home. The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants.Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful.The episode is embarrassing for TVP but police believe it will not affect the success of the investigation.The arrest followed information that emerged from theEpsteinfiles. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein. Police began searching the former duke’s residence on the Sandringham estate and the Royal Lodge on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized.Late last year,King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a princeand of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clearthis should not be used to fund the judicial review.Explore more on these topicsAndrew Mountbatten-WindsorMonarchyJeffrey EpsteinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ed Davey faces growing revolt against leadership as senior Lib Dem MP quits | Ed Davey | The Guardian
description: Treasury spokesperson Charlie Maynard reportedly resigned in attempt to unseat leader as party slips in polls
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Treasury spokesperson Charlie Maynard reportedly resigned in attempt to unseat leader as party slips in polls
Content: Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, gives his keynote speech at the party’s conference in September.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEd Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, gives his keynote speech at the party’s conference in September.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesEd DaveyEd Davey faces growing revolt against leadership as senior Lib Dem MP quitsTreasury spokesperson Charlie Maynard reportedly resigned in attempt to unseat leader as party slips in pollsAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentFri 9 Oct 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 16.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEd Davey is facing a growing revolt against his leadership of theLiberal Democrats, after the resignation of a senior frontbench figure on Friday.Charlie Maynard, the Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, has resigned in an attempt to unseat Davey after months of frustration over concerns that the party is failing to cut through with voters, the Guardian understands.Daisy Cooper, the party’s deputy leader, immediately backed Davey, saying he enjoyed the support of the “vast majority of MPs”, who wanted him to lead them into the next election and were “furious at this distraction”.“We Liberal Democrats are the last line of defence against a Reform UK government, and Ed is determined to lead a strong and united party into the next general election whenever it comes,” Cooper said.“As Ed said at conference, we are in the fight of our lives against the right who want to turn our country into their version of Trump’s America.”Maynard’s resignation, first reported by the Financial Times, came four days after Alison Bennett, the Lib Dem care and carers spokesperson, stood down from the frontbench.Davey has led the party since 2019, first as acting leader and then officially from August 2020. At the 2024 general election, he steered the party to its most successful result in more than 100 years. The party now has 71 MPs, and is the third largest party in the House of Commons.But the Lib Dems have slipped to fourth or fifth in national opinion polls, behind the Greens and Reform UK, and frustration has mounted over the party’s failure to attract voters in a fragmented political landscape.At the party’s conference in Brighton in September, Davey played down criticism from a Liberal Democrat council leader who questioned whether he was the right person to lead the party. Julian Brazil, the leader of Devon county council, said the party was “sleepwalking into irrelevance” and “lacking ambition”.Davey announced a plan fora £17bn income tax cutin a speech aimed at shoring up the party’s support among former Conservative voters. He said the cut would be paid for entirely by increased growth generated by rejoining the EU’s single market and customs union.However, Davey faced opposition by Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference to change the pension triple lock to help fund a national care service. One said his defence of the current policy “gaslights an entire generation into believing it’s for our benefit”.Explore more on these topicsEd DaveyLiberal DemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gromit finally gets a voice … and it’s Martin Freeman | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: After 37 years, the staunchly silent dog will speak for the first time in the audiobook of his autobiography – and it turns out he sounds like a hobbit
Author: Alexi Duggins
Headline: After 37 years, the staunchly silent dog will speak for the first time in the audiobook of his autobiography – and it turns out he sounds like a hobbit
Content: ‘Who could possibly be the voice of a character everyone feels they know, but nobody’s actually heard?’Photograph: PRView image in fullscreen‘Who could possibly be the voice of a character everyone feels they know, but nobody’s actually heard?’Photograph: PRTelevision & radioGromit finally gets a voice … and it’s Martin FreemanAfter 37 years, the staunchly silent dog will speak for the first time in the audiobook of his autobiography – and it turns out he sounds like a hobbitAlexi DugginsFri 9 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe has been on screen for 37 years, but he has never uttered a word. Now, Gromit will speak for the first time – with the voice of the Hobbit starMartin Freeman.The claymation dog, who has partnered with his eccentric inventor-owner Wallace in a series of Oscar-winning films including The Wrong Trousers, A Close Shave and Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit, is releasing an autobiography this month – including an audiobook edition.“When you create a character who has no voice and whose facial expressions are everything, what do you do when your publisher reminds you there’ll be an audiobook?” said Nick Park, the animator and film-maker who created the series. “Who could possibly be the voice of a character everyone feels they know, but nobody’s actually heard?View image in fullscreen‘He’s reading Gromit’s story as Gromit put it’ … Martin Freeman.“The more I thought about it, the more I realised Martin Freeman was the obvious choice, really. I was genuinely thrilled and honoured when he said yes.”Freeman previously honed the role of put-upon sidekick in his Bafta- and Emmy-winning turn as Dr John Watson toBenedict Cumberbatch’s unpredictable detective in Sherlock. It should stand him in good stead to voice Gromit – who has had to put up with Wallace variously falling in love with a serial killer, welcoming in a hardened criminal penguin as a lodger, and inventing a hackable robot gnome that spawned an army of evil garden decorations.Freeman won’t be taking too much creative licence with the character, however. “Martin is not doing a Gromit ‘voice’ as such,” said Park. “He’s reading Gromit’s story as Gromit put it: his inner thoughts, his candid insights and endless witticisms, bringing to them his usual colour, thoughtfulness and wry humour.”View image in fullscreenThe book is not the only spin-off of the franchise in the works.Larger Than Life, an immersive, behind-the-scenes experience projected across four 11-metre walls, will open on 14 October at the Lightroom in King’s Cross, London.Grand: The Autobiography of Gromit, as told to Nick Park, will be published on 22 October.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioAudiobooksTelevisionWallace & GromitAnimation on TVMartin FreemannewsShareReuse this content

title: Does Polanski have to go? Greens at the crossroads after Holborn and St Pancras | Green party | The Guardian
description: Pressure is building on the party leader after byelection defeat, a damaging row over Zionism and polls that show him less popular than Nigel Farage
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Pressure is building on the party leader after byelection defeat, a damaging row over Zionism and polls that show him less popular than Nigel Farage
Content: A discarded Green party leaflet for Zack Polanski on the pavement in King's Cross after his byelection loss.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA discarded Green party leaflet for Zack Polanski on the pavement in King's Cross after his byelection loss.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockGreen partyDoes Polanski have to go? Greens at the crossroads after Holborn and St PancrasPressure is building on the party leader after byelection defeat, a damaging row over Zionism and polls that show him less popular than Nigel FarageAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentFri 9 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 13.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Zack Polanski addressed his campaignersflush with victoryafter the Gorton and Denton byelection in February, he declared: “Labour’s electoral stranglehold is over.” The election of Hannah Spencer as the new Green MP for the Greater Manchester seat was a seismic victory, he continued: “I said we were here to replace Labour and this is what replacing looks like.”But in the wake of Polanski’s defeat in theHolborn and St Pancras byelectionon Thursday, and a calamitous row over the party’s stance on Zionism, the debate around what, or who, could be replaced has shifted to Polanski himself.On Friday the leader of the Green party in England and Wales was defiant after losing toLabour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali, who took 45% of the vote, to Polanski’s 33%. Asked what was going wrong in his party, which has fallen from highs of 21% in some pollsafter the victory in Gorton and Dentonto around 10-11%, Polanski, responded: “If things are going wrong by the fact that we just tripled our vote share and had our second best byelection result in Green party history, you know what? I’ll take that.” While emphasising that Green members would ultimately decide who they wanted as leader, he said: “Of course I can carry on.”.That the last few months have been difficult for the Greens – and Polanski in particular – is beyond doubt. Polanski himself is, according to new polling from More in Common, now less popular with voters than Nigel Farage, and is the least popular major UK party leader, falling by four points to a -28 net approval.His standing, bruised by a series of controversies over a failure to pay council tax and the sharing of a post criticising police, has been further damaged by acontroversial motionthat was adopted at the Green party conference in Brighton last weekend, equating Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism. Polanski’s decision to abstain from the debate and the vote to instead campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, was condemned by his detractors, but also, more significantly, criticised by senior figures in his own party.The former Green leader Caroline Lucas told BBC Newsnight on Thursday that Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”. Asked if he should stand down, she said: “I think let’s just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this byelection.” Following his defeat she appeared to temper her position, saying Polanski had “transformed the party” and she hoped he would now “help resolve huge issues we face and transform our internal structures”.On Friday, pressure mounted, as the leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein,called for Polanski to step down, saying it was a “big mistake” for him not to have spoken and voted for amendments stating that any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians, rather than impose a one-state system.But there was bullishness among the Polanski faithful, with Greens Organise, the leftwing faction that backed his leadership bid, saying he should stay on. A statement from the group said that “not all growth and success is linear, there will be ups and downs; the real test for a political organisation is how we deal with failure”. It added: “We have reshaped the British political landscape. TheGreen partycan still become the ecosocialist party we need. Zack is still the leader who can get us there.”Green party supporters pointed out that the party achieved a 13-point swing from Labour in Holborn and St Pancras, traditionally a safe Labour seat. The Camden councillor Hamza Chowdhury – who was overlooked as the candidate in the constituency in favour of Polanski – went as far as saying the result was “a huge win for the Green party and the wider movement”.Polanski supporters point out that since he was elected leader in September 2025, the party has quadrupled its membership to more than 230,000. As well as the winning of its first ever seat in the north of England, he presided over the Greens’ best-ever performance in May’s local and mayoral elections, including gaining their first-ever directly elected mayoralty, in Hackney, eastLondon.Nonetheless, the result in north London exposed the dual challenge Polanski now faced, said Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common. At the same time as the replacement of Keir Starmer with Andy Burnham had brought disillusioned progressives back to Labour, Polanski had become a more polarising figure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion15:19Did the Zionism row lose it for Zack Polanski? | Politics WeeklyA series of missteps, starting when heshared a social media post critical of policeafter the Golders Green stabbings, had damaged his popularity with the wider UK public, added Tryl. “It was just one of those moments which gave soft Green supporters pause for thought. Similarly, many people don’t vote directly on something like the Zionism is racism motion, but it adds to that sense of ‘oh, I thought these were nice guys who were focused on the environment’.”The result in north London was a “good one” for Labour, he added, despite the drop in its majority. While governing parties usually get hit hard in byelections, the drop in Holborn was below the average for defending a seat at byelections in any postwar parliament, he noted.But Labour hopes of the death of the Green party were likely to have been exaggerated. “I think writing off the Greens is premature,” he said. “Burnham has managed, for now, to unite the left, but a lot of big decisions, including on North Sea oil drilling and, more importantly, the budget, are coming down the line.”As for Polanski, the path towards rebuilding the popularity that saw him win the support of young voters desperate for hope and change would lie in a return to his original economic messaging around “rip-off Britain” and generational fairness, rather than divisive internal battles, said James Baggaley from UCL’s Policy Lab. “The question for the Greens and Polanski now is: do they want to reassure voters on questions of antisemitism and also get back to what they were actually winning on, which was the economy?”Explore more on these topicsGreen partyZack PolanskiHolborn and St Pancras byelectionLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Be more Jagger? How BBC’s Matt Brittin could follow up Elvis appeal to staff | Matt Brittin | The Guardian
description: Director general called for ‘a little less conversation, a little more action’ – but from what other songs could he have drawn inspiration?
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Director general called for ‘a little less conversation, a little more action’ – but from what other songs could he have drawn inspiration?
Content: Matt Brittin, right, urged BBC staff to channel their inner Elvis in an all-staff call earlier this week.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMatt Brittin, right, urged BBC staff to channel their inner Elvis in an all-staff call earlier this week.Composite: Getty ImagesMatt BrittinBe more Jagger? How BBC’s Matt Brittin could follow up Elvis appeal to staffDirector general called for ‘a little less conversation, a little more action’ – but from what other songs could he draw inspiration?Stuart HeritageFri 9 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe BBC director general, Matt Brittin, has started the job at a time of huge crisis. Money is short, jobs are being cut and it’s likely entire channels will be culled to stem the tide. This is a moment that requires great motivational charisma, which is why, in a recent all-staff call, he urged BBC employees to be “a bit more Elvis– a little less conversation, a little more action”.Clearly, this isn’t great. But maybe this is how things are now. Perhaps, if you really want to unite a flagging workforce against a vast and inevitable decline, you need to start quoting song lyrics at them. With that in mind, here are some more that Brittin could use in his next call.Be more Rolling Stones – you can’t always get what you wantView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersThis may be a better tactic, given the sour mood at theBBCright now. Sure, employees may wish for lots of things – like a bigger commissioning budget, more exclusive coverage of big sporting events, and a functioning BBC Three. But Mick Jagger was right. You can’t always get what you want, but if you try sometimes, you just might find you get what you need. Note: this only really works if what you need is having Romesh Ranganathan present everything.Be more Queen – the show must go onView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tom Hill/WireImageIt doesn’t matter how many cuts the BBC faces. It doesn’t matter how many staff it has to lose. The corporation’s ethos is to inform, educate and entertain, and that’s what it will do, no matter what. If that means Sophie Raworth has to do the news over Zoom from inside a wardrobe, so be it. If it means the Olympics have to be replaced by footage of raindrops racing each other down a window for several hours at a time, bring it on.Be more Bee Gees – stayin’ aliveView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesThe media landscape is going through a stage of permanent transformation. Maybe the idea of an elderly institution such as the BBC thriving in this new environment is too much to ask. Perhaps the real motivating war cry should be about clinging on to life at any cost. What do we want? Survival, if only in a heavily diminished capacity. When do we want it? Now!Be more the Smiths – there is a light that never goes outView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Cronin/RedfernsThe BBC finds itself in a moment of extreme belt-tightening, and every penny must be utilised to its best advantage. As such, turning on the office bathroom lights is too expensive and therefore banned. Your phone has a torch, doesn’t it?Be more XTC – making plans for NigelView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Paul Natkin/WireImageThis one speaks for itself. An enormous part of running the BBC involves figuring out what to do with Nigel Farage. If Brittin wants to maintain any form of continuity with the previous administration, this will mean putting him on television at every possible opportunity. Does it hurt the corporation to give so much airtime to someone who wants to abolish the licence fee? Absolutely. But also, could he guest host The One Show for a couple of weeks? Couldn’t hurt to ask.Explore more on these topicsMatt BrittinBBCTelevision industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Stark warning – does new footage in Avengers: Endgame reveal the truth about Doctor Doom? | Movies | The Guardian
description:
Warning: contains spoilers
The four short scenes added to the new version has made the film the highest-grossing of all time – but the only people really enjoying this are the Disney accountants
Author: Ben Child
Headline: Warning: contains spoilersThe four short scenes added to the new version has made the film the highest-grossing of all time – but the only people really enjoying this are the Disney accountants
Content: ‘I’m putting together a pub quiz team’ … Robert Downey Jr and Chris Evans in Avengers Endgame: Encore.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘I’m putting together a pub quiz team’ … Robert Downey Jr and Chris Evans in Avengers Endgame: Encore.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyMoviesStark warning – does new footage in Avengers: Endgame reveal the truth about Doctor Doom?Ben ChildWarning: contains spoilersThe four short scenes added to the new version has made the film the highest-grossing of all time – but the only people really enjoying this are the Disney accountantsFri 9 Oct 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 19.03 EDTShareDoes it really matter which film is the highest-grossing of all time at the global box office? Will James Cameron be lying awake at night staring into the darkness and pondering whether to withdraw humanity’s access to giant, blue-skinned space elves out of sheer spite, just because Avatar has been dethroned once again byAvengers: Endgame? It seems unlikely. Are the Russo brothers at this very moment leaping and capering with wild abandon because adding a few new scenes and releasing their film for the umpteenth time has led to this momentous changing of the guard? Probably not. Is a Disney accountant somewhere holding a tiny awards ceremony in which every nominee is himself? Well yes, absolutely, because the mouse house ultimately owns both films.And yet the most interesting thing about Avengers: Endgame’s return to cinemas is not how much money it has made – for the record, the rerelease, titled Avengers Endgame: Encore, had brought in another $126m worldwide by last weekend, taking its lifetime total to approximately $2.925bn (just ahead of Avatar’s $2.923bn) – but whatMarveladded to the picture while we were all busy counting.Premium-format presentations of the new version feature a new scene at the end of the film and another three during and after its credits, with some also appearing in standard screenings. The idea is presumably that these tantalising snippets will segue viewers smoothly into the upcomingAvengers: Doomsdaywith the sort of spring in the step that can only come from being convinced that they are now three tiny clues away from understanding the mind of Kevin Feige.View image in fullscreen‘I’ve got to do what now?’ … Mark Ruffalo as Hulk in Avengers Endgame: Encore.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyThe original Endgame featured a closing shot of Chris Evans’ Steve Rogers, who has apparently used Tony Stark’s discovery of time travel to return to the 1940s, dancing contentedly with Hayley Atwell’s Peggy Carter. In the new version, the couple are interrupted by a knock at the door, only to find Tom Hiddleston’s Loki standing outside offering to help them. Given that the Norse trickster ended Loki season two holding the branching timelines of the multiverse together, this is unlikely to be just a neighbour popping round to complain about the hedge. We are presumably meant to infer that whatever is about to go wrong with reality is serious enough to reach Steve even in his carefully arranged retirement, and that his happy ending may now have to be put on hold. The man has defeated the Nazis and helped reverse the extinction of half of all life, but apparently still hasn’t accrued enough annual leave to finish a dance.Scene two turns up during the credits, and finds Bruce Banner holed up in an underground facility following the events ofSpider-Man: Brand New Day, trying to keep his inner Hulk under control. As if matters couldn’t get any worse, the voice of Robert Downey Jr’s Doctor Doom is heard announcing that he has come to “collect” the troubled scientist. Whether he wants Banner’s genius, the Hulk’s muscle or something considerably less agreeable remains unclear, but it seems safe to assume he is not putting together a pub quiz team.A second mid-credits scene sees the Time Variance Authority’s Mobius (Owen Wilson), OB (Ke Huy Quan) and Casey (Eugene Cordero) – whose organisation is tasked, following the events of Loki season two, with protecting the branching timelines it once ruthlessly pruned – watching in horror as universes collide and vanish in their thousands. Crucially, the reality inhabited by the X-Men during the 20th Century Fox era is among those that are threatened. In the comics, similar incursions unfold through Jonathan Hickman’s Avengers and New Avengers, culminating in the Time Runs Out storyline and leading into the 2015 event Secret Wars. The main Marvel and Ultimate universes are the last to be destroyed, after which Doctor Doom assembles remnants of ruined realities into the patchwork planet Battleworld. Might Doomsday see the Fox universe, the retro-futuristic reality occupied by the Fantastic Four and the main Marvel Cinematic Universe similarly stitched together, with Doom appointing himself ruler of whatever survives?View image in fullscreenGonna need a bigger hammer … Chris Hemsworth as Thor in Avengers Endgame: Encore.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyEncore’s final scene arrives after the credits, and reworks Endgame’s original audio farewell: Tony Stark building his first Iron Man armour in an Afghan cave. The new version pairs the blows of the hammer with flashing images, culminating in a final, ominous shot of Doctor Doom’s mask. Is Marvel trying to tell us that the Latverian sorcerer really is a Stark variant after all? Or is the studio just exploiting the unsettling associations of a familiar din coming from the wrong metal visage? Either way, the film-makers clearly want us to carry the memory of Tony Stark into Doomsday, and perhaps ponder how much of the man who saved the universe might lurk inside the one now threatening it.Marvel looks like it’s about to abolish the Multiverse saga. Isn’t that cheating?Read moreThis is, admittedly, a more intriguing setup than we might expect from a common-or-garden Marvel mashup. If Doom has the face of a lost friend and the power to offer ravaged worlds the merest glimpse of a future beyond torture and oblivion, resisting him could require more than Thor locating a larger hammer than usual.What is clear is that Marvel has somehow persuaded audiences to pay again for a film they already know, then rewarded them with the news that retirement is cancelled, the Hulk’s attempts to retreat from public life have failed and existence itself is falling apart. Somewhere, that Disney accountant is probably giving himself a lifetime achievement award.Explore more on these topicsFilmMarvelAvengers: EndgameSuperhero moviesAvengers: DoomsdayTom HiddlestonHayley AtwellcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Sometimes she publishes notes she’s scribbled on her hand’: Édouard Louis on 10 reasons to love Anne Carson | Nobel prize in literature | The Guardian
description: The French author discovered Carson on a bus while stranded in a snowstorm and has been enthralled by her fearless imagination ever since
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The French author discovered Carson on a bus while stranded in a snowstorm and has been enthralled by her fearless imagination ever since
Content: Carson doesn’t try to ‘make literature’ … Louis on the Nobel-winning writer.Photograph: Golli/Kjartan ÞorbjörnssonView image in fullscreenCarson doesn’t try to ‘make literature’ … Louis on the Nobel-winning writer.Photograph: Golli/Kjartan ÞorbjörnssonNobel prize in literature‘Sometimes she publishes notes she’s scribbled on her hand’: Édouard Louis on 10 reasons to love Anne CarsonThe French author discovered Carson on a bus while stranded in a snowstorm and has been enthralled by her fearless imagination ever sinceWhere to start with Anne Carson‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne CarsonÉdouard LouisFri 9 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 18.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1.Anne Carsonis one of the greatest writers of our time. I discovered her work on a Peter Pan bus from New York to New England. I’d bought Antigonickin a bookstore a few days earlier, almost randomly. From the very first lines, I was enthralled. While we were on the bus, a snowstorm suddenly blanketed the roads, and the other passengers and I found ourselves stuck for 10 hours in rural America, surrounded by an entirely white landscape. I took my computer out of my backpack and started to translateAntigonick into French. Spontaneously. I was so absorbed by the power of Carson’s text that I didn’t notice the hours pass.2. One of Carson’s greatest strengths is that, unlike so many other contemporary writers, she doesn’t try to “make literature”. She writes. Sometimes clouds do the speaking, in her work, and sometimes monsters do; sometimes, in the middle of a collection of poems, she lets an imaginary Catherine Deneuve take over the narration. Sometimes she writes a letter to her own sleep and sometimes she publishes notes she’s scribbled on her hand. She writes about Homer, but also Rosalía; about Brecht, but also Marilyn Monroe.3. In Carson’s work, time is upside down – out of joint, as Shakespeare writes in Hamlet. This is one of the strangest aspects of her work and it has fascinated me from my first reading. In her rewriting of Antigone, in the first scene, Antigone and her sister Ismene talk about Hegel. And yet, in Carson’s play, the conversation happens as if entirely normal, as if the ancient Greek Antigone and Ismenereally haddiscussed Hegel together. One day, my friend Ivo van Hove decided to put on Sophocles’ Antigone and called Carson to ask her if she would do a new translation. Carson responded, “I already did a translation, titled Antigonick.” Ivo said, “Of course, but that’s not a literal translation of Sophocles – in the first scene, the two sisters talk about Hegel.” Carson responded, “That’s what’s written in Sophocles’ text. All I did was translate.”View image in fullscreenA tribute to Carson’s brother … Nox.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian4. One of Carson’s most wrenching texts is called Nox. In it, she tells the story of her brother, or rather, the story of her brother’s absence. When he was very young, her brother was convicted by a Canadian court. Rather than go to prison, he fled. He hid in Europe and Asia for decades under false identities. During the time of his disappearance, he would sometimes send his family a brief letter, or a postcard with quick phrases scribbled on the back. On a few occasions he called, just for a few minutes. One day, the Carson family received a call informing them of his death in Copenhagen. Carson gathered the photos she had of this brother who had just died and whom she hardly knew, and also the letters he had sent her, and she wrote fragments about her memories of him interspersed with an analysis of a poem by Catullus. She added in reflections on Herodotus and history, and very personal notes on pain and loss, reminiscent of Barthes’s Mourning Diary. Then she put all these notes into a box. And later Nox was published in the form of this box, with a single sheet of paper folded accordion-style inside bearing all the notes and images and fragments that she had accumulated. Never had a book looked like this – a shoebox with an enormous accordion foldout inside.5. Carson thus spurns the limits of what a book is; her work Float is made up of several booklets on different subjects gathered together in a plastic envelope. Nox is indeed a box. H of H Playbook is a wide rectangular facsimile edition, impossible to put on a bookshelf. Lots of writers across history have tried to reinvent writing. Very few of them have also had the idea of reinventing what a book is, or transforming the book-object itself. Anne Carson did.6. But Carson’s formal inventiveness should not lead us to forget the powerfully political dimension of her work. In Autobiography of Red, she takes inspiration from the ancient poet Stesichorus to tell the story of the monster killed by Hercules during his 12 labours. She chooses to tell the story of the monster, the victim, rather than repeat the tale of the hero, the executioner. She imagines a story in which a young Hercules and Geryon have a devastating homosexual affair. In her books, Carson often places herself in the position of the defeated.7. For a long time she identified with Oscar Wilde, to the point of having a Wilde outfit that she regularly wore during her adolescence.8. Women are also at the heart of her work, and always have been. In Norma Jeane Baker of Troy, one of her most beautiful texts, she makes Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy into one and the same character: two women who, despite the centuries between them, remain the object of the same masculine violence, the same dictates of obligatory beauty. Carson has also translated Sappho’s poems. And in her version of Euripides’s Bacchae, she gives an unheard-of psychological depth to the female characters.9. On a more personal level, I can say that Carson has a distaste for the kind of social interaction that tends to come with a literary life. I sincerely believe that she likes nothing more than to be at home, writing. One day when we were signing copies of our books side by side, she said to me, “I really hate this!” Another time, after a performance we did together at the House of Literature in Oslo, she proposed that we quickly head for the restaurant in order to avoid the small talk.10. Recently, we were talking about a trip I’m getting ready to take to Iceland, where she lives. I suggested to Anne that we do a performance together, with two voices, like we had done in the past. Then I felt bad about adding work to her life and so I sent her a follow-up message saying, “But we don’t have to do something public. We can just relax and enjoy ourselves.” Anne responded: “I prefer working. That way I don’t have to think about the world. Or myself.” How better to sum up the greatness of Anne Carson?Translated by Josh CohenExplore more on these topicsNobel prize in literatureAnne CarsonAwards and prizesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Privileged and proud: how nepo babies took fashion month by storm | Fashion | The Guardian
description: From commanding the catwalks to acting as plus-ones for their famous parents, celebrity kids are bang on trend
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: From commanding the catwalks to acting as plus-ones for their famous parents, celebrity kids are bang on trend
Content: Apple Martin makes her catwalk debut for Chloé during Paris fashion week.Photograph: Kristy Sparow/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenApple Martin makes her catwalk debut for Chloé during Paris fashion week.Photograph: Kristy Sparow/Getty ImagesFashionPrivileged and proud: how nepo babies took fashion month by stormFrom commanding the catwalks to acting as plus-ones for their famous parents, celebrity kids are bang on trendChloe Mac DonnellFri 9 Oct 2026 10.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKnee-length skirts andbras worn as topswere two of the main takeaways from fashion month, which wrapped up this week. But the biggest trend had nothing to do with clothing. From New York and London to Milan and Paris, the shows were the ultimate proof of a nepo baby takeover.John Travolta’s daughter, Ella Bleu, 26, made her Paris catwalk debut atMiu Miu. Apple Martin, 22, the daughter of Chris Martin and Gwyneth Paltrow, walked the Chloé show.Meanwhile, the Vogue World event in Milan featured the Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli’s son Matteo, 29, Nick and Susie Cave’s son Earl, 26, Ava Phillippe, 27, the daughter of the actors Reese Witherspoon and Ryan Phillippe, and many more nepo babies in attendance.View image in fullscreenAva Phillippe at Vogue World: Milano 2026 at Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II in Milan, Italy.Photograph: Stefania M D’Alessandro/Getty Images for VogueMark Borkowski, a PR consultant, described the nepo baby phenomenon as “a wonderful cocktail of youth, nostalgia and inherited glamour”.Fran Hoepfner, the author of The Field Guide to Nepo Babies, said it was vital that a nepo had both a family connection and a direct or adjacent industry connection. “Simply having rich parents does not automatically make someone a nepo baby,” she said. “It just makes you lucky.”Previously, the children of famous people tended to downplay their family connections or even change their surnames. Nicolas Cage was born Coppola – his uncle is the legendary US film-maker – while Angelina Jolie dropped the Voight from her surname in an attempt to distance herself from her actor father, Jon Voight.View image in fullscreenElla Bleu Travolta modelling for Miu Miu at Paris fashion week.Photograph: Estrop/Getty ImagesAccording to Borkowski, we are now seeing play out “the industrialisation of inherited fame”. He described it as a cultural shift. “For years people tried to escape from the shadow of their parents because it actually hindered their career. Now they are no longer apologising for their privilege.”Nicole Kidman brought her daughter Faith Urban, 15, to Chanel, while The Diplomat star Keri Russell’s plus one at the Louis Vuitton show was her 13-year-old daughter, Willa. Elsewhere, the supermodels Karen Elson and Kristen McMenamy danced with their daughters Scarlett Teresa White, 20, and Lily McMenamy, 32,on the H&M catwalk.Four years after New York magazine declared 2022the “year of the nepo baby”, the boom is showing no sign of slowing down. The appeal for brands is simple: the casting of a nepo instantly captures mass audience attention.View image in fullscreenMatteo Bocelli, son of the Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli, at Vogue World.Photograph: Valentina S Frugiuele/Getty Images for VogueIt is not limited only to fashion. The newSense and Sensibility’s film credits read like a nepo roll-call. Samantha Morton’s daughter Esmé Creed-Miles plays Marianne Dashwood, while Sting’s non-binary child Eliot Sumner stars as Mr Palmer. Meanwhile, Cillian Murphy’s son Aran is currently on TV screens as Sharon Horgan’s son in Youth, and Kate Winslet’s son Joe Anders stars in Netflix’s adaptation of John Steinbeck’s 1952 novel East of Eden.“It’s a marketing tool,” Borkowski said. “Casting an unknown model or actor is one thing, but casting the daughter of a Hollywood legend gives a brand all that inherited fame and decades of cultural recognition.”The internet has been crucial to the nepo baby coup. In an age where anyone with a phone and internet access can become famous, why not lean into those existing famous family roots? “You don’t have to have any real talent to develop a fanbase,” Borkowski said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenNicole Kidman with her daughter Faith Urban at the Chanel show in Paris.Photograph: Swan Gallet/WWD/Getty ImagesIn 2023 Romy Mars, the daughter of the film-maker Sofia Coppola and musician Thomas Mars, went viral after posting about being grounded because she had tried to charter a helicopter to have dinner with a friend using her father’s credit card.In the now deleted video, she also revealed she wasn’t meant to have a social media account. “They don’t want me to be a nepotism kid but TikTok is not gonna make me famous, so it doesn’t really matter,” she said. Three years later she has amassed nearly 800,000 followers, starred in a film directed by her grandfather and released an album. Her debut music video was directed by her mum.Hoepfner described Mars’s behaviour as “sheer nepo baby perfection”. She said today’s generation had “learned lessons from their older millennial peers, who either deflected or tried to play off their privilege with some degree of false humility.”Elsewhere, Francesca Scorsese is a budding actor and film-maker, but it is her TikTok videos starring her Goodfellas director dad, Martin, that have led to millions of followers. In one, she asks him to identify “feminine items” including a menstrual cup, which Scorsese mistakes for a drinks container; in another, she tests him on gen Z slang.Even if someone does try to move beyond their family name, they often continue to leverage their connections. In January, in a six-page Instagram statement, Brooklyn Beckham said he was cutting ties with his parents. That decision led to him becoming more famous than ever. Borkowski described the continuing attention that unfolded as a cross between “the Big Brother house and a soap opera”, with fans of each member of the family waiting to see what happened next.Hoepfner said: “The fact of the matter is that there’s nothing they can really do about the fact that they’re a nepo baby, so they might as well own it. The best way to go about that at this point might as well be by doing it brazenly, with some degree of style or panache – especially if they aren’t really sorry about it.”Explore more on these topicsFashionCelebritySocial trendsFashion weeksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lost generation: the AI threat to Britain’s next great directors  | Film industry | The Guardian
description: Commercials once launched careers from Ridley Scott to Guy Ritchie, now automated production is cutting costs – and the chance to learn by doing
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Commercials once launched careers from Ridley Scott to Guy Ritchie, now automated production is cutting costs – and the chance to learn by doing
Content: Director Ridley Scott, left, and Paul Mescal on the set of Gladiator II.Photograph: Aidan Monaghan/APView image in fullscreenDirector Ridley Scott, left, and Paul Mescal on the set of Gladiator II.Photograph: Aidan Monaghan/APFilm industryLost generation: the AI threat to Britain’s next great directorsCommercials once launched careers from Ridley Scott to Guy Ritchie, now automated production is cutting costs – and the chance to learn by doingMark SweneyFri 9 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Ridley Scott was awarded the UK’s highest accolade for a glittering career directing films fromAlien and Blade Runner to Gladiator and The Martian, he reminded those attending the Bafta event eight years ago that making commercials had been his“film school”.The advertising industry has long been a breeding ground for British film and TV talent who havegone on to make the jump to Hollywood productions, including Guy Ritchie, who started out making music videos and commercials, and Paddington in Peru director Dougal Wilson, whose credits include a number of John Lewis’s famous Christmas ads.But thepanicked race to introduce AI technology across the advertising industry, to cut client costs and avoid being pushed aside by big tech, has raised fears of a lost generation who may be denied the opportunity to develop into great British film and TV directors.“100%, yes, I have fears,” says Luke Scott, who runs the group that includes Ridley Scott Associates, the media production company that was co-founded by his father in the 1960s.“I’m grown up enough to recognise that change is inevitable. But what I’ve seen generally in terms of generative AI output is a very mixed bag. You can turn to it and do something and say ‘Look what I made and isn’t it edifying’. But that is very misleading and sort of introducing us to an ersatz creativity.“The grave danger is the monoculturalisation of everything. The creative business is something you learn by doing. It is in the doing that is most valuable. Flying a drone isn’t like flying, there isn’t that visceral feeling to it, you are not actually flying. What do you do with that lost generation?
