title: A promising future now looks perilous for election loser Zack Polanski. He sowed, now he reaps | John Harris | The Guardian
description: There was a real chance of a Green byelection win in Holborn and St Pancras. He made bad decisions and cost his party dear, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: There was a real chance of a Green byelection win in Holborn and St Pancras. He made bad decisions and cost his party dear, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Zack Polanski, left, watches on as Sagal Abdi-Wali speaks, following her victory in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in the early hours of 9 October 2026.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenZack Polanski, left, watches on as Sagal Abdi-Wali speaks, following her victory in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in the early hours of 9 October 2026.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockOpinionGreen partyA promising future now looks perilous for election loser Zack Polanski. He sowed, now he reapsJohn HarrisThere was a real chance of a Green byelection win in Holborn and St Pancras. He made bad decisions and cost his party dearFri 9 Oct 2026 03.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.08 EDTShareAs ever, among all the noise triggered by Labourholding the seat of Holborn and St Pancras, the most plain-spokenand undeniable analysiswas provided by that sage and national treasure John Curtice, of Strathclyde University. The result, he said, echoed national opinion polls and reflected two undeniable facts: that the Greens are in need of a period of contrition and reflection, and Labour ought to be slightly less than ecstatic.Andy Burnham’s party, with a majority of 3,364, he said, showed they “are in a much better position than they were six months ago, but still not as popular as they were in 2025”. The Greens, meanwhile, remain “a more significant player than historically they have ever been”, but have lost much of the ground they gained during Zack Polanski’s first year as leader, when the serial failures of the local MP – one Keir Starmer – provided him and his party with such a glorious succession of political opportunities.Do not forget: the Greens’success earlier this year in Gorton and Dentonplayed a massive part in Starmer eventually leaving the political stage, and the man he barred from being the Labour candidate snatching his job. But now? Publicly, Polanski seems largely unrepentant aboutthe “Zionism is racism”motion passed at his party conference, and confident he can resume where he left off. But his party’s claim that it tripled its previous vote share in the seat is very specious indeed: as the pollster Peter Kellnerputs it, “the leftwing vote two years ago was divided between the Greens’ 10.4% and an independent, Andrew Feinstein’s, 18.9%. Together, they won 29.3%.” The true increase in the leftwing anti-Labour vote, therefore, is only 3.5 percentage points, and Polanski has thus taken such a significant blow that his experience of the next few weeks and months could be very choppy indeed.Over the last week, I spent two days in the constituency, filming another episode of the Guardian’sAnywhere But Westminster video series, and got a deep sense that our politics remains in a state of unpredictable flux. So many people and the conversations we had come to mind. The young people of colour in the pinched neighbourhood of Somers Town – the urban village right next to Euston station – who were all voting Green, and talked of Gaza and the impossibility of living in our capital. The woman in upmarket Primrose Hill who told us she no longer told people she was Jewish for fear of instant uproar and upbraiding about Israel, a country she had last visited 15 long years ago. But most of all, a 24-year-old trainee teacher called Tom, who reluctantly still lives with his parents, and has no idea how he is going to hold down a job in his home city. He had once been an enthusiastic Green member and activist, he told me, and had every intention of voting for them, untilthe Zionism motionsuggested a party perfectly happy to inflame the UK’s sense of division and polarisation. He decided to switch to Labour.The searing summer should have provided the Greens with another boost, and a real chance of another byelection win. But now? Polanski –who endorsed the ideathat Zionism is a form of racism eight days before his party’s conference began – looks not just morally questionable, but distinctly weak: one central bit of symbolism in this whole affair, let us not forget, was his absence from the Zionism debate and vote at his party conference.And so to a geographical jump to a few other parts of the country. As I may have written once or twice in the past, I live in Frome, in Somerset: a 25,000-population settlement whose affinity with the Greens has been deepening for the last decade or so. They provide four of the six councillors who represent the town on our new unitary council. The rurality and climate-fear in the villages that surround us chimes with Ellie Chowns’s seeminglyout-of-the-blue election two years agoas the Green MP for North Herefordshire andAdrian Ramsay’s successin the East Anglian seat of Waveney Valley. But there are also elements of the maverick, future-facing attitudes that waft down into our neck of the woods from Bristol Central, the seat held since 2024 byCarla Denyer, the former Green party co-leader. I think I know what was holding those two elements together, and partly powering the Greens’ resurgence: a mixture of radical, empathetic social democracy and urgency about the fate of the planet that also seems to have taken root in some of England’s suburbs.With the possible exception of Bristol, if you wanted to completely wreck the Greens’ successes in all those places, you would bin that approach and accelerate exactly what Polanski has facilitated: not just a politics of no-surrender and provocation, but the entry into the partyof embittered former Jeremy Corbyn supportersand assorted ultra-leftists, bringing with them a flimsy, pious gesture politics.The party’s former leaderCaroline Lucasand the longstandingGreen activist Rupert Readare about to publish a mini-manifesto titledClimate Popularism: a guide to “breaking the grip of rightwing populism through a new politics of crisis resilience”, to be formally launched on 15 October. Written before the antisemitism meltdown, it rather minces its words about Polanski’s project, but makes it pretty clear why things have now gone wrong. “Some observers have wondered whether this new eco-populism has at times been a little tooquietabout the ‘eco’ part,” Lucas and Read write. “On the doorstep, at least, this may be an understandable strategy … [But] as recent heatwaves have made abundantly clear, the salience of climate impacts will make adaptation concerns a doorstep issue before long.”Lucas and Read make the case for “centrally funded, locally appropriate action to adapt neighbourhoods, infrastructure and ways of life, to prepare for the broad, cascading impacts of human-triggered climate change”. They propose a domestic retrofit programme that would entail a lot of “secure green jobs”. They also write, very perceptively, about an “exhausted majority” tired of our shrill politics, and suggest the “depolarisation” of the climate issue in the face of plain facts – which sounds like the direct opposite of how Polanski operates. There is talk of a politics of “courage, hope, love of place” – and, crucially, a decisive turn into the use of citizens’ assemblies. This is the kind of turn the Greens should undoubtedly take – but even if they do, they will now be starting in a deeply troubled and weakened state.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham, meanwhile, still has no end of work to do. For what it’s worth, many of us have long believed that the substantial presence in British politics of a radical party free of Labour’s pussyfooting around the climate crisis and the harsh realities of inequality was an absolute necessity, and the Greens’ fitful growth was nothing but a good thing. Now, by contrast, as the fallout from Polanski’s sudden crash only deepens, they have a massive amount of self-questioning and reinvention to do. Whether they will even have the inclination is another question entirely.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsGreen partyOpinionHolborn and St Pancras byelectionZack PolanskiByelectionscommentShareReuse this content

title: Heathrow’s third runway is a bottomless money pit. Stop it now | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: It won’t promote growth, will take decades and will swallow up billions of taxpayers’ money, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: It won’t promote growth, will take decades and will swallow up billions of taxpayers’ money, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: ‘Heathrow and HS2 are plagued by extravagant planning horizons and consultancy-driven budgets in which each contractor has a vested interest in cost inflation.’Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Heathrow and HS2 are plagued by extravagant planning horizons and consultancy-driven budgets in which each contractor has a vested interest in cost inflation.’Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty ImagesOpinionHeathrow third runwayHeathrow’s third runway is a bottomless money pit. Stop it nowSimon JenkinsIt won’t promote growth, will take decades and will swallow up billions of taxpayers’ money. The only winner will be the airport’s ownersFri 9 Oct 2026 06.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 06.47 EDTShareInfrastructure sends politicians berserk. Propose more money for the health service or reopening youth clubs and frowns break out all round. Can we afford it? But shout infrastructure and cheers go up. The word suggests glamour, chest-beating and “growth”. Reason flies out of the window.The saga of Heathrow’sthird runwaybeggars belief. Aforeign-owned private companywants to make more money out of its cramped west London investment. The airlinesare scepticaland passengers will have to paysurcharges higherthan any in Europe. Meanwhile fields lie empty round its rival, Gatwick, and capacity atLondon’s third airport, Stansted, is underused.The third runway is a nightmare. The official price tag is now a staggering £49bn but the overall budget for Heathrow’s expansion and operating expenditure couldsoar beyond £100bn. An unknown proportion of this willfall on the taxpayer. Theproposal has been debated for 20 yearsand the opening constantly postponed. A date of 2035 has now become 2039. I would not take bets on 2045.Sixty years ago, the British government agreed it was totally inappropriate for crowded and polluted Heathrow to expand in densely populated westLondon. Nor could an expanded Gatwick meet demand. The debate was over where to locate a new third airport. Sites in the Thames estuary and at Cublington and Stansted were researched. Stansted won. It already had an RAF base and it would service the expected growth in demand from London’s growing eastern reaches. Stansted opened in 1991.The Tories privatised London’s airports. This turned what should have been a planned expansion into a battleground of feuding rivals. Each airport became a matter not of orderly growth but of quick profits, self-serving airline slots and a shifting army of amateur officials. Commissions came and went, in the grip of overpaid lobbyists. A Heathrow runway proposed by businessman Surinder Arora within the existing airport curtilage wasbrushed aside as insufficiently bold. As for Stansted, it was taken over by Manchester airport and is now hardly mentioned as an alternative to a third runway.Airport public relations endlessly suggests it is about “business” and therefore relevant to “growth”, as if it were part of Andy Burnham’s re-industrialisation of Britain. Heathrow claims its new runway willcreate 100,000 jobs. Butfewer than 15%of air travellers claim to be “on business”, and whatever happened tovideo conferencingreducing the need for intensive business air travel? As for Heathrow’s claim to be Britain’s leading cargo airport – “a quarter of all UK trade by value” – that is based, ludicrously, on thevalue of the gold ingotsthat form roughly 60% of the goods it transports. What banks shifting bullion has to do with growth is unclear.Heathrow now has eerie echoes of HS2. Even its upper cost limit of £100bn is much the same. Both are plagued by extravagant planning horizons and consultancy-driven budgets in which each contractor has a vested interest in cost inflation. A third similar project is Hinkley Point nuclear power station, its cost currently rising through £50bn. Both the railway and the power station have beensavaged by the National Audit Office. These projects are widely considered political white elephants and years from completion. Few dare say so. Meanwhile we should note that a new general hospital costs £1bn, aswould rebuilding 50 secondary schools.Stupefying sums are here being channelled into London and the south of England. That they have been born of the age of Boris Johnson’s “levelling up” and Burnham’s tilt to the north is bizarre. This week, conference politicians have cited budgets with endless savings: half a million off student exchanges here, a billion off quangos there. Yet no one mentioned thatevery yearfor the next decade John Healey’s Treasury willblow about £7bnjust to relieve overcrowding on trains from London to Birmingham. This is almost70% of his total rail investment.The fact is that big infrastructure is monumental and sexy. No one boasts about building a care home, rather a fancy train or a nuclear power plant. One ofParkinson’s lawsstates that, while tiny items of corporate spending are debated for hours, big ones go through on the nod. They are too big to check and easy to promote.It is absurd for the government to spend the next two decades upheaving Heathrow and tearing apart the M4 corridor for the profit of a band of foreign investors, when a simple alternative lies in growing Gatwick and Stansted. This whole debate is about tourism, and tourists can surely suffer the mild inconvenience of using the other two venues, as was intended half a century ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe rest of us – politicians not least – should realise that this is serious money. There are serious uses to which it should be put.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsHeathrow third runwayOpinionHeathrow airportAir transportInfrastructureTransportLondonAirline industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: You have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents. So what went wrong? | Devi Sridhar | The Guardian
description: Some change in our lifestyles and environments over a generation has caused this increased risk. What, exactly, is a mystery, says chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Devi Sridhar
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: Some change in our lifestyles and environments over a generation has caused this increased risk. What, exactly, is a mystery, says chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Devi Sridhar
Content: A patient undergoing a CT scan.Photograph: JohnnyGreig/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA patient undergoing a CT scan.Photograph: JohnnyGreig/Getty ImagesOpinionCancerYou have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents. So what went wrong?Devi SridharSome change in our lifestyles and environments over a generation has caused this increased risk. What, exactly, is a mysteryProf Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghFri 9 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTShareIn the field of global health, we often talk about each generation living longer and healthier lives than their parents. We’ve seen this in the gains in life expectancy, the sharp decrease in child mortality and in the near elimination of many vaccine-preventable diseases. But since the turn of the century this progress has stalled, and in some cases several health metrics have gone backwards.Take cancer, which was long thought to be a disease linked to old age. While most cancers do indeed still occur in elderly people, a new report highlights that a number of cancersare increasing in people who are under 50, often referred to as “early onset cancer”. The report, undertaken by the World Cancer Research Fund, looked at data from 12 different cancer types in England, the US and the Netherlands over the past 20 years. What they found isn’t pretty.While there were slight variations among the three countries, larger patterns are clear. Among women who are under 50 in England, breast, bowel, uterine, kidney, liver, pancreatic and stomach cancershave increased. For men under 50 in England, there were increases in bowel, kidney, liver, pancreatic and prostate cancers. This is the opposite of what we would hope to achieve in public health – and no, it isn’t only because we have better diagnostic tools, or are doing more testing. While this explains some of the increase, it doesn’t account for it all. The data indicates that younger generations are experiencing a higher incidence of some cancers than previous generations at the same age. Put more simply: you have a higher chance of cancer at a younger age than your parents.Scientists are now working to unpick what has changed between generations that might be driving this uptick, especially trying to find things people may have been exposed to during childhood or adolescence in the 1990s that they wouldn’t have been in the 1950s.Here are some potential explanations: what we eat has changed significantly over the past 50 years, with the rise in ultra-processed and fast foods as well as sugary drinks. We also are more sedentary as a population. These changes are linked to rising levels of excess weight and obesity. Body fat, especially around the vital organs and waist, is a risk factor for chronic inflammation, insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction, all of which are linked to higher cancer incidence. Globally, obesity rates havemore than doubledamong adults and quadrupled among adolescents since 1990. Data collected in 2024 found that about 66% of adults in England were eitheroverweight or living with obesity.Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research findsRead moreBut diet, physical activity and excess body weight doesn’t fully explain the rise of certain cancers – such as breast cancer – in young people. Studies have shown that for women before menopause, a higher BMI is, in fact,linked to a slightly lower risk of cancer(which is in contrast to older women, where a higher BMI significantly increases risk of developing breast cancer.) Going further, scientists are looking at the health impact of sustained exposure to environmental toxins like air and water pollution, chemicals and plastics that have become widespread and almost impossible to avoid over the past 50 years.It has been scientifically challenging to identify one toxin that explains the global increase in cancers.Cancercan develop long after exposure to a toxic chemical, and over our lives we encounter a range of chemicals and pollutants. Saying which one, or whether it was during childhood, in utero, or adulthood, is difficult to pin down.On the positive side, one area that we have made progress with in young people is lung cancer, largely driven by anti-smoking campaigns and widespread awareness of the links between smoking and lung cancer. So not everything is getting worse.None of the continuing research into risk factors for early onset cancer should mean attaching blame to patients. One of the first human impulses when getting a diagnosis is to think “what caused this?”, and even further, “what have I done?” – and this isn’t helpful. In addition, scientists estimate that only 40% of cancers at a population level are because of an “individually modifiable” behaviour like smoking, alcohol consumption, diet, physical activity, or weight. The other 60% is a mix of ageing, genetic susceptibility, infection, possible environmental factors, and sometimes just bad luck.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith the research and investment continuing into scientific research, we will eventually learn what’s driving the rise in cancer in younger people. But for now, that mystery is still to be uncovered.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghExplore more on these topicsCancerOpinionYoung peopleHealthObesityCancer researchMedical researchcommentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: Don’t worry about the plague, go and read some Anne Carson | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: The world may be going to hell in a handcart, but at least now I get to say I know a Nobel prize winner
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: The world may be going to hell in a handcart, but at least now I get to say I know a Nobel prize winner
Content: ‘I went hiking with the Nobel prize winner Anne Carson in Iceland last year … OK, it was a short walk up a rocky incline.’Photograph: TT News Agency/Alamy stock photo/Alamy live newsView image in fullscreen‘I went hiking with the Nobel prize winner Anne Carson in Iceland last year … OK, it was a short walk up a rocky incline.’Photograph: TT News Agency/Alamy stock photo/Alamy live newsDigested weekNobel prize in literatureDigested week: Don’t worry about the plague, go and read some Anne CarsonEmma BrockesThe world may be going to hell in a handcart, but at least now I get to say I know a Nobel prize winnerFri 9 Oct 2026 07.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.46 EDTShareMonday“Anyone worried about pneumonic plague?” This is a friend – a medic – texting me after reading reports at the weekend of the 28-year-old Russian woman whodied while working at a “plague research lab” in Siberia. Relying on details from the famously open Russian state guaranteed the presence of a certain dark subtext to the tantalisingly short news item. Namely: lab-grown disease cultivated for reasons unknown and with a 100% mortality rate escapes Russian facility into general population, eight hours’ flying time from London. In other words, we’re all going to die.My first thought was: is this better or worse than the time that guy who’d been exposed to Ebola took the subwayto go bowling in Brooklyn? The answer to which of course is that post-Covid, it’s worse: we know exactly how these things go, how they start small, with a news in brief buried 20 pages deep in the paper, moving glacially up the news list every few days until a lonely death in a Siberian laboratory leads, step by incremental step, to the zombie apocalypse.Meanwhile, the word “plague” remains outlandishly unrelaxing, despite the best efforts of the New York Times to contextualise it. Elucidating the various different types of plague that can kill you – pneumonic, septicemic and bubonic – I have to say my money would have been on bubonic as the worst, what with theBlack Deathand all. Apparently, however, the most virulent form of plague is the one in question, pneumonic, spread by a cough or a sneeze and causing “a severe rapid-onset lung infection” that can kill within a few days. Advice from my medic friend in New York: “Get antibiotics for everyone.” Alternatively, invest in a sense of proportion.TuesdayI did not have “let’s have more firing squads” on my bingo card of talking points this week, but that is the serious discussion under way in the US after the horrific,botched execution of Christa Pike, the convicted murderer on death row who regained consciousness and started talking on Tuesday after the state of Tennessee failed to kill her.This was the second botched execution by the state this year, and one of the apparently7%of all executions in the US since 1972 that have not been effective, among the most commonreasons citedbeing expired drugs and untrained executioners, but also malfunctioning electric chairs that set fire to their occupants.As a result, the single method of executing a prisoner in the US that has resulted in no failed attempts whatsoever is the firing squad, a phrase that raises images, incomprehensible in a supposedly modern world, of a semicircle of shooters, none bearing sole responsibility, firing in the direction of the condemned’s head. For the first time in the US military since 1945, one such execution is due to happen at Fort Hood, Texas, in December, which this week Pete Hegseth, the US defence secretary,promised to livestreamin defiance of anything resembling normal human behaviour.WednesdayAll hail the Kult of Kemi – captain, coach and owner of the Conservatives | John CraceRead moreThere’s likely a joke about the failure of the Tory party to lie down and accept its fate after so many lethal injections, but I can’t quite bring it home. Instead, at party conference this week in Birmingham, we saw a chipper-seemingKemi Badenoch step out on stageto perform her pantomime version of common sense, smartly referring to the Reform party as “that” – as in “we are not uniting with that”. The Tory leader does an extremely good job of appearing to be a plain-spoken and regular human in contrast with Reform, on the one hand, and what might delicately be called the unusual makeup of the Greens on the other.It’s worth remembering what Badenoch looks like when the mask slips. If Boris Johnson’s real face was the rictus of an underbriefed, overconfident man white-knuckling his way through government while chuckling to himself like a toy in a horror movie, Badenoch strikes me as someone who is stuck on the gimlet-eyed setting of victory at all costs. Meanwhile, footage of YoungConservativespartying at conference never gets old, offering a strong rival for most embarrassing moment to the 30,000-word policy document the Tory leader – hide your face – has self-christened “Kemistry”. Someone tell her you can’t coin your own nicknames.ThursdayAnne Carson has won the Nobel prize for literature and, forgive me, but very occasionally when life gives you the opportunity to be insufferable, you can’t not take it. So, in response to this news, I would like to say that when I went hiking with the Nobel prize winnerAnne Carsonin Iceland last year the thought struck me …There was no thought; I just wanted to get it on the table about the hike – OK, it was a short walk up a rocky incline – it was with the Nobel prize winner Anne Carson, who I have loved forever and have known since we met in Michigan many years ago. She is brilliant and funny and wise, and I could cite so many lines from her poetry but one of my favourites is this, from the poem Lines in her 2005 collection Decreation: “To my mother / love / of my life, I describe what I had for brunch.” I feel the same way about this line that Madonna used to say she felt about Frida Kahlo’s self-portrait, which is that if you don’t feel it vibrate through your system, I can’t ever really be your friend. (I’m aware most people would be fine with that.)FridaySublime to ridiculous, Carson to Elon Musk, who is the subject of Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary that launched this week and which I can’t wait to see. Pre-publicity has focused on the contributions to the film of Justine Wilson, Musk’s ex-wife, who along with MacKenzie Scott (formerly Bezos) is part of the tech titans’ first wives club via which one can measure the journey taken by very rich men from marriage to regular women to women with no apparent interior lives. “He was constantly remarking on the ways he found me lacking,” said Wilson, who alsotold Gibneyher ex-husband once said to her: “If you were my employee, I would fire you.” No amount of money in the world, am I right?Digested week in picturesView image in fullscreenThe Tories demonstrate how they can ruin ordinary pleasures like dogs and beer just as efficiently as Reform.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I write the songs that make the whole world cry, I write the … ’Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreen‘The key is only to make eye contact when it’s not being returned.’Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/AFP/Getty ImagesExplore more on these topicsNobel prize in literatureDigested weekAnne CarsonElon MuskInfectious diseasesConservative conferenceKemi BadenochConservative conference 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents | Gordon Brown | The Guardian
description: We have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policy, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Author: Gordon Brown
Headline: We have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policy, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Content: Andy Burnham and Mark Rutte inspecting a robotic dog at RAL Space, the UK's national space laboratory, at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus, Didcot, 16 September 2026.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA Pool/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Mark Rutte inspecting a robotic dog at RAL Space, the UK's national space laboratory, at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus, Didcot, 16 September 2026.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA Pool/APOpinionScienceBritish households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talentsGordon BrownWe have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policyGordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010Fri 9 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.53 EDTShareThe coming 10 years are almost certain to be the decade that sees the greatest scientific breakthroughs in a century. The question is whether advances now under way in AI, quantum computing and biology can address cancer, find ways to treat or prevent dementia, and overcome thegrowing resistanceto antibiotics. Can we find sustainable ways to address our energy needs and protect the environment at the same time? Can AI transform the way we deliver education, health and social care to the benefit of millions, as well as advance modern manufacturing strength? And what role can Britain’s inventors, investors and industrialists play in developing these transformative technologies?While the US and China are the world’s obvious innovation powerhouses, the UK also has enormous assets, as the Innovation Nation Conference in Manchester addressed by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will hear today. We are home tofour of the world’stop 10 universities and 16 of the top 100, five of which are in Europe’s top 10 for spin-outs, startups based on intellectual property produced through a university’s research. With less than 1% of the world’s population, theUK produces6% of the world’s research papers, nearly 9% of citations and 12% of the most highly cited research.Our research expertise is one of the many reasons we have been at the forefront of recent inventions:from AlphaFold, which predicts how proteins behave, to viral-vector vaccine technology and AI that detects cancer as reliably as radiologists. Britain already sits at the intersection of AI, quantum computing and synthetic biology. The question then is: why, having led the first Industrial Revolution, should the UK not be the world’s great innovation nation once again?We know the public have an entrepreneurial spirit, and back this vision. New polling for this week’s conference finds that75% of peopleagree that innovation is essential for creating UK economic growth.But it is disappointing thatonly 36%of the British publicbelieves the country is a world leader in science. It is time for innovation to move to the forefront of government policy and the10-year planthe government is preparing. If we were to raise Britain to Swedish or Japanese levels of innovation intensity we would, over time, leave every household £5,000 better off (according to my calculations), and increase our national income by £150bn a year as higher investment in research and development feeds through into productivity. And a jobs plan on the scale thatOur Scottish Futurehas proposed for Scotland would mean about 3m new jobs across the UK.We can identify the major hurdles to overcome. While the UK is good at startups and spin-outs, we are slow to turn startups into scale-ups, and even slower to turn scale-ups into global success stories. Per head of population, the US has double the number of $1bn companies and nearly three times as many $10bn-plus companies than the UK. And even when we do scale up at home, three-quarters of venture capital investment comes from overseas.Turning this around will require a government to keep tackling the bottlenecks that are inevitably created from innovation. Speakers from future-facing companies at today’s conference will set out the steps that we need to consider. These will range from making sure firms can access the money they need to grow from UK investors, to new incentives for investors, to public-private partnerships – as happens in Germany, France and Italy – capitalised by theBritish Business Bankand thenational wealth fund. Competition policy must favour new entrants against vested interests and be aligned with a favourable tax regime, such as through research and development credits that favour companies of all sizes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money | Chris Stokel-WalkerRead moreResearchfor the conferencehas identified 127 innovative clusters covering every region and nation of the UK, many of which will succeed if we are willing to give long-term support to the infrastructure, skills training and research and development support from UK Research and Innovationthey need to grow. In order to harness this potential, more power needs to be devolved to enable mayors and regional authorities to act locally while ensuring access to global markets.Britain does not lack genius or great assets. Every nation, including ours, must do more to find its “lost Einsteins” – the young people in lower-income areas who have the talent but not yet the opportunity to show their creative genius. What we need now is to create a chain of hope that connects all people to intellectual discovery and deployment, to startups and scale-ups, and to global leadership – all aligned around a shared national purpose.Sixty-four years ago, John F Kennedy declared that the US would lead a nationwide effort to be first on the moon. But the space initiative was not his first choice. He had wanted a national project that everybody could feel part of, and revealed he would have preferred to have chosen a project on Earth – if he could have found one with the same power to inspire a national mission that the whole population could enthusiastically embrace.Today, we can choose to be the innovation nation. “This generation does not intend to founder in the backwash of the coming age,” said Kennedy of the US. And this generation of Britons has no intention of being left behind as the age of AIaccelerates. Today’s event, spearheaded by the prime minister in Manchester – itself a city of innovation – will send a message that we mean to be in the global vanguard; not because, as Kennedy said, it is easy to do, but even though it is hard. For the challenge now is to do more than invent the future. We must invest in it, manufacture it and, wherever possible, own it here in Britain.Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010Explore more on these topicsScienceOpinionTechnology sectorTechnology policyUniversitiesAI (artificial intelligence)Medical researchcommentShareReuse this content

title: Execution TV? Pete Hegseth has taken the once ‘greatest democracy’ to a horrific new low | Paul Daley | The Guardian
description: A proposal to livestream the killing of Nidal Hasan by firing squad opens a window ever wider to the Trump administration’s complete moral vacuity
Author: Paul Daley
Headline: A proposal to livestream the killing of Nidal Hasan by firing squad opens a window ever wider to the Trump administration’s complete moral vacuity
Content: ‘The world has become inured to Donald Trump’s monstrous narcissism and maladministration,’ writes Paul DaleyPhotograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The world has become inured to Donald Trump’s monstrous narcissism and maladministration,’ writes Paul DaleyPhotograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionTrump administrationExecution TV? Pete Hegseth has taken the once ‘greatest democracy’ to a horrific new lowPaul DaleyA proposal to livestream the killing of Nidal Hasan by firing squad opens a window ever wider to the Trump administration’s complete moral vacuityThu 8 Oct 2026 21.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 01.43 EDTShareMore fool me! Here I was thinking nothing that America’sTrump administrationcould do or say, no matter how politically and morally bankrupt, no matter how venal or violent, was capable of shocking me any longer.Then I woke to today’s news that one of the Trump cabinet’s bigger boofheads – the uber Christian nationalist, crusader-fantasist and “secretary of war”Pete Hegsethhad announced that America wouldhave a public firing squad executionof murderer Nidal Hasan.Reckless global militarisation including athreat at the UN to annihilate Iran, a litany ofsexual misconduct allegationsagainst the commander in chief, claims of blatantpresidential corruption… they have all ceased to surprise and shock us, so inured has the world become to Donald Trump’s monstrous narcissism and maladministration.But now we have execution TV. Tune in to the livestream on Thursday 3 December to watch a military firing squad shoot the life out of Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at a US army base in 2009.Pentagon says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamedRead moreState-sanctioned killing as entertainment! Yes, the world’s supposedly greatest (or formerly greatest) democracy has arrived at an horrific new moral nadir.The fact that America remains Australia and the west’s most relied-upon and trusted ally despite the global wrecking ball the second Trump administration has proved to be, was already cause for deep concern.But being so closely allied to a country that now wants to turn the execution of a human being – no matter what their crimes – into a live entertainment event, promises to redefine depravity.Given that American statescontinue to execute so manyconvicted criminals, where might the United States ultimately draw the line? No doubt the ilk of Hegseth in American society – and elsewhere – will count down the days until they can tune in to the live coverage of Hasan’s execution in droves. Might the audience cry out for more – for livestream cameras in the death chambers across theland of the free?How would this populist administration respond? If you think it’s a fanciful question, consider how far American governance and presidential values have slid in the moral murk in the past two years alone.Meanwhile, it’s hard to contemplate a more audacious appeal to American society’s darker angels than this looming entertainment event.But there we are. We have arrived.Pass the popcorn, Don and Pete!It would be heartening today to hear political leaders the world over condemn Hegseth and Trump’s planned introduction of Ghoul TV.But let’s please start in Australia, where federal governments have for a long time opposed capital punishment – let alone turning it into a public spectacle. Will the prime minister and his senior ministers stand up and condemn without qualification this depraved plan for America to livestream an execution? What about the leaders of other political parties here,some of whomhave, after all, supported capital punishment?We’re waiting.Meanwhile, how much further into the moral quagmire must America wallow beforeAustralia rethinksits craven military dependence on Washington – not least via the reckless shackling of our strategic reliance to the US via the $368bn (and counting)Aukus submarine deal?Announcing America’s decision to turn killing into a form of entertainment, Hegseth said: “It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”America’s defense department later confirmed the execution would be livestreamed.This represents a significant lurch in the US from civilisation towards savagery.You can’t choose your family. But you can choose your friends and allies. And you can also tell them firmly when they’ve careened off the ethical rails.Actions speak louder than words.And this planned livestreamed execution says it all about what is happening in America today, opening the window ever wider on the Trump administration’s moral vacuity and its paucity of human decency.Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionPete HegsethUS politicsUS militaryCapital punishmentAustralian foreign policyDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Labour and the Greens: winning trust takes more than words | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A byelection win is a fillip for Andy Burnham and shows Zack Polanski must confront the failures damaging his party’s credibility and appeal
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A byelection win is a fillip for Andy Burnham and shows Zack Polanski must confront the failures damaging his party’s credibility and appeal
Content: ‘As Mr Polanski’s profile has grown, it seems the public have become less convinced by his political talents.’Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘As Mr Polanski’s profile has grown, it seems the public have become less convinced by his political talents.’Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersOpinionHolborn and St Pancras byelectionThe Guardian view on Labour and the Greens: winning trust takes more than wordsEditorialA byelection win is a fillip for Andy Burnham and shows Zack Polanski must confront the failures damaging his party’s credibility and appealFri 9 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTShareByholdingHolborn and St Pancras, Andy Burnham’s Labour has shown it can attract liberal and left-leaning voters. Theseathas substantial numbers of young adults, students, professionals and Muslims – offering fertile ground for the Greens’ ecopopulism. However, Labour prevailed. Having won leave-voting Makerfield in June, Mr Burnham can now claim an appeal that bridges Labour’s divided electorate. It’s worth noting that turnout in London was low and Labour’s vote share fell 3.7 points. But that compares with an average19.3-point fall in four byelectionsunder Mr Burnham’s predecessor. The new leader clearly has bought Labour breathing space and checked the Green advance.The Greens more than tripled their vote share in the constituency to 33%. But they were beaten. Labour’sSagal Abdi-Walitook 45% in Sir Keir Starmer’s former seat, leaving Zack Polanski’s ambition of entering parliament unfulfilled. For a party that began the year promising to turn voters’ hunger for change into a serious challenge to Labour, this was a sobering moment. The passing of amotiondeclaring “Zionism is racism” at its conference probably cost the party support – though the result in central London alone cannot definitively say that. There is a separate question of leadership. Mr Polanski nowsayshe would have voted against the motion. Why, then, did he not make his opposition clear when it mattered last weekend?Heintendsto remain leader – and the expanded, radical membership has given Mr Polanski a base in the party that likely insulates him from an instant coup. But withcalls for his resignationgrowing, he has to try to stay in the job while restoring confidence in the Greens’ electoral chances. Clouds had emerged on the horizon long before the party’s conference. Its spring polling surge has faded. In March,YouGovput the party second nationally to Reform, on 21%. Mr Burnham has since stolen much of the Greens’ rhetorical thunder by consciously evoking a more leftwing agenda. The party is now in fourth place, polling10% nationally.View image in fullscreenSagal Abdi-Wali.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesAs Mr Polanski’s profile has grown, it seems the public have become less convinced by his political talents. Since the beginning of the year his net favourability rating hasfallen from -6 to -29. The Greens are not to be discounted. Mr Burnham has yet to turn hope into lasting support. That will depend on what his government delivers, especially as prices rise, rather than whom it defeats.In aninterviewwith the BBC, Jonathan Bartley, the Greens’ former party co-leader, warned that the influx of members has changed the party and that some newcomers are unaware of its traditions of consensus and opposition to political “purity tests”. Significantly, Mr Polanski’s deputy, Rachel Millward, said that the party structures needed to become “fully democratic and strategic”. This may not be enough for the Green MP Siân Berry, whosaidshe wanted to “fix the serious flaws” in the controversial Zionism motion.Leadership is missing, and responsibility for that falls squarely on Mr Polanski. He has shown that he can communicate persuasively. Now, if he remains in post, he must show that he can acknowledge what went wrong and build support for changing thecontroversial Zionism policy. Mr Polanski claims credit for Labour’s leftward turn. But the Green leader now needs to put his own party’s house in order.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the 90s revival: the end of the analogue age | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The new exhibition at Tate Britain is part of a wider cultural resurgence from 30 years ago. This is nostalgia for a pre-digital era
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The new exhibition at Tate Britain is part of a wider cultural resurgence from 30 years ago. This is nostalgia for a pre-digital era
Content: ‘Kate Moss was the face of the era.’Photograph: Rose Hartman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Kate Moss was the face of the era.’Photograph: Rose Hartman/Getty ImagesOpinionCultureThe Guardian view on the 90s revival: the end of the analogue ageEditorialThe new exhibition at Tate Britain is part of a wider cultural resurgence from 30 years ago. This is nostalgia for a pre-digital eraFri 9 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTShareEach generation imagines itself to be cooler than the one that went before it, and weirder than the one that comes after it, toupdateGeorge Orwell. Gen X is no exception. “It felt like something was happening,” Pulp’s Jarvis Cocker writes in the catalogue forThe 90s: Art and Fashion, which opened at Tate Britain this week. “Something good. It felt like the weirdos were taking over.”The exhibition, curated by the former editor of British Vogue, Edward Enninful, is part of a wider 90s cultural revival. Oasis’s Wonderwall was the UK’sunofficial World Cup anthemthis summer, after last year’s selloutreunion tour. Pulp have also just completed a world tour. The 1993 novelTrainspottinghas become a musical; less surprisingly, so has 90s-set romanceOne Day, which found a new audience with 2024’sNetflix series.Love Story, which fictionalises the doomed relationship between John F Kennedy Jr and Carolyn Bessette, broke streaming records. Cult dramaThis Lifeis now on iPlayer. Vogue has described the era as “fashion’s most revisited decade”.And there’s more in the pipeline. The National Theatre’s 2027 season will include two new plays celebrating the“optimism” of the 1990s: James Graham’s dramatisation of John Major’s rise to No 10 and Moira Buffini’s imagining of the lead-up to the 1998 Good Friday agreement.View image in fullscreenThe Face magazine, January 1997.Photograph: TheFrontPage/AlamyThis sense of optimism is surely behind the resurgence. Between the fall of the Berlin Wall and of the twin towers in New York, democracy, economics and creativity thrived, at least for some. The Young British Artists and Britpop put the UK on the contemporary cultural map. The common people could become pop stars, fashion designers and prize-winning artists. Magazine photoshoots were elevated to art. Kate Moss was the face of the era. Daring, youthful and “real” – this was Cool Britannia. No wonder theNew Labour governmentwas quick to get in on the act after its 1997 victory.Nineties grunge is seen as a reaction against the excesses of the Thatcherite 80s. Yet, as last year’s exhibitions showcasingLeigh Bowery and The Face magazineshowed, a youth counter-culture had emerged. In the 90s it became mainstream.In hindsight Cool Britannia looks more than a little London-centric and elitist. And life wasn’t glossy for everyone. Racism, Aids and sexism form the backdrop to the Tate exhibition. Many of the images explore what it meant to be a young woman at a time when “girl power” was an empty slogan in the creative industries. One of the era’s greatest cultural legacies is that these female artists now command solo exhibitions, such as Tracey Emin’sblockbuster retrospectiveat Tate Modern this spring.This 30-year renaissance cannot just be put down to the“nostalgia pendulum”, whereby influential figures like Enninful are able to curate their own past. The 1990s was the last decade of the analogue age. This nostalgia speaks to a longing for a time without smartphones, social media, selfies and streaming. People watched TV, listened to music and danced together. It was a period of freedom, possibility and fun for young people. It’s not hard to see why it appeals to Gen Z. Like the magazines set up to capture the zeitgeist, that world has gone for ever. We don’t look back in anger, but in sorrow.Explore more on these topicsCultureOpinionJarvis CockerPulpOasisTrainspottingDavid NichollsJohn F Kennedy JreditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Zionism, racism and the Green party in turmoil | Green party | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to articles on the Green party’s motion
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to articles on the Green party’s motion
Content: The Green party conference in Brighton, 3 October 2026: ‘This decision is a shot in the foot, risking the alienation of British Jews and others who, like me, support peace and reconciliation.’Photograph: Sopa Images/LightRocket/GettyView image in fullscreenThe Green party conference in Brighton, 3 October 2026: ‘This decision is a shot in the foot, risking the alienation of British Jews and others who, like me, support peace and reconciliation.’Photograph: Sopa Images/LightRocket/GettyGreen partyLettersZionism, racism and the Green party in turmoilReaders respond to articles on the Green party’s motionFri 9 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.25 EDTShareAs ever, Jonathan Freedland is on the money in his article (The Green party’s anti-Zionism motion is yet another attempt to tell Jews how we should think, 3 October). As a non-religious Jew-ish Londoner, I am appalled at the passing of the motion to declare Zionism as a form of racism, and I am seriously considering leaving the Green party as a result.While I condemn the Israeli government’s actions against the Palestinian people, and I am not a Zionist myself, Zionism as defined by the motion is only one political interpretation and completely ignores ancient religious and cultural definitions held by many Jews who also condemn the current Israeli government.I have worked with Palestinians and Israelis on the West Bank and in Jerusalem in the cause of peace and reconciliation, and firmly believe in equal rights for everyone in Israel and the occupied territories. That cause will be set back by this decision, which will give fuel to antisemites who hide their racism under an anti-Zionist guise.This decision is a shot in the foot for theGreen party, risking the alienation of British Jews and others who, like me, support peace and reconciliation, believe in equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians, and strongly oppose the actions of the current Israeli government.Simon LawsonLondonJonathan Freedland is right that Zionism means different things to different people, and that Jewish historical attachment to Israel cannot simply be dismissed. But that complexity can also become a way of avoiding the more important question: what has Zionism produced in practice?“Fire is destructive” does not mean every use of fire is destructive. It means fire has destructive potential, which is why we recognise boundaries around its use. The same applies to Zionism. Jewish self-determination is not inherently racist; but when a political project pursued in its name produces permanent occupation, settlement, displacement, unequal rights and Palestinian subordination, it is legitimate to ask whether the project has crossed those boundaries. Therefore, “Zionism is racist” can be a true description of the manifestation of Zionism embodied in the current Israeli state.The issue, therefore, isn’t whether a benign definition of Zionism can be imagined. It plainly can. The issue is whether the political reality created in its name conforms to that definition. We should be able to examine Zionism as we examine any other political ideology: by its effects, its institutions, and the boundaries it recognises. Criticising a political ideology or the actions of a state is not the same thing as attacking Jews orJudaism.Raymond O’BrienLondonThose who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it. Green party success in the EU elections in 1989 saw a huge increase in membership and a wave of entryism. By 1991 it was fragmented and irrelevant. Zack Polanski’s election as leader of the Green party also saw a wave of entryism.It was never tenable to allow a gathering composed of those who can afford, or choose, to turn up to be the party’s policymaking body. But for many Greens it is an article of faith; proof of the party’s commitment to “democracy”. They were called “fundis” (fundamentalists) in my day. A group of us (“realos”) tried to change things in 1990 with a motion arguing that a “leadership” structure was necessary in a world where we were under the media microscope. The motion passed, but the party split.It is tragic to see a party that has pulled itself up by its bootstraps since the early 1990s, that has worked hard to win representation locally, and that has won seats in Westminster under a voting system that disadvantages newcomers, being stopped in its tracks by its lack of internal democracy.Here’s a suggestion from an oldie. Organise an internal referendum on the motion and let the whole membership decide. And put an end to the travesty of democracy that saw it adopted in the first place.Lyn DadeTwickenham, LondonAs a member of the Green party, I was dismayed by the profoundly counterproductive “Zionism is racism” motion passed at conference on Sunday. Since his election as leader and his success in broadening the party’s appeal, opponents of Zack Polanski and the Greens have repeatedly sought to portray the party as antisemitic. This motion hands them the ammunition they have been looking for.Until now, the Greens have stood out among UK political parties in their willingness to describe Israel as an apartheid state and to condemn its actions in Gaza as genocidal. That argument risks being obscured by an entirely avoidable debate over accusations of antisemitism.The motion is also historically and politically flawed. While the form of Zionism represented by the Israeli state today is exclusionary and discriminatory, it does not follow that all forms of Zionism are racist.Zionism emerged, in large part, as a response to the persecution of Jews in Europe. To erase that history from our understanding of Zionism is to overlook the reality of anti-Jewish racism that helped give rise to the movement.I hope the Green party leadership can find a way to distance itself from this damaging motion and refocus attention on holding the Israeli government accountable for its treatment of the Palestinians.Prof Benjamin SelwynUniversity of SussexHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Farewell, Marina Hyde. Thank you for brightening so many of our days  | The Guardian | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers gasp at the news that their beloved columnist is leaving the Guardian after 25 years
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers gasp at the news that their beloved columnist is leaving the Guardian after 25 years
Content: ‘It’s devastating news to know that I can no longer laugh, cry, squirm, gasp, disagree and love your columns.’Photograph: Jay Brooks/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It’s devastating news to know that I can no longer laugh, cry, squirm, gasp, disagree and love your columns.’Photograph: Jay Brooks/The GuardianThe GuardianLettersFarewell, Marina Hyde. Thank you for brightening so many of our daysReaders gasp at the news that their beloved columnist is leaving the Guardian after 25 yearsFri 9 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.17 EDTShareHow could you let this happen (It’s true: this is my final column. You have exactly 24 hours to complain before my inbox self-destructs, 2 October)? You have some truly great writers, and for them I will continue to support the Guardian, but it’s Marina Hyde’s column that many of us look forward to most. She is uniquely and reliably smart, funny and spot-on. Is it money? Like Nye Bevan with consultants, fill her mouth with gold if you have to; you can clean it up afterwards. But I fear I’m too late, and all that’s left to say is: Thank you, Marina, for brightening so many of our days, and for putting our thoughts so brilliantly into words. And thank you, Guardian, for giving her the space to do so.Richard O’BrienHighbridge, SomersetThe honour is all ours, Marina. It’s devastating news to know that I can no longer laugh, cry, squirm, gasp, disagree and love your columns. I have looked forward to reading your words for the last 25 years and you will be very much missed. Thank you, and go well.Gill EmpsonAston-on-Trent, DerbyshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: When Zeal and Lytchett’s eyes met across the village square | Rural affairs | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Adrian Chiles’s article on the sweet spot between quaint rural place names and nominative determinism
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Adrian Chiles’s article on the sweet spot between quaint rural place names and nominative determinism
Content: ‘Worth, a one-nation Tory and local vicar with a floppy fringe.’ The Square and Compass at Worth Matravers, Dorset.Photograph: Christopher Nicholson/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Worth, a one-nation Tory and local vicar with a floppy fringe.’ The Square and Compass at Worth Matravers, Dorset.Photograph: Christopher Nicholson/AlamyRural affairsLettersWhen Zeal and Lytchett’s eyes met across the village squareReaders respond to Adrian Chiles’s article on the sweet spot between quaint rural place names and nominative determinismFri 9 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.24 EDTShareHow could Adrian Chiles have overlooked Dorset, where quaint village-naming meets nominative determinism (From Bentley Pauncefoot to Yetts O’Muckhart, I’m obsessed with Britain’s weirdly named villages, 7 October)?The county is home to the three Matravers brothers: dark and cruel Langton, squandering the family fortune at the gambling tables; Worth, a one-nation Tory and local vicar with a floppy fringe; and youngest brother Lytchett, who was probably something of an afterthought for his parents and who launches social projects but never quite follows them through.Meanwhile, I can help Adrian out with Zeal Monachorum: she’s a young Quaker environmentalist who has recently moved to Dorset, having fallen in love with Lytchett Matravers, and will be the good woman he needs to redeem the family name by setting up a successful alternative community.Janet FraserTwickenham, LondonWhat a treat to read Adrian Chiles’s piece on weird place names. West Yorkshire has lots to offer the etymologically inclined, with time assigning different meanings to them. My favourite is the village of Slack, which naturally has Slack Bottom, Slack Top and Mid Slack, perhaps a practical indication of the human effort required to reach each location. In Australia’s southernmost state, Tasmania, there are villages named Nowhere Else and Paradise. The trouble there is that visitors remove the name signs as soon as the previously stolen ones are replaced.Madonna GrehanMelbourne, AustraliaMy wife and I thought we were alone in applying personas to obscure village names on our travels. One particular favourite of ours is Moreton Jeffries, whom we envisage as a somewhat pompous, blazer and cravat clad ex-major, as per the late David Niven’s character in Terence Rattigan’s Separate Tables. And don’t get us started on Acton Trussell!David and Anthea CollinsKidderminster, WorcestershireAdrian Chiles mentions some places named Green. I have also noticed that some apply to me. There is a Little Green (5ft 3in and shrinking), Broad Green (that happens with age) and Cross Green (when I stub my toe). The headlines in the paper often have my family responsible for many things at the moment, and the shortened version of my first name, where artificial intelligence is Al, for very many other problems.Alan GreenLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Elvis Costello is twice as honest as the average musician | Elvis Costello | The Guardian
description: Letter: His integrity is one reason I’ve stuck with him, says Nick Davey
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: His integrity is one reason I’ve stuck with him, says Nick Davey
Content: Elvis Costello in 1984.Photograph: Adam Beeson/AlamyView image in fullscreenElvis Costello in 1984.Photograph: Adam Beeson/AlamyElvis CostelloLettersElvis Costello is twice as honest as the average musicianHis integrity is one reason I’ve stuck with him, saysNick DaveyFri 9 Oct 2026 12.11 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTShareElvis Costello has been a role model since I was a bespectacled teen and he appeared on the music scene to provide some credibility for NHS glasses. I no longer keep the scrapbook, but did cut the clipping from the Guardian in 2022 when he nominatedhis Honest playlist. His integrity as an artist and a human being has been one reason I’ve stuck with him for 49 years. I was delighted, therefore, to see consistency in his picks for his second Honest playlist (4 October), with Georgie Fame as his alpha and Louis Armstrong’s Keepin’ Out of Mischief as his omega. He seems, however, to have forgotten about his teen party listening. And we’d better not ponder the reasons for his change in response to “The best song to have sex to”. Thanks for keeping my hero in the spotlight.Nick DaveyChesterfield, DerbyshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
