title: Two Latvians arrested at RAF base in Cambridgeshire released on bail  | UK news | The Guardian
description: Men found inside RAF Molesworth, used by US and Nato for intelligence, freed on strict conditions as police continue investigation
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Men found inside RAF Molesworth, used by US and Nato for intelligence, freed on strict conditions as police continue investigation
Content: RAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe.Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe.Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty ImagesUK newsTwo Latvians arrested at RAF base in Cambridgeshire released on bailMen found inside RAF Molesworth, used by US and Nato for intelligence, freed on strict conditions as police continue investigationPriya BharadiaandDan SabbaghFri 9 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo Latvian men have been released on bail after being arrested at an RAF base in Cambridgeshire used by the US military and Nato.The two men, aged 32 and 26, were arrested at 2am on Thursday after they were discovered inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, which is used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations.An investigation had begun four hours earlier, when military police found an abandoned vehicle near the facility at around 10pm on Wednesday.Military police, joined by officers from Cambridgeshire police, discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence, before finding and arresting the two men inside the base.The suspects, both Latvian nationals currently resident in the UK, were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and causing criminal damage. They were then further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023, namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.They have since been released on bail, with strict conditions, as the police continue their investigation.Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said they were “very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites”, but that there was nothing from their investigation so far to suggest a connection to an incident near RAF Fairford in September.“Our investigation continues and we are working closely with colleagues from the Ministry of Defence police and Cambridgeshire constabulary on this. A key line of inquiry remains to identify any potential motivation behind why the men were at that location, and this includes whether it may be connected to any criminal activity,” she added.Officers have since carried out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation. The abandoned vehicle was also taken to a nearby police location.Located west of Huntingdon, RAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Abolish ICE’: Mamdani, AOC and other Democrats urge action after New York shooting | New York | The Guardian
description: Immigration officer shot man in car where five-year-old child was sitting, sparking fierce protests
Author: Auzzy Byrdsell
Headline: Immigration officer shot man in car where five-year-old child was sitting, sparking fierce protests
Content: A demonstration at NewYork-Presbyterian Allen hospital in New York on Thursday.Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersView image in fullscreenA demonstration at NewYork-Presbyterian Allen hospital in New York on Thursday.Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersNew York‘Abolish ICE’: Mamdani, AOC and other Democrats urge action after New York shootingImmigration officer shot man in car where five-year-old child was sitting, sparking fierce protestsAuzzy ByrdsellandJosé Olivaresin New YorkFri 9 Oct 2026 16.51 EDTFirst published on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeading New York Democrats expressed anger and demanded curbs on Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) violence after a federal officer shot a man driving a car in which his five-year-old son was sitting, sparkingfierce protests.At least seven shots were reportedly fired and the man was hit in the neck late on Thursday afternoon as children were coming home from school in the busy Marble Hill neighborhood ofNew YorkCity. Marble Hill is considered part of Manhattan, but is physically located in the Bronx.Federal authorities on Friday morning identified Oscar Belgal as the man shot, saying he was undocumented, from the Dominican Republic and had a felony record and gang affiliations.ICE agent shoots man in New York City with five-year-old reportedly in carRead moreBelgal was later booked into the Metropolitan Detention Center, Brooklyn, federal lockup, which is newly being used to detain immigrants, according to his attorneys and a US prosecutor who spoke during a hearing on Friday afternoon.He still has a “bullet in his body” and has not been able to communicate with his family, his attorneys said during the hearing.ICE took Belgal on Thursday from a New York hospital into New Jersey. He reportedly spent the night inside the Elizabeth Contract Detention Facility, a privately run ICE facility, before being brought back into New York and being booked into MDC Brooklyn.Meanwhile, Belgal was able to have only one phone call with lawyers on Friday, his attorney Paige Austin with Make the Road New York said.A New York federal judge on early Friday morning ordered ICE to keep Belgal in the area, after his attorneys filed emergency motions requesting his release.The justice department is likely to argue that Belgal’s transfer into New Jersey took place before the judge’s order, making the order requiring ICE to keep him in the area moot. And Belgal’s attorneys have indicated that they will continue challenging his detention.The Justice Department will likely argue that Bergal’s transfer into New Jersey took place before the New York judge’s order, which would make the judge’s order requiring ICE to keep him in the area moot. Bergal’s attorneys will continue to challenge his detention.Marcos Charles, a senior ‌ICE official, said Belgal refused ​to exit his car when approached by ‌federal officers who were trying to arrest him, and then accelerated, ‌struck two ICE vehicles and drove towards other officers. An ICE officer then shot Belgal and Charles said the wound was “superficial”.Footage showed a man in a high-visibility construction vest, possibly with a badge on a lanyard, carrying an assault-style rifle and standing close to Belgal, who is sat on the street, while another officer appears to hold a hand to his neck and shoulder area.New York police officers in uniform shortly afterwards carry the man to an unmarked car and lay him in the back seat, handcuffed behind his back.But Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York congresswoman, andZohran Mamdani, the city’s mayor – all of whom are Democrats – led strong condemnation of ICE’s conduct.Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic New York candidate, rushed to the protests and was knocked over in the chaos as local police and demonstrators clashed.View image in fullscreenDarializa Avila Chevalier at a protest after an ICE officer shot a man in New York, on Thursday.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAThe wounded man was conscious and hospitalized,authorities said.A joint statement from Bronx and Manhattan borough presidents Vanessa L Gibson and Brad Hoylman-Sigal, respectively, said their constituents “stand united in outrage” over Belgal’s shooting.“The frustration, pain, anger and trauma stoked by this incident extends far beyond an individual,” the statement said.Mamdani called the incident “unconscionable” and said on Thursday night that ICE,part ofthe Department of Homeland Security (DHS), had “whisked him away” from the New York-Presbyterian Allen hospital in upper Manhattan.Asimilar incident occurredin Texas last month after a man was shot by an ICE officer in Austin and despite abullet lodgedin his back was taken by the federal authorities from a local hospital to ICE detention about 140 miles away.Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani demanded ICE be abolished.Both Hochul and Mamdani spoke to Donald Trump and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, by phone on Thursday night.Gone in 90 seconds: an ‘invisibilized’ ICE is arresting more people than everRead more“I have been on ​the phone with President Trump and Secretary Mullin negotiating ‌the release of the man ICE agents ‌shot. Those negotiations were unsuccessful,” Mamdani told a press conference. He demanded from the Trump ‌administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City. “ICE is rotten to its core,” he said.ICE has beenstepping uparrests all year despite withdrawing massed militarized ranks from Minneapolis in January andadoptinga more covert approach toenforcement.Both Hochul and Mamdani demanded that ICE cease enforcement operations in New York and the governor said she expressed outrage to the Trump administration on behalf of all New Yorkers.Hochul added that the incident could easily have ended in tragedy.“No child should ever have to experience the terror of gunfire,” she said. The child was being looked after by his family on Friday.1:58ICE officer shoots man in New York City – videoThe streets where the shooting and protests took place were calm on Friday morning but many residents remained shocked and angry.“Here’s an innocent child that was caught in the crossfire,” said Calvin Hayden, a south Bronx native. “That child could have been killed.” Hayden heard about the shooting the night before and said he was immediately disturbed. He came to Marble Hill, the northernmost part of Manhattan, to see the aftermath.“I don’t believe ICE has any reason or right to be in New York City,” he said, adding he thought New York was already equipped on its own to handle immigration disputes without ICE presence.“There’s a lot of individuals who are not committing crimes and they just want to make a better life for themselves,” he said.Some drivers on 225th Street yelled anti-ICE sentiments as they drove past the scene.View image in fullscreenA vehicle with a bullet hole and a shattered window at the scene of the shooting.Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersMullin said on Friday morning that the ICE officers involved in the shooting did not know there was a child in the vehicle and defended the agency’s actions. But he pointed out that Belgal would have obviously known the child was in his car when he drove it at officers. The exact sequence of events leading up to the shooting have not yet become clear.Mullin said that Hochul had asked the DHS for a pause on enforcement in New York.“No, we are not putting a pause on enforcement,” he said.Mullin criticized New York’s“sanctuary” policies, ​which restrict how much city agencies and police cooperate with immigration authoritie.Belgal, 28, has prior convictions, was serving five years of probation for felony grand larceny and was also arrested on drug charges in 2025, a case that is still pending, according to the New York police department.“What happened today was an outrage,” Mamdani said late on Thursday, adding: “When ICE agents opened fire, a five-year-old child – a five-year-old child! – was in the back seat of that car. Thank God that child is physically unharmed.”Witnesses told local media they heard the child yelling at the officers after the shooting. At least 20 people havebeen shotby federal immigration agents under the second Trump administration, as well as a rise in deaths in detention.Three deaths, three states, 24 hours: one day in ICE’s quiet but ‘gruesome’ surgeRead more“ICE is a rogue, lawless and paramilitary surveillance agency. It does not belong in New York City and it should not exist in the United States of America. Abolish ICE,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement.The representative also condemned the retail company Target for allowing federal enforcement teams to use its parking lots as staging areas from which to launch arrest operations.Protesters held signs saying:“Jail all killer ICE agents” and “Leave our neighbors alone.”View image in fullscreenDemonstrators protest near the scene of the shooting.Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters“ICE, get the fuck out of our neighborhood,” shouted Gibson, the Bronx borough president. “I’m angry that we have to be here … We are a working-class community. We don’t deserve this type of treatment from the White House.” She encouraged the crowd to get involved in opposing ICE, saying: “There are more of us than there are of them. I want this to be a moment that we turn into a movement.”Protesters gathered at the hospital where Belgal was taken. The police set up barricades and protesters quickly clashed with officers in a chaotic scene.Demonstrators banged drums and shouted: “Shut it down,” and “ICE out!” as cars driving by honked in support.Standing outside the hospital, Murad Awawdeh, the president of the New York Immigration Coalition, said he wanted to see an independent investigation into the shooting led by New York officials.“The pain that you’re witnessing is people who are witnessing their neighbors, their family members, their friends being ripped away,” he said.ICE has arrested more than 19,500 people in New York and nearly 18,000 in New Jersey during the second Trump administration, mostly Latin American immigrant men without criminal histories,Gothamist reportedearlier this week using government data, adding that those totals were more than double the number of such arrests in the last 18 months of the Biden administration.Lex McMenamin and Joanna Walters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsNew YorkICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Zohran MamdaniUS immigrationProtest (US)US policingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Headteachers threaten strike ballots after losing confidence in Ofsted | Ofsted | The Guardian
description: Unions tell government to fix ‘overbearing mess’ of inspection regime and its impact on staff wellbeing – or risk industrial action
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Unions tell government to fix ‘overbearing mess’ of inspection regime and its impact on staff wellbeing – or risk industrial action
Content: An Ofsted spokesperson said it would ‘keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve’.Photograph: Russell Hart/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn Ofsted spokesperson said it would ‘keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve’.Photograph: Russell Hart/AlamyOfstedHeadteachers threaten strike ballots after losing confidence in OfstedUnions tell government to fix ‘overbearing mess’ of inspection regime and its impact on staff wellbeing – or risk industrial actionRichard AdamsEducation editorFri 9 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTensions between England’s headteachers and Ofsted are developing into a crisis after school leadership unions said they had no confidence in the watchdog and would hold strike ballots unless “significant wellbeing issues” caused by Ofsted’s inspections regime were fixed.The Association of School and College Leaders​ (ASCL), which includes senior leaders in many secondary schools, described Ofsted’s inspection system as “an overbearing mess” and urged the government to pause inspections to stop teachers leaving the profession.A spokesperson for ASCL said that “if change is not forthcoming” the union would seek to hold an indicative ballot on industrial action.New Ofsted inspection regime damaging teachers, survey saysRead moreThe National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said it would also consider steps including strike action at a meeting of its leadership next week.The combative moves come after a survey published by Ofsted showed 88% of schools reported that recent inspections had negatively affected staff wellbeing.The Guardianreported last weekthat Lucy Powell, the education secretary, wants Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” and overhaul the framework introduced last year. The new framework was intended to lower the strain and workload caused by inspections, but many heads say the opposite has happened.In response to ASCL’s announcement, a spokesperson for theDepartment for Educationsaid: “Inspection and accountability are vital, but they must reflect the reality of what is happening in schools, recognise the context they are working in, and support improvement rather than add to the pressures they already face.“That’s why we are working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better, so every child gets the education they deserve.”An Ofsted spokesperson said: “We have worked hard to reduce the pressure of inspection in recent years, but we know workload and wellbeing remain a challenge.“We are working with the Department for Education on this and we will keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve what we do.”​Hostility ​towards Ofsted has been heightened since the death of Ruth Perry, a popular headteacher in Reading. In 2023 a coroner found that anOfsted inspection contributedto Perry’s mental health deterioration and her death. Labour pledged to reform school inspections in its 2024 election manifesto.But ASCL said it had “seen no meaningful progress on the part of Ofsted to address significant wellbeing issues caused by inspections, and that it is increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale of members”.England school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaintsRead moreThe motion of no confidence in Ofsted passed by ASCL’s executive stated: “We fear that the disproportionate stress and anxiety exerted by the inspection system will lead to school leaders deciding to leave their posts with a consequent impact on schools, children and young people.”Pepe Di’​Iasio, ​ASCL’s general ​secretary, said: “​Our repeated attempts to resolve our concerns through discussion and negotiation have hit a brick wall … The current system is not fit for purpose. It is an overbearing mess and urgently needs to be reviewed.”Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the NAHT, said: “Our deep concerns about this Ofsted framework and the impact it is having on professionals are longstanding. Our executive committee will be meeting at the end of next week and debating the next steps NAHT will take. We fully expect that debate to include the option of pursuing industrial action.”Explore more on these topicsOfstedSchoolsTrade unionsDepartment for EducationTeachers' workloadEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: NHS faces exodus of ADHD and autism services staff to private clinics | NHS | The Guardian
description: Brain drain of psychologists, psychiatrists and nurses leaves NHS ‘weaker’, driving patients to seek care elsewhere
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Brain drain of psychologists, psychiatrists and nurses leaves NHS ‘weaker’, driving patients to seek care elsewhere
Content: Unite members protest against public funding waste and employment shortfalls in the NHS in Manchester.Photograph: Gary Roberts Photography/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenUnite members protest against public funding waste and employment shortfalls in the NHS in Manchester.Photograph: Gary Roberts Photography/ShutterstockNHSNHS faces exodus of ADHD and autism services staff to private clinicsBrain drain of psychologists, psychiatrists and nurses leaves NHS ‘weaker’, driving patients to seek care elsewhereFull report |NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry findsDenis CampbellHealth policy editorFri 9 Oct 2026 13.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 16.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNHSis facing an exodus of staff quitting its ADHD and autism services to join private clinics amid huge demand from children and adults to get a diagnosis.The loss of specialist personnel to the private sector has already forced one NHS trust in Englandto limit accessto its neurodevelopmental service to only the most urgent cases.The brain drain of psychologists, psychiatrists, nurses and other staff are leaving the NHS “weaker” and making it more likely that people will be forced to seek private healthcare.The NHS care watchdog announced on Friday it will start inspecting private clinics that offer diagnostic assessments for ADHD and autism, which are unregulated. The Care Quality Commission’s move follows thepublication of the government-commissioned reviewof mental health and neurodiversity urging ministers to ensure all service providers are properly regulated amid claims of a “wild west” of private firms offering diagnostic tests.No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are realRead moreScores of private clinics have been set up in recent years offering assessments and treatment for ADHD and autism. They have capitalised on the large number of people who have been unable to access NHS care because services have been overwhelmed by an explosion in demand for diagnoses of neurodiversity, creating long waits for help and large backlogs.Adrian James, the CQC’s interim inspector of mental health care, said: “This new responsibility will … close a significant gap in our oversight, meaning that people receiving these diagnoses can have far greater confidence in the service they are receiving.”Prof Peter Fonagy’s report – thought to be the biggest inquiry of its kind in the world to date – voiced concern that private firms face the temptation of “financial incentives” to wrongly diagnose and treat patients whose symptoms mean they should not qualify for either.The CQC already regulates services offering diagnosis and treatment. But the change means non-NHS clinics offering only diagnostic assessments will in future have to register with them.Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said the tighter regulation means “people can be confident that assessments are high quality and that the NHS is not being overcharged by independent or private providers”. About 810,000 children and adults inEnglandare waiting for an assessment for ADHD or autism.The risks to the NHS of losing staff to the private sector was highlighted last week when the Health Service Journalrevealedthat the Herefordshire and Worcestershire health and care NHS trust had been forced to restrict children and young people’s access to its neurodevelopmental service for that reason.A paper presented to the trust’s board reported: “Neurodevelopmental staffing is reduced significantly, with the majority of leavers choosing to take up employment with ISP [independent sector providers] and RtC [Right to Choose] providers for ND [neurodiversity].”Right to Choose gives NHS patients the right to have an NHS-funded ADHD or autism assessment with a private provider to help them receive care more quickly.The trust responded to the exodus last month by limiting access by under-18s to only those with the most serious symptoms. It will revert to a normal service on Monday. A total of 1,298 people have already waited at least two years for an ADHD or autism assessment with the trust.Thea Stein, the chief executive of the Nuffield Trust and a member of the government’s ADHD taskforce, said NHS services suffered when staff joined private operators, as also happens in physiotherapy and child and adolescent mental health services.She said: “Some staff stay with the NHS part-time when they get a private-sector job, but many will walk away entirely, leaving the health service in a weaker position and under greater pressure.“Concerning inequalities will widen further if the NHS can’t keep fully staffed teams or expand them to meet increasing demand for ADHD support. If these services continue to haemorrhage staff, some people will get much quicker support if they can afford to pay for private care,” Stein added.The NHS Alliance, which represents trusts, confirmed the continuing exodus of staff. “We’re increasingly dealing with one ADHD workforce spread across different providers, both in the NHS and private sector,” Rebecca Gray, the director of the alliance’s mental health network, said.“The significant growth in the private sector market, where people accessing services can often be seen more quickly than in stretched NHS services, will make working in the independent sector attractive to some staff.”The Independent Healthcare Providers Network (IHPN), a trade body that represents many non-NHS firms, welcomed the CQC’s enhanced new role.Sean Phillips, the IHPN’s head of policy, said: “While all of IHPN members who deliver ADHD and autism assessments are CQC registered – with 83% rated good or outstanding – we have long called for greater ‘end-to-end’ oversight of neurodevelopmental provision and it’s welcome to see that the CQC haveconfirmedthey will now be regulating all providers of ADHD and autism assessments.”Explore more on these topicsNHSAutismPrivate healthcareHealthAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderNeurodiversityMental healthShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: the ‘black box’ wastewater trade that rakes in millions for UK utility companies | Water | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Firms made more than £340m last year from processing industrial and commercial wastewater at sewage works that are unable to remove many chemical pollutants
Author: Rachel Salvidge
Headline: Exclusive: Firms made more than £340m last year from processing industrial and commercial wastewater at sewage works that are unable to remove many chemical pollutants
Content: A sewage treatment works operated by Thames Water in Isleworth, west London.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenA sewage treatment works operated by Thames Water in Isleworth, west London.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAWaterRevealed: the ‘black box’ wastewater trade that rakes in millions for UK utility companiesExclusive:Firms made more than £340m last year from processing industrial and commercial wastewater at sewage works that are unable to remove many chemical pollutantsRachel SalvidgeFri 9 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWater companies in the UK made more than £340m in revenue last year by pouring billions of litres of industrial and commercial wastewater into sewage treatment works that experts say are not designed to remove most chemicals, leaving pollutants to pass into rivers, seas and farmland.Water companies in England are required by law to take industrial wastewater and issue permits called “trade-effluent consents” that allow businesses to send it to sewage works, though water companies can refuse applications.However, no independent regulator oversees the trade-effluent process and there is no central register, so Watershed Investigations, the Guardian and the campaign group River Action compiled a database of 26,000 consents, providing the first ever national picture of the system.The investigation found an annual total of up to 608bn litres of industrial wastewater entering sewage works from sites such as power stations, pharmaceutical plants, food factories, hospitals, abattoirs and waste facilities.The permits are issued and enforced by the water companies themselves, with environmental regulators having no direct role. “It’s a bit of a black box,” one industry expert said.Most sewage works only have biological treatment facilities, which are not designed to remove industrial chemicals, including flame retardants,Pfas, solvents and pharmaceuticals. Some permits on the database feature chemicals such as cyanide, chromium, cadmium and mercury. Watershed hasmapped every sewage treatment worksand the industrial companies permitted to send waste to each one.Pollutants that survive treatment are discharged into rivers, lakes and seas as “treated effluent”, while those captured in sewage sludge are spread on farmland as fertiliser. The waste also adds to the overloading of sewer networks that triggersraw sewage spills, which have caused outrage, community protests and calls for the industry to be nationalised so that profits can be reinvested in improving the system rather than going to shareholders.United Utilities made the most revenue from industrial waste last year, at £61.6m, followed by Yorkshire Water at £48.8m. However, these companies included revenues from tankered waste in their figures, while some others did not. Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water, Scottish Water and Wessex Water said they routed commercial tankered waste through separate companies within their groups.Chart showing UK water companies’ earnings through ‘trade-effluent consents’ by financial year from 2020-21 to 2025-26Thames Water has the largest volume of permitted industrial sewage, at 113bn litres, followed by United Utilities at 105bn litres and Severn Trent Water at 79bn litres.Chart showing amount of industrial and commercial sewage taken in by UK water companies each yearAcross the sector, revenues from receiving industrial and commercial wastewater have risen sharply in five years, with Anglian Water’s increasing by 62%.The industry expert said water companies had “a financial incentive to accept far more toxic material than they should”.The permit regime was very old and not fit for purpose, they added. “Currently theEnvironment Agencydoesn’t know exactly how much of this waste is going into waterworks each year.”Waste handlers also drive tankers carrying industrial effluents, landfill leachate and other liquid wastes to sewage works. An Environment Agency (EA) officer said landfill leachate was its “greatest concern” because of the harmful chemical cocktail it can contain.Both the officer and the industry expert identified Davyhulme wastewater treatment works in Manchester, operated by UnitedUtilities, and Avonmouth, operated by Wessex Water, as big receivers of tankered waste. “Carriers will drive [long distances] to dispose of their wastes here … You can see lines of tankers queueing outside Avonmouth,” the expert said.Checks by water companies across the sector can just involve taking a sample and carrying out basic pH and metals analysis, but even more advanced testing does not always pick up a wide range of potentially harmful substances, “and by the time you’ve identified [that] it had something nasty in it, it’s already gone”, the EA officer added.But “ignorance is no defence”, said the officer. “They should be seeking sufficient information from the producer of that waste to satisfy themselves so they can treat it properly.”The industry expert said the UK needed a dedicated liquid-waste treatment sector rather than relying on a “dilute and disperse” model.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRevealed: how companies ‘secretly’ use billions of litres of public water in drought-hit EnglandRead moreAmy Fairman, the head of campaigns at River Action, said: “Industrial pollution must not become a lucrative business for water companies … Polluters must be held to account and made to pay, rather than passing the costs and consequences down the line.“The public has a right to know what is being put into our sewage works and where those pollutants ultimately end up. The government has promised to clean up [England’s] rivers through the clean water bill – it must confront this hidden industrial wastewater trade and address the serious failures exposed by this investigation.”“Water companies should never profit from pollution,” said a spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. “We know the water industry hasn’t been working in the public interest for far too long and that’s why we are reforming it, including how wastewater is disposed of.”An EA spokesperson said the trade-effluent framework was “developed over 30 years ago”, before many of today’s concerns aboutPfaswere fully understood, and that it was working to improve how contaminants in wastewater were managed.View image in fullscreenWater flows from an outlet pipe into the Mersey, near the United Utilities wastewater treatment plant in Stretford, Greater Manchester.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersA spokesperson for the trade association Water UK said: “Water companies [in England] are legally obliged to accept trade effluent and charges are set by Ofwat. The Environment Agency sets the permit conditions, but they make no account of the fact that sewers are not designed to treat a range of toxic substances such as forever chemicals and mercury, which is still, sadly, used by many dentists.“That’s why we have long called for the government to ban these toxic substances and to force the manufacturers to pay the costs of removing them from the environment.”A United Utilities spokesperson said it had “strict consent and control processes” operating under “regulatory requirements designed to protect public health and the environment” and that it “assesses, monitors and treats wastewater”. It added that tankered waste, including landfill leachate, was accepted only at specifically permitted sites.NI Water said applications involving “priority substances” were referred to the Northern Ireland Environment Agency, and dedicated teams sampled sewer and tanker effluent to “oversee compliance”.Scottish Water said it assessed trade-effluent applications based on factors including sewer and treatment capacity, protection of infrastructure and staff, and compliance with environmental standards. All water companies included in this article were contacted for comment.Companies can also discharge industrial wastewater directly into rivers and seas, but this is subject to permits issued by the environmental regulators.In England, water companies are regulated by Ofwat and the Environment Agency, with policy set by Defra. Ofwat also covers Wales, but environmental regulation sits with Natural Resources Wales and policy with the Welsh government. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own regulators and publicly owned water companies, with policy set by their devolved governments.This article was amended on 9 October 2026 to add context on the policy and regulatory framework within the devolved administrations of the UK; to note that the cited figure of 608bn litres of trade effluent is a maximum annual total based on applied consents; and to clarify a reference to harmful substances that can be missed by most routine water analysis.Explore more on these topicsWaterUtilitiesPfasPollutionUnited UtilitiesSevern TrentThames WaternewsShareReuse this content

title: Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence | Cop31 | The Guardian
description: ‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in Fiji
Author: Adam Morton
Headline: ‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in Fiji
Content: The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, speaks with Turkey’s climate change minister, Murat Kurum, at the pre-Cop31 summit in Fiji.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, speaks with Turkey’s climate change minister, Murat Kurum, at the pre-Cop31 summit in Fiji.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesCop31Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in FijiAdam Mortonin Nadi, FijiFri 9 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 08.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said.But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet inTurkeynext month.Kurum, the Turkish climate change minister, told the Guardian the world was “already in a transition” and suggested fossil fuel use could be addressed indirectly through other steps.Kurum was among national leaders and ministers, officials and civil society members in Fiji this week to prepare for Cop31, which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya in November. Australia, which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31, had pushed to hold the pre-Cop meetingin the Pacificto bring attention to island nations.View image in fullscreenFijian dancers perform at the summit’s welcome ceremony.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesGeopolitical turmoil from war, a historic energy crisis and an unpredictable and climate-denying US administration – combined with the knowledge that many would be attending the main climate summit in a few weeks – meant only 13 national leaders joined Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the Fijian city of Nadi, and most were from the Pacific.But there were also about 30 ministers, including from India and European nations, representatives from the big emitters China and Saudi Arabia, the heads of global agencies and about 4,000 other attenders.On Tuesday, a delegation flew north to seeTuvalu, a low-lying atoll country of about 10,000 people that is among the most at risk from the climate crisis. They were shown a 20-hectare (49-acre) land reclamation project and heard stories of life in a country that is mostly only about 2 metres above sea level, and where rising waters, storm surges and intensifying extreme weather pose an accelerating threat to survival.In a powerful speech, Melelusi Sokotia, 13, told the visitors her friends’ dreams to be “teachers, doctors, builders” were being subsumed by the question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.Back in Nadi, Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, was moved to tears and received a standing ovation during her closing address. She urged delegates to “remember the people you met” and “carry something of the Pacific with you”.Tabuya said: “This pre-Cop draws to a close tonight. Our responsibility does not.”View image in fullscreenFiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya (centre), receives applause during the summit’s closing session on Thursday.Photograph: Pacific pre-Cop31/AFP/Getty ImagesThe governments of about 190 countries will head to Antalya with clear evidence that responsibility is not being met. A recent report by the UN environment programme warned that under the most optimistic future, global heating wouldreach at least 1.8C, well beyond the 1.5C ceiling of the Paris climate agreement. It called for immediate and sustained emissions cuts and said every fraction of a degree of heating avoided would save lives and reduce economic losses.Throughout the pre-Cop, Pacific leaders repeated their demands: that countries must act to “keep 1.5C alive”, that climate finance must be easily accessible for poor and vulnerable communities who have not caused the problem but are most at risk, and that the health of oceans must be prioritised.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAustralia and Turkey criticised for hosting UN climate conference while embracing coalRead moreAustralia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said only 0.2% of global climate finance was spent helping small island developing countries adapt, and that the countries that needed it the most, such as Tuvalu, “get it the least”. “That has got to change,” he said. “It’s a key priority ofCop31.”Kurum said Nato countries should be much more focused on climate spending. He said they had promised to increase their defence budgets to 5% of GDP by 2035 as a result of “concerns for their own safety and security”, but had committed much less to addressing the climate crisis despite expressing concerns and it posing an even greater risk.Asked if he thought as much should be spent on climate as defence, he said: “Much more.”View image in fullscreenLeaders attend a session at the summit.Photograph: Getty Images“The climate issue is the security issue itself,” Kurum told the Guardian through an interpreter. “If you don’t spend one unit of money prior to the disasters, then you are left in a position where you have to spend 10 units of money after the disaster. It’s cheaper pre-disaster.”Kurum and Bowen reiterated they would focus in Antalya on winning support for a global goal of 35% of the energy needed to run homes, businesses, factories and vehiclescoming from electricityby 2035. Now it is about 21%.But the question of what direct action the global community should agree to take to phase out fossil fuels remains far more vexed.Both host countries backed a multi-country statement in Fiji that supported a global “transition away from fossil fuels”, echoing language adopted by the global communityat Cop28 in Dubai three years ago. But both faced criticism, and accusations of hypocrisy, for continuing toback new coal and gas developmentsand beinglargely silent before the pre-Copon the need to phase out fossil fuels.View image in fullscreenChris Bowen, a Cop31 president-designate and Australia’s climate minister, chairs a session on Thursday.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesBowen said the way to stop using fossil fuels was not to cut supply of the dirty fuel but to build enough renewable energy so there would be no need for fossil fuel power plants.Kurum said the world was “already in a transition” and suggested the focus at climate talks on wording about transitioning away from fossil fuels might not be productive as he did not think further progress could be made. Delegates from some countries, including Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states,strongly opposed naming fossil fuels at Cop30in Brazil.Dozens of countries frustrated with what they see as a UN stalemate on the issue met separatelyin Colombiathis year to discuss a path away from fossil fuels. They are due to meet again next July in Tuvalu, and want the issue to be in an agreement in Antalya.Tzeporah Berman, the chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, said Pacific leaders had been clear in Nadi that there should be an urgent fossil fuel phaseout.“This means no new projects,” she said. “You can’t phase something out by building more of it.”Explore more on these topicsCop31Global climate talksClimate crisisTurkeyFijiTuvaluPacific islandsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Animals crossing: the simple solution to stop roadkill in the Amazon | Conservation | The Guardian
description: Installation of eight canopy bridges in Alta Floresta has enabled 15,000 safe crossings by animals including spider monkeys and marmosets – and more bridges are planned elsewhere
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Installation of eight canopy bridges in Alta Floresta has enabled 15,000 safe crossings by animals including spider monkeys and marmosets – and more bridges are planned elsewhere
Content: A black-faced black spider monkey (Ateles chamek) crossing one of the multilayered bridges.  Photograph: Sergio LealInstallation of eight canopy bridges in Alta Floresta has enabled 15,000 safe crossings by animals including spider monkeys and marmosets – and more bridges are planned elsewhereBySuzana CamargoFri 9 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy about 7am, with dense fog blanketing the landscape, Gabriel Falquetto had already come across several road-killed animals along the ES-164 highway in Brazil’s Espírito Santo state. The biologist was on his way to Kaetés private natural heritage reserve (RPPN) in the Atlantic Forest, where he monitors wildlife and roadkill.Then he spotted the lifeless body of a primate on the pavement. It was a buffy-headed marmoset (Callithrix flaviceps), a specieslisted as critically endangeredon the International Union for Conservation of Nature red list. An estimated 2,500 individuals remain in the wild, making it one of the world’s most threatened primates.“It was extremely painful and discouraging,” Falquetto said. “We travel through this region every day monitoring wildlife, and we celebrate every encounter with groups of buffy-headed marmosets in the forest. Finding an individual in those conditions brings a feeling of sadness and helplessness. Beyond the loss of that animal, the incident reminds us of the impacts our activities have on biodiversity.”About 1,800 miles away, on a road leading to Alta Floresta, a small Amazon town in the far north of Mato Grosso state, there have been no cases like the buffy-headed marmoset’s roadkill recorded since 2024. That year, eight canopy bridges were installed, connecting fragmented forest patches. Camera trap footage revealed that over 15 months the aerial wildlife crossings enabled 15,000 safe crossings by arboreal animals – and in that time there was not a single road kill.View image in fullscreenBiologist Fernanda Abra, the founder of Reconectam, with one of the canopy bridges.Photograph: ReconectaThe bridges are part of a programme involvingProjeto Reconectaand the municipal government, along with local organisations and business owners who are eager to conserve the unique biodiversity of their town and promote ecotourism, and were alarmed by the growing number of wildlife-vehicle collisions.Fernanda Abra, an associate researcher at the Smithsonian national zoo and the Conservation Biology Institute in the US, and the founder of Reconecta, recalled that just hours before installing the first bridges in Alta Floresta, she found two Schneider’s marmosets (Mico schneideri) dead. The species is endemic to the Brazilian Amazon and isthreatened with extinction.“A canopy bridge serves two purposes,” Abra said. “The first is to improve connectivity for wildlife, allowing animals to move from one side to the other in these fragmented forest areas. As a result, we also reduce roadkill.”All bridges have two camera traps, one facing the crossing to record which animals are using it and the other facing the forest to observe which animals arrive there but decide not to use it.Among the primate species recorded using the bridges during the first months of the programme were the black-faced black spider monkey (Ateles chamek), the Purús red howler monkey (Alouatta puruensis), the tufted capuchin (Sapajus apella), Schneider’s marmoset and the Alta Floresta titi monkey (Plecturocebus grovesi).‘Cries of delight’ as Sumatran orangutan filmed using canopy bridge to cross road for first timeRead moreDescribed only in 2019 and soon afterclassified as critically endangered, the Alta Floresta titi monkey has become the symbol of the initiative, which is now entering a new phase thanks to its positive results.“In August, we will install eight more bridges in the city’s urban area,” Abra said. “The only difference is that the electric utility will first need to lower the power lines and insulate them so that if animals jump from the bridge on to the wires, they won’t be electrocuted.”The project under way in Alta Floresta is not Reconecta’s first. In 2021, working alongside the Waimiri-Atroari Indigenous people, the teaminstalled 32 canopy bridges over BR-174, the highway that crosses their territory and the Amazon between the Brazilian states of Amazonas and Roraima.The Waimiri-Atroari helped Abra identify the best locations for the artificial bridges. Over the past five years, cameras mounted on the bridge poles have documented about 1,250 crossings by primates, including the golden-handed tamarin (Saguinus midas), a species that is not strictly arboreal and often descends to the ground in search of food, making it particularly vulnerable to roadkill.“The outcomes of the BR-174 project have been incredible,” Abra said. “We were able to test different bridge designs to find out which ones the animals prefer.”After years of working along Brazilian highways, she had always sought a solution that was simple, low-cost and durable. The current bridge features a multilayer design that accommodates primates with different modes of locomotion – from species that rely on their prehensile tails to move through the canopy, to brachiating species such as spider monkeys, which swing using their arms, both of which are common in the Amazon, as well as species that simply walk across the network of crossed ropes. Other small terrestrial mammals including opossums, sloths and mouse opossums have also been recorded using the bridges.View image in fullscreenA Schneider’s marmoset crossing one of the bridges in Alta Floresta.Photograph: Maelle Lima de FreitasAbra said it was important to keep in mind that this was a long-term project, and results were not always immediate. BR-174 was built in the 1970s, and animals take time to adapt to a new crossing alternative. Reconecta’s monitoring has shown that use of the structures increases over time.“Very often, our sense of urgency in conservation doesn’t take into account the timing of the impact,” she said.In Alta Floresta, tufted capuchins took seven months before using one of the bridges for the first time, which may indicate that each species has its own pace of adaptation.Home to the world’s greatest diversity of primates, Brazil also has the world’s fourth largest road network – a deadly combination for animals living along forest edges that have been split apart to make way for highways.“From our human perspective, roads mean connection and development. But for wildlife, they represent disconnection, barriers and a threat to survival,” Abra said.View image in fullscreenA howler monkey on a bridge. Cameras mounted on the bridge poles document the crossings.Photograph: ReconectaNearly 9 millionmammals are killed on Brazil’s roads every year, a 2022 study found. A data compilationpublished in the journal Naturein 2025 found that the country ranked among those with the highest mortality rates of terrestrial vertebrates killed on roads.Prof Fabiano Rodrigues de Melo, a primatologist at the Federal University of Viçosa in Minas Gerais, said: “Habitat loss is one of the main drivers of population declines, especially among threatened species, but the impact of roadkill is still greatly underestimated.”Beyond roadkills, highways bring confinement to fauna. Amely Branquinho Martins, an environmental analyst at the ICMBio, Brazil’s federal agency for conservation units, and a coordinator of theGenomics of the Brazilian Biodiversity project, said: “When populations become isolated, they grow smaller and more vulnerable to threats.”One of those threats is inbreeding, which occurs when closely related individuals reproduce. “Habitat loss and degradation can prevent an individual from one population from migrating to another – what we call gene flow. Without it, the species’ genetic diversity declines,” Martins said.The consequences continue to multiply in a domino effect, Melo said. The loss of primates, especially fruit-eating species, can alter forest composition, because they play a key role in seed dispersal and even contribute to pollination. “A whole network of ecological interactions is ultimately lost with the disappearance of these species,” Melo said.One of the hopes for reducing wildlife roadkill is the passage of a bill under consideration in Brazil’s congress that would establish a national road safety plan for wildlife, which calls, among other measures, for the placement of wildlife warning signs, speed-reduction devices and the construction of overpasses, aerial crossings and underpasses along highways.The bill has been approved by the chamber of deputies and is now awaiting a vote in the senate.If approved, the canopy bridge model developed by Reconecta could be implemented nationwide. In 2026, Brazil’s national department of transport infrastructure designated the design as therecommended standard for highways.Abra’s efforts to protect primates have earned international recognition. She received a Future for Nature award in 2019, followed in 2024 by a Whitley award, often referred to as the Oscars of environmental conservation. In June she was named as one of the recipients of the 2026Wayfinder award, joining a select group who receive funding from the National Geographic Society for their projects.View image in fullscreenA dead anteater on the BR-262, known as the ‘highway of death’, in Terenos, Mato Grosso.Photograph: AGB Photo Library/AlamyThe support comes at the right time, as Abra plans to expand Reconecta, including new chapters in Suriname and Lucas do Rio Verde, a municipality in Brazil, which will install 10 canopy bridges.Abra also hopes to bring her canopy bridges to other biomes, including the Pantanal and the Atlantic Forest, helping prevent the deaths of monkeys such as the buffy-headed marmoset.Expectations are especially high for bridges over BR-262, one of Brazil’s longest highways, which cuts across the Pantanal and isknown as the “highway of death”. Approximately2,000 animalsare killed on the road every year.Abra said: “I envision a future with Reconecta biomes. We already have Reconecta Amazon, and we’ll soon launch Reconecta Pantanal. I also see canopy bridges in the Atlantic Forest for the primates that live there, including muriquis and howler monkeys, which are both highly threatened.”She stressed that for this vision to succeed, the continued engagement of government agencies, private companies and local communities would be essential, just as it was in Alta Floresta and the Waimiri-Atroari Indigenous territory. “When everyone is involved, everyone values the initiative and works harder to make it succeed,” she said.Thisarticlewas originally published inMongabay.Explore more on these topicsThe alternativesConservationWildlifeAmazon rainforestBrazilAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find | Plants | The Guardian
description: Species with leaves large enough to be seen from space is already critically endangered – and plans are afoot to protect it
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Species with leaves large enough to be seen from space is already critically endangered – and plans are afoot to protect it
Content: Jeremiah Harris in one of the pictures he posted on Instagram that was seen by waterlily expert Carlos Magdalena.Photograph: Jeremiah HarrisView image in fullscreenJeremiah Harris in one of the pictures he posted on Instagram that was seen by waterlily expert Carlos Magdalena.Photograph: Jeremiah HarrisPlantsHow a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily findSpecies with leaves large enough to be seen from space is already critically endangered – and plans are afoot to protect itPippa NeillEnvironment reporterFri 9 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA chance social media encounter has led to the race-against-time discovery of a new species of giant waterlily that has until now been hidden in the depths of Colombia’s jungle.But the plant, which is so huge it is visible from space, is already considered critically endangered.Giant waterlilies, which can measure up to three metres across and carry the weight of a small child, are one of the oldest flowering plants in the world still alive today. They existed before the continents split apart and are present throughout culture, from the Egyptians to Monet.Three years ago, while scrolling through Instagram, Carlos Magdalena, a world-renowned waterlily expert at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, came across a photo of someone swimming among several giant waterlilies in the Inírida River in Guainía, Colombia.Jeremiah Harris, who took the photo and who runs a carnivorous plant nursery in the US, was not aware of its significance, having mistakenly identified the waterlily as the more common Victoria amazonica.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueHowever, when Magdalena saw the photo, he “immediately suspected” something was unusual as the natural range of the Victoria amazonica does not extend to the Inírida River.He messaged Harris to track down the exact location and spent several years analysing satellite imagery and securing the funds and necessary permits to allow him to verify the presence of the waterlily for himself.Along with a team from the Jardín Botánico in Bogotá and members of the local indigenous reserves, Magdalena went on a five-day expedition deep into the rainforest.They spent several days exploring the flooded jungle with no luck, until, at the last moment, their driver advised them where to look. With only 10 hours left until their return flight, the team sailed overnight in total darkness to a small lake deep in the flooded rainforest, where they located a population of the waterlilies.View image in fullscreenCarlos Magdalena with a Victoria colombiana leaf.Photograph: Mauricio Bernal/Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew“It was so emotional I shed a tear, it was one of those moments that will remain with me for life,” Magdalena said. “Coming across something like this is absolutely totally fascinating, it’s jaw dropping.“Giant waterlilies give away their secrets slowly,” he said. “It’s remarkable. We believe we know everything but the reality is we don’t, there’s lots of things still to be discovered and protected.”The team collected the material needed to begin a formal identification, with a paper published on Friday in the journalPhytotaxaconfirming it as a new species to science. The waterlily has been given the official name Victoria colombiana. There are just three other known giant waterlilies.Newly identified waterlily species is world’s largestRead moreHarris, who is an author of the study, said his friends always teased him for taking selfies with plants, but the fact this one ended in the discovery of a new species was “incredible”.“I was just so excited, absolutely elated,” he said.Magdalena said: “This is one of those extraordinary stories where indigenous and horticultural knowledge with the help of social media and technology came together to uncover a truly extraordinary botanical achievement.”The team estimates there are between 30 and 50 of the Victoria colombiana waterlilies in the wild, making them extremely rare and at risk of extinction.Maarten Christenhusz, a plant taxonomist who analysed the sample, said new species were found all the time, but few were as “large, spectacular and emblematic as this one. This new giant waterlily can even be seen from space, which is a striking reminder of how much we still don’t know about life on our planet.”View image in fullscreenResearchers inspect the newfound discovery.Photograph: Royal Botanic Gardens, KewThe team is working towards an official International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List designation.Efforts are also under way to support the long-term conservation of the waterlily, including the possibility of establishing a naturalised population in a more accessible lake within indigenous territory. The researchers hope to continue efforts to collect the plant’s seed, with the aim of cultivating it in Bogotá. If these efforts are successful, there is a chance the waterlily may be grown atKew Gardens.Explore more on these topicsPlantsWildlifeColombiaAmericasResearchConservationEndangered speciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK coastguard agency chief faces calls to resign over ‘misleading’ claims in pay row | Emergency services | The Guardian
description: Regulator says poll data did not sufficiently back up claim of support for plan to stop remunerating rescue officers
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Regulator says poll data did not sufficiently back up claim of support for plan to stop remunerating rescue officers
Content: It is understood the option of not paying coastguards is no longer on the table.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIt is understood the option of not paying coastguards is no longer on the table.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/Getty ImagesEmergency servicesUK coastguard agency chief faces calls to resign over ‘misleading’ claims in pay rowRegulator says poll data did not sufficiently back up claim of support for plan to stop remunerating rescue officersKevin RawlinsonFri 9 Oct 2026 12.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head of the UK coastguard agency is facing calls to resign after she was found to have used unverified data to back up her controversial plan to strip rescue officers of their pay.Virginia McVea, the chief executive of the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA), claimed more than 90% of coastguard rescue officers supported the proposal, citing an official survey. Now, after an Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) investigation, the agency has admitted its poll did not sufficiently back up the claim.Nicola Savage, a national officer for theGMB union, which represents coastguard rescue officers (CROs), said: “If Ms McVea is unable to produce the reports she refers to, we would consider this as a deliberate attempt to mislead. If this is the case, she should resign – as hundreds of coastguards have already asked her to do.”Joe Robertson, one of several MPs who have campaigned on CROs’ behalf, accused McVea of misleading MPs and coastguards during three separate meetings at which he said she cited the figure.He called on her to “do the right thing and apologise for misleading MPs, CROs and the public”, adding: “Please also give a written account of how you came to repeat this false line over and over again and why you still have not published the surveys which you promised to MPs in our meeting on 24 June.”Minister and maritime boss accused of misleading MPs over plan to stop coastguard officers’ payRead moreThe MCA’s plan to strip coastguards of their pay was a reaction to a court defeat. A judge affirmed that while CROs volunteered for service, they were classed as workers with the right to minimum wage and holiday pay because they were paid for their time, among other factors. Rather than respect this status, the MCA tried to stop remunerating CROs in an attempt to reclassify them as volunteers.This led to heavycriticism from MPs, CROs and coastal communities, with the GMB union saying nearly 600 CROs had backed its vote of no confidence in McVea.Seeking to defend the plan, McVea cited the 90% figure, but MPstold the Guardian in Julythey felt misled by her.Ina letter to McVeathis week, the OSR’s director general, Ed Humpherson, said: “Neither of the surveys [cited] asked CROs directly about their support for the proposed volunteer model, so do not provide evidence relating to the reported claims. [The] MCA has been unable to provide any further evidence to underpin the reported claims.”Leaked results of an MCA survey, revealed by the Guardian in July, showed CROs had actually been asked how volunteer and worker models would affect their availability.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe results suggested the MCA had included people who said they would become less able to respond to calls if they were volunteers, as well as those who replied “other”, among those in support of the volunteer model.The agency said at the time: “Survey findings were considered alongside a range of operational, legal and practical factors.” But it refused to say how.Theplan was ultimately scrappedby the maritime minister, Keir Mather, as he responded to near universal criticism. CROs are still waiting to find out what system will be adopted, but it is understood the option of not paying coastguards is no longer on the table.The MCA has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsEmergency servicesVoluntary sectorGMB unionPublic sector payTrade unionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bragging rights for Burnham, blues for Farage: conference season winners and losers | Politics | The Guardian
description: While the Labour and Conservative leaders will be delighted with their showing, Nigel Farage, Ed Davey and Zack Polanski have less reason for cheer
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: While the Labour and Conservative leaders will be delighted with their showing, Nigel Farage, Ed Davey and Zack Polanski have less reason for cheer
Content: From left: Polanski’s conference was consumed with controversy; Burnham’s was praised as ‘one of the best’. Badenoch also had a successful season, but Farage’s gathering was gatecrashed by protesters.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Polanski’s conference was consumed with controversy; Burnham’s was praised as ‘one of the best’. Badenoch also had a successful season, but Farage’s gathering was gatecrashed by protesters.PoliticsBragging rights for Burnham, blues for Farage: conference season winners and losersWhile the Labour and Conservative leaders will be delighted with their showing, Nigel Farage, Ed Davey and Zack Polanski have less reason for cheerAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentFri 9 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 08.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWinnersAndy Burnham2:20Andy Burnham fights tears as he speaks of his dad at Labour conference – videoEven his fiercest critics would struggle to argue that Andy Burnham’s first conference as Labour party leader was anythingbut a success. There was the requisite rapture among the Labour faithful after hisdeeply-personal speech, delivered without a tie or a lectern and, at times, with tears in his eyes. But even figures on the right, such as the broadcaster Piers Morgan, described it as “one of the best, and most powerfully delivered, by a British politician in a very long time”.The prime minister’s policy offering packed a punch too. He put forward radical progressive policies on social care, promising to“rip the plaster off”and make changes to the pensions triple lock, electoral reform and Europe.AYouGov poll after the conferenceshowed that it had boosted the “Burnham bounce”, with Labour opening up a five-point lead over Reform UK in the polls. The upcoming budget, and next year’s spending review, will sorely test whether he can keep that momentum going and make good on his promises. Burnham’s success at the Labour conference was capped by a victory at the Holborn and St Pancras byelection a few days laterseeing off a challenge by the leader of the Green party Zack Polanski.Kemi Badenoch1:44Kemi Badenoch refuses to ‘unite’ with Reform UK in Conservative conference speech – videoThis time last year, Kemi Badenoch was hanging on to her role as leader of the opposition by a thread. But in the past 12 months her personal favourability ratings have continued to improve, according toMore in Common research. This was a conference where she tightened her grip over the Conservative party and leaned hard into her own brand, telling GB News’s Christopher Hope: “We are under new management. There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively, which is all me.”While Badenoch’s speech lacked the emotional firepower of Burnham’s, she was assured and disciplined in her focus on the economy – not mentioning small boats or other elements of the culture wars which have energised her in the past. Promised giveaways to wealthy individuals, such as free childcare for those earning more than £100,000 and abolishing inheritance tax on family homes for the 5% of households that pay it, were designed to appeal to the Conservative’s traditional base, one of the first indications of a resolve to win back the “blue wall”.The most powerful moment of the speech came as she drew a line in the sand between the Tories and Reform, thunderously telling her audience there would be no uniting the right: “I don’t want to live in a country run by people who threaten journalists, call veterans traitors and debate whether my mixed-race children are English.” Whether she will reject any deal with Reform if the electoral circumstances dictate remains to be seen.Online, all the time, communicationsView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch and the Tories are pleased with their ‘tapestry’.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesBoth the Conservative and Labour communications teams can congratulate themselves on a job vigorously done in the past few weeks. The coup of the conference season came in the guise of a 27-metre (88ft) graphical retelling of the past two years in British politics in the style of the Bayeux tapestry, as seen through Conservative eyes. Senior party figures and members alike enjoyed the “Birmingham tapestry”, for itspointed jabs at defector Robert Jenrick, but the canniest move was including depictions of high-profile journalists, most of whom duly posted images of the propaganda to their sizeable social media followings.The team at theLabourparty conference successfully projected the “hopey-changey” vibes they had intended, mainly by producing as many posters and placards declaring there was “hope again” as there were participants at the conference. But special mention should also be given to the socials team at Labour HQ, whose snipes during their rivals’ conferences (“Who was less sure whether he’d finished, the shadow chancellor or the audience?”, they asked after Andrew Griffith’s less than assured end of speech exit) was a masterclass in side-eye.The battle of political ideasThis conference season saw the most sharply defined battle lines between right and left in a generation. Burnham used his speech to attack neoliberalism, saying: “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time. Deindustrialisation. Deregulation. Privatisation. Austerity. Brexit.”He was instantly accused by theConservativesof indulging in a “socialist fever dream” of the 1970s. They went on to proclaim a love of Thatcher while simultaneously belting out the national anthem. In her speech, Badenoch pitched the fight against Labour as “a battle for the soul of this nation”, trotting out the well-worn Tory treatise that “what people earn belongs to them, not government”.Sidekicks with main character energyView image in fullscreenEd Miliband is enjoying his time as foreign secretary.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianEd Miliband lolloped through Liverpool’s conference centre with the ease of a man who appears to be very much enjoying his time as foreign secretary. In a lineup easily swallowed by the gravitational pull of the leader’s speech, Miliband delivered a deft piece of politics, telling assembled members theywere “right”to be moved by the plight of the Palestinian people.Over at the Conservative conclave, the Conservatives’ candidate for mayor of London, James Cleverly, also had a jolly time away from the main stage. “[Kemi Badenoch] knows, as I do, that our best bet of getting her into No 10 is getting me into City Hall,” he tolda panel convened by the Centre for Policy Studies (CPS).LosersNigel FarageView image in fullscreenNigel Farage was overshadowed by the suspension of close aides.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAReform UK billed its largest ever gathering at the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham as “the most talked about event of 2026”. Its leader, Nigel Farage, wanted to use the conference to outline a series of policy pledges for a Reform government’s first 100 days in office.Instead the opening was overshadowed by the suspension of his close aides Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr, after anundercover investigation by reporters from a group called Verbatim. Reform UKcleared them of breaking laws that ban foreign donationson Wednesday, but the matter remains under police investigation.Farage’s own speech was interrupted by protesters, who appeared to be roughed up as they were thrown out of the hall. A man was later given a police caution after footage appeared to show one woman having her hair pulled and being hit with a walking stick.Zack PolanskiZack Polanski started his run in to the Green party of England and Wales’s conference by asking, unsuccessfully,if it could be delayed so he could focus on campaigningin theHolborn and St Pancras byelection. He may now wish it had been cancelled altogether.The party’s gathering in Brighton was consumed by controversy, after members voted in favour ofan official policy statingthat Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, is a type of racism. Polanski absented himself from the most toxic internal debate the party has faced for years, choosing instead to leave to campaign, and the party is still reeling from the fallout.Shortly after the Greens’ triumph in February’sGorton and Denton byelectionit was polling above 20%; itnow stands on 11%.Ed DaveyView image in fullscreenEd Davey: ‘We care! We fight!’Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAAt first it seemed as if the Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, had come through his party’s conference in Brightonrelatively unscathed, despite going unexpectedly viral for a speech in which he enthusiastically, if not entirely successfully, attempted to rally a chant of “We care! We fight!”. But his opposition to Labour’s proposals to change the pension triple lock was met with opposition by senior and backbench Lib Dems, with one saying his defence of the current policy “gaslights an entire generation into believing it’s for our benefit”.John HealeyThe chancellor used the word hope 21 times in his personal conference speech that, while warmly welcomed by Labour party members, managed to say very little about actual policy over quite a long period of time. In the days that followed, senior Labour figures privatelyvoiced unease about Healey’s approach to his crucial first budgetthis month, noting it lacked detail about policy on investment and growth or any pitch-rolling for possible tax rises.Andrew Griffith0:34Andrew Griffith speaks at the Conservative party conference – videoAmong all the gaffes, the spills, the wrong names and forgotten policy details of this season of party conferences, one performance really did stand out.Griffith, the shadow chancellor, was described by Badenoch as having “more business experience than the entire Labour cabinet combined” – attenders at Conservative party conference were left wondering if any of it had involved public speaking. After an address variously described as “an historic clunker”, “curious” and “the worst speech ever heard”, Griffith’s speech appeared to simply peter out and the shadow chancellor wandering awkwardly off stage, leaving the audience not knowing whether to clap, or simply follow him out of the room.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onplatform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies.
