title: Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts | Palantir | The Guardian
description: Former Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Former Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns
Content: Tom Watson at the Labour party conference in Liverpool last month.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTom Watson at the Labour party conference in Liverpool last month.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesPalantirPalantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contractsFormer Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdownsJamie GriersonFri 9 Oct 2026 03.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Watson, the former Labour deputy leader who recently joined Palantir, has warned against “mob rule” when it comes to awarding public contracts.Lord Watson, now a senior vice-president at the US tech corporation, said UK ministers could get themselves “in a lot of trouble” as he was questioned about concerns raised about the government working with his new employer.Palantir was co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel and has providedAI-powered software to the Israeli military and the White House’s ICE immigration crackdown, leading to a public and political backlash against its deepening involvement in British public services.The prime minister,Andy Burnham, is under significant pressure from Labour MPs and unions to ditch Palantir from government contracts, including a £330m software deal with the NHS.The company is also fighting Sadiq Khan in court over theLondon mayor’s block on a £50m contractto use its AI in Metropolitan police investigations. It is seeking to win more public sector work in the UK, where it already has an annualturnoverof £427m.Watson told the BBC podcast Political Thinking with Nick Robinson: “One of the things I’d say to my former colleagues is: do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices? Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one.”He added: “I think we are very targeted by the people that are targeting Israeli companies. We’re not an Israeli company, but because of our work in Israel we found ourselves in the middle of the row of the Gaza protests.”Watson told the podcast he would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns if the situation arose, saying: “We don’t actually work in that sector, but yes, of course we would.”He calledPalantir“the most interesting company on the planet” as he announced his new role last month. The company said his job would be, in part, to “deepen the social and economic value its work creates through better British public services, jobs and skills”.Watson was a defence minister and a minister for digital engagement in Gordon Brown’s government. Since stepping down from parliament in 2019, he has been an adviser to the gambling and music industries and, since 2024, he has been a part-time adviser to Palantir.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPalantir said Watson had taken a leave of absence from the House of Lords and had relinquished his parliamentary pass while he worked for the company inLondon.The Labour MP Chi Onwurah, who chairs the science, innovation and technology committee, which has raised concerns about Palantir, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “Tom is not the first politician to be blinded by tech hype. The key issue is we can’t be so dependent on one company. It’s a US company, subject to US legislation regarding access to our data.”Explore more on these topicsPalantirTom WatsonPublic services policyNHSMetropolitan policeSadiq KhanAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour chair of housing committee calls for urgent funds for affordable homes in England | Housing | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Abena Oppong-Asare urges chancellor to unlock billions of pounds, as housing associations say they could build 41,000 homes in 10 years
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Abena Oppong-Asare urges chancellor to unlock billions of pounds, as housing associations say they could build 41,000 homes in 10 years
Content: Oppong-Asare said families on social housing waiting lists needed to ‘see action now’.Photograph: London Portrait Photoqrapher-DAVID WOOLFALL/UK ParliamentView image in fullscreenOppong-Asare said families on social housing waiting lists needed to ‘see action now’.Photograph: London Portrait Photoqrapher-DAVID WOOLFALL/UK ParliamentHousingLabour chair of housing committee calls for urgent funds for affordable homes in EnglandExclusive: Abena Oppong-Asare urges chancellor to unlock billions of pounds, as housing associations say they could build 41,000 homes in 10 yearsKiran StaceyPolicy editorFri 9 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Labour chair of the Commons housing committee is urgingJohn Healeyto bring forward billions of pounds of planned spending on social and affordable homes in England, after housing associations said they were ready to build tens of thousands more.Abena Oppong-Asare called for the chancellor to allocate money from the £39bn Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) as soon as possible, rather than after the election as planned.Housing associations have said they could build an additional 41,000 homes outside London over the next 10 years if they had more government funding.They said the extra units would help the government get closer to its target of building 1.5m new homes across this parliament – though the housing secretary, Angela Rayner,recently admittedthat it would be difficult to achieve.Oppong-Asare said: “The government should use theupcoming budgetto increase the building of social homes by ensuring a significant proportion of the Social and Affordable Homes Programme is allocated during this parliament.“Families stuck on social housing waiting lists need to see action now. I urge the chancellor to ensure a significant sum of the £39bn SAHP is allocated during this parliament and that truly affordable social rent homes are prioritised as part of this package.”Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves,announced the £39bn10-year fund last year, having changed the government’s borrowing rules to allow her to borrow more for capital projects.The money was due to be spent on a mix of council houses and a number of other types of affordable housing, including affordable rents and shared ownership schemes.Free land for those who will build social homes on it. Is this the radical solution to the UK’s housing problem? | Phineas HarperRead moreBefore he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had said the scheme should be reallocated entirely to social rent housing.But when the first £10bn was allocated under his government in August, it went to a mix of councils and housing associations outside London to spend on avariety of types of subsidised homes.Ministers said the money would help build 70,000 new homes. But housing associations said they could have built an additional 41,000 – including 25,000 for social rent – if the government had given them all the money for which they bid.They said they could start construction work on 15,000 of those in the next three years – though some associations have come under fire for selling their homes to the private sector.The National Housing Federation (NHF), which represents housing associations, said ministers would have to allocate an additional £5.3bn from the programme to build the extra homes.Ministers have said they are planning to allocate £6bn to London immediately. But of the remaining £13bn, they said they planned to hand out “significant sums” in the second half of the scheme, which would come after the next election.Kate Henderson, the chief executive of the NHF, said: “Housing associations submitted bids with plans to build tens of thousands of affordable homes, but many organisations with sites ready to go and proven track records did not receive the funding needed to deliver these homes.“With additional investment now, it is possible to help transform the lives of families in urgent need of an affordable home.”A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing said: “We’ve already announced nearly £10bn of allocations from the Social and Affordable Homes Programme so we can start building more than 70,000 council, social and affordable homes across England.“Our record investment will help families trapped in temporary accommodation or stuck on housing waiting lists into safe, secure homes.”Explore more on these topicsHousingSocial housingJohn HealeyBudgetCommunitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau | Vaccines and immunisation | The Guardian
description: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers
Author: Melody Schreiber
Headline: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers
Content: A child receives a hepatitis B vaccine in Lomé, Togo, on 7 August 2015.Photograph: BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA child receives a hepatitis B vaccine in Lomé, Togo, on 7 August 2015.Photograph: BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesVaccines and immunisationControversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-BissauRecommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchersMelody SchreiberFri 9 Oct 2026 17.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.It is a central part of the vaccine vision forRobert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants inGuinea-Bissauin the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said wassuspendedafterinternational uproarearlier this year.Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.Experts fear ‘unethical’ vaccine trial in Africa is ‘prototype’ for US studies under RFK JrRead moreThe US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) hasreportedlyset aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday byCIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University inDenmark.According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held adual appointmentwith Bandim as recently as December.Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchersfound no effectsat all.This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”Explore more on these topicsVaccines and immunisationGuinea-BissauAfricaHealthRobert F Kennedy JrDenmarknewsShareReuse this content

title: Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Israeli airport, UAE prosecutors say | Flydubai plane incident | The Guardian
description: Hammam al-Hammami is believed to have been targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Hammam al-Hammami is believed to have been targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv
Content: Hammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersView image in fullscreenHammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersFlydubai plane incidentFlydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Israeli airport, UAE prosecutors sayHammam al-Hammami is believed to have been targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel AvivJason Burke, international security correspondentFri 9 Oct 2026 16.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was planning to launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Israel’s international airport, prosecutors in theUnited Arab Emiratessaid on Friday.Hammam al-Hammamiattacked the plane’s Indian pilotwith an emergency axe, but failed to prevent his badly injured colleague from opening the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower his assailant.Passengers then tried to control the aircraft, which was safely landed inSaudi Arabiaby an off-duty relief pilot who was among about 180 passengers.Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney-general of the UAE, said on Friday that al-Hammami, who is in Emirate custody, had admitted he had tried to execute a “premeditated terrorist plot to … launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv, with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”.The 29-year-old, who was hired by flydubai, a government-owned low-cost airline, began a process of radicalisation while studying in Australia when he was influenced by the hardline takfiri ideology through reading extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks, al-Shamsi said in a statement.“[Al-Hammami] subsequently developed … ideas advocating violence and terrorism. He also drew inspiration from the 11 September 2001 attacks, and the idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking. According to his confession, this was linked to his decision to pursue a career in aviation.”Over the weekend, Australian security agencieslaunched an investigationafter it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. Heleft the country without completing his engineering degree.New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation after police confirmed al-Hammami underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.There has been widespread concern about how al-Hammami was able to pass vetting and join a crew flying toIsrael. An Omani national, he earned a distance-learning aviation management degree from Buckinghamshire New University in 2023 and was employed by Oman Air from 2020-24, joined Royal Air Maroc in early 2025 and worked there for several months before moving to flydubai in January 2026.Security officials have been keen to understand if al-Hammami was acting alone or had become involved with a group such as al-Qaida or Islamic State, which could suggest further such attacks might be planned. Emirate authorities believe this is not the case.“In the presence of his lawyer and with all legally prescribed safeguards ensured, the suspect provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution. He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim,” al-Shamsi said.Investigators have found al-Hammami had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route ‌and the airport”, the Emirati state news agency WAM reported.The passengers on board the aircraft were overwhelmingly Israeli, with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailing them and the pilot for their bravery after the foiled attack.Explore more on these topicsFlydubai plane incidentAir transportMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelDubaiSaudi ArabiaUnited Arab EmiratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: US imposes new sanctions on international criminal court | International criminal court | The Guardian
description: Trump administration says US ‘doesn’t need’ ICC after accusing court of unfairly targeting Americans for war crime charges
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: Trump administration says US ‘doesn’t need’ ICC after accusing court of unfairly targeting Americans for war crime charges
Content: The international criminal court (ICC) in The Hague.Photograph: Remko de Waal/ANP/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe international criminal court (ICC) in The Hague.Photograph: Remko de Waal/ANP/AFP/Getty ImagesInternational criminal courtUS imposes new sanctions on international criminal courtTrump administration says US ‘doesn’t need’ ICC after accusing court of unfairly targeting Americans for war crime chargesAriana Baioin New YorkFri 9 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTFirst published on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe United States was accused of launching “an assault” on the world’s legal order after imposing more sanctions on theinternational criminal court(ICC).Unveiling the Trump administration’s latest escalation against the court, which it has accused of politicization and unfairly targeting Americans for war crime charges, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, declared: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”The ICC accused Donald Trump’s officials of attempting to “obstruct the course of justice” as Rubio, just hours aftera former ICC judge was awarded the Nobel peace prize,announced in a videothat the US would move to impose financial sanctions.Alarm at UN over sanctions threatened by US on international criminal courtRead more“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us. Because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” Rubio said in a video posted on X. “We don’t need that court and we don’t want it.”In a statement, the court warned that “history will judge this moment” and urged other members to ensure it can continue the function. “It is an ⁠attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what ⁠it was created to do. It is an assault ​on the rule ‌of law and ‌on the very foundations of the international legal order,” ‌the ICC said.The new set ofsanctionswill block any assets the ICC has in US jurisdictions and gives US companies or individuals six months to wind down business with the tribunal court.But the sanctions also allow the ICC to address the US government’s concerns, and certain transactions are exempt.The Trump administration has repeatedly condemned the ICC for issuing arrest warrants for Israeli officials, including Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. It also opened an investigation into the actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, although the case has been closed.The ICC was established in 2002 as an international tribunal to hold countries accountable for war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity.Trump has long targeted the ICC. During his first term, he imposed sanctions on the court, which were later reversed under the Biden administration.But when Trump returned to office in 2025, hesigned an executive orderimposing sanctions on the ICC for the court’s investigations into Israelis and Americans. From there, the administration has continued to impose more sanctions.The administration added sanctions on judgesand lawyers at the ICC. In August, it placed additional sanctions on the ICC president, Tomoko Akane.Explore more on these topicsInternational criminal courtUS politicsUS foreign policyTrump administrationMarco RubionewsShareReuse this content

title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law | Nobel peace prize | The Guardian
description: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza
Content: 1:11Nobel peace prize winner Navi Pillay jokes about sharing award with Donald Trump – videoNobel peace prizeICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international lawCommittee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in GazaJulian BorgerandRachel SavageFri 9 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTFirst published on Fri 9 Oct 2026 05.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commissionthat concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.That commission concluded last year that the state of Israelwas guilty of genocidal actsin Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,”the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.“In awarding this year’sNobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.Hours after the announcement, the Trump administrationunveiled broad new sanctionsagainst the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in SouthAfrica, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in theAkayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establishrape and sexual violence as weapons of war– a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January byhanding her winner’s medalto Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”Explore more on these topicsNobel peace prizeNorwaySouth AfricaInternational court of justiceHuman rightsAfricaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: China agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark deal  | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs
Content: BYD cars being loaded on its cargo ship at Nantong Port in Jiangsu Province of China.Photograph: Xu Congjun/VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBYD cars being loaded on its cargo ship at Nantong Port in Jiangsu Province of China.Photograph: Xu Congjun/VCG/Getty ImagesAutomotive industryChina agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark dealBrussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobsLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentFri 9 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations withChinasince June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EV – but it’s too long for UK parking spacesRead more“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.China has beenflooding Europe with cars, including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs.Šefčovič said the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building in every member state in Europe with “literally thousands of job losses” at risk because of the flood of cheap imports from China across many sectors including chemicals and textiles.He said EU leaders were “clearly expecting very fast action” from the European Commission and the Chinese recognised that.“I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” he said.“This ‌is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told ‌reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold ​talks with his Chinese counterpart.Earlier this week senior EU officials said they were heading to Beijing to seek whatthey called a “proof of concept”or pilot scheme with one sector which they hoped could then be expanded to other areas under pressure from Chinese competition.Šefčovič said he put “so much emphasis” on the negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop” a trade war once it was declared.As part of a 16-point agreement, Beijing and Brussels will continue negotiating on cars, export restrictions on rare earths and access to China for more food and drink from the EU.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChina said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” for hybrid cars suggesting one method of curbing sales would be to set higher minimum price tags for Chinese cars sold in Europe.The EU commissioner will brief EU diplomats in Brussels on Sunday ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday.A statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce said China is “willing … to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”.It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”.While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryEuropean UnionChinaEuropeElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tory tax break for banks has cost UK public purse £6bn, says TUC | Banking | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Chancellor urged to reverse Jeremy Hunt’s tax surcharge cuts to claw back billions in lost revenue
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Exclusive: Chancellor urged to reverse Jeremy Hunt’s tax surcharge cuts to claw back billions in lost revenue
Content: TUC analysis found cuts to the bank surcharge – an extra levy on lenders’ profits – from 8% to 3% led to £6bn in lost tax revenues over three years.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTUC analysis found cuts to the bank surcharge – an extra levy on lenders’ profits – from 8% to 3% led to £6bn in lost tax revenues over three years.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesBankingTory tax break for banks has cost UK public purse £6bn, says TUCExclusive: Chancellor urged to reverse Jeremy Hunt’s tax surcharge cuts to claw back billions in lost revenueBusiness live – latest updatesKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentFri 9 Oct 2026 09.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTax cuts for big banks have deprived the UK government of £6bn in revenues, according to campaigners, who are calling on the chancellor,John Healey, to increase taxes and force lenders to pay their “fair share” in the budget.Calculations by the Trades Union Congress (TUC), which represents unions with more than 5.3 million members across England and Wales, shows that the public purse is billions of pounds worse off as a result of tax cuts introduced under the Tory chancellor Jeremy Hunt in 2023.The then government agreed to slash the bank surcharge – an additional levy on lenders’ profits – from 8% to 3% that year. The move was meant to offset a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%, after the industryargued higher taxes would put them at a competitive disadvantagecompared with other big financial centres such as New York.However, the cuts came just as lenders started reaping handsome earnings, thanks torising interest rates. The UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group – have now generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years.The TUC says the 2023 cuts ultimately robbed the UK purse of tax revenues. Its analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the UK public lost out £2.3bn in 2023-24, a further £1.7bn in 2024-25, and £2bn in 2025-26 – totalling £6bn over three years.With banks pocketing record profits, the TUC said the surcharge should now be increased beyond its pre-2023 level at the 28 October budget. That could raise up to £60bn, which could be used to cover rising household bills as part of prime minister Andy Burnham’s drive to tackle the cost of living.“The Tories’ tax break for banks has cost the UK public purse £6bn and counting. It’s time to end it and to make sure banks pay their fair share,” the TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, said.“At a time when families are struggling with soaring energy costs, taxing banks’ booming profits to cut bills is just plain common sense. There is a mountain of evidence to suggest that banks can afford to pay more tax – not least the record £25bn bonus pool they paid out last year.“This month’s budget is an opportunity to put things right.”Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against bank tax rises, after narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget. Jamie Dimon, chief executive of the largest US bank, JP Morgan,warned Burnham and Healeyagainst further levies during a meeting last month, saying it could put investment and jobs at risk.Earlier this year, Dimon warned that hecould scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquartersif the UK government became hostile to banks.The TUC has said raising the surcharge to 16% – double the rate prior to Conservative cuts – could raise £24bn in tax revenues over the next four years. Meanwhile, a 35% bank surcharge, which would match the windfall tax rate that Conservatives imposed on energy companies, would deliver £60bn over four years. Even reversing the surcharge cuts and setting it at 8% would raise £9bn over that same period, the union body said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Reversing the last government’s tax cuts is the very least this government can do to claw back some of the lost billions it’s handed to banks in recent years,” said a spokesperson for campaign group Positive Money, which has also been pushing for bank tax rises at the budget. “Banks are making record profits without lifting a finger, thanks to the higher rates being paid to them, by both customers and the Bank of England.”David Postings, the chief executive of banking lobby group UK Finance said that a strong banking sector was essential for a strong UK economy and that profitable lenders would be able to invest in better services for customers, issue more loans, and deliver “returns” – such as shareholder dividends – that supported people’s savings and pensions.“Banks also make a major contribution to the public finances and already face a materially higher total tax rate in the UK than in other leading financial centres,” he said.“Further tax increases would weaken the UK’s competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government’s ambition to deliver growth in every postcode.”The Treasury was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsBankingFinancial sectorJohn HealeyRishi SunakTax and spendingTUCTrade unionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI surveillance startup Flock to cut several hundred jobs amid backlash, sources say | Surveillance | The Guardian
description: Company, which grown rapidly in recent years, has been under scrutiny as privacy concerns grow
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Company, which grown rapidly in recent years, has been under scrutiny as privacy concerns grow
Content: A Flock Safety camera in Troy, New York, on 16 March 2026.Photograph: Albany Times Union/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Flock Safety camera in Troy, New York, on 16 March 2026.Photograph: Albany Times Union/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesSurveillanceAI surveillance startup Flock to cut several hundred jobs amid backlash, sources sayCompany, which grown rapidly in recent years, has been under scrutiny as privacy concerns growReutersFri 9 Oct 2026 15.46 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 16.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlock Safety plans to shed about 18% of its employees, people with direct ⁠knowledge of the plans said on Thursday, as the maker ofAI-poweredsurveillancecameras and license-plate readers facesmounting oppositionto its products from communities and ⁠lawmakers.The people said the job ⁠cuts came after ​a voluntary buyout program and were expected to affect roughly 270 employees at Flock, a surveillance technology startup that has seen rapid growth in recent ⁠years. Employees will leave the company at the end of the month.Sources declined to be identified as the company has yet to make the plan public.Their cities dropped Flock surveillance cameras. They’re still being watchedRead moreFlock declined ⁠to comment.In September, Flock announced a voluntary separation program, asking employees to apply if they wanted to ​leave the company, as Wired reported. The ‌company has about 1,500 employees.Flock faces ‌growing scrutinyfrom regulators, lawmakers and privacy advocates, despite drawing strong investor interest among venture capitalists. A ‌recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed Americans are divided on whether Flock cameras are a good idea. About 38% of the country supports the use of Flock cameras in their community, compared with 47% who oppose their use.Across 49 states, Flock’s network of about 120,000 AI-powered cameras, affixed to streets and highways, automatically read license plates and record vehicles as they pass.The company, based in Atlanta and founded in ‌2017, has raised more than $950m from venture capital investors, with its latest $275m round in March led by Andreessen Horowitz valuing the company at $7.5bn. The funds have supported a ​new US manufacturing facility and an upcoming push into drone products, according to the company.Flock provides cameras and software to more than 4,800 law enforcement agencies and nearly 1,000 businesses. The company says its technology helps investigate and solve crimes, but it has come under increasing scrutiny over alleged privacy violations and data-sharing practices.Public backlash ⁠has grown. In September, Florida banned automated license plate readers from state highways, ​citing privacy risks tied to Flock’s ​cameras.Home Depot investors recently demanded reviews ​of the retailer’s partnerships with surveillance technology vendors after reports that Flock’s data was used ​in immigration enforcement.Flock also ‌faces legal challenges, such ​as a privacy ​lawsuit in Virginia alleging that the widespread deployment of its AI-powered cameras constitutes warrantless surveillance.Together with AI datacenters, Flock cameras have emerged as a flashpoint ahead of November’s midterm elections, with candidates increasingly attacking their opponents by tying them to the technology.Explore more on these topicsSurveillanceAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Christian Bittar has conviction for rigging interest rates quashed | Libor | The Guardian
description: Former City banker becomes eighth to clear their name, just days after five others were acquitted
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Former City banker becomes eighth to clear their name, just days after five others were acquitted
Content: Christian Bittar in 2016.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/ReutersView image in fullscreenChristian Bittar in 2016.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/ReutersLiborChristian Bittar has conviction for rigging interest rates quashedFormer City banker becomes eighth to clear their name, just days after five others were acquittedJoanna PartridgeFri 9 Oct 2026 11.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormer City trader Christian Bittar has become the eighth person to have his conviction for rigging interest rates quashed, just days after five other former bankers alsosuccessfully cleared their names.Christian Bittar, who previously worked for Deutsche Bank, was convicted in 2018 of conspiracy to defraud.On Wednesday, the court overturned the convictions of Jay Vijay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon and Colin Bermingham, all of whom worked atBarclays.This week’s acquittals come just over a year after the UK supreme courtoverturned a decade-old rulingagainst the former UBS and Citigroup trader Tom Hayes and former Barclays trader Carlo Palombo. Their victory opened the door for the other traders to challenge their convictions.Bittar said after his acquittal: “I have waited a very, very long time for this day. Finally, the injustice of what I and others suffered has been recognised. I am so grateful for those who stood by me through this ordeal and those who worked so tirelessly to correct it.”Bittar and the five other former traders were all sentenced to jail on charges of manipulating the euro interbank offered rate (Euribor) or the now defunct London interbank offered rate (Libor).The Euribor and Libor rates affected the value of ordinary people’s pensions, mortgages and savings, as well as hundreds of trillions of pounds and euros worth of financial products around the world. Nine bankers accused of rigging the rates were given fraud convictions.The supreme court overturned the convictions of Hayes and Palombo after finding faults in the original trials, ruling that trial judges had given “inaccurate and unfair” instructions to the juries, that had ultimately “deprived” the men a fair trial.Friday’s ruling marks a further blow for the Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which brought the original charges against the former traders.While the SFO did not contest the appeals of the five men acquitted on Wednesday, it did contest Bittar’s appeal, stating his conviction was safe.Jason Williams, head of division at the SFO, said:“We argued for a different outcome but respect the court’s decision in relation to Christian Bittar. The SFO remains committed to tackling the most complex fraud, bribery and corruption.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBen Rose of law firm Hickman and Rose, who represented Bittar, said it was a “scandal that the SFO has consistently failed to uphold its duty to ensure that these trials are fair”.Peter Johnson, the ninth former trader who was convicted of rate rigging, also intends to appeal against his conviction. He pleaded guilty to conspiring to manipulate Libor in 2014.Ellen Gallagher, a partner at Vardags, who represents Johnson, said: “Peter’s fight to clear his name continues.“As the court made clear today, he has taken the first steps towards that appeal by filing provisional grounds.”Explore more on these topicsLiborBankingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m lovingly making fun of everyone I’ve ever met’: on the set of Leo Reich’s gen Z sitcom | TV comedy | The Guardian
description: The comedy wunderkind shot to fame with his show Literally, Who Cares?! and a role in Lena Dunham’s Too Much. Now he’s bringing his take on self-involved zoomers to the TV screen. Just don’t call him the voice of a generation
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: The comedy wunderkind shot to fame with his show Literally, Who Cares?! and a role in Lena Dunham’s Too Much. Now he’s bringing his take on self-involved zoomers to the TV screen. Just don’t call him the voice of a generation
Content: Squat goals … Leo Reich.Photograph: Raphael Neal/Channel 4View image in fullscreenSquat goals … Leo Reich.Photograph: Raphael Neal/Channel 4TV comedy‘I’m lovingly making fun of everyone I’ve ever met’: on the set of Leo Reich’s gen Z sitcomThe comedy wunderkind shot to fame with his show Literally, Who Cares?! and a role in Lena Dunham’s Too Much. Now he’s bringing his take on self-involved zoomers to the TV screen. Just don’t call him the voice of a generationRachel AroestiFri 9 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeo Reich’s new Channel 4 sitcom is “Girls meets Peep Show. That’s always my favourite part of pitching anything: choose two really good things and say it’s a mix of those!” says the comedian with a slight smirk. Still, it’s a fair summary: It Gets Worse is a bracingly candid, occasionally provocative hangout comedy about twentysomethings floundering professionally and personally in the big city that comes accompanied by a strong stench of British bleakness (see: the title, for a start). Yet it does fail to flag one key aspect. While Girls and Peep Show covered the travails of millennials and gen X respectively, It Gets Worse is happening now – making it the UK’s first true gen Z sitcom.Or not. “I’m sceptical of the idea that generations have any real unifying features across the board, so I don’t want it to be like: this is a gen Z sitcom!” says the 28-year-old. In fact, it soon becomes clear that It Gets Worse is deliberately USP-less. We first meet Reich’s Ethan – “a middle-class loser gay guy” – and his pals Sam and Abi as they’re packing up their London flatshare, having been forced out because of a rent hike. But this isn’t the start of a meditation on the cost of living crisis – or anything else. “The point isn’t there’s some big concept where everyone’s a superhero, it’s: these are some people dot dot dot.” When I ask how closely the final show resembles his original idea, Reich looks askance. “The idea, I would say, was quite broad …”I’d wager that the real idea – the main idea, the only idea – was to give a sitcom (any sitcom) to Reich, who since the pandemic has established himself as the future of comedy with remarkable ease. Following a stint in Footlights at Cambridge and a lockdown that birthed a few cleverly mordant TikToks (“for us, there were no rules! Apart from obviously don’t go outside,” he quips in one clip captioned “telling my kids about my wild 20s”), Reich took his debut standup show to the Edinburgh fringe in 2022. Literally, Who Cares?! saw him pose as a heightened parody of a stereotypical zoomer: “a deliriously self-involved, fragmentarily informed, habitually self-pitying, comprehensively cynical member of Generation Z”, as a celebratory New Yorker profile put it the following year. (A British reviewer likened his character to a 21st-century Rick from The Young Ones.) Reich performed his ingenious script, which merged pastiche with drolly accurate observations about the modern world, looking like a pre-Raphaelite club kid: dramatic eye shadow, short shorts, mop of curls. It was an immediate hit, and swiftly picked up for a HBO special – unheard of for a fledgling British comedian. No wonder he’s been given carte blanche to bring his sensibility to TV.View image in fullscreenFlat broke … Reich with Olive Gray (left) and Emily Fairn.Photograph: Jack BarnesIt’s an autumn day when I visit the set of It Gets Worse in south-east London, where a former spice warehouse is doubling as the squat Sam has moved into. Reich is in this scene – an awkward sex party – but still finds time to swing by the monitors to see how things are looking and – I quickly realise from the script in my hand – ad lib half of Ethan’s ludicrous small talk (there’s nothing on the page about Tutankhamun or the idea that as a society “we need to get back to the land”).Afterwards, in a liminal space upstairs, Reich is vaping and sipping a canned coffee. He encourages improvisation: the show “is about mess and people being fucking stupid and delusional, so I think it suits a level of roughness … thank God!” Yet as a longtime standup fanatic (as a teenager he’d make his mum take him to the now defunct alternative north London comedy club the Invisible Dot; his heroes included Simon Amstell and James Acaster), he remains serious about the art of comedy. He describes his on-set role as “a sort of joke warden”, who steps in when “the rhythm’s a little bit out” in his castmates’ delivery. I notice one particular line about a party guest – “Leon’s cousin from Tring” – is non-negotiable in terms of both syntax and cadence.double quotation markThis is a very specific time to be looking down the barrel of the rest of your lifeReich may shrug off any voice of a generation label, but It Gets Worse does feel distinctly of the moment. That’s partly thanks to the protagonists: “a campy gay guy, uptight northern girl and mixed-race artist” have typically been restricted to “side character” status on screen in the past, he says. But it also has a lot to do with that depressing title. While gen Z isn’t a monolith, its members do all have something significant in common: they are coming of age during the permacrisis, the omnipresent financial, political and ecological precarity that is making the future feel hopeless for many. “Trying to say this without being cringe, but it’s a very specific time to be looking down the barrel of the rest of your life,” says Reich. “All of these traditional institutions like marriage and climbing the career ladder don’t really exist, or if they do exist you can’t trust them. There’s a vague sense of massive anxiety.”Reich is, presumably, not feeling the fear to quite the same degree. Since his breakthrough he has appeared in Lena Dunham’s Netflix comeback Too Much (she returns the favour here by playing Abi’s boss, one of a host of big-name cameos including Andrew Scott and Zadie Smith) and now, obviously, has his own sitcom. But that doesn’t mean he can’t identify with his characters. It Gets Worse isn’t an issue-led drama but an attempt “to recreate a mood or feeling of helplessness, which isn’t about success in a brutal material way. It’s an existential feeling of being lost and stupid and not knowing what to do.”In the show, all three leads have “radically different responses to the broader existential anxiety”, says Reich. Ethan sees himself as “a charming clown” whose philosophy is “fuck it, let’s just have a laugh, live in the moment so you don’t have to plan your future”. He is easily the luckiest of the trio – his living situation is solved when he moves back in with his London-based mum (a sublimely irritable Vicki Pepperdine) – but far from aspirational. There’s an arch Fleabagian nihilism to his humiliating sexual experiences (including one with a therapist played by Scott), which dovetails with the sense that Ethan is “being fucked by life but kind of enjoying it”, says Reich, who tends to think of sex as inherently hilarious (“it’s such an insane thing to do!”).Meanwhile, Abi, played by Emily Fairn (The Responder, House of Guinness), takes the good girl route, chasing the hallmarks of an Instagrammable lifestyle via industrious perfectionism. Sam (Olive Gray) is a tutor and wannabe writer who pursues the same meaning and control by building her “own kind of life and rejecting social norms”, says Reich. Her cynicism has also led to a kind of radical independence. “I think,” says Gray, “that she’s the type of person who believes no one owes anyone anything and everyone is responsible for themselves – to her own detriment and the detriment of the people around her, unfortunately.”Unlike many messy millennial dramedies, It Gets Worse clearly aims to replace myopia with multiplicity. Fairn appreciated the show’s acknowledgment of class dynamics, like how “Ethan makes fun of Abi for working so hard, but that’s how she affords her rent”. She was encouraged to keep her native Liverpool accent and channel her own experiences as a “working-class northerner” into Abi, who leans into or plays down her accent depending on the situation – and occasionally slips in some scouse slang. (It was Fairn’s suggestion for Abi to call Sam a “jarg writer. Leo was like: I don’t even need to know what that means, that sounds hilarious!”)Even so, Ethan is quite obviously the comic engine. Like Reich himself, he is winningly self-deprecating, disarmingly frank, hyper-articulate and endlessly amusing company. There is naturally some crossover between him and Reich’s chronically narcissistic persona in Literally, Who Cares?! (he’s another “quite irritating gay guy because I can’t really do anything else”), but Ethan is aware of his own ridiculousness and can laugh at himself. And whereas the standup show was a precision-tooled piece of satire, It Gets Worse is a heartfelt paean to friendship and, in a weird way, a bit of “wish fulfilment” for its creator: he’s never lived in a grotty flat with friends, moving straight from his parents’ home to his own place.Leo Reich review – uproarious Gen-Z narcissist blazes throughRead moreThat said, any sentimentality is countered by a fierce joke rate, plus Reich’s aversion to cosy earnestness: he is still trying to send up his peers, just in a slightly more subtle way. “Sometimes I want to be made fun of by TV and I think the point of this is really lovingly making fun of everyone I’ve ever met.” Despite the real difficulties faced by gen Z, this is ultimately a show about “people who don’t have really, really serious problems complaining all the time”. For that reason, he’s anticipating at least some intergenerational pushback. “I don’t know if everyone’s always in the mood to hear a fine 27-year-old going: actually, being kind of scared of the future is really hard! It’s like: well, it’s not!”It Gets Worse begins 22 October on Channel 4 in the UK and Binge in Australia on 23 October.Explore more on these topicsTV comedyComedyTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content
