we learnedTate Britain missed the mark with breathlessly superficial exhibition of 90s art and fashionWhy children have always adored taking pictures – and what their images can tell usWhether your brain can handle a show that only has white paintingsThe Greek goddess Aphrodite was thrown on the rubbish heap in OxfordAustralia’s historic theatres and cinemas are the stuff of ritzy glamourA £110m gallery can still run the risk of looking like a fashion magskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTories could be in hot water after using Stanley Chow’s cartoon portrait of Andy ‘Bottler’ Burnham without consentMasterpiece of the weekAn Angel in Red With a Lute by Giovanni Ambrogio de Predis, c1495–1499View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Album/AlamyLeonardo da Vinci is said to have been sent to the court of Milan by Lorenzo de’ Medici to play on a bizarre stringed instrument of his own invention. His drawings do include inventions for novel musical devices. This painting is closely influenced by Leonardo: not only does it imitate his shadowed, dreamy style but it was originally part of the same altarpiece in Milan as his National Gallery masterpiece The Virgin of the Rocks. Leonardo, De Predis and every other Renaissance artist associated music with the mathematics of Pythagoras and the harmony of the universe: the angel here is playing, could we but hear it, such heavenly music. But it is the lute that suggests a very direct influence by Leonardo. The precise and detailed, entrancing way that De Predis depicts its nine strings and the angel’s highly realistic fingering echo Leonardo’s fascination with machinery and technology – in this case the sweet machinery of music. Painted under the hypnotic sway of the Tuscan polymath who was Milan’s court artist, this painting holds you charmed and soothed by the sound of silence.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in touchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsLondon listingsScotland and Ireland listingsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: In the Shadows review – true tale of Ramla Ali’s remarkable rise through the boxing ranks is a knockout | Movies | The Guardian
description: Jasmine Jobson goes the distance as the British-Somalian boxer battling pain from her past and her family’s disapproval in a heavyweight, tick-the-boxes production
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Jasmine Jobson goes the distance as the British-Somalian boxer battling pain from her past and her family’s disapproval in a heavyweight, tick-the-boxes production
Content: Fraught with danger … Jasmine Jobson in In the ShadowsView image in fullscreenFraught with danger … Jasmine Jobson in In the ShadowsMoviesReviewIn the Shadows review – true tale of Ramla Ali’s remarkable rise through the boxing ranks is a knockoutJasmine Jobson goes the distance as the British-Somalian boxer battling pain from her past and her family’s disapproval in a heavyweight, tick-the-boxes productionPeter BradshawFri 9 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe true-life success story of boxer Ramla Ali is confidently told in this capable picture from screenwriter Ursula Rani Sarma and documentary director Anthony Wonke, in his feature-film debut. Ali is the British-Somali boxer who escaped to the UK from the Somali civil war with her family as a refugee, and in 2021 became thefirst person to box for Somalia at Olympic Games. The boxing significance of her last name is actually not mentioned in the film – and I never noticed it until it flashed up in a kind of “fight card” intertitle before her first competitive bout.She is fiercely played by Jasmine Jobson, from TV’s Top Boy; her supportive white Muslim-convert husband Richard – a hugely important figure in enabling Ramla to break away from her disapproving family and do as she wants – is played by Finn Cole, and her abusive trainer Clinton is Gershwyn Eustache Jr. This is a film that takes you through the classic boxing-movie scenes fluently enough: the nervous first appearance in the gym, the overbearing quasi-parental coach, the heartstopping fight debut. It was good to see the traditional closeup of post-fight sore fists in the ice-bucket. All in all, the film works better thanGiant, the recent biopic of British-Yemeni boxer Prince Naseem, who is in fact briefly mentioned here.But devotees of the boxing film could be wondering … when will we see the all-important scene showing the boxer receive the character-building experience of failure? Of actually getting beaten? Well, Ramla suffers a concussion during a sparring match, but only because sinister and controlling Clinton deliberately puts her in the ring with someone of a higher weight class.This, though, is a boxing film with a difference and not just due to gender. Young Ramla fundamentally has to learn to box in secret. Her family would never allow such a pastime for a Muslim girl; she lives at home, with a job in a legal firm, having to train after work and telling her mum she is being kept late at the office. She genuinely appears to have no plan for what to do when they find out, although the idea of marrying Richard may have been a more fully formed idea than the film suggests. This means there is a layer of concealment and denial that doesn’t exist in women’s boxing films like, say, Clint Eastwood’s Million Dollar Baby with Hilary Swank or David Michôd’s Christy with Sydney Sweeney. There, the female boxer’s vocation, though naturally fraught with danger and patriarchal disapproval, is not frowned upon in the same way by her own community; perhaps a working-class white woman from a tough (but secular) background can afford to fight and has less (or nothing) to lose. That was not the case for Ali.In the Shadows is perhaps not groundbreaking, but it is a film with a real story to tell: a story about the pain that Ali suffered as a child inSomaliaand the heartbreak the family endured there, revealed indirectly in flashback, which was mysteriously transformed into her determination to box her way out of the tragic past. It is a strong performance from Jobson.In the Shadows screened at the London film festival and is in UK and Irish cinemas from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsBoxingBiopicsSomaliaOlympic GamesAfricareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tenzing review – reconstruction of first summit of Everest puts Sherpa at the centre of the story | Movies | The Guardian
description: Genden Phuntsok brings charm and innocence to his portrayal of Tenzing Norgay, while Tom Hiddleston is suitably frank as Edmund Hillary
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Genden Phuntsok brings charm and innocence to his portrayal of Tenzing Norgay, while Tom Hiddleston is suitably frank as Edmund Hillary
Content: ‘Not exactly a bromance’ … Tom Hiddleston and Genden Phuntsok in Tenzing.Photograph: Apple TV/APView image in fullscreen‘Not exactly a bromance’ … Tom Hiddleston and Genden Phuntsok in Tenzing.Photograph: Apple TV/APMoviesReviewTenzing review – reconstruction of first summit of Everest puts Sherpa at the centre of the storyGenden Phuntsok brings charm and innocence to his portrayal of Tenzing Norgay, while Tom Hiddleston is suitably frank as Edmund HillaryPeter BradshawFri 9 Oct 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 14.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a well intentioned, watchable, if sometimes soft-edged film with some NatGeo production values and VFX jeopardy on high mountain peaks. The subject is the triumphantMount Everestexpedition of 1953, in which the ultimate ascent was achieved by Nepalese-Indian mountaineer Tenzing Norgay and New Zealander Edmund Hillary.Tenzing, a former Sherpa guide whose unparalleled knowledge of the mountain and exemplary climbing skills earned him promotion to full team member, is played here by Tibetan actor Genden Phuntsok, while Hillary is robustly portrayed by Tom Hiddleston. Screenwriter Luke Davies and director Jennifer Peedom have the decent aim of restoring Tenzing’s achievement to the centre of the narrative, a tale which at the time was resoundingly claimed for Hillary and the British empire: a glorious redemption of Scott’s Antarctic ordeal 41 years earlier and a sign of divine approval for the imminent coronation of Queen Elizabeth II.For years, many assumed that Tenzing was somehow Hillary’s servant or military-style batman, a Sancho Panza figure to whom Hillary had just been sentimentally loyal. But Tenzing is the hero of this story, and the narrative of the great climb with Hillary and expedition leader John Hunt (Willem Dafoe) is interspersed with flashbacks to his early life – not Hillary’s – starting with his awestruck childhood encounter with the legendary British alpinist George Mallory, played in cameo by Johnny Flynn. He starts as an eager boy, passionate about the mountain, for which he uses the Tibetan name Chomolungma (though the name “Mount Everest” is not here stigmatised like “Ayers Rock” or “Snowdon”). His biddable good nature and instinctive mastery of the terrain makes him indispensable to other countries’ expeditions (although these are not featured in the flashback sections) and, finally, to the British.There are vertiginous moments of peril in the climb, but this is not exactly a bromance between Tenzing and Hillary; it is more a romance between Tenzing and the mountain. Nor is it specifically a rebuke to British imperial arrogance; both men were in their way outsiders to the stiff-upper-lip British club. Hiddleston plays Hillary as frank, thoughtful, practical, with no side to him; Phuntsok maintains Tenzing’s boyish innocence. Would a Tibetan film-maker have immersed us even more thoroughly in Tenzing’s world and excluded the British more? Maybe. At any rate, Genden Phuntsok’s charm carries the picture.Tenzing is in Australian cinemas from 8 October, UK and US cinemas from 9 October, and on Apple TV from 16 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsBiopicsMountaineeringMount EverestNepalSouth and central AsiareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Other Mommy review – Jessica Chastain’s demonic double horror isn’t nightmarish enough | Jessica Chastain | The Guardian
description: There’s some effectively unnerving imagery and a cleverly icy dual lead performance but this kept-from-critics shocker is a bit of a jumble
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: There’s some effectively unnerving imagery and a cleverly icy dual lead performance but this kept-from-critics shocker is a bit of a jumble
Content: Jessica Chastain in Other Mommy.Photograph: Photo Credit: Bernard Walsh/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreenJessica Chastain in Other Mommy.Photograph: Photo Credit: Bernard Walsh/Universal PicturesJessica ChastainReviewOther Mommy review – Jessica Chastain’s demonic double horror isn’t nightmarish enoughThere’s some effectively unnerving imagery and a cleverly icy dual lead performance but this kept-from-critics shocker is a bit of a jumbleBenjamin LeeFri 9 Oct 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe buzz surrounding theviral, limb-bending trailerof pre-Halloween horror Other Mommy was such that screen grabs became memes, official YouTube channel views ran up to 30m-plus and BuzzFeed used the extremely BuzzFeedheadline: “The Lady Sitting Next To Me SCREAMED”: This Trailer Playing Before The Odyssey Is Scaring Moviegoers, And These Hilarious Reactions Have Me Crying.Matchbox: the Movie review – as pointless as a film based on a toy car could beRead moreSure, Universal releasing it exclusively attached to the second biggest film of the year played a considerable part but the imagerywasefficiently direct and frightening, a derivative scared child/creepy demon set-up turned into something that felt hard to deny and increasingly impossible to avoid. But then what had seemed like the surest slam-dunk horror of the season seemed to slither away. The marketing continued (there was a second trailer that didn’t quite break the internet in the same way) but the reviews never appeared, a choice made to hide the film from critics until the day it opened. It’s a strategic decision that implies a disaster, Universal eager to keep pre-ticket sales high (it’s predicted to win the weekend with $20m-plus) and bad reviews at bay. But instead, as is often the case, it’s less of a one-star train wreck and more of a two-star mess, likely to frustrate rather than enrage.It’s based on the Bird Box author Josh Malerman’s acclaimed novel Incidents Around the House and the more obvious title change is the clearest indication of what’s shifted from page to screen. Other Mommy is less interested in the slow-burn and more focused on the instant blaze, a rickety fairground ride filled with loud jolts and skin-tearing gore. British director Rob Savage has bragged that his film features 50 jump scares, that’s about one every two minutes, a boast that also indicates his exhausting priorities.What’s strange is how unjumpy the film then is and how more interesting it feels when Savage isn’t trying to spill our popcorn. The Other Mommy is a double of working mother Ursula (Jessica Chastain), who has become a secret friend of young daughter Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark). She’s a demon who wants to become human and by impersonating Bela’s mother, she hopes that faking a deep connection will allow her “into her heart”. In a rather rushed fashion, Other Mommy’s campaign goes from teaser to full-court press.Chastain is an actor who isn’t always a great fit, her admirable avoidance of being typecast leading to a too-wide variety of roles that just don’t always feel well suited. But her elegant iciness works wonders here, selling both a hard-working parent who struggles to soften at home and an untrustworthy monster trying to find the right emotional mode and facial expressions to convince a child that she isn’t nefarious. Both mommies are desperate to win her over and Chastain works hard to win us over in the process even if her overpronounced smile, used as the poster’s main image, is a little too reminiscent of the Smile series.The rules of Other Mommy can also get a little scrambled. In trying to make Bela believe she is the gentle, loving and understanding parent she really needs, I’m not quite sure why she would keep presenting in such ghoulish and monstrous ways other than to scare those of us watching. The little blips are effective – the wrong amount of fingers, an accidental skin slip on her face – but too soon we have full-on gloopy body horror. The film can often feel like a loosely connected series of set pieces rather than a complete and cohesive story, something Chastain has experienced before in the It movies, which felt more like overlong trailers.Savage managed to make one of the only genuinely necessary Covid movies with the ingenious Zoom horrorHost, but his studio outings have so far lacked the same creative spark. Technically he proves himself once again here – as he did in the slickly made yet generic Stephen King adaptationThe Boogeyman– but he’s in danger of becoming a studio horror director for hire rather than one with his own clear voice. There’s a slight sense of confused panic to his choices as he throws a little too much at the wall, Other Mommy’s abilities and guises so varied that she starts to lose any real distinctiveness as a villain, turning into just some industry standard monster to be mechanically expelled. It’s even more of problem when the set-up of the film itself is already so familiar (even in the last decade, it recallsImaginary,M3gan,ZandCome Play) and, as is often the case with so many horror films in this moment, a lot less would do so much more.It’s also unclear how the two worlds are separated and operate, and while it’s refreshing to see characters all on the same page early on (both parents see Other Mommy within the first 20ish minutes), it’s then a struggle for the Succession screenwriter Nathan Elston to convincingly choreograph what comes next. Wouldn’t dad be a little more horrified earlier? Wouldn’t the police come calling after a gnarly midpoint death? Wouldn’t they not risk letting their daughter out of their sight? It’s amusingly grounded for a while (do we Google priests or mediums?) and there’s a neat and funny twist on what’s otherwise a rote Insidious-aping sequence, but the smarter ideas are mostly picked up briefly then dropped in favour of more basic funhouse horror. The psychological chaos inflicted by Other Mommy – pitting Bela against her parents, doing her bidding to try to impress her, forcing her to decide between the love she wants and the love she needs – is far scarier than yet more snappy but repetitive VFX. This wrestle is most apparent in the finale, which goes full house-rattling Poltergeist hokum and lightens the novel’s bleaker ending.There’s a chillier, quieter version of Other Mommy that could have really crept under our skin, but Savage is too busy trying to give us a heart attack to care if he gives us nightmares.Other Mommy is out in cinemas nowExplore more on these topicsJessica ChastainHorror filmsThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Old-timey fascism was kept secret. Now you don’t have to hide it’: Martin McDonagh, John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell on Wild Horse Nine | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: McDonagh’s latest film has Malkovich and Rockwell shooting the breeze as CIA agents in 1973 on Easter Island. They discuss grandchildren, swimming with turtles and who shot JFK
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: McDonagh’s latest film has Malkovich and Rockwell shooting the breeze as CIA agents in 1973 on Easter Island. They discuss grandchildren, swimming with turtles and who shot JFK
Content: I now pronounce you … Sam Rockwell, John Malkovich and Martin McDonagh.Photograph: Giulia ParmigianiView image in fullscreenI now pronounce you … Sam Rockwell, John Malkovich and Martin McDonagh.Photograph: Giulia ParmigianiVenice film festivalInterview‘Old-timey fascism was kept secret. Now you don’t have to hide it’: Martin McDonagh, John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell on Wild Horse NineXan BrooksMcDonagh’s latest film has Malkovich and Rockwell shooting the breeze as CIA agents in 1973 on Easter Island. They discuss grandchildren, swimming with turtles and who shot JFKFri 9 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Earmuffs!” says Sam Rockwell, pausing his gushing tribute mid-flow and turning to faceJohn Malkovichon the couch. Rockwell loves Malkovich and has been discussing his work at some length. Malkovich, he says, is charismatic and dangerous, half masculine, half feminine; a unique combination and the perfect sparring partner. He’s one of the world’s finest actors and annoyingly modest to boot. “Earmuffs!” says Rockwell and pivots back towards me. “He hates hearing all this. That’s why I keep saying ‘earmuffs’.”Malkovich frowns. “I don’t mind it,” he says.“Hates it,” says Rockwell. “He truly hates all this stuff.”In Martin McDonagh’sWild Horse Nine, Malkovich and Rockwell play bickering CIA agents who may also be the best of friends. Chris and Lee are fresh from plotting the 1973 coup in Chile and are spinning their wheels on Rapa Nui, amid the crashing waves and the moai statues. They’ve seen too much and sinned too greatly and now Chris has cancer, which is hardly helping his mood. So he takes Lee aside and asks for one last big favour.Ahead of the film’s premiere, the production team commandeer suites at an opulent Venice hotel and hand out hats and T-shirts to each new arrival. The lobby becomes a sea of merch. The harried concierge has to raise his voice to be heard. He says: “Second floor for the Six White Horses press interviews.”McDonagh makes films that are playful and volatile, spring-loaded with violence and spiced with absurdist black comedy. Wild Horse Nine nods to In Bruges andThe Banshees of Inisherinwith its odd-couple antics and explosive side notes. But its mood is more mournful, death-haunted, with one eye on the past. McDonagh – once the upstart enfant terrible of London theatre – is now a silver-haired 56-year-old who comes at life from a different angle. “I’m getting older,” he says. “Maybe this is my first old-man movie.”On sitting down to script Wild Horse Nine, the film-maker wrote GUILT and REGRET at the top of page one, as though setting his course with a compass and sextant. His film opens in Santiago before relocating to the South Pacific. From there it homes in on Malkovich’s CIA veteran, a leaky repository of cold war horror with his memories of the Bay of Pigs and Dealey Plaza. Chris is likely dying and wants to go out with a bang. He claims that he knows who killed JFK and is about to spill the beans.View image in fullscreenIn focus … Sam Rockwell as Lee and John Malkovich as Chris in Wild Horse Nine.Photograph: Diego Araya Corvalán/Searchlight PicturesThe Kennedy assassination is the God particle of conspiracy theories. It marked the loss of US innocence, or the start of the rot of disinformation and fake news. McDonagh knows the official version and remains breezily unconvinced. “I definitely think there was something going on,” he says. “I’m definitely a believer in the conspiracy. Exactly what that was, we’ll never really know. Was Lee Harvey Oswald involved? More than likely. Was he the lone gunman? I don’t believe that for a second.”Martin McDonagh says CIA has ‘done awful things all around the world’Read moreHe’s made several pictures with Woody Harrelson. Wasn’t Harrelson’s father once rumoured to have been involved in the killing? McDonagh sits up and mimes zipping his lip. “I know nothing,” he says.Wild Horse Nine was never intended as a comment on the present-day United States. Except that history has a tendency to repeat and the shoot coincided with Donald Trump’s strike on Venezuela. Operations like that used to be more covert, conducted via proxies, whereas now they seem brazen, the equivalent of a smash-and-grab raid. “But I don’t think Trump is the worst president that we’ve had,” he says. “I don’t even think he’s the worst in the past 60-years. Nixon was more of a fascist pig. George W Bush probably killed more people than Trump. And then if you look at Vietnam, there’s Johnson. The difference is that with old-timey fascism, you at least had to keep it secret. These days you don’t have to hide it any more. Is that more fucked? Or is it more honest?”McDonagh sits behind one closed door; Rockwell and Malkovich behind another. On-screen or off, the two actors have different energies, different speeds, so that the interview feels like a private performance: the Energizer Bunny versus the all-seeing Sphinx. One of these men has left his sunglasses on the floor. Inevitably it is Rockwell, who is altogether more bouncy and heedless. “My Guccis,” he cries. “Oh man, I would have stepped on those.”View image in fullscreenOn location … the director Martin McDonagh with John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell in Rapa Nui.Photograph: Diego Araya Corvalán/Searchlight PicturesRockwell won an Oscar for playing the bumptious small-town deputy in McDonagh’sThree Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri. Malkovich may well follow suit thanks to Wild Horse Nine, which goes on to receive a rapturous 13-minute ovation at the premiere. The 72-year-old is on fabulously flavourful form as Chris, a tragicomic monster who is simultaneously melting down and seeing the light, lashing out and making amends. The character plays to the actor’s natural strengths, mining his innate theatricality and enigmatic air. But he explains that the role required some heavy lifting as well. Endless rehearsals and hours of line-readings, he says. “Sam and I did each scene at least a thousand times.”A thousand? Malkovich is so self-contained and unblinking, it’s hard to know when he’s joking.Rockwell chips in. “Yeah, about a thousand times. We ran it on the weekends. John’s a workhorse.”“You are, too,” Malkovich says. It’s good to have a co-star to rehearse with, he adds, although every good actor has their own way of working. Clint Eastwood, for instance, prefers to hit the ground running. “You have to be a slick talker to get more than two takes out of Clint. You have to be pretty convincing, because he doesn’t take that lightly. As I know from experience.”They were on Rapa Nui for six weeks, which helped with the process. “I have two granddaughters, so it was a long time away from them,” he says. “I don’t like being away from my grandchildren. But it’s a great place to shoot because there’s nothing else to do. You can swim with the turtles but that’s about it. Your work days are long. You’re always prepping for tomorrow. If it weren’t for a movie, I’d probably go nuts.”Rockwell enjoyed it. “We had a great time,” he says. “Every night we had a little Chile wine and some rum. And there was a drink made with sugarcane, what the hell was it called? They put an egg-white in it.”You can handle the truth! Why cinema suddenly loves conspiracy theoriesRead moreHis partner, the actor Leslie Bibb, has materialised in the doorway. “Pisco sour,” she says.“Pisco sour!” He’s delighted to see her and glad of the intel. Bibb has swung by to check when Rockwell breaks for lunch. He introduces her to me and indicates Malkovich on the couch. “But you can’t miss John,” he says. “Look at him, he’s beautiful.”Marooned on his island, Chris plans to write his memoirs and come clean. His bosses are terrified he’ll mention “the Dallas parts” of his story. Some secrets, they feel, must be taken to the grave.Malkovich has played heroes and villains. He’s been Tom Ripley, Biff Loman and the Vicomte de Valmont. But his career has been long and he’s covered this particular topic before. In 1994, he adapted and directed a stage version of Libra, Don DeLillo’s novel about Lee Harvey Oswald. He studied the Zapruder footage of JFK’s final moments and wandered down several conspiracy rabbit holes. The Warren Commission’s findings, he concluded, were either flawed or a lie. And if that makes him a crank, he’s hardly in the minority.“Well, I think 60% of the American public don’t believe it,” he says. “Could the official story be true? Yeah, I guess. So could Keebler elves. The government tells us all kinds of things. Some of them may be true but not the majority of them, that’s my experience.”View image in fullscreenHeading for trouble? John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyI’ve read that he hasn’t voted since the 1972 presidential election, when the liberal George McGovern lost in a landslide to Nixon. He nods; this is true. “I’m not a believer,” he says.Not a believer in what? Democracy? Malkovich shrugs. “In the whole thing, really. As they say in France: ‘Je ne pratique pas’, I’m not practising. I remember the night McGovern lost. I was talking to my father on the phone and I said: ‘Well, I’m done.’ He said: ‘My God, John, you can’t be done.’ I was 19 years old but that was it, I was done. I concentrate on what I can make and leave it at that.”What about Rockwell? Is he still practising? “Yeah, well, I vote,” he says glumly. “I vote with faint hope. Hoping Obama will come back.”The publicist sticks her head around the door. She reports that lunch is almost ready, which means that we’ve reached the last question. Rockwell perks up. “No pressure,” he says.Let’s finish with death. That’s where the whole film is leading. Chris has decided he wants to die on Rapa Nui. Then he changes his mind and opts for Venice instead. Assuming that a death can be scripted like a film, where in the world would be the ideal place to bow out?Malkovich thinks for a moment. “Probably on stage,” he says. “About 15 years ago I toured with a new opera based on Casanova’s memoirs. It started with Casanova chasing a chambermaid around the stage, as he was known to do, and then he has a heart attack. The play stops and people come out with a stretcher and then everyone breaks into song. Before the performance, I always made sure to tell all my friends: ‘It’s just the beginning of the play. I fake a heart attack. Don’t pay any attention.’ But forgot to tell my then-agent and I don’t think she has ever forgiven me.”A few nights after that, he made the exact same mistake. “I have a friend, Barbara Sturm, who is a knee doctor in Düsseldorf. She came to see me and I suddenly realised I hadn’t warned her either. So I tried to text from the dressing room but of course she already had her phone switched off, being a well-mannered person. And so blah-blah-blah, the whole thing happened again.”The production was pure chaos, but it was also rather funny. Every night he’d fake a coronary and see the panic sweep through the audience like wildfire. “As many as 20 people would run up to the stage. You’d have the doctors and a stretcher and then everybody starts singing.”Rockwell is laughing. “That’s good acting,” he says.“Well no, it’s terrible,” says Malkovich. “But still, it wouldn’t be the worst way to go.”Wild Horse Nine is released in the US, UK and Ireland on 6 November and in Australia on 5 NovemberExplore more on these topicsVenice film festivalMartin McDonaghSam RockwellJohn MalkovichJohn F KennedyFestivalsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the fizzing fuzz-pop racket of Pushbike and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Drawing from post-hardcore, twee and emo, the Exeter trio’s intoxicating energy feels like an invitation to form your own band
Author: Huw Baines
Headline: Drawing from post-hardcore, twee and emo, the Exeter trio’s intoxicating energy feels like an invitation to form your own band
Content: A rowdy proposition … Pushbike.Photograph: Courtesy of Molly BonifaceView image in fullscreenA rowdy proposition … Pushbike.Photograph: Courtesy of Molly BonifaceAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the fizzing fuzz-pop racket of Pushbike and the week’s best new tracksDrawing from post-hardcore, twee and emo, the Exeter trio’s intoxicating energy feels like an invitation to form your own bandHuw Baines,Michael CraggandBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 9 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromExeter, UKRecommended if you likeBoyracer, the Promise Ring, Rites of SpringUp nextLittle Bastard EP out nowIt’s tempting to view any half-decent scene as either a magical happening or a simple quirk of geography and timing. In reality, they’re more like monuments to the importance of showing up. For that to continue to happen, you need bands like Pushbike. Rattling through four songs in well under 10 minutes, each crooked hook, euphoric yelp and cheesewire guitar lead on their Little Bastard EP feels like an invitation to form a band, draw a flyer, or book a show.The trio – guitarist-vocalists George Gravell and Niall Ivie, alongside drummer Tom Grogan – are part of a Sarah Records-esque network orbiting Exeter’s Cavern venue, sustained in part by their own label, Spinning Sister, plus a smattering of zines and interlaced groups, from the wonkily brilliant powerpop outfit Bramwell to Ivie’s intriguing tape-hiss indie project Maeries.Pushbike are a rowdier proposition, cribbing from the abrasive ambition of mid-80s Washington DC post-hardcore as much as the twee racket of Boyracer, with their insistent fuzz-pop melodies calling to mind midwest emo grandees the Promise Ring. On Little Bastard, they cross these streams on the fizzing Pure Hate, which builds towards a throat-stripping display of emotion, while I Am the Pilot’s mile-a-minute drums create an irresistible, almost reckless, sense of momentum. Similarly, the loud-quiet-loud rager Rainham Steel will make you want to stomp a distortion pedal through the floor. Be honest: what’s stopping you?Huw BainesThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenPrepare for takeoff … Uniique3.Photograph: Lisa PerssonUniiqu3 – Airplane ModeDown your duty-free vodka, move your tray table to the upright position and party in the aisle: on the lead track from her newly announced debut album, the Jersey club ambassador turns air steward for this slamming peak-time slayer.BBTfawn burke– we can’t pretendA fizzy soda pop bop from the Los Angeles-based artist, vocalist, and songwriter that feels like the halfway point between a neon-streaked, hyperpopped Caroline Polachek and a big EDM head-knocker.MCLorenzo Senni – Art Life & Skateboarding (ft Chad Muska and Jamie Thomas)The Italian trance postmodernist is the purveyor of the most intensely euphoric live set imaginable, but has been away for six years. This welcome return features more gorgeous synth compression, plus pro skaters pondering life.BBTStar Moles – Born AgainPhiladelphia’s Emily Moales follows her critically lauded Highway to Hell album with this new single, a beautifully off-kilter indie-pop gem that focuses lyrically on the overwhelm of big emotions.MCSlayyyter – i think he’s got a girlThis year’s most likely to “do a Chappell Roan”, AKA upgrade from cult concern to bona fide pop superstar, returns with a chunky, guitar-slathered future live favourite anchored by a big, dumb throat-shredding chorus.MCPeverelist – Wreck IIAn absolutely addictive two-note electro motif propels this new one by the Bristol bass master, who keeps the dancefloor held down as a centrifugal whirl of sound thrums around it.BBTThe Cat’s Miaow – If You’re Lost, You Can Follow Me HomeMelbourne’s number one purveyors of elegantly crumpled jangle-pop return. Essentially 100 seconds of lilting guitar riffs and softly brushed drums, this latest single is a beautiful ode to those who care for the world’s lost strays.MCSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistPop and rockIndiePunkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Branford Marsalis Quartet and Dianne Reeves: Dedicated to You review – eloquent Coltrane tribute | Jazz | The Guardian
description: This elegant contemporary reinvention of 1963 album John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman pairs Marsalis’s post-bop sax with Reeves’ agile vocals, to time-stopping effect
Author: John Fordham
Headline: This elegant contemporary reinvention of 1963 album John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman pairs Marsalis’s post-bop sax with Reeves’ agile vocals, to time-stopping effect
Content: We say it’s wonderful … Branford Marsalis and Dianne Reeves.Photograph: Courtesy of Shervin LainezView image in fullscreenWe say it’s wonderful … Branford Marsalis and Dianne Reeves.Photograph: Courtesy of Shervin LainezJazz album of the monthJazzReviewBranford Marsalis Quartet and Dianne Reeves: Dedicated to You review – eloquent Coltrane tribute(Blue Note)This elegant contemporary reinvention of 1963 album John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman pairs Marsalis’s post-bop sax with Reeves’ agile vocals, to time-stopping effectJohn FordhamFri 9 Oct 2026 04.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early 1960s, the Impulse! label tried to steer its star saxophonist John Coltrane away from increasingly uncompromising and experimental music that it feared might be scaring its customers. Label boss Bob Thiele suggested a more palatable all-ballads album with a little-known African American supper-club singer called Johnny Hartman, whose warm, Bing Crosby-like baritone but bracing absence of schmaltz had already impressed Frank Sinatra and Tony Bennett. Coltrane and Hartman hit it off perfectly, and the 1963 album, John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman, was an unexpected mini masterpiece of restraint, flawless timbral expressiveness, and mutual understanding.View image in fullscreenBranford Marsalis and Dianne Reeves: Dedicated to You album coverInvited by Blue Note Records in Coltrane’s centenary year to curate his own tribute, post-bop sax luminary Branford Marsalis made that album the template for Dedicated to You – done as contemporary reinventions, not mere cover versions. Marsalis invited Dianne Reeves, a vastly experienced jazz singer with a Sarah Vaughan-like mix of flawless intonation and agile spontaneity, to take the vocal role. “Listening to all the great singers coming up”, Reeves has said, “I learned that they stood in the band, not in front of the band. They saw themselves as co-creators of the sound.”Marsalis’s tenor murmurs and twists behind Reeves’ juggling of nostalgia and hope on Autumn Serenade, and the title track makes time stand still in its cherishing of every word and sound. Lush Life’s famous small-hours ruminating on life’s mistakes is reinvented in Reeves’ almost defiant resignation and the sleepy languor of the tenor sax and piano, while her slyly taunting stretch of the syllables of “won-der-ful” unerringly nails the love-is-fab irony of They Say It’s Wonderful.Marsalis adds Trane instrumentals from the same period here, including the exhilaratingly beboppish soprano feature Big Nick, a hurtling Charlie Parkeresque genuflection on the uptempo 26-2, plus three bonus tracks engagingly balancing the vocal and jazz-instrumental eloquence of this fine album.Also out this monthThe prodigiously eclectic German pianistMichael Wollnyreleases the solo-piano set Eine Winterreise (ACT), a rumination on the Schubert song cycle that the pianist typically recasts as “a meditation on walking – on moving forward without having any reliable guidance, without a fixed destination”. Wollny relishes abstract sound, improv, and jazz phrasing, but his idiomatic range is profound. Alongside Schubert’s themes, Kate Bush’s Snowflake gets a glisteningly awestruck treatment here, as does Björk’s Aurora, as Wollny continues – unintentionally – to reinforce his stature as a piano visionary in the league of Jarrett, Hancock or Mehldau. London harpist/vocalistTara Mintonunveils a sensitive interweaving of Latin American rhythmic ideas and Spanish and English lyrics on her distinctive autobiographical set The Devil Invites You to Dance (Adhyâropa Records), while pianist/composerMyra Melford’s Fire and Water Quintet, including guitarist Mary Halvorson and cellist Tomeka Reid, delivers Sure Grand Out (RogueArt), her compelling third exploration of sonic parallels for the physicality, animation and grace of painter Cy Twombly’s work.Explore more on these topicsJazzJazz album of the monthalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Jess Williamson: A Mile South of Heaven review – alt-country singer’s love-hate affair with LA | Music | The Guardian
description: Following 2023 breakout Time Ain’t Accidental, the best songs here are when Williamson strips back country music, rebuilding it as something familiar yet different
Author: Aimee Cliff
Headline: Following 2023 breakout Time Ain’t Accidental, the best songs here are when Williamson strips back country music, rebuilding it as something familiar yet different
Content: Nostalgic … Jess Williamson.Photograph: Courtesy of  Jackie Lee YoungView image in fullscreenNostalgic … Jess Williamson.Photograph: Courtesy of  Jackie Lee YoungMusicReviewJess Williamson: A Mile South of Heaven review – alt-country singer’s love-hate affair with LA(New West)Following 2023 breakout Time Ain’t Accidental, the best songs here are when Williamson strips back country music, rebuilding it as something familiar yet differentAimee CliffFri 9 Oct 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn her essay Goodbye to All That,Joan Didion writes that she left New York City when “the golden rhythm was broken”. Texas-born alt-country singer Jess Williamson borrows the title for the aching opening track of her sixth solo album, on which she contemplates whether she has had enough of Los Angeles. But while Didion was looking back on leaving the city of her youth behind, Williamson is still in LA, wrestling with competing desires to stay or flee.View image in fullscreenJess Williamson: A Mile South of Heaven.Photograph: Courtesy of  Jackie Lee YoungThis tumultuous love-me, love-me-not is set to Williamson’s most traditional soundscapes to date: “Deep in the woods I feel the hum of the city,” she sings on Hum of the City in her strongest Texas drawl over mournful strings and twiddling banjo. Gone are the iPhone-programmed drums that made her 2023 breakout Time Ain’t Accidental so appealingly offbeat, and while the Americana flourishes give weight to Williamson’s nostalgia for her native Dallas, at times they make the album stodgier and less imaginative than her previous record.A Mile South of Heaven’s most intriguing moments come when she strips country music back to its bare essentials, rebuilding it as something that looks uncannily similar yet different. Take the sparse climate anxiety meditation Tracking the Tropics, backed by eerie Mellotron, with even the hand claps sounding sinister. Or album closer The Gem and Mineral Show, in which Williamson recalls sipping champagne with a pop star, and chills with a visceral, unadorned ending as she sings of the loneliness of being a perpetual tourist. On this record, homesickness is a constant no matter where you go, and every note is packed with yearning.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Shostakovich Symphony No 8 album review – composer’s cry of despair in a remarkable and resonant new recording | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Conductor Alain Altinoglu brings weight and purpose while the instrumental solos are piquant and precise.
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Conductor Alain Altinoglu brings weight and purpose while the instrumental solos are piquant and precise.
Content: Glorious … Frankfurt Radio Symphony.Photograph: Ben KnabeView image in fullscreenGlorious … Frankfurt Radio Symphony.Photograph: Ben KnabeClassical musicReviewShostakovich Symphony No 8 album review – composer’s cry of despair in a remarkable and resonant new recordingFrankfurt Radio Symphony/Altinoglu(Alpha)Conductor Alain Altinoglu brings weight and purpose while the instrumental solos are piquant and precise.Clive PagetFri 9 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf the Leningrad was Shostakovich’s official response to the second world war, the Eighth Symphony was his answer to the question: “Will you tell us what you really think?” Written while the fighting was still under way, its immediacy remains striking today, a quality reflected in Alain Altinoglu’s purposeful interpretation with the Frankfurt Radio Symphony orchestra.View image in fullscreenSchostakovich Symphony No 8 album coverYou hear that directness at once in the way the strings dig deep, bringing remarkable colours to a 26-minute Adagio that, in the wrong hands, can sound merely bleak and black. Not that Altinoglu shuns the horrors: his phrasing and textural dynamics bring fearsome weight and a sense of wide-eyed terror to the composer’s protracted cry of despair. The orchestra covers itself in glory with instrumental solos that are piquant and precise. Resonant details are captured by an outstanding German production team that manages to outdo the Berlin Philharmonic’s excellent 2020 account under Kirill Petrenko (Shostakovich fans will need both).The second movement, a portrait perhaps of the Nazi war machine, and the third with its visceral depiction of the battlefield, shriek with terror and, here and there, the blackest humour. The passacaglia that follows is a keening survey of what has come before, leading to a shellshocked finale that balances cynicism with compassion. With persuasive accounts of the fourth and fifth symphonies released last year, this is shaping up to be an important series.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: AK Blakemore: ‘The Goldfinch by Donna Tartt was extremely silly and bad’ | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The poet and author on F Scott Fitzgerald’s perfect novel, losing faith in Ernest Hemingway – and the recent debut that blew her away
Author: AK Blakemore
Headline: The poet and author on F Scott Fitzgerald’s perfect novel, losing faith in Ernest Hemingway – and the recent debut that blew her away
Content: ‘I often find myself revisiting Virginia Woolf’s Orlando’ … AK Blakemore.Photograph: Alice ZooView image in fullscreen‘I often find myself revisiting Virginia Woolf’s Orlando’ … AK Blakemore.Photograph: Alice ZooThe books of my lifeFictionAK Blakemore: ‘The Goldfinch by Donna Tartt was extremely silly and bad’The poet and author on F Scott Fitzgerald’s perfect novel, losing faith in Ernest Hemingway – and the recent debut that blew her awayAK BlakemoreFri 9 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryLynley Dodd’s Hairy Maclary from Donaldson’s Dairy – where an assortment of differently shaped dogs go on a walk – wormed its way into my subconscious when I was very young. The great dane (Hercules Morse, as big as a horse), the dalmatian (Bottomley Potts, covered in spots), the dachshund (Schnitzel Von Krumm with a very low tum) … I could probably still recite most of it from memory.My favourite book growing upI had a lot of picture books illustrated by the great Korky Paul, and remember being obsessed – even as quite a young child – with the intricate grotesquerie of it all. He’s probably best known these days for illustrating the Winnie the Witch books, but my favourite was The Rascally Cake by Jeanne Willis, in which a rotund, green-haired man called Rufus Skumskins O’Parsley makes a cake out of disgusting things (rotten eggs, spider legs, garden snails and so on), only for the cake to come to life and attempt to eathim. Probably more than a little bit of Skumskins found its way into the protagonist of my second novel, The Glutton.The book that changed me as a teenagerI studied F Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby for my English GCSE and it entirely reshaped my brain. I still think it’s about as near to perfect as it’s possible for a novel to be. All the stupid loveliness and yearning in the world, distilled down into image after image, with a core of white-hot rage, at the way extreme wealth enables – necessitates, really – extreme cruelty. There’s functional alcoholism, and then there’s whatever Fitzgerald was doing in 1923. Everyone should read it.The writer who changed my mindI had a baby in May, and in the first weeks post-partum I read Of Woman Born: Motherhood as Experience and Institution, by the poet and activist Adrienne Rich, while my son was napping on my belly.It made me realise that I’d wrongly – though, perhaps, understandably – held on to this notion that mothering would necessarily mean setting aside the work of the imagination, and a narrowing of my horizons, creatively. But Rich writes so thrillingly of parenthood as a politically radicalising and artistically activating experience. Rich’s work has made me excited for the years to come as a writer, as well as a mother. I wish I’d read her a long, long time ago.The book that made me want to be a writerPortrait of My Lover As a Horse by Selima Hill.I bought it with a book voucher in Foyles on Charing Cross Road, when I was about 14. I’d never heard of Hill, but I picked it up based on the strangeness of the title and cover. All of Hill’s poetry collections, as published by Bloodaxe, have this naive, under-designed quality to them. I read the whole collection front-to-back on the train home, and then again back-to-front. By the next day I was trying to emulate Hill’s guileless, cryptic style in my own – far less masterly – little poems. That was basically my apprenticeship as a poet.Theauthor I came back toJane Austen. Until my mid-20s I subscribed to that surprisingly common, reductive view of her as the author exclusively of novels about rich people having dinner at each other’s houses. But now I’m a rich person (in global terms, at least – I mean, I have Chanel foundation and a mortgage) who likes having dinner at other people’s houses, I’m like,this rules.The book I rereadI often find myself revisiting bits of Virginia Woolf’s Orlando. In case you aren’t aware of it, it’s about a gender-swapping and functionally immortal Elizabethan nobleman who spends several languid centuries falling in and out of love and eventually achieving something like self-knowledge. Such a totally exhilarating, audaciously fun bit of work from an author who was – bless her – a bit of a Debbie Downer overall.The book I could never read againThe Sun Also Rises. I was worryingly into Ernest Hemingway, for a teenage girl, whereas now I think he’s a bit of a pillock.The book I discovered later in lifeI’m 35 so I flatter myself nothing I could say really counts, but: I thought I’d use my maternity leave to finally give some Donna Tartt a go. I staggered through The Goldfinch and thought it was extremely silly and bad.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe book I am currently readingI just finishedWhat Am I, a Deer?by Polly Barton, and I was totally blown away by it. It’s about how we have fun and what we find funny, how we choose our friends and construct our pet fantasies, and I loved it, and I love how Barton’s brain works. She thinks so profoundly about the minutiae of modern life and modern social dynamics and I somehow found myself feeling strangely optimistic about the world and the eccentricities of the people in it. A banger.Doom Painting by AK Blakemore is published by Granta. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFictionThe books of my lifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundup | Science fiction books | The Guardian
description: The Ballad of Black Tom by Victor LaValle; As You Wake, Break the Shell by Becky Chambers; The Eye of Goliath by Diego Muzzio; Our Cut of Salt by Deena Helm
Author: Lisa Tuttle
Headline: The Ballad of Black Tom by Victor LaValle; As You Wake, Break the Shell by Becky Chambers; The Eye of Goliath by Diego Muzzio; Our Cut of Salt by Deena Helm
Content: The Eye of Goliath reimagines The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, adapted for film in 1931.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Eye of Goliath reimagines The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, adapted for film in 1931.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyScience fiction roundupScience fiction booksReviewThe best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundupThe Ballad of Black Tom by Victor LaValle; As You Wake, Break the Shell by Becky Chambers; The Eye of Goliath by Diego Muzzio; Our Cut of Salt by Deena HelmLisa TuttleFri 9 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenThe Ballad of Black Tomby Victor LaValle(Penguin, £9.99)This short novel won almost every genre award following its 2016 US publication. As a Black writer, LaValle had a conflicted relationship with the works of HP Lovecraft. As a child, he loved the tales of cosmic horror, but grew to recognise the racism and other prejudices of the author. Unable to “throw the man’s stories away” because of how formative they were on his own imagination, he decided to write his own response to one of the most obviously racist, The Horror at Red Hook, recasting it through the perspective of a musician and hustler from 1920s Harlem later known as Black Tom. It’s a powerful tale of horror – both everyday and the occult – told with sheer brilliance.View image in fullscreenAs You Wake, Break the Shellby Becky Chambers(Hodderscape, £22)In this cosy science fiction love story set on a distant planet, life is a constant struggle for the human colonists. As the book opens, botanist Signy is yet to meet the love of her life, Cora, a rorqual pilot. Rorquals are gigantic interplanetary creatures, trained by human pilots whose implants allow them to communicate with the beasts as they transport supplies. Chapter 1 is followed by chapter 764, set more than a decade later, when the two women are blissfully married. The non-linear narrative may reflect what we’re told is the rorqual view of time, but it also removes much suspense. The characters are adorable, and the details of growing plants in an artificial environment, or Cora’s relationship with her rorqual, are enjoyable, but readers may grow impatient with the glacial pace and reiterations of their feelings for one another. Even the “naturally solitary” rorqual is given to declaring its love for Cora. In the final pages there’s a tonal shift that ends on a cliffhanger: how Cora and Signy survive is to be revealed in a sequel.View image in fullscreenThe Eye of Goliathby Diego Muzzio,translated by Rahul Bery(Pushkin, £12.99)This first novel by an award-winning Argentinian writer is an old-fashioned tale of madness and the horrors of war. In an asylum on the outskirts of Edinburgh, circa 1920, Dr Pierce hopes to cure severely traumatised patients by hypnosis. All the men, including the doctor, carry wounds from the first world war. His latest case, David Bradley, was an engineer, but is now unable to do anything but desperately attempt to swim on dry land, until overcome by exhaustion. Bradley’s diary reveals the reason behind the man’s gradual descent into madness, as, cold and starving in an abandoned lighthouse, the rescue he expects keeps failing to arrive. Bradley’s own discovery of papers left behind by the last lighthouse keeper, a naturalist with a talent for taxidermy who murdered his family, adds another interlocking piece to this irresistible, haunting gothic horror.View image in fullscreenOur Cut of Saltby Deena Helm(Orbit, £22)In 2002, Marina is a young American of mixed heritage who takes a trip to Haifa, the city where her Palestinian grandmother Nuhad was born and lived as a child, until the family was driven out by the Israeli occupation in 1948. Nuhad never spoke about that terrible time, and now that she is dead, Marina wants to understand. When she finds her grandmother’s house, it is empty, for sale, and generally known to be haunted. Previous occupants have either vanished or died in mysterious circumstances. Entering, she feels anger, but then a flood of happy memories from Nuhad’s childhood. The house is more than simply haunted – it has become a vessel for vengeance, channelling death while longing for a return of the family it loved. The author allows the house to speak, which jars with the more realistic approach taken elsewhere. Despite a few missteps, this is a powerful, affecting novel about Palestinian loss and trauma.Explore more on these topicsScience fiction booksScience fiction roundupFantasy booksHorror booksFictionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Queerest of Folk by Russell T Davies review – the groundbreaking screenwriter tells it like it is | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: From Coronation Street to It’s a Sin, Davies’ memoir of a career in TV is also a rallying cry for creativity
Author: Rebecca Nicholson
Headline: From Coronation Street to It’s a Sin, Davies’ memoir of a career in TV is also a rallying cry for creativity
Content: A scene from Aids-era drama It’s a Sin (2021)Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyView image in fullscreenA scene from Aids-era drama It’s a Sin (2021)Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyBook of the dayAutobiography and memoirReviewThe Queerest of Folk by Russell T Davies review – the groundbreaking screenwriter tells it like it isFrom Coronation Street to It’s a Sin, Davies’ memoir of a career in TV is also a rallying cry for creativityRebecca NicholsonFri 9 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 03.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTelevision is an intimate art form, once beamed into living rooms, now on devices right in front of our faces. The screenwriter Russell T Davies understands that intimacy. Whether discussing his early days developing lost-to-history soap spin-offs, making a splash with the pioneering gay seriesQueer As Folk, or reviving Doctor Who to great acclaim, he makes it feel as if you’re at the pub with him, settling in for the night, ready to hear his best stories.This warm and gossipy autobiography offers a peek behind the curtains of the British TV industry, and as such, it goes light on Davies’s own life story. Instead, he gallops through five decades in the business, using the framework of his TV shows to propel the book forward at great speed. He was born in Swansea in 1963, to a family who loved watching TV. While he was studying English at Oxford, a friend suggested that, as he thought television was so great, he should consider doing it as his job.That proved to be a lightbulb moment. Davies worked on children’s television, writing for puppets, before cutting his teeth at Granada Studios in Manchester, alongside Sally Wainwright, Paul Abbott and the great, late Kay Mellor. A little later, having created a period drama called The Grand, he found that viewers were turning off. Ladling on the misery with abuse, murder and a hanging obviously wasn’t working. There is another revelation: a friend tells him he is funny, so he should write like that. Afterwards, there is no stopping him.Humour drives Queer As Folk, one of his defining creations. It is hard to overstate the impact of the Channel 4 show, which came out in 1999. Back then, queer stories were still vanishingly rare and largely miserable. Industry people dismissed the idea, assuming that a story about gay men would be earnest and dull. The arrival of this funny, Technicolor and defiantly explicit series changed all that. In one of many amusing asides, Davies notes that it was going to be called Queer As Fuck, until a publicist pointed out that it would never be discussed by Richard and Judy. “That was a red line for me,” he quips.His other megahit was Doctor Who. He had written Doctor Who fandom into Queer As Folk, and when he revived the beloved sci-fi series in 2005 it appears to have been the fulfilment of a lifelong dream. His first Doctor was Christopher Eccleston, followed by David Tennant, and he returned after a long gap with Ncuti Gatwa, whose tenure was short-lived. Davies writes about it all with love, so anyone hoping for gossip will be disappointed. Even the collapse of a Disney deal and his second departure from the show are handled with grace.Early in the book, Davies pre-empts criticism by writing that he is going to call a lot of people “lovely”. He does. He loves Abbott and Mellor. He loves Billie Piper and David Tennant. Producers, directors: many of them, too, are lovely, and he loves them. But neither does he mince words when he feels like it. Gwyneth Paltrow, who said that she would feel “stifled” by the use of intimacy coordinators for sex scenes, gets short shrift. “How remote and numbed and privileged you are,” he writes, scathingly. He recalls a money meeting with Harvey Weinstein, and how unsettling it was to notice the producer’s “baleful power”. He had tense discussions with the producers of A Very English Scandal, who lectured him on how to make high-end television. “But you’ve never made any!” he retorted, adding that “Old Etonians should never take on a Swansea comprehensive boy in a scrap.”If, at times, Davies’ lightness of touch is tactful to the point of seeming coy, then elsewhere, his bluntness is bracing. His husband Andrew died of brain cancer in 2018, after eight years of illness. He writes about these years with a forceful and moving honesty. When people tell him that Andrew is looking down on him, he writes: “I always think, I fucking hope not!”He ends it with a manifesto for the future: a rallying cry for invention and creativity, a call for hope and optimism in the face of ongoing threats to the arts from autocrats, AI and collapsing budgets. He cheers for the likes of Baby Reindeer and I May Destroy You, while also celebrating The Traitors and The Chase. If Davies has an ethos of television, then it is that there is no high or low. He is thrillingly democratic about it all, whether a straight-to-VHSVegas-based Coronation Street specialorIt’s a Sin, his award-winning drama about the Aids epidemic. This is a warm and rousing tribute to British television.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: End Of Abyss review – a creepy dollhouse take on Resident Evil and The Thing | Games | The Guardian
description: This fetchingly presented horror game brings style and scares, but overextends itself with repetition
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This fetchingly presented horror game brings style and scares, but overextends itself with repetition
Content: Your little bobble-headed hero … End of Abyss video game screenshot.Photograph: Section 9/Epic Games PublishingView image in fullscreenYour little bobble-headed hero … End of Abyss video game screenshot.Photograph: Section 9/Epic Games PublishingGamesReviewEnd Of Abyss review – a creepy dollhouse take on Resident Evil and The ThingPlayStation 5 (version played), Xbox, PC; Epic Games PublishingThis fetchingly presented horror game brings style and scares, but overextends itself with repetitionAlex SpencerFri 9 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsmall band of soldiers enters an abandoned facility, where puckered flesh sprouts from cold steel. It’s a promising but familiar start to a sci-fi horror story, with heavy overtones of Alien and The Thing. Neither of those, though, were so … dinky.End of Abyss’s facility is presented as a kind of a model-village recreation of The Thing’s Outpost 31 that you peer into from above. Your little bobble-headed hero takes up a tiny fraction of the screen, with most of the remainder drenched in foggy darkness, or even blanked out entirely. This is a world of Usborne-style cutaways, where anything outside the walls is total blackness.This combination of cute and eerie immediately marks End of Abyss as part of the Scandi-chiaroscuro style pioneered by Limbo and Inside (from Playdead, in Copenhagen) and Little Nightmares (from Malmö-based Tarsier Studios, where the founders of End of Abyss developer Section 9 cut their teeth). Those games, though, were all puzzle-platformers. End of Abyss is a survival-horror game in the mould of PS1-era Resident Evil, which took a similarly zoomed-out approach, using fixed, CCTV-reminiscent camera angles. It’s a great way of controlling each scene’s composition for maximum aesthetic value – and, of course, to set up scares.View image in fullscreenDrenched in darkness … End of Abyss.Photograph: Section 9/Epic Games PublishingEnd of Abyss delights in lovingly decorated dioramas, with bodies and viscera laid outjust so, illuminated by the flickering light of a CRT screen and some orange-glowing item (a valuable key or weapon upgrade) dangling just out of reach. As you’re studying these details, trying to figure out how you might reach that desirable object, at the edge of your vision a monster will peel itself from the darkness and attack before you can consciously register its presence.What follows is a dance of backpedalling and firing your pistol, praying that it’s loaded with enough ammo to finish off the advancing assailant before it can catch up to you. Or, worse, your retreat carries you into another nest of monsters. These are foundational thrills of the genre, and End of Abyss keeps them intact as it shrinks them down to dollhouse size. They might be scarier still, in fact, because manually aiming a gun from a top-down perspective can be fiddly, and End of Abyss’s control scheme is so confounding (who puts reload on the right thumbstick?) that you’re fighting muscle memory as much as the monsters.On top of this survival-horror foundation, though, End of Abyss layers elements of Dark Souls, Metroid and Hollow Knight – and here it overextends. This facility is big and complex enough for you to get lost in, filled with doors that only open from the other side and seemingly separate zones that join up in unexpected ways. These can be some of video games’ finest pleasures, when done right, but they make for an uncomfortable fit in a game that relies on a character so slow-moving that they can be threatened by a shambling zombie.View image in fullscreenStriking gloomy style … End of Abyss.Photograph: Section 9/Epic Games PublishingThat striking gloomy style, meanwhile, is something of an achilles heel when you’re trying to tell one room from another. It’s not helped by a pause-screen map that struggles to convey the interlocking territory, and, at the time of playing, is prone to getting confused over questions as fundamental as which doors are locked.This leads to a lot of unnecessary backtracking and, with every repeat visit, those carefully staged scenes lose some of their sheen. A composition that had you gawping the first time can’t hope to maintain that effect on the dozenth visit, while the shadow-peeling scares turn out to run on the clockwork logic of a fairground ghost train. Reaching the final boss after 12 hours, with much of the map still greyed out and other stretches tromped over endlessly, I’m left feeling exhausted, with little inclination to explore the other half of the game that (according to the completion percentage) remains unseen. Contrary to its fetchingly diminutive presentation, End of Abyss might be just too big for its own good.End of Abyss is out now; £22.69Explore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5reviewsShareReuse this content

title: End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland review – Murakami’s marvel brilliantly brought to life | Theatre | The Guardian
description: With a dual narrative set in Tokyo and a world of dreams, Philippe Decouflé’s epic production is as bewitching as its balletic unicorns
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: With a dual narrative set in Tokyo and a world of dreams, Philippe Decouflé’s epic production is as bewitching as its balletic unicorns
Content: Beautiful but dangerous … Kiita Komagine and Misato Morita in End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBeautiful but dangerous … Kiita Komagine and Misato Morita in End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewEnd of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland review – Murakami’s marvel brilliantly brought to lifeBarbican theatre, LondonWith a dual narrative set in Tokyo and a world of dreams, Philippe Decouflé’s epic production is as bewitching as its balletic unicornsArifa AkbarFri 9 Oct 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow to stage Haruki Murakami’s epic, dual-narrative novel without leaving the audience in a muddle? Director-choreographer Philippe Decouflé goes big, filling the enormous Barbican stage with a kaleidoscope of dream worlds for Ako Takahashi’s adaptation. It could have become a scramble of stories and inquiries into memory, technological advances in society and the imagination. Instead, it is turned into one long immaculate coup de théâtre.There are two versions of the protagonist, Watashi(Tatsuya Fujiwara) – oneisin Tokyo, the other in a world comprising dreams. The city is noirish while the latter is beautiful but dangerous, with a complicated storyline involving the sundering of humans from their shadows, a walled city, roaming animals and a professor (Narushi Ikeda) who collects their skulls to channel past experiences through sound.View image in fullscreenRabbit hole of wonderlands … Miu Tomita plays Woman in Pink and Tatsuya Fujiwara is Watashi.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe professor’s 17-year-old granddaughter (Miu Tomita) accompanies Watashi in Tokyo and appears like a kitsch version of the prophetess who goes with Aeneas into the underworld. Watashi seeks escape, so he can be reunited with his shadow (Shuntaro Miyao), but is drawn to this strange world too and has a romance with a librarian (Misato Morita).Initially, it spirals into a rabbit hole of wonderlands, with kooky humour and references to western canonical and pop culture, as is Murakami’s way, from ancient myth to Lewis Carroll’s Alice and Luis Buñuel’s Un Chien Andalou. A playful set, designed by K Ishihara, shows its own theatrical construction with cheeky playfulness.View image in fullscreenNoirish … one version of Watashi is in Tokyo.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe visual pyrotechnics suck you in, from big projections to the speed, flow and agility of dancing that gestures at anime. They bring forth Murakami’s many creatures, from underground “murks”, with porcupine spikes, who flip and cartwheel, to a herd of balletic unicorns.Decouflé’s choreography is unsurpassable in its elastic grace and athleticism without seeming circus-like. The aesthetics on the whole are so ravishing that it doesn’t matter if the story is not easy to grasp in the first half. At least not for some because, while Murakami fans will know that the unity of the story is to come, initiates to his work may be left punch-drunk and befuddled by the onslaught of worlds and images.View image in fullscreenMurakami’s creatures include unicorns.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianIt becomes clear after the interval that this is controlled and deliberate confusion, reflecting Watashi’s state of mind. The dance becomes imbued with feeling as Murakami’s world reveals its underlying themes of loneliness, grief, the fear of disappearing and of death.Franz & Marie review – Woyzeck folk musical finds heart amid the horrorRead moreBut the story of lost shadows, representing the “true” self, bears bigger socio-political echoes that feel contemporary, and even prescient (the book was published in 1985). This world looks like Neo’s in The Matrix, and its technology chimes with ideas in Naomi Klein’s book,Doppelganger: A Trip into the Mirror World. The sinister side of the perfectionism that this dream society has cultivated could be a comment on postwar Japan, or on our world of AI, real and fake selves, code and machine-constructed subjectivity.At almost three hours, it leaves you with the sense that you have been dreaming, collectively, about a world of dead animals, lost shadows and unfeeling humans, but also of unicorns, impossible beauty and an ocean-like imagination. It is both of our world, and other.AtBarbican theatre, Londonuntil 11 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreHaruki MurakamireviewsShareReuse this content
