title: Jerry Hall deserves murder on Celebrity Traitors – but legends live beyond logic | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: Her unintentional buffoonery and disregard for the game makes Hall this season’s incredible agent of chaos
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Her unintentional buffoonery and disregard for the game makes Hall this season’s incredible agent of chaos
Content: Some of the contestants are playing chess. Some are playing 4D chess. Meanwhile, Hall is barely even aware there’s a game going on at all.Photograph: Cody Burridge/Studio Lambert/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenSome of the contestants are playing chess. Some are playing 4D chess. Meanwhile, Hall is barely even aware there’s a game going on at all.Photograph: Cody Burridge/Studio Lambert/BBC/PAThe TraitorsJerry Hall deserves murder on Celebrity Traitors – but legends live beyond logicStuart HeritageHer unintentional buffoonery and disregard for the game makes Hall this season’s incredible agent of chaosFri 9 Oct 2026 07.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 13.01 EDTShareBy rights,Jerry Hallshould not still be a participant on The Celebrity Traitors. If there was any justice in the world, the traitors would have murdered her in cold blood at the very start of this Thursday’s episode. The fact they did not speaks volumes about what an absolute legend the woman is.The crime that should have condemned her to death happened on last Friday’s show, during a mission where everyone had to be buried alive with a partner. Contestants had to choose between waiting to be dug up, or shouting the word “haggis”, which would release them but also make them eligible to be murdered. Needless to say, Hall shouted “haggis” approximately one solitary nanosecond after the game started. Nobody else shouted “haggis”. For sheer weakness in the face of adversity, she deserved to die.View image in fullscreenWhen given a choice between staying buried or risking being murdered, Hall immediately opted for the latter.Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio LambertHowever, perhaps the traitors did the right thing in letting her live, because it has become perfectly apparent that Hall functions best on the show as an agent of chaos. Some of the contestants are playing chess. Some are playing 4D chess. Meanwhile, Hall is barely even aware there’s a game going on at all. She is treating the whole endeavour as an excuse to drift around blurting out whatever mad nonsense happens to pass through her mind at any given juncture.A case in point. During Thursday’s episode, Hall and Hannah Fry walked into breakfast together. The expectation had been that one of them would be murdered. Suspicion immediately rocketed among everyone. What devious shenanigans could have taken place to ensure they both made it through the night intact?For her part, Fry realised the heat would be on and acted accordingly. Hall, meanwhile, wailed “WHAT ABOUT RICHARD?” like a newly grieving widow, apropos of absolutely nothing. Nobody knows why she did it. Was it a strategy? Was it a ploy? Or, as may well be the case, does she simply live inside a bubble unaffected by simple things like causality or logic?View image in fullscreenHall arriving at Studio 54 with Mick Jagger in 1979.Photograph: Allan Tannenbaum/Getty ImagesIn fairness, this is probably what we all expected from Hall. To say the woman has lived a life would be an incredible understatement. This is a woman who spent the 1970s ping-ponging between Bryan Ferry and Mick Jagger. She has played at Glastonbury and been the Joker’s girlfriend. She has judged the Whitbread prize and starred in adverts for Bovril. She was married to Rupert Murdoch. If all of these things had happened to you, you’d be forgiven for living inside a self-made reality shield as well.However, this does make her a brilliant participant on The Celebrity Traitors. It means that, after a week and a half of being abjectly wrong about absolutely everything, she still has the total confidence to boast about being a leg-wrestling champion in high school.There is no telling where this will end. Maybe the other contestants, sick of her unintentional buffoonery, will round on her. Maybe she’ll confuse and beguile everyone so much that she ends up winning the entire thing. Maybe she’ll become a traitor by accident and accidentally demolish the castle. This is Jerry Hall we’re talking about. All bets are off.Explore more on these topicsThe TraitorsJerry HallTelevisioncommentShareReuse this content

title: The new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our age | Movies | The Guardian
description: Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning shows how public opinion has changed around billionaire CEOs since The Social Network’s release
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning shows how public opinion has changed around billionaire CEOs since The Social Network’s release
Content: A straitjacketed simmer … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: SonyView image in fullscreenA straitjacketed simmer … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: SonyMoviesThe new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our ageJeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning shows how public opinion has changed around billionaire CEOs since The Social Network’s releaseDan MilmoGlobal technology editorFri 9 Oct 2026 07.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen The Social Network came out, Mark Zuckerberg organised a staff viewing of a film hedescribed as “fun”.A group corporate outing to the sequel is unlikely.The Social Network hardly portrayed the Facebook founder and his company in a hagiographical light (Zuckerberg laterdescribed the film as “hurtful”), but there was at least an element of the plucky upstart to the rise of Zuckerberg as he takes Facebook to 500 million users and a valuation of $25bn (ridiculously small numbers now – Meta has 3.6 billion users and is worth $1.8tn).By the end of that film, though, a steely CEO is emerging and his company is on the brink of global hegemony. The Social Reckoning picks up from there, with a clear perspective that both the founder and his company – as well as the industry they represent – are corporate villains now.This is set to be underlined by the release of theOpenAIdrama, Artificial, where its CEO, Sam Altman, is reportedly given a deeply unflattering portrayal. Elon Musk completes the villainous trilogy by appearing as himself – aside from the odd deployment of an AI avatar – in Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary, Musk, about the world’s first trillionaire.Tech is the obvious thread joining these films, but another is the scathing portrayal of the company leaders in them. Film villains used to be hoodlums, ex-deep state operatives, people with posh British accents. Tech execs are the new Darth Vader.View image in fullscreenDeeply unflattering … Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonThis is underlined by the casting ofJeremy Strong, who looks a touch on the old side to be playing 2019-2021 era Zuckerberg (the Meta CEO was in his mid-30s at the time of the film’s events whereas Strong is 47), but is embedded in our minds as the tortured Roy family scion Kendall in Succession.Strong also brings a straitjacketed simmer to the role here, one that breaks slightly at the end as he backtracks on being a “free speech absolutist” under intolerable pressure. It is the most human Zuckerberg moment in the entire film.Peter Bradshawdescribes Strong’s performanceas a “very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet”. It is much less sympathetic than Jesse Eisenberg’s in The Social Network and is a sort of corporeal representation of Meta as the monolithic, corporate bad guy.Elements of the portrayal chime with some former Meta employees, including a whistleblower, Arturo Béjar,who describes it as “accurate”. Another former employee tells the Guardian that Zuckerberg was “unemotional” in meetings (perhaps what you’d expect from a $1.8tn company CEO, admittedly). Well, Strong’s performance certainly is that.There had already been a turning point in public perception of Facebook beforethe Haugen leaks, with theCambridge Analyticascandal, which raised questions about the privacy of account holders’ data and how it is used.Haugen’s revelations in 2021 compounded this disquiet. By the time of the2022 inquest for British teenager Molly Russell, who took her own life after watching harmful content on Instagram, regulation of social media around the world was inevitable.The tone of The Social Reckoning and Strong’s performance reflect this shift. In the UK, screenings of the film are carrying an advert for the online safety charity established by Molly’s family,in which her father says: “‘Instagram helped kill my daughter”.Responding to Russell,Metasays it has worked to improve the safety of its platforms.The regulatory, legal and political backlash against social media – as well as the release of The Social Reckoning – reflects a lack of trust in such statements.Strong’s Zuckerberg says in the film that “the debate is over”. If it is, The Social Reckoning portrays a world where Meta is on the wrong side of it.Explore more on these topicsFilmMetaMark ZuckerbergOpenAIJeremy StrongSocial mediaDigital mediaShareReuse this content

title: ‘Is death necessary?’: why Peter Greenaway’s assisted dying drama is stuck in post-production hell | Movies | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Three years after filming began on the contentious Lucca Mortis, starring Dustin Hoffman, the British director is still in dispute with producers over which version to release, and a battle over rights rumbles on
Author: Geoffrey Macnab
Headline: Exclusive: Three years after filming began on the contentious Lucca Mortis, starring Dustin Hoffman, the British director is still in dispute with producers over which version to release, and a battle over rights rumbles on
Content: Peter Greenaway pictured in Madrid, Spain, in 2015.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeter Greenaway pictured in Madrid, Spain, in 2015.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesMovies‘Is death necessary?’: why Peter Greenaway’s assisted dying drama is stuck in post-production hellExclusive:Three years after filming began on the contentious Lucca Mortis, starring Dustin Hoffman, the British director is still in dispute with producers over which version to release, and a battle over rights rumbles onGeoffrey MacnabFri 9 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeter Greenaway’s new movie was supposed to mark a glorious swansong for him and his lead actor Dustin Hoffman, the Oscar-winning star of The Graduate and Tootsie. Both men were in their 80s when shooting began in Lucca, Tuscany, in late 2023. Neither knew the storms ahead or that this was going to turn into arguably the most troublesome project in Greenaway’s career.Turn the clock back to 2023 and Greenaway, who has been based in the Netherlands for the last 20 years, could hardly conceal his excitement during a Q&A at International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA) in the huge art deco Tuschinski theatre in Amsterdam in November 2023, after receiving a lifetime achievement award from the festival. He told the audience that he would be flying toItalythe next morning “and that, all being well, we will start shooting seriously in the next couple of days”.The film was then called Lucca Mortis, and Greenaway explained that it explored death. He said he had already made “quite a number of films” about sex (“Eros”) “but the other thing was Thanatos (death). There are, and have been, some extremely good films made about old age. I am thinking of [Ingmar] Bergman’s Wild Strawberries, for example, but not that many.”View image in fullscreenDustin Hoffman at the premiere of Twiggy in Los Angeles last week.Photograph: Variety/Getty Images“Our film is really about notions of death and it asks the rather absurd and ridiculous question – is death necessary? The popular media is absolutely covered now in considerations about assisted death, about euthanasia, about the legitimacy of suicide. I believe that we must take death more seriously.”Greenaway’s pitch was that Lucca Mortis isn’t a horror picture “full of coffins and skulls and macabre activities”. Instead, it a drama about a New York writer contemplating his mortality; a man who wants to round off his life in the neatest, most elegant way possible. Jacob Zucchine (Hoffman) was adopted as a kid and eventually grew up in the US. He returns to Lucca in Tuscany in search of his Italian roots. The film is set around the time of 9/11. Like New York, Lucca is dominated by looming towers and these inspire the author to write stories but also to feel that death is stalking him.Ominously, Lucca Mortis encountered difficulties right from the outset. In late 2023, the director and his crew arrived in Lucca but the lead actors weren’t yet there. Dozens of trucks filled with technical gear turned up from Rome: sets were built and the crew sat waiting for several weeks for work to begin – but it never did and they were eventually sent home. It appeared that the production had already hit cashflow problems.View image in fullscreenAnne Bancroft and Dustin Hoffman in The Graduate from 1967.Photograph: Cinetext Bildarchiv/Lawrence Turman\embassy/AllstarSuch a delay, though, is not unusual in film production. It is often a mad scramble to complete the financing for an ambitious independently funded film such as this. Production finally got under way in early 2024 – and this time with actors.The trade press reported that Lucca Mortis had a €15m (£12m) budgetand that it would use 25 locations in Lucca. The city threw itself behind the movie. Many of the locals were involved andthe Tuscan press reporteda carnivalesque atmosphere during shooting akin to that on a Fellini movie, with the Livorno-based publication Il Tirreno saying: “For a few months, Lucca became an open-air film set, with the citizens acting as unwitting extras and the historic centre crisscrossed by cameras, dolly shots and familiar faces.”However, the charm soon wore off as constant delays ate up large chunks of the budget. Produced by Facing East (whose previous credits include Robbie Williams biopic Better Man and Liam Neeson thriller, In The Land of Saints and Sinners) the budget for the film came mainly from private financiers Jumpy Cow Pictures in Switzerland. There was extra support through Italian and Dutch tax rebates.When most of the shooting was completed, Greenaway and Saskia Boddeke (his Dutch wife and creative partner) set to work with their team. A first draft assembly of the film was delivered in late 2024 and was reportedly warmly received. However, it was at this point that tensions threatened to reach breaking point. Sources close to Greenaway have said that the director’s contract gave him final cut, but that the producers subsequently decided to make their own, more “commercial” cut without the director’s involvement. Their position was that they were entitled to intervene because the film had gone over budget. Facing East has not responded to requests for comment.View image in fullscreenAlan Howard, Richard Bohringer, Helen Mirren and Michael Gambon in Peter Greenaway’s 1989 film The Cook, The Thief, His Wife & Her Lover.Photograph: Palace Pictures/Sportsphoto/AllstarThe net result is that there are two different versions of the film in circulation, neither of them fully completed (although the producers’ cut is said to be more advanced). There is also an ongoing row about who controls the rights to the movie – which is now stuck firmly in limbo.And the citizens of Lucca are not happy. Three years on from the start of production, there is still no sign of the movie made in their back yard and which they embraced with so much enthusiasm and affection. Lucca councillor Remo Santini commented earlier this week: “We’re disappointed because, as a municipality, we’ve spent time and energy making this film. We even had a sneak preview of it, months ago, and it really made a great impression on us. Yet, despite filming having wrapped over two years ago, all is quiet. Unfortunately, this stalemate isn’t our fault.”The city says it has made repeated requests to the production and the director for explanations about what has happened to the movie, “and no one has contacted us since”. This, then, clearly wasn’t a smooth or happy shoot. Even the title is proving contentious. Partly because the city of Lucca isn’t keen to be associated with death, the film is now called Tower Stories.The irony is that those who have seen the two cuts say they are not that different. Whichever way the film is edited, it is still based on the same dense and digressive Greenaway screenplay, which takes the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein’s gnomic observation “death is not an event in life; we do not live to experience death” as its starting point. Some have talked admiringly of the picture’s visual splendour, lush musical score, operatic set-pieces and narrative intricacy. Hoffman is said to give a very poignant performance as the elderly writer, a character who appears to be partially based on Greenaway himself.“It’s a great legacy for Greenaway and not only for him, but for Dustin – a great performance. It’s a movie that needs to be finished and needs to be released,” one frustrated member of the production crew told me last week.View image in fullscreenGreenway’s The Draughtsman’s Contract from 1982.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyThere is, though, something quixotic about the very idea of Lucca Mortis. Greenaway is the grand old visionary of British cinema. He has dozens of credits to his name, shorts, features and documentaries, all with his firm authorial imprint. Whether he is dealing with cannibalism (The Cook, The Thief, His Wife & Her Lover), Shakespeare (Prospero’s Books) or garden design (The Draughtsman’s Contract), his approach remains the same: magical realism, obtuse ideas, puns, and plenty of visual flamboyance.This could be Greenaway’s final feature, but whether it will be seen in the way he intended is now in serious doubt. The longer it is stuck in postproduction purgatory, the less chance that its director, 84, and its star, who turned 89 in August, will be fit and able enough to promote it properly. There are also obvious questions over whether distributors and festivals will accept a Greenaway film over which the director hasn’t had the final say.The talk is now of trying to protect the “dignity” of Lucca Mortis. For that to happen, everyone involved will need to accept what surely should have been obvious from the outset, namely that when you commission Peter Greenaway to make a film, that’s exactly what you are going to get – a Peter Greenaway film – and you risk disaster if you try to turn it into something else.Explore more on these topicsFilmPeter GreenawayDustin HoffmanItalyEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘My dog’s built her own fashion community’: how canine companions stole the fashion week spotlight | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Our four-legged friends are turning heads from Louis Vuitton to Schiaparelli – but what does their presence in the most exclusive of spaces say about the industry’s changing attitudes?
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Our four-legged friends are turning heads from Louis Vuitton to Schiaparelli – but what does their presence in the most exclusive of spaces say about the industry’s changing attitudes?
Content: Furry and fabulous … a guest gets ready for Paris fashion week.Photograph: Raimonda Kulikauskienė/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFurry and fabulous … a guest gets ready for Paris fashion week.Photograph: Raimonda Kulikauskienė/Getty ImagesFashion Statement newsletterFashion‘My dog’s built her own fashion community’: how canine companions stole the fashion week spotlightOur four-legged friends are turning heads from Louis Vuitton to Schiaparelli – but what does their presence in the most exclusive of spaces say about the industry’s changing attitudes?Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereChloe Mac DonnellFri 9 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe front row at a fashion week show is a known hotspot for celebrities. During the most recent iteration that wrapped up on Tuesday, sightings included Heathcliff, AKA Jacob Elordi, high-fiving the Adolescence star Owen Cooper at Bottega Veneta; Rihanna arriving 63 minutes late to the Matières Fécales show; and Dua Lipa gossiping with Nicole Kidman and Pedro Pascal at Chanel. But peppered in among the Hollywood crowd was another type of guest going head-to-head for the photographers’ attention: dogs.From a cavapoo at Louis Vuitton to a shih tzu at Schiaparelli, four-legged companions – rather than designer bags – sat on the laps of many showgoers. At the Balenciaga show,Brooklyn Beckham and Nicole Peltz sat next to Miranda Priestly– no, not Meryl Streep in her Devil Wears Prada character, but the brand’s creative director Pierpaolo Piccioli’s rescue dog. Tommy Hilfiger took his post-show bow with a fluffy samoyed – a look-a-like of Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift’s pup who stars with Kelce in a campaign for the brand. Elsewhere, a miniature schnauzer in goggles and a chihuahua wearing a puffer jacket took over the catwalk at Chopova Lowena.While Demi Moore’s1.2lb chihuahuaPilaf was once a regular guest at shows (RIP), and Prince Tokyo Gizmo Hilton made his front-row debut with Paris Hilton at a Gucci show, dogs on the laps of more regular guests, and not just A-listers, are becoming more widespread. In July,Vogueran a story on Poppy, a tiara-wearing shih tzu who has become a regular on the couture circuit.Madeleine Rothery, a freelance fashion writer, has been bringing Disco, a five-year-old boston terrier, to fashion shows for the last two years. “People find her quite entertaining,” Rothery says. “I think people can feel quite self-conscious and uptight at shows, and she just makes everyone feel at ease, loosen up a little and talk among each other, rather than be glued to their phones.”View image in fullscreenStar of the show … Demi Moore with Pilaf in 2024.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesThis new doggy dominance is reflected in wider culture, where from treat jars at local pubs toa surge in specialist clothingand dedicatedfashion magazine covers, the central role that dogs play in many people’s lives is increasingly being celebrated.Prada, an appropriately-named five-year-old teacup pomchi (a crossbreed between a pomeranian and a chihuahua) who lives in London, has become a familiar face at shows over the past two years. “The street style photographers always call her name to look at the camera when we’re heading into a show,” says her owner, Tori West, the editor of Bricks magazine. “She’s built her own fashion community, which is super cute.”Disco, who lives in Paris with Rothery, travels to Copenhagen each season. “In Paris, I’ve never dared take her to a show because most of the venues are cultural institutions, and I just know she wouldn’t be allowed in, so there’s no point asking,” says Rothery.Copenhagen is usually more pooch-friendly, but for one particular show in August, Rothery turned up to discover access meant passing through a museum where dogs were banned. The security guard told Rothery that if she hid Disco, he would “turn a blind eye”.“It turned into a really lovely act of kindness towards us both,” Rothery says. “It’s hard to be negative when a dog’s around. They just make everyone feel good about life.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCanine couture … Madeleine Rothery and Disco.Photograph: Anasteisha DangerWhile Prada enjoys the spotlight, her attendance at fashion week is as West’s registeredsupport animal – her role is to help provide stability to West, who has anxiety. “I feel way more safe and comfortable having her with me at events than not,” West says. This time at London fashion week, she joined West at every show, aside from two where West was given a head’s up that the music would be too loud. “If an event isn’t pooch-friendly, it’s usually one that isn’t chill, so then I know it would stress me out being there anyway,” West says. “I’ve learned I don’t want to be in spaces that wouldn’t allow my dog.”West says the increased visibility of dogs at fashion week suggests that the industry may be reconsidering the wider needs of its guests. “It’s such a busy, stressful schedule, and I think people who have children, carers, or assistance animals have historically been somewhat forgotten about in these hyper-controlled fashion environments,” West says.For Rothery, Disco’s presence is a reminder of her life outside the fashion week bubble. “No matter how stressed or overwhelmed I start to get, I always have to walk her and tend to her,” she says. “That just brings me back down to earth.”To read the complete version of this newsletter – complete with this week’s trending topics in The Measure –subscribe to receive Fashion Statementin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFashionFashion Statement newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Why you've probably been thinking about narcolepsy all wrong | Medical research | The Guardian
description: The sleep disorder has been the butt of jokes and a comedic plot point, but the reality of living with narcolepsy is anything but funny. Things could be about to change for people with the condition though, after the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the first ever drug to treat narcolepsy itself, rather than just its symptoms. Madeleine Finlay tells Ian Sample how the scientific breakthrough came about, and Julie Flygare, who has narcolepsy and founded the non-profit Project Sleep, explains what it is like to live with the condition and how the drug could be gamechanger

title: The best sunrise alarm clocks in the UK, tried and tested for gentler mornings | Sleep | The Guardian
description: Our reviewer sheds some light on the best dawn simulation alarms, from Lumie and Philips to Dreamegg
Author: Pete Wise
Headline: Our reviewer sheds some light on the best dawn simulation alarms, from Lumie and Philips to Dreamegg
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSleepReviewThe best sunrise alarm clocks in the UK, tried and tested for gentler morningsOur reviewer sheds some light on the best dawn simulation alarms, from Lumie and Philips to DreameggThe best eye masks to help you sleep betterPete WiseFri 9 Oct 2026 05.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo wake each day in darkness is a plight you wouldn’t wish on your worst enemy, yet that’s what many of us do routinely throughout winter. Getting up in the dark decouples our life from our circadian rhythm (our body clock), with bodily processes such as cognition and metabolism put to work before they’re fully prepped.Thank heavens, then, for sunrise alarm clocks. These “dawn simulation” devices glow with gradually intensifying brightness as your wake-up time approaches, kickstarting your circadian rhythm before you get out of bed. For many users, this results in a happier, healthier start to the day.Sunrise alarm clocks can differ vastly – for instance, only some are bright enough to be medically certified as light-therapy devices forSad(seasonal affective disorder) and other disorders. We’ve indicated the two alarms that have this certification in their specs below.I tested 10 wake-up lights from Lumie, Beurer, Philips, Dreamegg, Blueair and Lexon to find out which would make the most difference to my mornings, and these are the eight I recommend. As a lifelong reluctant riser, I’ve found the experience of testing these devices a gamechanger – in fact, I’m now using one daily. Perhaps mornings aren’t so bad, after all …At a glanceBest sunrise alarm clock overallLumieBodyclock Glow 150£118.96 at AmazonBest budget sunrise alarmLumieSunrise Alarm£39.99 at AmazonBest sunrise alarm clock for heavy sleepersLumieBodyclock Spark 100£98.46 at HealfBest sunrise alarm for late-night readingPhilipsSmartSleep£181.99 at AmazonBest mini sunrise alarm clockLexonMina Sunrise£79.90 at John LewisBest sunrise alarm clock for couplesBeurerWake-up Light WL50£57.56 at John LewisWhy you should trust meMornings, eh? I’ve often felt lousy first thing, after waking up to a minutes-long medley of smartphone alarms.When, at last, I drag myself out of bed, I frequently spend the day reviewing all kinds of gadgets, from Sad lamps to electric heaters. It’s a freelance job I’ve been privileged to do since 2017 – and as we tumbled dimly into 2025, the Filter gave me one of my most quietly life-improving assignments yet: reviewing sunrise alarm clocks. I tested three additional models in winter 2025/26, and one of these has emerged as my favourite of all.The extent to which these gadgets have improved my mornings has surprised me – although it was greater in some cases than others. Frankly, I’d like other groggy wakers to feel the same benefit, and my reviews are written and ranked with this in mind.Some brands did not want the sunrise alarm clocks I sourced for testing back, so those will be donated for fundraising toCat Action Trust 1977, a small national charity dedicated to the welfare of feral cats.How I testedView image in fullscreenEach sunrise alarm clock, including the Beurer Wake-up Light WL50 (pictured), was tested over at least two nights.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianThe only proper way to test a sunrise alarm clock is by using it to wake up each morning – so that’s what I did.I used each model for at least two nights, testing out multiple light and alarm sound settings, and assessing the quality of wake-up for each device. I considered the brightness of each alarm, how close the glow felt to real sunlight, and the audio quality. Above all, I reflected on how lively and refreshed I felt after waking up with each one.Many sunrise alarm clocks also have a sundown function, so I used this where available too. I also tried using each sunrise alarm clock as a reading light, to help me finish the day – as well as start it – smartphone-free.Some sunrise alarm clocks go even further, with additional features such as app operability, multiple alarm profiles and mood lighting. To ensure a thorough review of each sunrise alarm clock, I played around with every possible customisation option and functionality.The best sunrise alarm clocks in 2026View image in fullscreenThe Lumie Bodyclock Glow 150, the Blueair Mini Restful sunrise clock air purifier and the Lexon Mina Sunrise.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianBest sunrise alarm clock overall:Lumie Bodyclock Glow 150LumieBodyclock Glow 150from£118.96£119 at Argos£118.96 at AmazonWhat we loveSuperior sunrise simulation; pleasant alarm tonesWhat we don’t loveIt’s relatively expensiveView image in fullscreen£119 at Argos£118.96 at AmazonLumie is the brand that pioneered consumer-grade sunrise alarm clocks in the early 1990s, and that pedigree still shines through.Equipped with a comprehensive set of wake-up sounds and medical-grade sunrise simulation, the Bodyclock Glow 150 is the best sunrise alarm clock of the many I’ve tested. It comes at a premium price, but could pay dividends for your sleep cycle.Why we love itThe sunrise effect is among the most convincing I’ve experienced, rivalling the less fully featured (but slightly cheaper) Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100, which is reviewed below. It feels like waking to daylight, or emerging into a clearing after walking through dense woodland.I found this model easy to control and configure via the five buttons surrounding the digital display. All of the personalisations that really matter are available, including sunrise light intensity and duration.Crucially, there’s a great selection of alarm tones to choose between – not always the case with Lumie models – ranging from the wonderfully gentle to the brusquely rousing. I preferred “tropical birds” and “waves” to “beep” or “steam train”, although I enjoyed imagining a train enthusiast waking contentedly to the latter.It’s a shame that …there’s only one colour available: black (with a white lamp). This will suit some bedroom design schemes better than others.Certification:UK MDR 2002 and EU MDR 2017/745 medical classificationModes:sunrise alarm, sunset, bedside lightFootprint:W19 x D12cmFeatures:light-sensitive auto-dimming displayBrightness settings:fiveSunrise duration:20, 30 or 45 minutesLumieBodyclock Glow 150from£118.96£119 at Argos£118.96 at AmazonWhat we loveSuperior sunrise simulation; pleasant alarm tonesWhat we don’t loveIt’s relatively expensiveRead our fullLumie Bodyclock Glow 150 sunrise alarm clock reviewBest budget sunrise alarm:Lumie Sunrise AlarmLumieSunrise Alarmfrom£39.99£49 at John Lewis£39.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value, with good sunrise simulation and soundsWhat we don’t loveLess bright than swankier Lumie modelsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£49 at John Lewis£39.99 at AmazonImagine telling one of your ancestors that you were awoken this morning by your lamp, which was purring at you. I’m not pulling your leg, you might say, it’s all thanks to the Lumie Sunrise’s “kittens purring” alarm tone, which sits sweetly alongside four other natural sounds, including goats bleating and birdsong.Why we love itIn all seriousness, this is an excellent sunrise alarm clock, and it comes at a standout price. Its sunrise light subtly brightens during the minutes leading up to your chosen alarm time, producing a lovely awakening that really did remind me of natural light.I found it easy enough to set the Sunrise Alarm’s time and alarm, although pressing some of the buttons can be fiddly. Do keep the instruction manual handy, as there are lots of options and buttons to get your head around.It’s a shame that …it lacks a little bedside table appeal. But having said that, this sunrise alarm clock has incredible performance for the price.Certification:noneModes:sunrise alarm, sunset, mood, bedside lightFootprint:W17 x D9cmFeatures:mood lighting (six colours)Brightness settings:10Sunrise duration:30 minutesLumieSunrise Alarmfrom£39.99£49 at John Lewis£39.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value, with good sunrise simulation and soundsWhat we don’t loveLess bright than swankier Lumie modelsBest sunrise alarm clock for heavy sleepers:Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100LumieBodyclock Spark 100from£98.46£98.46 at Healf£98.96 at AmazonWhat we loveOutstanding sunrise simulationWhat we don’t loveLack of gentler alarm soundsView image in fullscreen£98.46 at Healf£98.96 at AmazonI woke up feeling great when I used the medical-grade Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100, which bathes the room in gradually intensifying, sun-like light for a set period before the alarm goes off.Why we love itThe device is supposed to realistically imitate the lightening shades of a sunrise – and it does so more convincingly than any other brand’s sunrise alarm clock. Depending on your chosen light intensity setting, it can get very bright.The Spark 100 also has a sunset feature that graduates through the same red, orange and white light colours used with the sunrise function, but in reverse order. After the sunset cycle, the light can either switch off entirely or remain in a gentle night-light mode, whichever you choose.Besides performing brilliantly as a wake-up light and sunset simulator, the Spark 100 is simply a nicely designed, well-made thing. I appreciated its soft-edged yet robust construction and handy features such as the cable organisation in the base. It’s a pleasure to have on the bedside table.It’s a shame that …the alarm tone sounds piercing at the higher three of its five volume levels. I found myself settling for a 2/5 – though very heavy sleepers may prefer (or even relish) the louder options.Certification:UK MDR 2002 and EU MDR 2017/745 medical classificationModes:sunrise alarm, sunrise, sunset, bedside lightFootprint:W19 x D12cmFeatures:tap to snooze, auto-dimming display, adjustable sunrise/sunset duration, adjustable digital display brightnessBrightness settings:fiveSunrise duration:30 minutesLumieBodyclock Spark 100from£98.46£98.46 at Healf£98.96 at AmazonWhat we loveOutstanding sunrise simulationWhat we don’t loveLack of gentler alarm soundsBest sunrise alarm for late-night reading:Philips SmartSleepPhilipsSmartSleepfrom£181.99£183.99 at Philips£181.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSolid design and good sunrise simulationWhat we don’t loveOne of the most expensive optionsView image in fullscreen£183.99 at Philips£181.99 at AmazonThis lamp soon felt like part of the furniture on my bedside table. In typical Philips fashion, it’s a good-quality, dependable product, with a solid middle-of-the-road design that won’t look out of place in many bedrooms.Why we love itSetup is slick – I was able to set my alarm time, sound and brightness by following the simple prompts on the device’s display, without having to consult the manual. Subsequently tweaking your alarm(s) takes practice, but you’ll master all the controls you need after a few days.The SmartSleep’s wake-up capabilities are impressive, combining brilliant light with a diverse choice of alarm sounds. It also has FM radio and 3.5mm auxiliary audio input options for the user who has tired of Alpine and gong bath soundscapes. There’s a 5V USB charging outlet at the rear of the lamp, too, which could free up a valuable bedside power socket.I loved using this model as a reading light, as well as a sunrise alarm. Even when a bright setting is selected, the light seems relatively mellow and restful, which helped me get to sleep after reading pulpy detective novels late at night. The light can be deactivated with a press.It’s a shame that …it costs such a lot. The SmartSleep has a hefty price to match its impressive performance.Certification:noneModes:sunrise alarm, sleep mode with sunset simulation, bedside lightFootprint:W22 x D12cmFeatures:FM radio, Aux audio input, “RelaxBreathe” breathing exercises, adjustable sunrise duration, snooze, up to two wake-up profiles (with separate alarms)Brightness settings:25Sunrise duration:20, 25, 30, 35 or 40 minutesPhilipsSmartSleepfrom£181.99£183.99 at Philips£181.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSolid design and good sunrise simulationWhat we don’t loveOne of the most expensive optionsBest mini sunrise alarm clock:Lexon Mina SunriseLexonMina Sunrisefrom£77.94£79.90 at John Lewis£77.94 at AmazonWhat we loveCute, chic designWhat we don’t loveAwkward controlsView image in fullscreen£79.90 at John Lewis£77.94 at AmazonMy only general gripe with sunrise alarm clocks is that many of them are an aesthetic downgrade on a conventional bedside lamp – but this charming mini model from French brand Lexon is a stylish exception.Why we love itThe obvious draw here is the design, which comprises a cute, mushroom-shaped light and colourful metal base with a wraparound digital display. It fits very neatly on to a small or well-utilised bedside table.The sunrise light function roused me gently before the alarm tone (also gently rousing) sounded, and I got up feeling alert. Even though this isn’t a very bright light, it evidently did the trick, and it was suitable for bedtime reading, too.You can choose from five alarm tones, all of which sound pleasantly full and rich. These include birdsong and water sounds, as well as some loud, piercing alarms that will suit particularly heavy sleepers. Beautifully finished and stoutly made, the Mina Sunrise is a cut above the rest in terms of build quality.It’s a shame that …the control buttons are on the base, and can’t be seen in the dark without a secondary light source such as a smartphone torch. You’d struggle to adjust the settings in the middle of the night.Certification:noneModes:sunrise alarm, sunset, bedside lightFootprint:W11 x D11cmFeatures:mood lighting (nine colours), snooze, cordless operationBrightness settings:fiveSunrise duration:30 minutesLexonMina Sunrisefrom£77.94£79.90 at John Lewis£77.94 at AmazonWhat we loveCute, chic designWhat we don’t loveAwkward controlsBest sunrise alarm clock for couples:Beurer Wake-up Light WL 50BeurerWake-up Light WL50from£54.99£57.56 at John Lewis£54.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s packed with featuresWhat we don’t loveNot all the features are usefulView image in fullscreen£57.56 at John Lewis£54.99 at AmazonThanks to its capability to save two alarms for different times (each with its own sound and light settings), the Beurer WL 50 is a great choice for couples who get up at different times. That’s a rare feature in any sunrise alarm clock – let alone in such a reasonably priced model.Why we love itThe sunrise mode itself is gentle yet effective, and it’s easy to activate the device as a reading light with a simple, groggy tap. I really liked the alarm sounds you get with the WL 50 too – which is just as well, as there are only two.Perhaps that narrow choice of alarm tones sounds a little stingy, but it seems less so when you explore the WL 50’s alternative audio options. It doubles up as an FM radio, with space to save up to 30 station presets, which you can listen to throughout the day or use as a livelier alternative to an alarm tone. Bluetooth connectivity and an AUX input expand your listening options further.Curiously, this sunrise alarm clock can be unplugged (when fully charged) and used on the go for up to three hours. It’s hard to imagine a situation wherein this would be useful, but I appreciate the gesture.It’s a shame that …the sound quality isn’t great (but it’s good enough for the half-awake).Certification:noneModes:sunrise alarm, sunset simulation, bedside light, radio/speakerFootprint:W11 x D11cmFeatures:FM radio, AUX audio input, Bluetooth audio, portable use (up to three hours), LED mood lightBrightness settings:adjustableSunrise duration:10, 20 or 30 minutesBeurerWake-up Light WL50from£54.99£57.56 at John Lewis£54.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s packed with featuresWhat we don’t loveNot all the features are usefulThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘A beautifully designed alarm clock’: the Dreamegg Sunrise 1.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianBlueair Mini Restful sunrise clock air purifierBlueairMini Restful sunrise clock air purifierfrom£169£169 at Blueair£169 at AmazonWhat we loveInnovative sunrise and air purification comboWhat we don’t loveToo bulky for the bedside tableView image in fullscreen£169 at Blueair£169 at AmazonBest for:an air-purifying sunrise alarm clockMost of us spend around a third of our time in bed, so a sunrise alarm clock that also purifies your bedroom air seems like a good idea. This model, the Blueair Mini Restful, is heralded as the world’s first.By sunrise alarm clock standards, it isn’t really mini. I found myself resting it on the floor, where I could see the digital display on the top, rather than putting it on my bedside table.The sunrise function proved effective, waking me reliably with warm, increasingly bright light before the alarm sounded. As for the purification, the Mini Restful certainly made my air feel fresher after a windowsill-sanding session had kicked up untold volumes of dust. The fan works exceptionally quietly, although I still preferred to run it only during the daytime (this can be automated via the Blueair app’s schedule feature).It didn’t make the final cut because …the sunrise alarm feature is only accessible via the Blueair app, and I feel that users should have the option to activate it manually. With that said, the app is a pleasure to use.Certification:none;modes:night light, sunrise alarm;footprint:W17 x D17cm;features:air purification, app control, alarm schedule;brightness settings:scale of 0-100%;sunrise duration:15-30 minutesBlueairMini Restful sunrise clock air purifierfrom£169£169 at Blueair£169 at AmazonWhat we loveInnovative sunrise and air purification comboWhat we don’t loveToo bulky for the bedside tableDreamegg Sunrise 1DreameggSunrise 1from£62.99£62.99 at Dreamegg£69.99 at AmazonWhat we loveNicely pairs a textured front with mellow lightingWhat we don’t loveRelatively dim lightView image in fullscreen£62.99 at Dreamegg£69.99 at AmazonBest for:soothing sleep soundsThis compact, great-looking device offers something different, with a selection of 29 ambient sounds that can be used as white noise to help you fall asleep. There are also five options for rousing you in the morning, including birdsong, a campfire crackling and, my favourite, waves breaking on a shore. For me, perhaps the only issue with this approach was that the sounds did a better job of putting me to sleep than they did of waking me up.The Sunrise 1 is a beautifully designed alarm clock, with a softly textured front and foolproof dimmer controls on either side to adjust the light level and digital display brightness. Reluctant risers will be pleased to note there’s a prominent snooze button at the top of the device – though, personally, I’ve rarely felt the need to use this feature while testing sunrise alarm clocks.It didn’t make the final cut because …its light is a little too dim for my taste.Certification:none;modes:sunrise alarm, white noise/sleep sounds, bedside light;footprint:W15 x D7.3cm;features:sleep sound timer, nine light colours, five wake-up sounds;brightness settings:adjustable;sunrise duration:Up to 60 minutesDreameggSunrise 1from£62.99£62.99 at Dreamegg£69.99 at AmazonWhat we loveNicely pairs a textured front with mellow lightingWhat we don’t loveRelatively dim lightWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenSunrise alarm clocks that are classified as medical devices, such as the Lumie Bodyclock Glow 150, may be better suited for users seeking a therapeutic effect.Are sunrise alarm clocks a fad?A cursory glance at Google Trends search data – or perhaps at your chosen social media platform – will tell you that interest in sunrise alarm clocks has grown sharply in recent years. You may wonder: is this overdue recognition for a useful technology, or is it a murkier wellness trend to file alongsidemouth tapingand stuffing onion slices into socks?While there hasn’t been a great deal of academic research into sunrise alarm clocks, some studies suggest they may benefit our sleep health. For instance, researchers from Ohio University found thattrial participants had significantly better sleep scoresand lower perceived stress and burnout after spending two weeks waking with a sunrise alarm clock while also avoiding smartphone use in bed.The ultimate test of whether sunrise alarm clocks are a fad will be time. I’m still using mine, as I approach a third winter.Do sunrise alarm clocks help with Sad?Sad bright-light therapy involves the use of intense light (in the region of 10,000 lux) to mimic the effects of bright sunlight. Sunrise alarm clocks tend to be far less bright than the average Sad lamp. With that said, light exposure around dawn and in the early morning can influence our circadian rhythms, so even a relatively dim sunrise alarm may still have benefits.If you’ve been diagnosed with seasonal affective disorder and are looking for a light-therapy device, it’s best to ask your GP which product to use and how to get the most benefit. Sunrise alarm clocks that are classified as medical devices (indicated in the specs each product above) are more likely to suit users seeking a therapeutic effect than models with no medical certifications.Why does it benefit us to wake with the sun?Getting up in the dark can feel awful, which makes a lot of sense because light helps our bodies wake up properly.Humans are diurnal, which means we’ve evolved to be more wakeful, energetic and capable of chasing mammoths over vast distances during daytime. When the brain recognises increasing light at dawn, it sends signals around other regions of the brain and to other organs to calibrate bodily processes including temperature regulation, hormone secretion and metabolism. And when darkness falls, the brain prepares us for sleep – a helpful effect that many of us compromise by looking at bright smartphone or laptop screens.These processes follow roughly 24-hour cycles known as our circadian rhythms. The term is derived from the Latin wordscirca(approximately) anddiem(day), meaning around a day.So, the sun is the original and best alarm clock – activating our minds and bodies with light, rather than startling us awake with sound. Think of your sunrise alarm as a plucky stand-in to rely upon during the star’s shorter winter shifts.Do sunrise alarm clocks work for heavy sleepers?Some users find the light from their sunrise alarm clock more rousing than others do. If you’re a heavy sleeper, there’s a heightened chance that the artificial sunrise will not wake you (although it might still help you feel more alert on waking).How you configure your sunrise alarm clock makes a difference. We all sleep more deeply during certain periods of our sleep cycle – and this includes particularly heavy sleepers. So, by setting your sunrise alarm clock to do a relatively long dawn simulation cycle (30 minutes is an option on several models), you give the gradually increasing light more time to rouse you. You’ll often have a choice between multiple light intensity settings, too, so select the brightest one available.If you’re worried about waking up on time, all of the sunrise alarm clocks featured in this guide can conclude their sunrise cycle with an audio alarm tone. So, they could serve perfectly well as a wake-up alarm, even if they don’t successfully start rousing you before the beep. To be on the safe side, I’d recommend choosing a louder model, such as the Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100.For more:The best mattresses to help you sleep betterHow to create the perfect bed: seven things our sleep expert swears byThe best sleep aids: 13 of the most-hyped remediesPete Wise is ajournalistwith more than a decade’s experience covering everything from global development and social causes to technology and music. He has written extensively on sleep-related topics, including Sad lamps,intermittent fasting, and the effects of caffeine consumption on sleep. title: Cocktail of the week: All Roads’ daiquiri – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: A touch of homemade scotch bonnet jam turns up the heat in this classic concoction
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A touch of homemade scotch bonnet jam turns up the heat in this classic concoction
Content: ‘As good for crisp autumn evenings as it is on a sunny day’: the All Roads daiquiri.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreen‘As good for crisp autumn evenings as it is on a sunny day’: the All Roads daiquiri.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: All Roads’ daiquiri – recipeA touch of homemade scotch bonnet jam turns up the heat in this classic concoctionMalika Green and Paschelle BrownFri 9 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOur daiquiri sums up whatAll Roadsis all about: familiar flavours with a little twist. Pineapple, rum and lime are a classic combination, and the addition of scotch bonnet jam brings a subtle warmth that makes this just as good for those first crisp autumn evenings as it is on a sunny day.All Roads daiquiriServes1For the pineapple and scotch bonnet jam75g fresh pineapple, roughly chopped30g caster sugar1small slicescotch bonnet chilli, or more to taste, or 1 pinch chilli flakesFor the drink10ml overproof white rum– we useWray & Nephew45ml white rum– we useHavana Club 3-Year-Old25ml fresh lime juice30g pineapple and scotch bonnet jam(see above and method)First make the jam. Put the pineapple and caster sugar in a saucepan and cook over a low heat until the fruit begins to soften. Blend smooth – we use a stick blender – then add the scotch bonnet to taste and keep cooking gently for 20-25 minutes, stirring regularly, until the jam thickens and turns lightly golden. Take off the heat, leave to cool completely, then lift out and discard the chilli (if using chilli flakes, leave them in). Decant into a small jar or container and keep in the fridge until needed.To build the drink, put everything in a cocktail shaker filled with ice, shake hard until well chilled, then double strain into a chilled coupe.Malika Green and Paschelle Brown,All Roads, London SW9Explore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodCaribbean food and drinkHerbs and spicesFruitrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for toffee apple Basque cheesecake | Food | The Guardian
description: Crisp surface, creamy centre, spicy, sticky topping – my go-to dessert
Author: Benjamina Ebuehi
Headline: Crisp surface, creamy centre, spicy, sticky topping – my go-to dessert
Content: Benjamina Ebuehi’s toffee apple Basque cheesecake.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.View image in fullscreenBenjamina Ebuehi’s toffee apple Basque cheesecake.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.The sweet spotFoodBenjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for toffee apple Basque cheesecakeA crisp surface and creamy core are the traits of this cheesecake with no base, here topped with spiced and sliced apples and a sticky, caramel sauceBenjamina EbuehiFri 9 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 05.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy go-to cheesecake these days is a burnt Basque. It’s so good it doesn’t even need a biscuit base, which might be the very reason some people aren’t fans. But Basque cheesecakes are rarely too sweet, because the burnt top provides just enough bitterness to balance things out and the insides stay ridiculously creamy. If I can give you one tip, though, it’s to make sure you take it out of the oven while it’s still really wobbly, to get the best set. An overbaked Basque is no fun at all.Toffee apple Basque cheesecakeI’ve given this an easy autumn spin with a generous topping of lightly spiced toffee apple slices.Prep5 minCook1 hr 10 minChillOvernightServes12750g cream cheese220g caster sugar1½ tsp vanilla bean paste4 large eggs, plus 1 egg yolk300ml double cream1 tsp fine sea salt20g plain flourFor the toffee apples3 eating apples60g butter80g dark brown sugar½ tsp ground cinnamon120ml double creamHeat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/465F/gas 9. Scrunch up two large sheets of baking paper, then smooth them out into the corners of a deep 20cm cake tin.Put the cream cheese, sugar and vanilla in a large bowl or stand mixer, and beat briefly until smooth. Add the eggs one at a time, followed by the extra yolk, making sure you don’t beat at high speed to avoid incorporating too much air. Stir in the cream and salt.Scoop about an eighth of the batter into a smaller bowl and sift the flour on top. Mix well to ensure there are no lumps, then scrape it back into the main mixture and stir well to combine.Pour the batter into the prepared tin and bake for 35-40 minutes, until the top is very well browned and the cheesecake still has a huge wobble. (If the top isn’t dark enough, just put it under a hot grill for a couple of minutes.) Leave the cheesecake to cool to room temperature, then chill in the fridge, ideally overnight. The next day, remove the cheesecake from its tin.To make the toffee apples, peel and core the apples, then slice them thickly into eighths. Heat the butter in a wide pan, then toss in the apples, turning to coat, and cook for three to four minutes, until they start to soften around the edges. Add the sugar and cinnamon, stir to combine, then, once the sugar has melted, pour in the cream. Cook briefly until the sauce is smooth, let it simmer for a minute, then take off the heat and stir in a pinch of salt.Let the apples cool, then spoon them and some of the caramel sauce on top of the cheesecake. Serve slices of cheesecake with extra sauce, if you like.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotCakeSpanish food and drinkCheeseFruitAutumn food and drinkEggsrecipesShareReuse this content
