title: I hitchhiked from Sydney to Perth, and found comfort in the company of strangers | Adventure travel | The Guardian
description: The lost practice of hitchhiking is a subculture, an art, and a way of travel that satisfies wanderlust like no other trip. Plus, it costs nothing
Author: Aston Brown
Headline: The lost practice of hitchhiking is a subculture, an art, and a way of travel that satisfies wanderlust like no other trip. Plus, it costs nothing
Content: ‘I smile, stretch out my arm and raise my thumb’: Aston Brown hitchhikes west in Australia, attempting to travel from Sydney to Perth.Photograph: Em JensenView image in fullscreen‘I smile, stretch out my arm and raise my thumb’: Aston Brown hitchhikes west in Australia, attempting to travel from Sydney to Perth.Photograph: Em JensenAdventure travelI hitchhiked from Sydney to Perth, and found comfort in the company of strangersThe lost practice of hitchhiking is a subculture, an art, and a way of travel that satisfies wanderlust like no other trip. Plus, it costs nothingGet our weekend culture and lifestyle emailAston BrownFri 9 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 20.20 EDTShareI’m alone, hunched over by a dusty road junction, and feeling the bite of the morning sun. I’ve already been waiting here, on the outskirts of Esperance on the south coast of Western Australia, for more than three hours. Another wave of traffic approaches. I smile, stretch out my arm and raise my thumb.Most drivers who pass wave or give me a thumbs up. One gives me the finger. There isn’t much traffic. Someone tosses a water bottle out their window at me.Just as I start to catastrophise in the dust, a four-wheel-drive quietly pulls off the road and comes to a stop behind me. I hoist my backpack around my shoulder, run over and jump in the passenger seat, thanking the driver profusely.One of my stranger interests is hitchhiking. I’m drawn to the idea of abandoning control and finding comfort in a stranger’s company. It’s a subculture, an art, and a way of travel that satisfies wanderlust like no other trip. Plus, it costs nothing.Once a popular way to travel in the 70s and 80s, these days it’s pretty rare to see a hitchhiker on the side of Australian roads. For starters, its reputation was overwhelmingly tarnished by its association withserial killer Ivan Milat, who murdered several hitchhikers in the early 90s. Australia is also one of the few countries in the world that make it legally fraught to hitchhike, with laws explicitly naming hitchhiking as an offence, though legislation differs between state and territories.View image in fullscreenDehydration while waiting for a lift is a concern for hitchhikers.Photograph: Aston BrownAccording toHitchwiki(Wikipedia for hitchhiking), most jurisdictions essentially prohibit a pedestrian from standing on or moving on to a road to hitchhike, though the wording and what legally constitutes “the road” varies. However, in the ACT hitchhiking is legal in most circumstances and Tasmania removed any reference to hitchhiking from its road rules in 2019.But safety and legal baggage aside, there are some signs hitching is making a comeback. Online resources such as the hitchhiker community Hitchwiki and its offshoot,Trustroots, which has more than 120,000 members, are steadily growing. And according to the University of Western Australia’s Dr Fang Liu, who studies adventure tourism,social media accounts sharing extreme ways of travellingare demystifying and normalising hitchhiking.View image in fullscreenHitching is making a comeback as social media influencers normalise hitchhiking.Photograph: Aston Brown“Young international travellersare seeing people online and think, ‘Oh, I can do that too,’ but they may be unprepared and unaware of the risks,” she says.“In a lot of places there’s no [phone] signal and you might have to wait hours for someone to stop. By then you’ve probably already dehydrated. Social media doesn’t convey that.”Confessions of an 82-year-old hitchhikerRead moreInside strangers’ carsI introduce myself to my latest ride. The driver is Doug Hilton, the boss of Australia’s national science agency, CSIRO. His job will make for good conversational fodder, but more importantly, he’s driving 500km west to Albany, his car has air conditioning, and the dusty intersection is in the rear-vision mirror.I’ve hitchhiked in Australia a few times before, once up Tasmania’s east coast and across Flinders Island on the Bass Strait, and another time from Canberra to Sydney. But never as far and never as ambitious as this latest leg – the plan is to go all the way from Sydney to Perth, mostly inside strangers’ cars.It’s the final leg of my journey and things have taken a fortunate turn.View image in fullscreen‘You’re the first hitchhiker I’ve seen in decades,’ Mike tells Aston Brown as they drive through South Australia.Photograph: Aston Brown‘Here we feel so safe’Five days earlier I’m fresh and clean-shaven, standing outside Broken Hill in outback New South Wales. I wait just five minutes before an SUV with a bull bar doubles back and offers me a ride.Inside is Miranda and her two children, originally from Zimbabwe. The car is crammed with pillows and baggage, but they find room for me. While I ram my backpack into the boot, Miranda’s teenage daughter moves to the backseat, squishing in beside her younger brother and an Esky packed with yoghurt cups and juice boxes.The family immigrated to the US a few years ago, but because of gun violence and immigration crackdowns decided to leave. “I never would have picked up someone there, but here we feel so safe,” Miranda says, the desert rushing by.View image in fullscreenMiranda with her two children in South Australia after giving Aston Brown a lift from Broken Hill, NSW.Photograph: Aston BrownThey now live in the regional Queensland town of Chinchilla, where Miranda says they’ve been embraced by the community. “We are so happy here,” she says. “Every day I thank God for where we have ended up.” From the backseat, her daughter says she wants to study medicine when she finishes high school.After four hours of meandering conversations between long silences, we part ways somewhere in rural South Australia. They’re headed to Adelaide to visit a family friend and make the most of school holidays. I’m going west.‘Milat changed things’Soon I’m racing through rolling hills of green oats and yellow canola flowers draped in golden afternoon light. Hulking wind turbines spin on the hilltops. Mike, 67, is in the driver’s seat of his Toyota troop carrier. He spends his retirement restoring century-old farm tractors and is headed to Cowell to pick up some engine parts. He says by sundown we’ll be in Jamestown, a small town with a pleasant campground by the river.“You’re the first hitchhiker I’ve seen in decades,” he says. “Milat probably changed things.”View image in fullscreenCanola fields whiz past in South Australia.Photograph: Aston BrownIvan Milat was convicted of the murder of five female and two male backpackers between 1989 and 1992 in NSW, several of whom had been hitchhiking. It’salleged he’s responsible for dozens more unsolved murders or disappearances.There’s no denying the act of hitchhiking is inherently risky. But I am a white male. Whatever the risks I face, they are not the samedangersa woman or female-presenting person can encounter hitchhiking alone. Hitchwikioffers specific safety advicefor female hitchers, but maintains “you have a right to be respected and it is not true that while hitchhiking you expose yourself to a risk at your own wish”. They also point out that women willusually spend less time waitingto be picked up.View image in fullscreenMike in front of his vehicle in Jamestown, South Australia.Photograph: Aston BrownOn my journey I follow the general rule of thumb when it comes to hitching safely: I stand well off the road, in places with good visibility, with enough room for cars to pull over, and slow-moving traffic. I stick to footpaths where I can.When a car does pull over I give the driver a once-over and follow my gut. If I feel uncomfortable or unsafe, I know I’m under no obligation to get in the car. Though that’s a hypothetical. Every experience I’ve had has been positive so far.View image in fullscreenThe wide open road in South Australia.Photograph: Aston BrownOver beer and dinner at the Jamestown pub, I learn about Mike’s extended family and how proud he is of his overachieving daughter. The next morning I tag along with him further west, snaking up a mountain pass before plunging into a treeless and barren plain below. Across the Spencer Gulf, grey and faint in the distance, is the Whyalla steelworks. Last monthmore than 500 of the plant’s employees lost their jobs.“People are feeling pissed off – there’s only bad news now and the major parties have no solutions,” Mike says. Talking about politics is a staple of the journey, though in a stranger’s car I prefer to do most of the listening. “Still, we are a lucky country, it’s just a lot of us don’t realise how lucky,” Mike says. An hour later we part ways.‘Middle of everything’By midday I meet Neil, a 79-year-old widower on the final leg of a four-month road trip across the continent. Neil, who lives in Geraldton in Western Australia, has stopped in his ute. His first joke is about hitchhiking.“A hitchhiker gets into a car,” Neil tells me. “He says to the driver, ‘You’re fairly brave picking up a hitchhiker these days. For all you know, I could be a mass murderer.’“The driver turns to him and says, ‘Well, what are the chances of us both being axe murderers?’”View image in fullscreenNeil provides a running commentary as they drive through South Australia.Photograph: Aston BrownAs we get comfortable, Neil’s running commentary begins. There’s a “ripper” wheat crop over there and another a few kilometres later, much the same. Over there is a slag heap from an abandoned iron ore mine. But where are all the sheep? And what could that truck be hauling?I learn about his life, too. Marrying at 21, raising a family, working 96-hour weeks driving trucks and saving prudently. We talk about relationships, love and getting to the “pointy end”. His motto is: “If you never go, you never never know.”At dusk we pull off the Eyre Highway at a truckstop and Neil disappears into his camper trailer for the night. I pitch my tent beside it. The ground is gravel and my sleep is restless. In the morning we set off at dawn and I doze off in the passenger seat.View image in fullscreenRain falls on the Nullarbor Plain along the Eyre Highway in Western Australia.Photograph: Aston BrownBy the time I wake the sun is high and the landscape has transformed, thickets of silver saltbush and red dirt as far as the eye can see. We’ve reached the Nullarbor, a vast arid plain stretching 1,200km across southern Australia. “Middle of nowhere,” I say. “Nah mate, middle of everything,” Neil replies, road trains swooshing by endlessly.Towing his camper, Neil sticks to about 80km/h for safety and fuel efficiency, so it’s slow going. In the afternoon we drive down the 90 Mile Straight, the longest straight road in the southern hemisphere, and that night, under a gibbous moon, we share a dark beer, dinner and a Magnum mini vanilla ice-cream by the fire, all courtesy of Neil.View image in fullscreenThe 90 Mile Straight on the Nullarbor Plain in Western Australia.Photograph: Aston BrownThree days and 1,900km since we met, Neil pulls up outside a campground in Esperance. We take a selfie and exchange a warm handshake. I know it’s probably the last time I’ll see him.A birding detourI don’t know it yet, but Doug from the CSIRO, 62, will be the last driver to pick me up before I hit Perth.I bookend my journey by talking to Doug about his passion for moths, his dream of inventing a way to eradicateferal cats, and the benefits of therapy to his mental health. Among other scientific pursuits, he’s on his way to Albany to meet with two Menang Indigenous elders who co-authored a paper with him about moths in the region, including three newly discovered species of primitive jaw moths.In the afternoon I take up his invitation to join him bird watching by the ocean. We park at a headland, Doug grabs a Nikon Z9 with a huge telephoto lens out of the boot, and we start walking through thick coastal scrub. At sunset we witness a brown blur scurry across a dirt track. Doug misses the photo but is nonetheless ecstatic and wraps his arm around me in joy.View image in fullscreenThe Nullarbor Plain.Photograph: Aston BrownApparently we’ve just seen one of Australia’s rarest birds, the noisy scrubbird, presumed extinct until it was rediscovered in 1961. The significance of the sighting is lost on me but Doug assures me I’ve just hit the peak of my bird-watching career. I didn’t know I’d started it.We pull into Albany at dark and Doug drops me off at a hostel. It reeks of marijuana and there’s no hot water but I’m just happy to be sleeping on a thick mattress. When I wake up it’s miserable outside so I make the call to take the bus for the final six hours of the route to Perth. I’m comfortable, but it’s decidedly dull as the sprawling suburbs of the world’s most isolated capital city start rolling by. I’ve spent 4,360km travelling across the most isolated inhabited continent on Earth, yet for all the distance, I’ve rarely felt alone.

title: ‘A candlelit spa, followed by an ice-cold plunge and a nightcap’: readers’ favourite European wellbeing breaks | Spa breaks | The Guardian
description: From a historic bathhouse in Sweden to forest bathing in Croatia, readers share their favourite places to relax and recharge
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From a historic bathhouse in Sweden to forest bathing in Croatia, readers share their favourite places to relax and recharge
Content: Centralbadet is a historic art nouveau spa in central Stockholm.View image in fullscreenCentralbadet is a historic art nouveau spa in central Stockholm.Readers' travel tipsSpa breaks‘A candlelit spa, followed by an ice-cold plunge and a nightcap’: readers’ favourite European wellbeing breaksFrom a historic bathhouse in Sweden to forest bathing in Croatia, readers share their favourite places to relax and rechargeTell us about asmall European ski resort– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 9 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn art nouveau spa in StockholmTucked away off a pretty shopping street in a beautiful art nouveau building is one of Stockholm’s oldest spas,Centralbadetwhere a day ticket costs from £23. As winter darkness descends, candles are lit around the pool and a quiet calm envelops you. Swimming by candlelight is a treat. Next a sauna followed by an ice-cold plunge. Afterwards a nightcap is in order so it’s a brisk walk in the cold crisp air toFotografiskarestaurant. It’s a great spot to savour one of Stockholm’s best views; the old town Gamla Stan and the twinkling lights on Lake Mälaren.Sarah Rochfort‘Completely timeless and immersive’: birdwatching in NorfolkView image in fullscreenA misty evening on Salthouse marshes.Photograph: Ernie Janes/AlamyBirdwatching at the Cley and Salthouse marshes in Cley-next-the-sea, Norfolk. The two bird hides are meditative and relaxed spaces. The windows open directly on to the pools of saltwater where many different species of birds obliviously wander around. It’s a place that is completely timeless and immersive. Your only job is to gaze out at the birds. It’s a very popular spot for birdwatching but the atmosphere is friendly and quiet. Someone even let us have a go with their binoculars. We particularly enjoyed watching a nest of baby swallows huddled in the corner of the hide. The marshes cover a wide area and are so important for biodiversity, providing an essential resting place for resident and migratory birds. You might even spot a spoonbill, which have returned to the UK from 2010 after being absent for hundreds of years. Well worth a wellness visit, even if you don’t really know anything about birds (like me).PetraHampshire’s Scandi sauna hutsView image in fullscreenHello Outdoors shepherd’s hut sauna.Photograph: Jason Ludlow/PRA fresh ginger concoction, orange slices and a friendly sauna master greeted us at the Hello Outdoorsshepherd’s hut sauna, which has a picture window overlooking the historicLymington Sea Water Baths. The deep blue of the sky and water, Swedish sauna hats, the calming scent of our chosen essential oil, a soothing soundtrack and the option to ease the sauna heat with an exhilarating plunge in an ice-cold tub or more genial dip in the sun-warmed sea baths made for a very enjoyable and restorative couple of hours away from real life. We didn’t want to leave.Claire EdwardsProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Forest bathing in CroatiaView image in fullscreenThe village of Radoboj.Photograph: Zvonimir Atletic/AlamyFor five days in Radoboj, northern Croatia, we forest-bathed beneath the trees, walked slowly, practised breathing and meditation and ate simple local food. No luxury spa, no expensive treatments – just nature and time. I wore an Oura smart ring throughout. My resting heart rate fell markedly and, by day four, the ring recorded four and a half hours of restorative time. More importantly, I felt profoundly different. It completely overturned what I thought wellness travel was. Sometimes the most restorative place isn’t a spa. It’s a forest.Bex HamiltonBath time near Sofia, BulgariaView image in fullscreenThe Bankya Central Mineral Baths.Photograph: PRThe natural mineral springs in Sofia mean bathhouses are a way of life. Bankya is on the outskirts of the city, so I travelled by bus to visit theCentral Mineral Bath Bankya. This opulent bathhouse is owned by the Sofia municipality, meaning the atmosphere is a mix of the everyday council baths and extraordinary architecture from the early 20th century. You can visit from under €10 and, as well as the promised health benefits of the natural spring water, there is a thermal zone, a salt room, aromatherapy, saunas and steam rooms with an array of massages too.Sarah CollingsThe perfect spa and skiing combo in PolandView image in fullscreenA winter landscape of Zakopane and the Tatra mountains.Photograph: Zoonar/AlamyWhile skiing in Zakopane, Poland, we made a lot of use ofTerma Bania, an incredible pool and spa centre right in the heart of the ski resort. There is something magical about watching the sun go down in blissfully warm water and surrounded by snow. There is an astonishing array of saunas, pools and steam rooms, surrounded by mountain views. We discovered there are also several thermal pool and spa complexes in the surrounding area, and ended up spending as much of our holiday in the spas as we did on the slopes!Francesskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSimmer by the loch in ArgyllView image in fullscreenThe sauna at West Coast Wellness.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe Lochside Sauna atWest Coast Wellness(£17 for 2.5 hours) in Evanachan sits on the shore of Loch Fyne. Hidden away from the single track road, a 10-minute walk takes you to one of the most peaceful saunas in the UK. From the giant window, sit back and watch the water of the loch (keep an eye out for dolphins), slowly preparing yourself to make the short walk down and take a dip in between the heat. Alternatively there is a cold water plunge which if anything is colder than the loch! The centre also offers yoga and pilates sessions and there’s the deliciousInverrestaurant just around the corner.LewisWild swimming and wildlife in North YorkshireView image in fullscreenWild swimming at Pool Bridge Farm.Photograph: PRWild swimming atPool Bridge Farmguarantees a wholesome retreat from the vibrant bustle of neighbouring York. Transformed from old fishing ponds, the sprawling site comprises four lakes and ample space for lounging and lunching. A revitalising dip is best paired with a stop in the sauna (£16.50), priming those brave enough for the raw, heady thrill of the next plunge. To top it off, head to nearbyWheldrake Ings nature reserve, one of North Yorkshire’s top wildlife destinations, especially for waterfowl. As the flood waters rise from autumn, so does the abundance of migratory birds. A serene natural scene to soothe the soul.FinSensory walk in the Black Forest, GermanyMy two teenagers and I stumbled on a wellness experience for the mind, body and soul while we were wandering around the Black Forest near our holiday base of Freiburg last summer. A friendly German walker with a tree branch for a stick and a large husky for a companion told us to try a barefoot sensory trail atPark mit Allen Sinnen(park of all the senses) as we walked along together through the forest. So we followed his advice. It involved walking barefoot over grass, sand, woodchips, stone, mud and more while trying to tune into our five senses. We began by putting our hands into hollowed-out trees with our eyes closed to guess what objects were placed there. There were bright, colourful flowers, natural scents to imagine and huts to relax and sit in full of sounds and smells to immerse ourselves in with eyes closed. We repeated these walks for three days, heightening our contact with our own senses – and treating ourselves to rye bread and cheese sandwiches with forest fruits berry juice from simple forest cafe cabins as a reward.HelenWinning tip: County Donegal’s peerless sauna on the pierView image in fullscreenA boat trip to the Sliabh Liag sea cliffs.Photograph: Christopher Hill /Scenic Ireland/AlamyIf you find yourself on the wild coast of south County Donegal, head to the Sliabh Liag Sauna at Teelin pier. After a day of hiking (and maybe one or two pints of porter the evening before), the small wood-fired sauna right on the pier was the perfect unwind. We followed it up by taking a sea dip in the bay just steps away. If you have plenty of time, combine the sauna with a nearby boat trip to the unforgettable Sliabh Liag sea cliffs towering 601 metres (1,972ft) above the sea.Peter HenryView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsSpa breaksReaders' travel tipsHealth and fitness holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Soil in need of some TLC? Then it’s time to make room for legumes | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: Crops such as vetch, field beans and forage peas can improve soil if you use them as a mulch
Author: Claire Ratinon
Headline: Crops such as vetch, field beans and forage peas can improve soil if you use them as a mulch
Content: Field beans are an ally to organic growers.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenField beans are an ally to organic growers.Photograph: AlamyGardening adviceSoil in need of some TLC? Then it’s time to make room for legumesCrops such as vetch, field beans and forage peas can improve soil if you use them as a mulchClaire RatinonFri 9 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIam locked in an eternal battle with my soil. Now, I adore the earth and believe it to be miraculous in its life-giving properties. But I’d be lying if I said I don’t sometimes (or often) feel deeply frustrated with the intransigence of the heavy clay I’m working with in my veg patch. Clay soil is especially miraculous in how nutrient dense it is. Yet, those nutrients are, somewhat ironically, more challenging for gardeners to access for their crops than with other soil types.The answer – as with almost all problems faced in a chemical free, mostly no-dig garden – is adding a mulch of organic matter (either compost or well-rotted manure) that can be incorporated into the earth by insects, who will improve its texture in the process. And yet, this trusty approach is tricky in my veg patch as we live on a hill and there is about a metre’s difference between one side of the site and the other. This situation (plus the stubbornness of soil made sodden by a wet winter and then solid by a heatwave summer) has meant the layers of compost I laid over the last year have been either washed away or not particularly well incorporated into the deeper soil.double quotation markThe root systems decompose in the ground… improving its structure and capacity to retain waterAll this is to say, I was not in a good position at the start of the growing season, and now autumn has arrived I’m considering what the soil needs for next year. Of course, I will continue to mulch enthusiastically, but I’m also looking at a key plant type that can come to the rescue – the legume. Capable of taking nitrogen from the air and capturing it in their bodies (with the help of some nifty bacteria) to be released for use by future plants, legumes are an effective ally to the organic grower who is working with soil that needs some extra TLC.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter a fiery summer, I’m choosing resilient crops to future-proof my gardenRead moreSown now, vetch (also known as winter tares), field beans and forage peas – whose ideal sowing time is September, but I suspect October will be fine in milder spots – will push their roots deep down into the soil during the coming months. Then, come spring, before they’ve had a chance to flower and while their stems are still soft, they can be cut down at the base and either incorporated into the soil if you’re inclined to dig, or if, like me, you’re not, they can be chopped into pieces and laid as a surface mulch, or put in the compost to rot down there.Either way, the root systems decompose in the ground, where they will be of most benefit to the soil, improving its structure and capacity to retain water as well as dispensing with any excess of it.While it does mean that those veg beds of mine won’t be planted with my favourite winter-ready or overwintering crops, it should mean that the soil is in a much better state to work with next spring.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensOrganic gardeningCompostSoilfeaturesShareReuse this content

Her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics, looks at the relationship between economic insecurity and the rise of the far right, arguing progressive politics must respond to the rise of authoritarianism by urgently addressing the economic pressures people experience in their daily lives. title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau | Vaccines and immunisation | The Guardian
description: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers
Author: Melody Schreiber
Headline: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers
Content: A child receives a hepatitis B vaccine in Lomé, Togo, on 7 August 2015.Photograph: BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA child receives a hepatitis B vaccine in Lomé, Togo, on 7 August 2015.Photograph: BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesVaccines and immunisationControversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-BissauRecommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchersMelody SchreiberFri 9 Oct 2026 17.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.It is a central part of the vaccine vision forRobert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants inGuinea-Bissauin the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said wassuspendedafterinternational uproarearlier this year.Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.Experts fear ‘unethical’ vaccine trial in Africa is ‘prototype’ for US studies under RFK JrRead moreThe US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) hasreportedlyset aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday byCIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University inDenmark.According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held adual appointmentwith Bandim as recently as December.Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchersfound no effectsat all.This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”Explore more on these topicsVaccines and immunisationGuinea-BissauAfricaHealthRobert F Kennedy JrDenmarknewsShareReuse this content

title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law | Nobel peace prize | The Guardian
description: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza
Content: 1:11Nobel peace prize winner Navi Pillay jokes about sharing award with Donald Trump – videoNobel peace prizeICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international lawCommittee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in GazaJulian BorgerandRachel SavageFri 9 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTFirst published on Fri 9 Oct 2026 05.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commissionthat concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.That commission concluded last year that the state of Israelwas guilty of genocidal actsin Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,”the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.“In awarding this year’sNobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.Hours after the announcement, the Trump administrationunveiled broad new sanctionsagainst the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in SouthAfrica, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in theAkayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establishrape and sexual violence as weapons of war– a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January byhanding her winner’s medalto Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”Explore more on these topicsNobel peace prizeNorwaySouth AfricaInternational court of justiceHuman rightsAfricaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season | Hurricane Isaias | The Guardian
description: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding
Content: Larry Smith boards up his home with plywood before Hurricane Isaias's expected landfall along the Gulf coast in Dauphin Island, Alabama.Photograph: Octavio Jones/APView image in fullscreenLarry Smith boards up his home with plywood before Hurricane Isaias's expected landfall along the Gulf coast in Dauphin Island, Alabama.Photograph: Octavio Jones/APWeather trackerHurricane IsaiasIsaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 seasonStorm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river floodingMegan Davies for MetDeskFri 9 Oct 2026 05.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 10.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).As a result ofthe strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama andMississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.View image in fullscreenPeople pick up sandbags in Mobile, Alabama, in preparation for Hurricane Isaias.Photograph: Octavio Jones/APInZimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.Explore more on these topicsHurricane IsaiasWeather trackerHurricanesUS weatherTexasLouisianaMississippiAlabamanewsShareReuse this content

title: Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues  | Global development | The Guardian
description: Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood
Content: Journalists with a symbolic coffin representing press freedom at a 2016 protest. Egyptian journalists say the arrests are part of mounting pressure against the media.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenJournalists with a symbolic coffin representing press freedom at a 2016 protest. Egyptian journalists say the arrests are part of mounting pressure against the media.Photograph: APGlobal developmentEgyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleaguesMatsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim BrotherhoodSupported byAbout this contentSaher Ahmed in CairoFri 9 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 15.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEgyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend aftersix colleagues were charged with terrorism offencesamid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawedMuslim Brotherhood.The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.In astatement issued on Wednesdayevening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detainedRead moreDarwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentPress freedomProtestNewspapers & magazinesEgyptMuslim BrotherhoodMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: How a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find | Plants | The Guardian
description: Species with leaves large enough to be seen from space is already critically endangered – and plans are afoot to protect it
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Species with leaves large enough to be seen from space is already critically endangered – and plans are afoot to protect it
Content: Jeremiah Harris in one of the pictures he posted on Instagram that was seen by waterlily expert Carlos Magdalena.Photograph: Jeremiah HarrisView image in fullscreenJeremiah Harris in one of the pictures he posted on Instagram that was seen by waterlily expert Carlos Magdalena.Photograph: Jeremiah HarrisPlantsHow a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily findSpecies with leaves large enough to be seen from space is already critically endangered – and plans are afoot to protect itPippa NeillEnvironment reporterFri 9 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA chance social media encounter has led to the race-against-time discovery of a new species of giant waterlily that has until now been hidden in the depths of Colombia’s jungle.But the plant, which is so huge it is visible from space, is already considered critically endangered.Giant waterlilies, which can measure up to three metres across and carry the weight of a small child, are one of the oldest flowering plants in the world still alive today. They existed before the continents split apart and are present throughout culture, from the Egyptians to Monet.Three years ago, while scrolling through Instagram, Carlos Magdalena, a world-renowned waterlily expert at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, came across a photo of someone swimming among several giant waterlilies in the Inírida River in Guainía, Colombia.Jeremiah Harris, who took the photo and who runs a carnivorous plant nursery in the US, was not aware of its significance, having mistakenly identified the waterlily as the more common Victoria amazonica.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueHowever, when Magdalena saw the photo, he “immediately suspected” something was unusual as the natural range of the Victoria amazonica does not extend to the Inírida River.He messaged Harris to track down the exact location and spent several years analysing satellite imagery and securing the funds and necessary permits to allow him to verify the presence of the waterlily for himself.Along with a team from the Jardín Botánico in Bogotá and members of the local indigenous reserves, Magdalena went on a five-day expedition deep into the rainforest.They spent several days exploring the flooded jungle with no luck, until, at the last moment, their driver advised them where to look. With only 10 hours left until their return flight, the team sailed overnight in total darkness to a small lake deep in the flooded rainforest, where they located a population of the waterlilies.View image in fullscreenCarlos Magdalena with a Victoria colombiana leaf.Photograph: Mauricio Bernal/Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew“It was so emotional I shed a tear, it was one of those moments that will remain with me for life,” Magdalena said. “Coming across something like this is absolutely totally fascinating, it’s jaw dropping.“Giant waterlilies give away their secrets slowly,” he said. “It’s remarkable. We believe we know everything but the reality is we don’t, there’s lots of things still to be discovered and protected.”The team collected the material needed to begin a formal identification, with a paper published on Friday in the journalPhytotaxaconfirming it as a new species to science. The waterlily has been given the official name Victoria colombiana. There are just three other known giant waterlilies.Newly identified waterlily species is world’s largestRead moreHarris, who is an author of the study, said his friends always teased him for taking selfies with plants, but the fact this one ended in the discovery of a new species was “incredible”.“I was just so excited, absolutely elated,” he said.Magdalena said: “This is one of those extraordinary stories where indigenous and horticultural knowledge with the help of social media and technology came together to uncover a truly extraordinary botanical achievement.”The team estimates there are between 30 and 50 of the Victoria colombiana waterlilies in the wild, making them extremely rare and at risk of extinction.Maarten Christenhusz, a plant taxonomist who analysed the sample, said new species were found all the time, but few were as “large, spectacular and emblematic as this one. This new giant waterlily can even be seen from space, which is a striking reminder of how much we still don’t know about life on our planet.”View image in fullscreenResearchers inspect the newfound discovery.Photograph: Royal Botanic Gardens, KewThe team is working towards an official International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List designation.Efforts are also under way to support the long-term conservation of the waterlily, including the possibility of establishing a naturalised population in a more accessible lake within indigenous territory. The researchers hope to continue efforts to collect the plant’s seed, with the aim of cultivating it in Bogotá. If these efforts are successful, there is a chance the waterlily may be grown atKew Gardens.Explore more on these topicsPlantsWildlifeColombiaAmericasResearchConservationEndangered speciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence | Cop31 | The Guardian
description: ‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in Fiji
Author: Adam Morton
Headline: ‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in Fiji
Content: The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, speaks with Turkey’s climate change minister, Murat Kurum, at the pre-Cop31 summit in Fiji.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, speaks with Turkey’s climate change minister, Murat Kurum, at the pre-Cop31 summit in Fiji.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesCop31Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in FijiAdam Mortonin Nadi, FijiFri 9 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 08.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said.But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet inTurkeynext month.Kurum, the Turkish climate change minister, told the Guardian the world was “already in a transition” and suggested fossil fuel use could be addressed indirectly through other steps.Kurum was among national leaders and ministers, officials and civil society members in Fiji this week to prepare for Cop31, which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya in November. Australia, which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31, had pushed to hold the pre-Cop meetingin the Pacificto bring attention to island nations.View image in fullscreenFijian dancers perform at the summit’s welcome ceremony.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesGeopolitical turmoil from war, a historic energy crisis and an unpredictable and climate-denying US administration – combined with the knowledge that many would be attending the main climate summit in a few weeks – meant only 13 national leaders joined Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the Fijian city of Nadi, and most were from the Pacific.But there were also about 30 ministers, including from India and European nations, representatives from the big emitters China and Saudi Arabia, the heads of global agencies and about 4,000 other attenders.On Tuesday, a delegation flew north to seeTuvalu, a low-lying atoll country of about 10,000 people that is among the most at risk from the climate crisis. They were shown a 20-hectare (49-acre) land reclamation project and heard stories of life in a country that is mostly only about 2 metres above sea level, and where rising waters, storm surges and intensifying extreme weather pose an accelerating threat to survival.In a powerful speech, Melelusi Sokotia, 13, told the visitors her friends’ dreams to be “teachers, doctors, builders” were being subsumed by the question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.Back in Nadi, Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, was moved to tears and received a standing ovation during her closing address. She urged delegates to “remember the people you met” and “carry something of the Pacific with you”.Tabuya said: “This pre-Cop draws to a close tonight. Our responsibility does not.”View image in fullscreenFiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya (centre), receives applause during the summit’s closing session on Thursday.Photograph: Pacific pre-Cop31/AFP/Getty ImagesThe governments of about 190 countries will head to Antalya with clear evidence that responsibility is not being met. A recent report by the UN environment programme warned that under the most optimistic future, global heating wouldreach at least 1.8C, well beyond the 1.5C ceiling of the Paris climate agreement. It called for immediate and sustained emissions cuts and said every fraction of a degree of heating avoided would save lives and reduce economic losses.Throughout the pre-Cop, Pacific leaders repeated their demands: that countries must act to “keep 1.5C alive”, that climate finance must be easily accessible for poor and vulnerable communities who have not caused the problem but are most at risk, and that the health of oceans must be prioritised.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAustralia and Turkey criticised for hosting UN climate conference while embracing coalRead moreAustralia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said only 0.2% of global climate finance was spent helping small island developing countries adapt, and that the countries that needed it the most, such as Tuvalu, “get it the least”. “That has got to change,” he said. “It’s a key priority ofCop31.”Kurum said Nato countries should be much more focused on climate spending. He said they had promised to increase their defence budgets to 5% of GDP by 2035 as a result of “concerns for their own safety and security”, but had committed much less to addressing the climate crisis despite expressing concerns and it posing an even greater risk.Asked if he thought as much should be spent on climate as defence, he said: “Much more.”View image in fullscreenLeaders attend a session at the summit.Photograph: Getty Images“The climate issue is the security issue itself,” Kurum told the Guardian through an interpreter. “If you don’t spend one unit of money prior to the disasters, then you are left in a position where you have to spend 10 units of money after the disaster. It’s cheaper pre-disaster.”Kurum and Bowen reiterated they would focus in Antalya on winning support for a global goal of 35% of the energy needed to run homes, businesses, factories and vehiclescoming from electricityby 2035. Now it is about 21%.But the question of what direct action the global community should agree to take to phase out fossil fuels remains far more vexed.Both host countries backed a multi-country statement in Fiji that supported a global “transition away from fossil fuels”, echoing language adopted by the global communityat Cop28 in Dubai three years ago. But both faced criticism, and accusations of hypocrisy, for continuing toback new coal and gas developmentsand beinglargely silent before the pre-Copon the need to phase out fossil fuels.View image in fullscreenChris Bowen, a Cop31 president-designate and Australia’s climate minister, chairs a session on Thursday.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesBowen said the way to stop using fossil fuels was not to cut supply of the dirty fuel but to build enough renewable energy so there would be no need for fossil fuel power plants.Kurum said the world was “already in a transition” and suggested the focus at climate talks on wording about transitioning away from fossil fuels might not be productive as he did not think further progress could be made. Delegates from some countries, including Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states,strongly opposed naming fossil fuels at Cop30in Brazil.Dozens of countries frustrated with what they see as a UN stalemate on the issue met separatelyin Colombiathis year to discuss a path away from fossil fuels. They are due to meet again next July in Tuvalu, and want the issue to be in an agreement in Antalya.Tzeporah Berman, the chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, said Pacific leaders had been clear in Nadi that there should be an urgent fossil fuel phaseout.“This means no new projects,” she said. “You can’t phase something out by building more of it.”Explore more on these topicsCop31Global climate talksClimate crisisTurkeyFijiTuvaluPacific islandsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sydney trader sacked for working from Singapore without permission wins unfair dismissal case | Industrial relations | The Guardian
description: Employee had also been in Bali when he told his manager he was working from home, Fair Work Commission hears
Author: Nino Bucci
Headline: Employee had also been in Bali when he told his manager he was working from home, Fair Work Commission hears
Content: Singapore’s city centre. The employee had previously asked if he could relocated to the city state but had been denied permission.Photograph: shih-wei/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSingapore’s city centre. The employee had previously asked if he could relocated to the city state but had been denied permission.Photograph: shih-wei/Getty ImagesIndustrial relationsSydney trader sacked for working from Singapore without permission wins unfair dismissal caseEmployee had also been in Bali when he told his manager he was working from home, Fair Work Commission hearsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastNino BucciCourts and justice reporterFri 9 Oct 2026 01.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Sydney currency trader who was sacked for working fromSingaporewithout approval has won an unfair dismissal case, but failed to be awarded compensation.The Fair Work Commission ruled on Wednesday that Charles Graham had been unfairly dismissed by HIFX Australia, trading as Xe, in December last year.Graham was sacked after his manager asked an IT worker to use his “FBI skills” and track the IP address on Graham’s laptop.They discovered he was working from Singapore. It was also later discovered he had previously worked from Bali after telling his manager he was working from home because he had a plumber “coming around to sort out some recurring bathroom issues”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailGraham was sacked as Xe found he knew he had to get prior approval to work overseas and was to attend the office three times a week.He said he had been holidaying in Singapore before his partner became ill with a bacterial infection, preventing him from returning to Australia.Home comforts: can remote work be better for the environment?Read moreHe provided documentation, which he said showed his partner required medical treatment.Graham had previously asked Xe if he could relocate to Singapore, but his request was denied.Fair Work Commission commissioner Alana Matheson said that after the company sent an email to Graham advising him of its discovery on 17 November last year, the “tone … had clearly pivoted” by the following day, when he was told “there was a case to answer regarding alleged breaches of company policy”.Over the following 10 days, a series of further email exchanges and a discussion between Xe managers took place.Graham said in his written response to Xe that he travelled to Singapore for a holiday and that there was no relation to his previous request to relocate there, that the decision to reschedule the return flight to Australia was made over a weekend, and that as there was no expectation or precedent that he contacted his manager outside business hours, he could not inform them of this.He said that when he did log on from Singapore rather than in Australia “he was bombarded with triaging hundreds of unread emails from his time off, fielding inbound calls and dealing with an eligible complaint from a high-value client”, and this took priority over telling his manager he was stuck overseas.Among his other responses was that he only intended to spend a short amount of time overseas, he had not been told about specific policies regarding hybrid work, and that he had intended to let his manager know he was overseas as soon as practicable.The company was not swayed and on 2 December last year sent him a termination letter that stated it had carefully reviewed his written submissions and found that he had not provided flight screenshots with his name, medical evidence that showed his partner was unable to travel, an adequate explanation for not telling his manager he was in Singapore, and had previously complied with “absence and approval processes”, demonstrating that he was familiar with them and had instead made “a conscious choice not to follow” them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toMorning MailOur Australian morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Your conduct represents a serious breach of company policy, a failure to follow lawful and reasonable instructions, and an irreparable breakdown of trust and confidence,” it said in the letter.Graham told the commission he worked remotely twice before November 2025: the previous year from Townsville, and in April and May 2025 from Bali. He had been employed by Xe for 20 months.But his manager said she had not been aware he had ever worked remotely from overseas.A Microsoft Teams message from Graham to his manager was included in evidence before the commission that detailed his claim he was working from home as he had a plumbing issue during one of the days he also told the commission he worked from Bali.Matheson found that she was satisfied that the dismissal of Graham was unreasonable because while there was a valid reason for his dismissal, the process followed was procedurally unfair.This was because Xe failed to fully raise the matters it was relying on in making the decision to dismiss Graham, Matheson said.She found that reinstatement was inappropriate but also decided against awarding compensation.This was, she said, in part because his misconduct contributed to the decision to dismiss him, and he was paid four weeks in lieu of notice.Explore more on these topicsIndustrial relationsSydneySingaporeAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women with PMOS should get subsidised weight-loss drugs, Australian advocates say | Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) | The Guardian
description: With GLP-1s to treat the condition not specifically approved by the TGA, patients are being prescribed them off-label
Author: Tess Ikonomou
Headline: With GLP-1s to treat the condition not specifically approved by the TGA, patients are being prescribed them off-label
Content: Symptoms of polyendrocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome include weight gain, hair loss and irregular periods.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenSymptoms of polyendrocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome include weight gain, hair loss and irregular periods.Photograph: James Manning/PAPolyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS)Women with PMOS should get subsidised weight-loss drugs, Australian advocates sayWith GLP-1s to treat the condition not specifically approved by the TGA, patients are being prescribed them off-labelGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTess IkonomouFri 9 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 19.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWomen living with a chronic hormonal condition should have access to taxpayer-funded weight-loss medications, advocates say.The Polyendrocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome Association of Australia (POSAA) is urging for GLP-1 drugs to be approved on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for people living with the condition.Formerly known as polycystic ovarian syndrome, PMOS affects one in eight women. Symptoms can include irregular periods, excess hair growth on the body and face, weight gain and hair thinning.New name for PCOS gives new hope to millions of womenRead moreThe lifelong condition, for which there is no cure, can lead to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and endometrial cancer.While GLP-1s are not specifically approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration to treat PMOS, patients are being prescribed the medications off-label.Half a million Australians are estimated to be using weight-loss medications regularly, aUniversity of New South Wales studyfound in July.Lorna Berry, a spokesperson for the POSAA who was diagnosed with the condition at 32, said she would welcome GLP-1s being subsidised for patients diagnosed with PMOS, in addition to funding for evidence-based research.“It’s important for people to have access to medications, irrespective of where they live or where they were born … it’s really important that there’s equitable access,” she told the Guardian.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailBerry said some women living with the condition were already missing out on being able to access the medications due to their high cost, which can set patients back several hundred dollars each month.Associate professor Magdalena Simonis, the women’s health spokesperson for the Royal Australasian College of Physicians, said the college did not currently have a position on whether GLP-1s were appropriate for the management of PMOS.“They’re not necessarily the only tool we have available to us, and that is important because long-term use is expensive, and it doesn’t look like these are going to be on the PBS anytime soon, and maybe not ever for conditions such as PMOS,” she said.“Because traditionally women’s conditions are not included in these changes.”Simonis, a GP with an expert interest in PMOS, said should research find the weight-loss medications more effective than existing treatments, a broader discussion about health equity would be needed.“That is a conversation that we’re having about obesity as a national issue,” she said.GLP-1 drugs – glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists – mimic a naturally occurring hormone which helps manage blood sugar levels and reduces hunger.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOzempic is listed by the PBS, but only for the treatment of diabetes.The Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee last November recommended Wegovy be subsidised for those with a body mass index above 35.The committee will meet next month when it will consider Novo Nordisk’s revised proposal to list Wegovy for obesity following protracted negotiations.The Danish pharmaceutical company produces both Ozempic and Wegovy.They contain the same active ingredient – semaglutide – but Wegovy has a higher dose.“Novo Nordisk is continuing to work constructively with the Department ofHealthto try to negotiate a solution for the PBS listing of Wegovy,” a company spokesperson said.“We remain committed to improving access for eligible Australians living with obesity.”QENDO, an organisation advocating for people affected by PMOS and other women’s health conditions, said it recognised “growing interest in GLP-1 medications for managing PMOS, particularly for people experiencing metabolic complications and challenges with weight management”.“While emerging evidence suggests potential benefits for some patients, further research is needed to establish their long-term effectiveness and safety specifically for PMOS,” QENDO’s acting chief executive, Kate Fisher, said.Explore more on these topicsPolyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS)HealthWeight-loss drugsWomen's healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: New spate of stabbings, overdoses and fires at Australian immigration detention centres run by ICE-linked US prison firm | Australian immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Federal government under scrutiny as documents reveal serious security lapses at Melbourne and Villawood immigration detention centres
Author: Christopher Knaus
Headline: Exclusive: Federal government under scrutiny as documents reveal serious security lapses at Melbourne and Villawood immigration detention centres
Content: Sydney’s Villawood immigration detention centre, where eight fires were reported to have been lit between February and May.Photograph: Daniel Munoz/ReutersView image in fullscreenSydney’s Villawood immigration detention centre, where eight fires were reported to have been lit between February and May.Photograph: Daniel Munoz/ReutersAustralian immigration and asylumNew spate of stabbings, overdoses and fires at Australian immigration detention centres run by ICE-linked US prison firmExclusive:Federal government under scrutiny as documents reveal serious security lapses at Melbourne and Villawood immigration detention centresGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastChristopher KnausandAriel BogleFri 9 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 19.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new spate of stabbings, overdoses and drug use in Australia’s immigration detention centres has put the Australian government in likely breach of laws designed to protect staff and detainees, internal documents show.Earlier this year,Guardian Australia revealedcatastrophic security failings across Australia’s onshore immigration network since Management and Training Corporation – a US private prison company used by Donald Trump to hold ICE detainees – won the $2.3bn detention contract in late 2024.The federal government has repeatedly attempted to take a stick to MTC and its local subsidiary Secure Journeys to improve its performance, including through financial penalties and a fiery meeting last year between the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, and the company’s global president.Escapes, fires, stabbing: catastrophic security failures revealed in Australia’s immigration detention networkRead moreBut new documents seen by the Guardian show serious security lapses have continued since, including through a spate of eight fire-related incidents at Villawood immigration detention centre and violence and drug use atMelbourneimmigration detention centre (MIDC). Those failings have again put the department itself in the crosshairs of Comcare, the federal work safety regulator.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe documents reveal a string of incidents at MIDC involving violence, aggression, illicit substances and improvised weaponry since August. That includes a violent altercation on 18 August between two groups that led to six detainees being hospitalised for “slashing and stabbing injuries made using improvised weapons”.On 10 September, a detainee was found overdosed in his room, requiring staff to administer Naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdose effects.The incidents at MIDC prompted Comcare to warn the government that it was failing to control the rising number of “incidents of this type at MIDC and across the broader immigration detention network”.
