That failure meant it was likely to be in breach of the law, the document said.“I have formed the reasonable belief that the department is contravening section 19 of the WHS Act by failing to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and other persons,” Comcare said in its notice. “In particular, the risks associated with violence, aggression, and the presence of illicit substances and improvised weaponry are not being adequately managed.“While the department has advised that a range of actions have been undertaken to address these risks, it has not sufficiently demonstrated that the control measures currently in place are effective in eliminating or minimising the risks, so far as is reasonably practicable.”Comcare said the information available indicates these hazards pose an ongoing risk of serious harm to workers and others in the centres.A separate Comcare document revealed that a series of eight fire-related incidents had taken place at Villawood immigration detention centre between February and May.View image in fullscreenFire damage to a room at VillawoodThe fires occurred despite prior warnings to government to intervene after previous fires lit inside Villawood exposed serious gaps in MTC’s preparedness. That includes one fire on 23 September 2025, when MTC staff rushed into a detainee’s room to save him from a fire without proper safety equipment, causing two workers to be hospitalised.The regulator found the department had not conducted its own systematic review of “all fire and smoke control measures falling within its influence or control”, a likely breach of work health and safety regulations.“The occurrence of multiple notifiable fire incidents over a period of approximately four months, particularly after previous regulatory intervention concerning substantially the same risk, provided repeated and compelling circumstances requiring the department to review the effectiveness of relevant control measures,” the Comcare document said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWorkers accuse new company managing Australia’s immigration detention centres of running them ‘like a prison’Read moreThe Guardian previously revealed a series of incidents across the centres since Secure Journey took over, including escapes, staff injuries and sick detainees missing medical appointments due to a lack of staff to escort them.Lyndal Ryan, national president of the United Workers Union, which represents workers in the centres, said the notices from Comcare show “the continuing dangerous situations facing workers and detainees inside detention centres, and Secure Journeys’ inability or unwillingness to address those issues”.The union hascontinually raised concernsabout understaffing in the centres, and Ryan said Comcare has made it clear that the department has the responsibility to pull Secure Journeys into line.“The list of eight fires at Villawood over a four-month period are signs of the instability and chaos our members are witnessing almost every day,” she said.A spokesperson for MTC’s local subsidiary, Secure Journeys, said:“In response to your questions, I can confirm that Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority.”An Australian Border Force spokesperson said it continually reviewed safety and security arrangements across the detention network.“Any regulatory notices issued by Comcare are assessed and responded to through established workplace health and safety processes,” the spokesperson said.“The welfare, safety and dignity of people in immigration detention, as well as the safety of staff, remain the Department’s highest priorities.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian immigration and asylumAustralian politicsMigrationMelbourneSydneynewsShareReuse this content

title: Adidas accuses Australian label White Fox of ‘trading off its reputation’ with use of four-stripe branding | Business | The Guardian
description: Global sportswear brand is suing online retailer in the federal court for selling clothes featuring ‘deceptively similar’ design
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Global sportswear brand is suing online retailer in the federal court for selling clothes featuring ‘deceptively similar’ design
Content: Adidas is suing White Fox for allegedly breaching its trademark of the three-stripe design.Composite: Federal Court of AustraliaView image in fullscreenAdidas is suing White Fox for allegedly breaching its trademark of the three-stripe design.Composite: Federal Court of AustraliaBusinessAdidas accuses Australian label White Fox of ‘trading off its reputation’ with use of four-stripe brandingGlobal sportswear brand is suing online retailer in the federal court for selling clothes featuring ‘deceptively similar’ designGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressFri 9 Oct 2026 02.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 02.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGlobal sportswear brand Adidas claims Australian label White Fox is trying to trade off its reputation by infringing its distinctive three-stripe trademark.Adidas is suing the online fast-fashion retailer in the Federal Court for selling clothes with a four-stripe design, which it argues is deceptively similar to its classic design.White Fox rejected repeated requests to stop selling and promoting clothing bearing the four parallel stripes, its rival claims.During the first mention of the dispute on Friday, Adidas’s barrister Patrick Flynn SC argued the Sydney-based company had been using the stripes as a trademark for months.Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over ‘deceptively similar’ four-stripe clothingRead moreHe pointed to a picture of a White Fox-endorsed influencer wearing the company’s four-stripe shorts with genuine Adidas shoes as a promotion that would confuse consumers.“There’s an intention to trade off our reputation,” Flynn said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailAdidas has held the trademark for a three-stripe design in Australia for more than 50 years and successfully sued another retailer for infringement over shoes bearing four stripes in 2013.It meant the action filed against White Fox in September was “not uncharted territory”, Flynn noted.“This is a pretty simple matter,” he said.White Fox’s barrister Ed Heerey KC said the Australian company would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label’s clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark.View image in fullscreen(L-R) Adidas track pants alongside White Fox track pants.Composite: Federal Court of AustraliaHe highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands such as fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons, and Shein.“Obviously Adidas has a reputation,” Heerey said.“Their own slogan is that it’s the brand with three stripes. Emphasis on the three.”The boutique will interrogate whether the use of four stripes was deceptively similar to Adidas’s trademark and whether any consumers would actually be misled.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe noted the 2013 judgment in favour of Adidas found it was common for branding to be placed on the side of shoes, but there was no such common practice for clothing.Adidas is seeking orders that will prevent White Fox making clothing with four stripes and force it to hand over profits it made on the products.Justice Ian Jackman – brother of one of Australia’s most famous exports Hugh Jackman – set the dispute down for a hearing in early 2027.It marks the first high-profile litigation of this kind against White Fox Boutique, which has become a major player in the retail industry since it was launched in Sydney in 2013.Co-founders Georgia and Daniel Contos, who own the company with Daniel’s mother Melina Maceri, focused on social media and influencer marketing to build their brand.The online retailer later expanded to the US and UK and generated $542m in revenue in the year to June 2025.Meanwhile Adidas, which generated a record $39.9bn in 2025, has vigilantly defended its three-stripe trademark across the globe with varying success.The sportswear giant recently lost its trademark infringement cases against luxury brand Thom Browne in the US, UK, and Germany.The upcoming battle in the federal court could prove to be a battleground for Adidas in a world of fast fashion and prolific imitation.Explore more on these topicsBusinessAustralian fashionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Firmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre company | Datacentres - Australia | The Guardian
description: The $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997
Author: Jonathan Barrett
Headline: The $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997
Content: Tim Rosenfield (left) and Oliver Curtis (right), who together with Curtis’s former brother-in-law Jonathan Levee are the trio behind Firmus, which shelved its IPO plans on Friday.Photograph: Firmus TechnologiesView image in fullscreenTim Rosenfield (left) and Oliver Curtis (right), who together with Curtis’s former brother-in-law Jonathan Levee are the trio behind Firmus, which shelved its IPO plans on Friday.Photograph: Firmus TechnologiesDatacentres - AustraliaFirmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre companyThe $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJonathan BarrettandJosh TaylorFri 9 Oct 2026 00.37 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirmus Technologies has scrapped what was set to be Australia’s biggest company listing in decades after investor demand for its much-hyped AI datacentre business failed to materialise.A Firmus spokesperson said the board decided that proceeding with the offer was no longer in the best interests of the company and its shareholders.“Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options,” the spokesperson said on Friday morning.Australia is building a lot of new homes. But is the datacentre boom holding us back? | Greg JerichoRead more“We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress.”Firmus, with an anticipated $44bn valuation, was expected to be the biggest ASX listing since Telstra in 1997.But it faced mounting scepticism over its huge valuation, and forecast earnings, for a company in its startup phase with just two, small operational sites.Backed by chip maker Nvidia and Wall Street firms Blackstone, Jane Street and Coatue, Firmus’s backers believed they could raise billions of dollars by selling shares in a public float with the help of five brokers.Thelack of demandmeans Firmus will need to raise money from private investors to fund its plans to build liquid-cooled “AI factories” in Australia and across Asia.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailFrantic discussionsThe polished Firmus pitch started to unravel midweek after it became clear the company’s bankers had vastly overestimated demand in their bid to raise $7bn from investors ahead of listing on the ASX on 23 October.This prompted discussions about a heavy reduction in the company’s proposed $11-a-share initial public offering, according to one investment manager briefed on the matter.The company ultimately decided to withdraw its application to list on the ASX altogether.Guardian Australia previously reported growing concern that early Firmus investors were going touse retail investors buying into the float as their “exit strategy”, leaving small investors exposed if the excitement dissipated.The datacentre company’s troubles have already rattled other parts of the market, with shares in Firmus investor Maas Group plunging more than 20% on Thursday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe anticipated financial worth of the founders – Oliver Curtis, his cousin Tim Rosenfield, and Curtis’s former brother-in-law Jonathan Levee – will also be greatly reduced.‘Diverging’ mission blamed for CDC splitVeteran datacentre firm CDC this week ended what was touted as a $73bn deal with Firmus named Project Southgate, which was aimed at building sovereign, renewable-powered AI infrastructure and which claimed Nvidia as its first customer.On Friday, appearing at the federal parliament’s joint standing committee on AI, CDC’s chief strategy officer, Dr Jack Dan, said the arrangements began when Firmus’s focus was “a lot more on Australia and creating sovereign AI capability in Australia.”“Their business model has then since evolved and probably the most blunt way of putting it is we have a very clear business model and a very clear mission for our company,” he said. “And when things start diverging significantly from that, we continue to follow our core mission.”The deal was first announced in October last year.Dan said Firmus had a “very different approach to developing datacentres” and CDC is “very much about critical infrastructure, very significant resilience … essentially 100% availability.”“That comes with a certain degree of assurance, a certain degree of rigor and a certain degree of process, which probably was or could have been construed as being a little bit too heavy for a more commercial type development.”Earlier in the hearing, Dan observed that CDC had been around for nearly 20 years, and until last year, “no one really cared who CDC datacentres was” but now datacentres were front and centre of the national conversation.Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - AustraliaBusinessAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Plans for Sydney’s controversial new public square in doubt after NSW government intervention | Sydney | The Guardian
description: State planning minister declares project ‘state significant’, wresting approval process away from local council
Author: Penry Buckley
Headline: State planning minister declares project ‘state significant’, wresting approval process away from local council
Content: Plans for the Sydney Town Square redevelopment featured a large clearing, trees and fountain.Illustration: JPW and ASPECT StudiosView image in fullscreenPlans for the Sydney Town Square redevelopment featured a large clearing, trees and fountain.Illustration: JPW and ASPECT StudiosSydneyPlans for Sydney’s controversial new public square in doubt after NSW government interventionState planning minister declares project ‘state significant’, wresting approval process away from local councilPenry BuckleyThu 8 Oct 2026 22.02 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlans for a grand new public square in the centre of Sydney are in doubt after theNew South Walesplanning minister declared the project “state significant”, wresting the approval process away from the City of Sydney.The lord mayor, Clover Moore,released rendersin August for the plaza opposite Sydney’s town hall. The design for the space, which the council had expected to be completed by 2031, include a semi-circular clearing projecting eastwards towards Hyde park, with a fountain and a grove of native trees.View image in fullscreenArtists render of the proposed Sydney Town Square redevelopment.Illustration: JPW and ASPECT StudiosThe plans have been the source of a battle between Moore and the NSW premier, Chris Minns, who has said he does not support the project, describing it as “too expensive, majorly disruptive for Sydney”, and said it would close down businesses in the area.It had also become a flashpoint in a culture war, ridiculed in the Sydney tabloid The Daily Telegraph, whichpublished AI-generated images of the new square heaving with protesters. The council led by Moore, who’s been the city’s progressive independent mayor since 2004, has previously received negative coverage from the publication for other proposals,including an Oxford Street cycleway first formally raised by the council in 2020.The council has now acquired the last of seven buildings needed to be bulldozed for the square. The demolition and construction was expected to cost $150m.But on Friday, the planning minister, Paul Scully announced he had declared the project a state significant development (SSD), after seeking advice from the NSW Independent Planning Commission, taking the decision for approval away from the council.“This process will allow for a rigorous whole-of-government assessment by the department and provide an opportunity for individuals, the community, and other stakeholders to have their say on any development application,” he said.The project has also been opposed by Woolworths, whose town hall store occupies one of the buildings that would be demolished under the plan. At a press conference outside the store on Friday, the Australian Retail Council’s chief executive, Chris Rodwell, welcomed Scully’s decision.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Look at this building. This is not a building that needs to be bulldozed … it’s home to Australia’s single busiest supermarket.”Scully said the IPC would make the determination on any proposal submitted by the City of Sydney. Under the SSD pathway, the planning minister himself is the consent authority, unless the IPC is delegated to take on that role.In a surprise statement on Friday, Moore, also welcomed the decision to declare the project state significant, saying, “I could not agree more”.“Regardless of who assesses it, we remain confident in the merits of the proposal and see no planning reason why it should not ultimately be supported.“The city owns the buildings, has responsibly saved the money over a 40-year period to deliver the project debt free, and has had some of the world’s leading designers and architects work on the plans.”She said the government had recently approved the acquisition of the final property required for the square. But she said the timing of Scully’s intervention “raises questions” and it would be “deeply disappointing” progress was delayed until after the March state election.Moore called on the minister to commit to “a transparent, genuine, fair and impartial assessment” that did not delay the project.Scully declined to comment.In its advice, the IPC noted the project involved “complex interfaces with state-owned transport infrastructure and requires coordinated assessment of engineering, construction, operational and stakeholder issues”.But it said the proposal would “deliver public benefits through the provision of significant civic and social infrastructure”, and had “the potential to generate significant economic benefits through increased tourism, events, cultural activity and visitation to Sydney’s CBD”.Explore more on these topicsSydneyNew South Wales politicsNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President says deal essential to lower US fuel prices but move set to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: President says deal essential to lower US fuel prices but move set to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies
Content: Trump in Washington on Wednesday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump in Washington on Wednesday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpZelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian dieselPresident says deal essential to lower US fuel prices but move set to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato alliesUS politics – live updatesRobert Taitin WashingtonFri 9 Oct 2026 19.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 20.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump was on a fresh collision course with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and European allies on Friday after a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine.Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with President Vladimir Putin of Russia,calling it“absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’sNatoallies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran.“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trumpwrote.“Based on the condition of their diesel refineries,Russiawill then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 tons of diesel fuel.”He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”Fuel prices have rocketed due to Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of the global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – with a gallon of fuel now averaging $4.20 – it is the soaring price of diesel, which last month rose to a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most political damage to Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm approach.Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need to operate machinery.The agreement was criticized by Democrats, who said it undercut a lawTrump signed last monthallowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions.“This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries,” the Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, joined by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, said in a statement. “Failure to follow the law and the bipartisan will of Congress that only weeks ago passed legislation aimed at cutting off revenue for Russia’s war machine and curbing purchases of Russian oil and gas.”Some Republicans were also critical of the agreement.“Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican,wrote on X. “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.”Perhaps the fiercest response came from Zelenskyy, whotold Axiosthat it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 earlier this week.In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump,saidthe deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.Trump announced the oil deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia accepted a reciprocal de-escalation plan that would stop Moscow attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.The agreement also comes on the heels of rising tensions between Russia and Washington’s Nato allies in Europe, amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.The latest development is likely to lead to a further deterioration of Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment in his failure to reach a deal.Trump’s willingness to reach an agreement with Putin that will lower fuel costs comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of American forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS politicsRussiaEuropeNatoUkrainenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk arrested in Montenegro | Montenegro | The Guardian
description: Founder of influential Rybar blog detained after warnings of attempts to destabilise Balkan country, officials say
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Founder of influential Rybar blog detained after warnings of attempts to destabilise Balkan country, officials say
Content: Mikhail Zvinchuk’s Rybar blog has more than 1.5 million subscribers on Telegram, and is one of the most popular Russian military blogs covering the war in Ukraine.Photograph: Francesca Ebel/The Washington Post/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMikhail Zvinchuk’s Rybar blog has more than 1.5 million subscribers on Telegram, and is one of the most popular Russian military blogs covering the war in Ukraine.Photograph: Francesca Ebel/The Washington Post/Getty ImagesMontenegroPro-Kremlin Russian military blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk arrested in MontenegroFounder of influential Rybar blog detained after warnings of attempts to destabilise Balkan country, officials sayPjotr SauerFri 9 Oct 2026 12.10 EDTFirst published on Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA leading pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger with reported ties to Russia’s intelligence services has been arrested inMontenegro, after warnings of attempts to destabilise the Balkan country, officials have said.Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the influential Rybar war blog, was detained on Friday alongside his wife and three other Russians by police and security agents in the Adriatic resort town of Risan, on suspicion of spreading Russian influence, local media reported.Montenegro’s prime minister, Milojko Spajić, confirmed Zvinchuk’s detention in a post on X, saying it followed warnings that the country would face attempts at destabilisation and hybrid warfare.The Montenegrin news outlet Vijesti reported later on Friday that Zvinchuk and the other detainees were to be expelled from the country on national security grounds.The Russian Telegram news channel Baza said officers detained Zvinchuk at the luxury Mövenpick hotel in Risan. It said the group was taken to Podgorica, Montenegro’s capital, for questioning and their phones and passports were confiscated.Founded in 2018 by Zvinchuk, a former press officer at Russia’s defence ministry, Rybar is one of the most popular Russian military blogs covering the war inUkraine, with more than 1.5 million subscribers on Telegram. It forms part of a sprawling online media ecosystem that promotes Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.But Rybar’s activities extend well beyond Ukraine, with the channel promoting pro-Kremlin narratives in Africa and the Middle East. More recently, it has been accused of amplifying far-right narratives surrounding the migration crisis in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in north Africa.“At the moment, the project team is in contact with Russia’s foreign ministry, which is working to resolve the situation. Since there were no violations of local legislation, we expect all detainees to be released,” the channel said on Telegram.View image in fullscreenMilojko Spajić, Montenegro’s prime minister, said the arrest followed warnings of attempts to destabilise his country and hybrid warfare.Photograph: Boris Pejovic/EPABritain sanctioned Zvinchuk and Rybar in December 2025 over their role in spreading Kremlin propaganda and undermining support for Ukraine. The British government said Zvinchuk received funding from the Russian state-owned defence conglomerate Rostec, and worked with members of Russia’s intelligence services.The US has separately accused Zvinchuk of attempting to interfere in the 2024 presidential election, offering a reward of up to $10m for information about those involved.Days before his arrest, Zvinchuk boasted on social media that he had managed to enter Montenegro despite being subject to western sanctions and an entry ban. He mocked a border guard who, he said, had searched his belongings but failed to check his name against a database.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Moscow was aware of Zvinchuk’s detention and would work to secure his release.Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev suggested Moscow could detain European and American citizens to use in prisoner exchanges to secure Zvinchuk’s release. “We will probably have to replenish our pool of prisoners for exchange with European and American idiots in order to get our own people back,” he wrote on social media.The arrest is likely to further strain relations between Montenegro and Russia, which have long been tense. In 2016, Montenegrin authorities accused Russian operatives of plotting with Serbian ultranationaliststo stage a coup, allegations Moscow denied.Montenegro, which joined Nato in 2017 and isseeking membership of the EU, imposed sanctions on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.The country recently approved plans to end visa-free travel for Russian citizens from 1 November, closing off a popular holiday destination for Russian tourists as it brings its visa policy into line with the EU.Explore more on these topicsMontenegroRussiaEuropeBloggingUkrainenewsShareReuse this content
