title: China agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark deal  | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs
Content: BYD cars being loaded on its cargo ship at Nantong Port in Jiangsu Province of China.Photograph: Xu Congjun/VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBYD cars being loaded on its cargo ship at Nantong Port in Jiangsu Province of China.Photograph: Xu Congjun/VCG/Getty ImagesAutomotive industryChina agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark dealBrussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobsLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentFri 9 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations withChinasince June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EV – but it’s too long for UK parking spacesRead more“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.China has beenflooding Europe with cars, including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs.Šefčovič said the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building in every member state in Europe with “literally thousands of job losses” at risk because of the flood of cheap imports from China across many sectors including chemicals and textiles.He said EU leaders were “clearly expecting very fast action” from the European Commission and the Chinese recognised that.“I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” he said.“This ‌is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told ‌reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold ​talks with his Chinese counterpart.Earlier this week senior EU officials said they were heading to Beijing to seek whatthey called a “proof of concept”or pilot scheme with one sector which they hoped could then be expanded to other areas under pressure from Chinese competition.Šefčovič said he put “so much emphasis” on the negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop” a trade war once it was declared.As part of a 16-point agreement, Beijing and Brussels will continue negotiating on cars, export restrictions on rare earths and access to China for more food and drink from the EU.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChina said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” for hybrid cars suggesting one method of curbing sales would be to set higher minimum price tags for Chinese cars sold in Europe.The EU commissioner will brief EU diplomats in Brussels on Sunday ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday.A statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce said China is “willing … to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”.It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”.While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryEuropean UnionChinaEuropeElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Israeli airport, UAE prosecutors say | Flydubai plane incident | The Guardian
description: Hammam al-Hammami is believed to have been targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Hammam al-Hammami is believed to have been targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv
Content: Hammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersView image in fullscreenHammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersFlydubai plane incidentFlydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Israeli airport, UAE prosecutors sayHammam al-Hammami is believed to have been targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel AvivJason Burke, international security correspondentFri 9 Oct 2026 16.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was planning to launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Israel’s international airport, prosecutors in theUnited Arab Emiratessaid on Friday.Hammam al-Hammamiattacked the plane’s Indian pilotwith an emergency axe, but failed to prevent his badly injured colleague from opening the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower his assailant.Passengers then tried to control the aircraft, which was safely landed inSaudi Arabiaby an off-duty relief pilot who was among about 180 passengers.Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney-general of the UAE, said on Friday that al-Hammami, who is in Emirate custody, had admitted he had tried to execute a “premeditated terrorist plot to … launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv, with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”.The 29-year-old, who was hired by flydubai, a government-owned low-cost airline, began a process of radicalisation while studying in Australia when he was influenced by the hardline takfiri ideology through reading extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks, al-Shamsi said in a statement.“[Al-Hammami] subsequently developed … ideas advocating violence and terrorism. He also drew inspiration from the 11 September 2001 attacks, and the idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking. According to his confession, this was linked to his decision to pursue a career in aviation.”Over the weekend, Australian security agencieslaunched an investigationafter it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. Heleft the country without completing his engineering degree.New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation after police confirmed al-Hammami underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.There has been widespread concern about how al-Hammami was able to pass vetting and join a crew flying toIsrael. An Omani national, he earned a distance-learning aviation management degree from Buckinghamshire New University in 2023 and was employed by Oman Air from 2020-24, joined Royal Air Maroc in early 2025 and worked there for several months before moving to flydubai in January 2026.Security officials have been keen to understand if al-Hammami was acting alone or had become involved with a group such as al-Qaida or Islamic State, which could suggest further such attacks might be planned. Emirate authorities believe this is not the case.“In the presence of his lawyer and with all legally prescribed safeguards ensured, the suspect provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution. He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim,” al-Shamsi said.Investigators have found al-Hammami had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route ‌and the airport”, the Emirati state news agency WAM reported.The passengers on board the aircraft were overwhelmingly Israeli, with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailing them and the pilot for their bravery after the foiled attack.Explore more on these topicsFlydubai plane incidentAir transportMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelDubaiSaudi ArabiaUnited Arab EmiratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company | Capital punishment | The Guardian
description: Only Iran and Afghanistan routinely carry out sentences in public, with Saudi Arabia appearing to have ended practice
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Only Iran and Afghanistan routinely carry out sentences in public, with Saudi Arabia appearing to have ended practice
Content: Pete Hegseth, the US defence secretary, said the execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad would be livestreamed.Photograph: Eric Lee/ReutersView image in fullscreenPete Hegseth, the US defence secretary, said the execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad would be livestreamed.Photograph: Eric Lee/ReutersCapital punishmentAnalysisPete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious companyJason BurkeOnly Iran and Afghanistan routinely carry out sentences in public, with Saudi Arabia appearing to have ended practiceUS politics – live updatesFri 9 Oct 2026 09.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 14.07 EDTShareIf the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans tolivestream the executionof a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years.Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according toAmnesty International.In April last year, the Taliban executed four men accused of murder in three different cities. All were shot dead in crowded public sports stadiums.Such events were commonwhen the hardline Islamist militia movement was in power in the late 1990s. Then as now, the Taliban claimed a due court process had been followed.In July,two young menaccused of killing police officers were hanged by Iranian authorities in the central square of Isfahan, Iran. Human rights monitors have reported about 30 public executions in Ithe country in the last five years, with an intensification in recent months after massive popular unrest earlier this year and the war with the US and Israel. Historically, many hangings have been carried out using a crane as a makeshift gallows.View image in fullscreenProtesters gathered last year in Paris and other cities around the world to demand an end to executions in Iran.Photograph: Siavosh Hosseini/LightRocket/Getty ImagesSaudi Arabia appears to have ended the practice after decades ofbeheading convicted criminalsin a square in the capital, Riyadh, and sometimes publicly in provincial cities.Legal experts and historians argue that public executions perform different functions. If the rule of law is shaky or there is doubt about the efficacy of the criminal justice system, they offer authorities seeking to win support a way of convincing the community that criminals will be punished. Such public spectacles can also be a way of cowing a population through terror.Armed militant groups have frequently resorted to public executions – often in an effort to assert their authority.Islamic State, which ruled a swath of Iraq and Syria between 2014 and 2019, conductedthousands of executionsfor alleged offences ranging from homosexuality to theft. Many of the executions took place in public or were videoed. A large number were deliberately choreographed to provide a spectacle for broadcast to terrorise enemies and potential dissidents as well as to radicalise IS supporters and attract new ones.In October 2025, as Hamas sought to reassert its control over the population of Gaza, it carried out a public execution of six men apparently accused of collaborating with Israel. In 2017, the group had executed three men accused of the same crime, partlylivestreaming the event on Facebook.View image in fullscreenThe planned public execution of Nidal Hasan would be the first in the US in many decades.Photograph: ReutersThe execution of Maj Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, at Fort Hood in Texas would be the first public execution in the US in many decades.In the US, the practice of public executions was largely stopped in the 1930s, though in 2001, some survivors and victims’ relatives were allowed to watch the executionby lethal injection of Timothy McVeigh, convicted of the 1995 bombing of a government office in Oklahoma City.Hasan’s executionhas been scheduled for 3 December. Hegseth, who has the authority to decide the conduct of the killing, has said that “of course” it would take place at the same time and in the same place as Hasan’s attack 17 years ago and would use firearms, as Hasan did.11:14‘Barbaric’ firing squad livestream ordered by Pete Hegseth - The LatestHasan can launch appeals within the civilian federal court system that could delay the execution for many years.In 2025, Amnesty International recorded 2,707 executions, the highest total globally since 1981, and an increase of two-thirds on the previous year. The sharp rise was mainly due to more than 2,100 executions byIran, its highest number of executions in decades.Amnesty said authorities had placed the death penalty “at the centre of flawed public security and ‘tough on crime’ narratives to assert control, project state power and score political points”.“This trend was strongest in countries where the authorities have tightened their grip on power by restricting civic space, silencing dissent and displaying disregard for protections established under international human rights law and standards,” the campaign group reported.Explore more on these topicsCapital punishmentFort Hood shootingsPete HegsethIranSaudi ArabiaAfghanistanHuman rightsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Three Saudis killed in Riyadh airport attack claimed by Houthis | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Attack is deadliest in kingdom since it launched major military offensive with allies against Houthis in Yemen
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Attack is deadliest in kingdom since it launched major military offensive with allies against Houthis in Yemen
Content: Smoke and flames rise from Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport after Houthis say they attacked it on Thursday.Photograph: Social Media/ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke and flames rise from Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport after Houthis say they attacked it on Thursday.Photograph: Social Media/ReutersSaudi ArabiaThree Saudis killed in Riyadh airport attack claimed by HouthisAttack is deadliest in kingdom since it launched major military offensive with allies against Houthis in YemenGuardian staff and agenciesFri 9 Oct 2026 05.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 22.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree Saudi citizens have been killed and several other people were wounded in attacks targeting Riyadh ⁠airport for which Yemen’sHouthisclaimed responsibility, Saudi officials have said.The attack late on Thursday was the deadliest inSaudi Arabiasince the kingdom and allied forces in neighbouring Yemen launched a major military offensive last weekend against the Iran-backed Houthis.It was also a significant escalation in the latest front in the Iran war, which has kept oil prices and markets jumpy.The first attack on Thursday afternoon targeted airport facilities, while the second struck aircraft, the Saudi statement said. It did not identify those responsible, though the Houthis claimed to have targeted the airport with a ballistic missile.Among the dead was Capt Hamoud Ali Alkalthami, the Saudia Group said in a statement. It appeared to be the first confirmed attack on the Saudi national carrier since the new offensive began. A separate Saudia Group statement said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers onboard.The aviation statement said the injuries to citizens and people of other nationalities “ranged from minor to serious”. The Saudia Group statement said operational activities at the airport returned to normal at 6pm on Thursday, hours after the attack.Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had destroyed three rocket launch platforms used by the rebels to threaten regional security.Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?Read moreThe Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in ​Yemen’s reignited civil war. Saudi Arabia says it isbacking an offensive by Yemen’s UN-recognised governmentto ‌take back territory from the Houthis.The Houthis have made a lightning advance across Yemen’s coastal plain over the last month,appearing to gain ground in the south-west on Wednesdayas the group approached the city of Taiz.Independent observers said earlier this week there was danger the group was on course to capture Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the government were pulling back to secure the major port city of Aden.Riyadh is due to host a meeting of energy policymakers, the WPC Energy Congress, this week.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaHouthisYemenMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: India’s ‘Cockroach’ party accuses government of mass detention of members ahead of weekend protest | India | The Guardian
description: Thousands expected to march in Delhi on Saturday, as anger mounts over controversial changes to voter lists in world’s largest democracy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Thousands expected to march in Delhi on Saturday, as anger mounts over controversial changes to voter lists in world’s largest democracy
Content: Protesters demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner over alleged voter-roll irregularities. The Cockroach Janta party has in part led the protest movement.Photograph: Abhishek Chinnappa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner over alleged voter-roll irregularities. The Cockroach Janta party has in part led the protest movement.Photograph: Abhishek Chinnappa/Getty ImagesIndiaIndia’s ‘Cockroach’ party accuses government of mass detention of members ahead of weekend protestThousands expected to march in Delhi on Saturday, as anger mounts over controversial changes to voter lists in world’s largest democracyGuardian staff and agenciesThu 8 Oct 2026 21.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndia’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.Opposition parties, their student units, and the“Cockroach” youth movementhave been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over acontroversial revision of ⁠voter lists.Thousands are expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday, amid mounting anger in the world’s largest democracy.AI cheating, leaked papers and marking errors: how exam protests went globalRead moreA spokesperson for the CJP, Ashutosh Ranka, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.Police authorities ⁠didn’t immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comments. Videos posted on social media platform X showed activists being taken away in vans.The CJP said that ‌among those detained was a group ‌of students from the western city of Pune who were headed for the 10 October protest in Delhi. It said they were being ‌taken away in a bus to an unknown location.The nationwide voter list review, known as the special intensive revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed against the deletions.The opposition says the removals disproportionately affect voters who support them, while voters more likely to back prime minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists.The election commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries.View image in fullscreenIndian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi is detained by police, during a protest organised by opposition parties demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi on 7 October 2026.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersThe campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organised street protests across the country.The protests present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar demonstrations led by the CJP forced the ​resignation of his education minister overexam paper leaks.In the lead up to Saturday’s planned demonstration, hundreds of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in tech hub Bengaluru on Thursday.Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.“I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who ⁠actually care about the future of India, they are just being (denied) voting rights,” said Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture ​student who attended the Bengaluru protest.There were also protests over ​police action against congress party leaders and the voter lists revisions.On Wednesday, the opposition Congress party accused police of ​using “brute force” to briefly detain ‌party leader Rahul Gandhi, his ​sister Priyanka Vadra, and other ​lawmakers as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.Delhi Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” the force.BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. The claims had “no base, not an iota of evidence”, he told reporters at a media briefing on Thursday.Police have barricaded the area in Delhi ahead of Saturday’s planned demonstrations.Explore more on these topicsIndiaNarendra ModiProtestSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Headteachers threaten strike ballots after losing confidence in Ofsted | Ofsted | The Guardian
description: Unions tell government to fix ‘overbearing mess’ of inspection regime and its impact on staff wellbeing – or risk industrial action
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Unions tell government to fix ‘overbearing mess’ of inspection regime and its impact on staff wellbeing – or risk industrial action
Content: An Ofsted spokesperson said it would ‘keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve’.Photograph: Russell Hart/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn Ofsted spokesperson said it would ‘keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve’.Photograph: Russell Hart/AlamyOfstedHeadteachers threaten strike ballots after losing confidence in OfstedUnions tell government to fix ‘overbearing mess’ of inspection regime and its impact on staff wellbeing – or risk industrial actionRichard AdamsEducation editorFri 9 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTensions between England’s headteachers and Ofsted are developing into a crisis after school leadership unions said they had no confidence in the watchdog and would hold strike ballots unless “significant wellbeing issues” caused by Ofsted’s inspections regime were fixed.The Association of School and College Leaders​ (ASCL), which includes senior leaders in many secondary schools, described Ofsted’s inspection system as “an overbearing mess” and urged the government to pause inspections to stop teachers leaving the profession.A spokesperson for ASCL said that “if change is not forthcoming” the union would seek to hold an indicative ballot on industrial action.New Ofsted inspection regime damaging teachers, survey saysRead moreThe National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said it would also consider steps including strike action at a meeting of its leadership next week.The combative moves come after a survey published by Ofsted showed 88% of schools reported that recent inspections had negatively affected staff wellbeing.The Guardianreported last weekthat Lucy Powell, the education secretary, wants Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” and overhaul the framework introduced last year. The new framework was intended to lower the strain and workload caused by inspections, but many heads say the opposite has happened.In response to ASCL’s announcement, a spokesperson for theDepartment for Educationsaid: “Inspection and accountability are vital, but they must reflect the reality of what is happening in schools, recognise the context they are working in, and support improvement rather than add to the pressures they already face.“That’s why we are working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better, so every child gets the education they deserve.”An Ofsted spokesperson said: “We have worked hard to reduce the pressure of inspection in recent years, but we know workload and wellbeing remain a challenge.“We are working with the Department for Education on this and we will keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve what we do.”​Hostility ​towards Ofsted has been heightened since the death of Ruth Perry, a popular headteacher in Reading. In 2023 a coroner found that anOfsted inspection contributedto Perry’s mental health deterioration and her death. Labour pledged to reform school inspections in its 2024 election manifesto.But ASCL said it had “seen no meaningful progress on the part of Ofsted to address significant wellbeing issues caused by inspections, and that it is increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale of members”.England school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaintsRead moreThe motion of no confidence in Ofsted passed by ASCL’s executive stated: “We fear that the disproportionate stress and anxiety exerted by the inspection system will lead to school leaders deciding to leave their posts with a consequent impact on schools, children and young people.”Pepe Di’​Iasio, ​ASCL’s general ​secretary, said: “​Our repeated attempts to resolve our concerns through discussion and negotiation have hit a brick wall … The current system is not fit for purpose. It is an overbearing mess and urgently needs to be reviewed.”Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the NAHT, said: “Our deep concerns about this Ofsted framework and the impact it is having on professionals are longstanding. Our executive committee will be meeting at the end of next week and debating the next steps NAHT will take. We fully expect that debate to include the option of pursuing industrial action.”Explore more on these topicsOfstedSchoolsTrade unionsDepartment for EducationTeachers' workloadEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant bans Drumcree parade | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Prospect of contentious Orange Order march through Garvaghy Road in Portadown has led to a nearly two-week standoff
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Prospect of contentious Orange Order march through Garvaghy Road in Portadown has led to a nearly two-week standoff
Content: A PSNI vehicle near Drumcree church in Portadown, where the parade would have begun.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenA PSNI vehicle near Drumcree church in Portadown, where the parade would have begun.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PANorthern IrelandNorthern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant bans Drumcree paradeProspect of contentious Orange Order march through Garvaghy Road in Portadown has led to a nearly two-week standoffRory CarrollIreland correspondentFri 9 Oct 2026 16.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNorthern Irelandsecretary of state has banned the Drumcree parade after a 13-day impasse between the Orange Order and nationalists.Chris Bryant announced on Friday night that it was “not in the public interest” for Orangemen to march the contested route through Garvaghy Road in Portadown, which Catholic residents had blocked.He said he took the decision after advice from Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of theNorthern IrelandPolice Service, that the parade “would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect” across Northern Ireland.The Parades Commission ruled two weeks ago that a small, circumscribed march could pass along Garvaghy Road – a reversal of 28 years of successive bans. But police prevented the Orangemen from marching after thousands of residents and supporters, including Sinn Féin leaders,blocked the road.Garvaghy Road residents welcomed the secretary of state’s decision, saying it brought relief and certainty after a tense standoff that revived memories of the 1990s, when Orangemen fought pitched battles with police in an attempt to march the route.It was the only “sensible, reasonable and logical outcome”, said Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition.TheSinn Féinleader, Mary Lou McDonald, and the party’s Northern Ireland first minister, Michelle O’Neill, said in a statement that residents had endured fear and anxiety. “There will be an enormous sense of relief within the community this evening.”The Irish government welcomed the decision and appealed to both sides to seek common ground. “This isn’t a time for triumphalism or claiming victories or anything like that,” said the taoiseach, Micheál Martin. “Those on the unionist, loyalist side will look at this through a different prism. We need to be conscious of that. We need to acknowledge that.”Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, accused Boutcher and Bryant of bowing to republican agitation and threats of potential violence. “These decisions are a mistake, and send profound signals that the country should be run on force of numbers and who shouts the loudest. The framework for both parading and protests now lies in tatters, and the rule of law has been fundamentally undermined.”Robinson asked the secretary to state to explain what the government will do to “restore confidence in the rule of law”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArtists including Noel Gallagher show support for Garvaghy Road residents in Drumcree disputeRead moreEarlier on Friday the chief constable asked Bryant to review the Parade Commission’s determination, made last month, that conditions in Portadown enabled the parade to go ahead.“I’ve looked at the changing situation in Portadown, the fact that it’s very difficult for that procession to proceed, and I’ve decided that it’s not in the public interest for it to proceed, and I’ve therefore banned the procession,” said Bryant.He thanked Portadown’s Orange Lodge for its “peaceful and law-abiding approach” and regretted that both sides could not reach a compromise, leading to a standoff. “With this in mind, I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions.”Boutcher said the dispute had affected relationships within and between communities and the police. “It is in everyone’s interest that time and space is now created for conversations about finding long-term solutions to this complex and sensitive issue.”The dispute has fuelled angry exchanges at the Stormont assembly and destabilised the executive, with unionists demanding O’Neill step down as first minister for allegedly breaking the law at aGarvaghy Road protest.Earlier on Friday, the PSNI sent the Sinn Féin deputy leader a letter probing alleged criminal offences relating to her involvement in the protest. O’Neill said she will cooperate with the investigation.Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandNorthern Irish politicsChris BryantnewsShareReuse this content

title: Parties prepare for byelection in Farage seat amid speculation over £5m gift inquiry  | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Tories said to be ready to fight in Clacton, with standards investigation rumoured to be nearing its end
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Tories said to be ready to fight in Clacton, with standards investigation rumoured to be nearing its end
Content: Conservatives are hopeful Nigel Farage will decide not to fight, but Reform sources insisted he would.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersView image in fullscreenConservatives are hopeful Nigel Farage will decide not to fight, but Reform sources insisted he would.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersNigel FarageParties prepare for byelection in Farage seat amid speculation over £5m gift inquiryTories said to be ready to fight in Clacton, with standards investigation rumoured to be nearing its endRowena MasonWhitehall editorFri 9 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 17.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage’s rivals are gearing up for a byelection in Clacton in the months ahead, amid speculation that the standards inquiry into his £5m gift is nearing a conclusion.Conservative sources said the party was ready to fight in Farage’s seat, although senior figures in the shadow cabinet are divided about whether it would be winnable, given Farage’s victory in abyelection over the summer.Other parties, including the hard-right Restore Britain, are also expected to put up candidates in the seat this time, after boycotting the August poll.Westminster is poised for a battle over the future of Reform if the sanction from the standards inquiry is a heavy one.The process could theoretically take place before Christmas if a decision is imminent, but the timelines of previous cases suggest it is more likely to be next year – if a serious sanction is imposed.In the cases of Margaret Ferrier, the SNP MP who broke lockdown rules, and Peter Bone, the Tory MP found to have bullied staff, it took well over six months from the conclusion of the commissioner’s report for a byelection to take place.The investigation into Farage’s gift began afterthe Guardian revealed in Maythat the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024.The Reform leader has said itwas a personal matter, not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.Under the process, if a serious breach is found, the commissioner will pass a memorandum to the standards committee of MPs and lay members.They would then have further discussions and call a further hearing or invite evidence from the MP before deciding on a penalty. That process can take weeks. The MP also has a right of appeal to the independent expert panel, which can take a further month or more.If parliament agrees with a penalty of more than 10 days of suspension from theHouse of Commons, a recall petition could be held, requiring signatures from 10% of voters in the MP’s constituency over a period of six weeks.In the cases of Bone and Ferrier, neither contested their seats, andConservativesare hopeful that Farage could decide not to fight. “There’s a question of whether he will stand again,” said one shadow cabinet minister.But Reform sources insisted Farage would fight for his seat again, having won the byelection against independent candidates including Count Binface by more than 11,000 votes.He has also recently embarked on a tour of the country, in an attempt to shore up his core support, and a reorganisation of his party HQ. This includes launching a new Reform TV channel to pump out the party’s message direct to voters, hiring a team of 12 “journalists” headed by the former GB News producer Aaron Lobo, who had been director of operations.Farage won a majority of 8,000 at the last general election, when he beat the sitting Tory MP, Giles Watling. The Conservative had previously won the seat with a majority of more than 25,000 in 2019, when there was no Brexit party candidate in the seat.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKConservativesHouse of CommonsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two Latvians arrested at RAF base in Cambridgeshire released on bail  | UK news | The Guardian
description: Men found inside RAF Molesworth, used by US and Nato for intelligence, freed on strict conditions as police continue investigation
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Men found inside RAF Molesworth, used by US and Nato for intelligence, freed on strict conditions as police continue investigation
Content: RAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe.Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe.Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty ImagesUK newsTwo Latvians arrested at RAF base in Cambridgeshire released on bailMen found inside RAF Molesworth, used by US and Nato for intelligence, freed on strict conditions as police continue investigationPriya BharadiaandDan SabbaghFri 9 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 13.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo Latvian men have been released on bail after being arrested at an RAF base in Cambridgeshire used by the US military and Nato.The two men, aged 32 and 26, were arrested at 2am on Thursday after they were discovered inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, which is used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations.An investigation had begun four hours earlier, when military police found an abandoned vehicle near the facility at around 10pm on Wednesday.Military police, joined by officers from Cambridgeshire police, discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence, before finding and arresting the two men inside the base.The suspects, both Latvian nationals currently resident in the UK, were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and causing criminal damage. They were then further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023, namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.They have since been released on bail, with strict conditions, as the police continue their investigation.Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said they were “very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites”, but that there was nothing from their investigation so far to suggest a connection to an incident near RAF Fairford in September.“Our investigation continues and we are working closely with colleagues from the Ministry of Defence police and Cambridgeshire constabulary on this. A key line of inquiry remains to identify any potential motivation behind why the men were at that location, and this includes whether it may be connected to any criminal activity,” she added.Officers have since carried out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation. The abandoned vehicle was also taken to a nearby police location.Located west of Huntingdon, RAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour hails byelection win as return of leftwing voters after Starmer era | Holborn and St Pancras byelection | The Guardian
description: Party now polling 15 points above Greens, who had been ahead of Labour before Keir Starmer resigned as PM
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Party now polling 15 points above Greens, who had been ahead of Labour before Keir Starmer resigned as PM
Content: The education secretary, Lucy Powell (left), with the newly elected MP Sagal Abdi-Wali, who won the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenThe education secretary, Lucy Powell (left), with the newly elected MP Sagal Abdi-Wali, who won the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAHolborn and St Pancras byelectionLabour hails byelection win as return of leftwing voters after Starmer eraParty now polling 15 points above Greens, who had been ahead of Labour before Keir Starmer resigned as PMSammy GecsoylerandPeter WalkerFri 9 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour is starting to win back voters on the left who became disillusioned under Keir Starmer’s leadership, the party’s deputy leader has claimed after it saw off Zack Polanski and the Greens to win theHolborn and St Pancras byelection.Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali took 45% of a relatively low turnout to keep Starmer’s old north London seat for the party, pushing Polanski, who had stood for the party he leads, into second place on 33%.While the result was broadly as predicted, Labour strategists were buoyed up by the party’s relatively straightforward route to victory in a diverse inner-city area of the sort the Greens have been targeting with recent success.The result “sends a clear message to those voters who lost faith in Labour in recent years”, said Lucy Powell, whocalled last monthfor the party to unite progressive voters under Andy Burnham if it wants to win the next election.After the byelection win, she told the Guardian: “We hear you, we’ve listened and we know we needed to be clearer about what we stand for and what type of country we want to see, proudly putting our values centre stage. We’re delighted so many of you are backing us once again.”The byelection came after the Green party voted at their conference last weekend to adopta hugely controversial policy equating Zionism with racism, and saying Israel should be replaced with a single Palestinian state.Polanski has been criticised for showing minimal leadership on the most toxic internal debate the Greens have faced in living memory, with the chair of Jewish Greens saying he should resign.The byelection, called after Starmerresigned his Commons seatshortly after he was ousted by Burnham, saw a low turnout of 38.7%, possibly due to the widespread predictions that Labour was set to win, despite a major campaigning effort from the Greens.The turnout also suggests Burnham could still face a battle to engage some voters in urban areas, particularly London, where the Greens took control of three councils in May’s local elections.In an emotional victory speech, Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, hit out at “those who seek to divide us”, in what appeared to be a response to Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, who suggested she was not British shortly after the byelection was called.“I hope this moment says something about who gets to belong,” she said. “For people who look like me, I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden, and this is Britain.”Responding to the defeat, Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, said that while the result showed his party remained a major threat to Labour, many voters had told him they wanted to “give Andy Burnham a chance”.It was the Greens’ second best-ever byelection result, more evidence of the party’s increased prominence and campaigning power since Polanski became leader 13 months ago.The best came in February, when the Greenstook an equally safe Labour seat, Gorton and Denton in Greater Manchester, in a major upset that weakened Starmer’s position. Around the same time, the Greens peaked at 21% in national polling, above Labour. They are now about 11%, more than 15 points behind Burnham’s party.Polanski’s position has come under scrutiny since the Zionism motion was passed, with critics accusing him of abdicating leadership after he missed the debate to campaign in the byelection, giving no clear message about whether or not he backed it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn interviews after the byelection loss, Polanski said he would have voted against the motion had he attended, given that two amendments he supported, both saying any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians rather than a one-state system being imposed, were voted down.On Friday, Vivien Lichtenstein, chair of Jewish Greens, said Polanski, who is Jewish, made a “big mistake” by avoiding the vote. Asked if he should continue in his role, she told Times Radio: “No, I think he should resign.”However, other members of Jewish Greens said Lichtenstein’s comments did not reflect the majority view in the group, and that a vote of no confidence in her had been tabled.Speaking shortly before the byelection result was announced, Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ former leader and first MP, said Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”.Speaking to Newsnight, she said: “I would have hoped that he would have really been a very strong critic of this motion, because the motion was flawed from top to bottom in my view. It’s dangerous, it’s divisive, it tries to have a singular definition of Zionism when we know that there are many.”Asked if Polanski should stand down, Lucas did not definitively say he should remain as leader: “I think let’s just see what happens in the … coming days and weeks.”There is no formal mechanism for ejecting a leader of the Greens. However, they are re-elected every two years, meaning Polanski, who took over in September 2025, will have to go before party members again in less than a year.Explore more on these topicsHolborn and St Pancras byelectionLabourGreen partynewsShareReuse this content

title: One person killed and nine injured in chain-reaction crash in New York City | New York | The Guardian
description: Motorist, reportedly trying to beat a traffic light, barrels through busy intersection and slams into pedestrians
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Motorist, reportedly trying to beat a traffic light, barrels through busy intersection and slams into pedestrians
Content: The scene in the Bronx after the crash that killed one person and injured nine on Friday.Photograph: Kyle Mazza/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe scene in the Bronx after the crash that killed one person and injured nine on Friday.Photograph: Kyle Mazza/SOPA Images/ShutterstockNew YorkOne person killed and nine injured in chain-reaction crash in New York CityMotorist, reportedly trying to beat a traffic light, barrels through busy intersection and slams into pedestriansMarina DunbarFri 9 Oct 2026 17.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least one person was killed and nine injured inNew York City’s eastern Bronx when a motorist barreled through a busy intersection, slammed into pedestrians and triggered a chain-reaction crash involving several vehicles, according to authorities and media reports.The horrifying collision happened shortly after 2pm in the Bronx’s Allerton neighborhood, with the driver at the center of the crash reportedly saying he was trying to beat a traffic light.Sources told theNew York Postthat four women, ranging in age from 50 to 60, were walking through a crosswalk when the Mercedes struck them.The victims were transported to Jacobi medical center, where one woman was pronounced dead. Two others were reported to be in critical condition, while the fourth was expected to survive, according to the Post’s sources.The New York fire department (FDNY) said that emergency medical crews treated nine people in the aftermath of the crash, according to the local outletNews 12.Surveillance footage obtained by News 12 captured a white Mercedes-Benz hurtling through the intersection, striking a group of pedestrians in the crosswalk before crashing into multiple vehicles waiting at a traffic light.According to the NYPD’s preliminary findings, the Mercedes rear-ended two vehicles with such force that both cars were pushed into two additional vehicles.The driver, who suffered minor injuries and remained conscious and alert, reportedly told a witness that he had been attempting to beat the traffic light, the Post said.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook | Federal Reserve | The Guardian
description: US president renews his efforts to oust Cook despite supreme court ruling that her firing was unconstitutional
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: US president renews his efforts to oust Cook despite supreme court ruling that her firing was unconstitutional
Content: Lisa Cook, a Federal Reserve governor, leaves the supreme court in Washington on 21 January 2026.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APView image in fullscreenLisa Cook, a Federal Reserve governor, leaves the supreme court in Washington on 21 January 2026.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APFederal ReserveTrump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa CookUS president renews his efforts to oust Cook despite supreme court ruling that her firing was unconstitutionalGaya GuptaFri 9 Oct 2026 14.05 EDTFirst published on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despitea June supreme court rulingthat her earlier firing was unconstitutional.Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published. Cook will be able to submit a written statement to present her own evidence and will be subject to examination from White House and her own legal counsel.“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump said in astatementposted to the White House’s website.Her legal team has maintained that the White House is “cherrypicking” facts and any claims of fraud are based on unrelated clerical errors.In response to the announcement, Cook’s lawyers said that they had “grave doubts” that the White House hearing would be “a legitimate one that would conform to the law”.“But if it is anything close to objective,” they continued, “the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from theFederal ReserveBoard.”They added that Cook “welcomes the opportunity to present the factsso she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her”.Cook was appointed by Joe Biden in 2022 to a 14-year term, becoming the Fed’s first Black governor. Before her tenure at the central bank, she taught at Harvard University and Stanford University and served on Barack Obama’s council of economic advisers.Cook’s battle with the White House began in August 2025 when she was abruptly fired after Trump said she committed mortgage fraud by listing two properties in Georgia and Michigan as her primary residence and failing to report rental income on her Atlanta property.Cook immediately sued theTrump administration, and the supreme court reinstated her after a 5-4 ruling that she could stay on as governor while fighting the fraud allegations.In June, the court ruled that Trump’s firing was unconstitutional because he did not follow proper procedure and give Cook an opportunity to dispute the allegations before she was fired.Cook was fired just as Trump was launching unprecedented attacks on the Fed’s chair, then Jerome Powell, in his blustering push to get the central bank to lower interest rates. Trump also launched a justice department investigation into Powell, which wasdroppedin April.Congress created the Fed to be an independent and non-partisan institution. Economists widely agree that a central bank unswayed by politics is essential for the stability of a country’s economy.Kevin Warsh, Powell’s successor, has repeatedly faced questions over how he will maintain the Fed’s independence. Before Trump picked him to lead the world’s most powerful central bank, he had echoed the president’s calls for cutting rates. But because of elevated inflation brought on by the war in the Middle East, the bank ultimately voted to raise rates in its last meeting, which drew the ire of the White House just more than a month before the crucial midterm elections.Explore more on these topicsFederal ReserveUS economyDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS supreme courtUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump immigrant purge could cut social security for Americans by $2,000 a year | US immigration | The Guardian
description: New report on economic cost of anti-immigration campaign projects 8.6% reduction in retirement payments by 2034
Author: Alexandra Villarreal
Headline: New report on economic cost of anti-immigration campaign projects 8.6% reduction in retirement payments by 2034
Content: Federal immigration agents arrest a man in the parking lot of an H-Mart grocery store on 31 October 2025, in Niles, Illinois.Photograph: Jamie Kelter Davis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFederal immigration agents arrest a man in the parking lot of an H-Mart grocery store on 31 October 2025, in Niles, Illinois.Photograph: Jamie Kelter Davis/Getty ImagesUS immigrationTrump immigrant purge could cut social security for Americans by $2,000 a yearNew report on economic cost of anti-immigration campaign projects 8.6% reduction in retirement payments by 2034Alexandra Villarrealin New YorkFri 9 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElderly Americans can expect to lose an average of $2,152 in annual social security benefits each, a projected 8.6% reduction in their retirement payments, by 2034 and every year after as a direct consequence of the economic fallout from the Trump administration’santi-immigration campaign, if that carries on, according to a new report shared exclusively with the Guardian.Already, US food prices are up, housing permits to build new homes are down – and even native-born Americans are losing out on potential jobs after the sudden exodus of 1.2 million foreign-born workers over the last two years as a result of Donald Trump’s policies, the report finds.“When the Trump administration says things, it’s not always data-driven. And we wanted to see what the data shows, and what other people have found the data shows,” said Michael Ettlinger, one of the report’s authors. “Turns out that refutes what the US president primarily is asserting.”The blowback on the economy from Donald Trump’s crackdown is wide-ranging, even as the federal government’saggressivemass deportation campaignquietlyramps upfurther.Gone in 90 seconds: an ‘invisibilized’ ICE is arresting more people than everRead more“We are just beginning to see the harms in terms of what is happening here domestically. But the impacts of these policies, of these efforts, are going to be long-lasting. And I think that is by design,” Vanessa Cárdenas, executive director of the pro-immigration reform organization America’s Voice, told the Guardian.The report, Economic Impacts of Trump Administration Immigration Policy, was commissioned by America’s Voice and conducted by researchers at Economic Insights and Research Consulting, a firm focused on economic analysis.Its conclusions underscore how recent federalpolicies revokingimmigrants’ legal protections or targeting them for enforcement have had dire effects on the nation’s affordability crisis and job market, especially in regions and industries that rely disproportionately on foreign-born workers.In the US agricultural sector, where 42% of crop workers are undocumented and 68% are foreign-born,farmersacross the country are warning that the vast majorityor in some cases allof their workforce has disappeared overnight, leaving produce to fall to, or rot in, the ground and go towaste.Food products heavily reliant on immigrant labor have experienced much sharper price increases than food overall since Trump retook the White House, according to the report.Examples of immigrant-reliant food price increases that have exceeded the average increase in grocery prices over the last 19 months, compared with the 19 months before Trump returned to office in January 2025, are: fresh whole milk up by 5.7%, canned vegetables up by 6.3%, and apples up by 7.2%, the report found.In that period before Trump’s inauguration, the vast majority of foods that principally depend on immigrant labor for production saw prices rise more slowly compared with other foods and some prices even fell outright, according to the report.“One thing that changed was the [immigration] policy. Before, the trend for all those goods was a lower inflation rate. And afterward, the trend was higher inflation. So the trend was reversed, and that was quite striking,” said Robert Lynch, one of the report’s authors.The construction industry, where foreign-born workers fill almost a third of all occupations, has also been severely affected. States more dependent on immigrant labor have seen costs for new single-family homes soar 10.9% in 2026, compared with the first eight months of 2024, bringing building projects’ monetary valuefrom an average of $305,752 to $338,752.And the issuance of housing permits to build single-family homes has dropped 10.6% nationwide since January 2025, with higher declines in regions more reliant on foreign-born workers, the research found.Meanwhile, native-born Americans are missing out on potential income in hard-hit states like California, Nevada, New Jersey, Florida and New York, where construction employment is on the decline – because when there are no immigrant roofers to build a home, American electricians and plumbers lose that project, too.“It’s not like someone can go work in construction and just not have any skills. And we’re losing people who have been here for decades working in construction. That could be fixed, but it’s going to take time,” Ettlinger said.Other industries with soaring costs and severe labor shortages includehealthcare, including home health care, nursing homes, adult daycare, lawn care, landscaping and groundskeeping, where immigrants have historically comprised a disproportionate share of the workforce and expertise.By September 2025, less than nine months into the second Trump administration, native-born workers had already lost an estimated 51,000 to 297,000 jobs because of changes to US immigration policy, the report said. The labor force shrunk by an estimated919,000 peopleduring the 18 months of Trump’s second term, whilejob growthhas slowed to roughly a third of the rate it was before he retook office.The federal government risks losing a large segment of the $26bn in payroll taxes from unauthorized immigrants who help to support the US social security fund that pays out to American seniors – while not being able to access those benefits themselves. Now, social security trustees,includingthe treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, health and human services secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, labor secretary, Keith Sonderling, and social security commissioner, Frank Bisignano, are warning that lower net immigration than expected is threatening worse finances for the flailing retirement benefits system, which could mean cuts to Americans’ entitlements.“The share of that annual loss due to the Trump immigration policy would be $2,152 [per person on average]. Thus, the Trump immigration policies, if continued, would reduce projected average annual Social Security benefits by 8.6% in 2034, and every year thereafter,” the report’s authors write.They told the Guardian that if the administration’s immigration agenda continues as expected, the implications for theUS economycould get even worse.“We would expect higher prices,” Lynch said. “We would expect more job losses, slower economic growth and the affordability crisis getting worse – partly because prices are higher, partly because people are losing their jobs and their incomes and they can’t afford as much.”Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationUS economynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘People are feeling the real impacts’: influencers are targeting private equity with satire and rage | Private equity | The Guardian
description: The trillion-dollar industry has taken over social media, inspiring skits and parody raps with millions of views
Author: Heather Timmons
Headline: The trillion-dollar industry has taken over social media, inspiring skits and parody raps with millions of views
Content: ‘A lot of people were being affected by this rampant rise in costs and wanted to know what was behind it. As it happens, private equity has changed a lot of industry landscapes.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘A lot of people were being affected by this rampant rise in costs and wanted to know what was behind it. As it happens, private equity has changed a lot of industry landscapes.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesConsumedPrivate equity‘People are feeling the real impacts’: influencers are targeting private equity with satire and rageSkits and parodies making fun of the trillion-dollar industry have taken over social media, racking up millions of viewsHeather TimmonsFri 9 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohnny Hilbrant Partridge kept getting stuck next to the same kind of finance guy at weddings – the one bragging about his family’s full-time nanny and lavish vacations whilename-dropping elite club memberships and private schools.To Partridge, a former fitness instructor, their shameless knack for self-promotion felt ripe for comedy. Using a filter that puts an exaggerated sneer on his face, Partridge donned a puffer vest and created “The PE Guy”, a caricature of the men who work in the private equity industry.“All we did is acquire some youth hockey complexes, implement dynamic pricing and put some people on recurring revenue subscription models,” Partridgescoffedin a video after lawmakersintroduced a billthis year to ban private equity from youth sports. “This country used to reward innovation, and suddenly it’s wrong to charge $11,000 for a development lacrosse weekend … give me a break.”World’s top 20 private equity firms produce more greenhouse gases a year than most countries, report findsRead moreSince he first debuted the character last year, “The PE Guy” has racked up millions of views onInstagramandTikTok, becoming the most popular player in a fast-growing ecosystem skewering private equity. The multitrillion-dollar industry has turned into a catch-all online for the ills of modern capitalism, inspiring“a day in the life” skitsandparody rap music videos.For many viewers, the draw is the dark humor, something that even the finance guys are embracing. Partridge said he gets invited to speak at insurance and private equity conferences and finance companies’ annual meetings as comic relief.But it’s also been a way many Americans are learning how the industry, which often operates out of view and without the same oversight or regulation as publicly traded corporations, is affecting their lives.Every business has bad actors, Partridge said, but he chose to focus on private equity because it is changing everyday things like healthcare so radically that “people are feeling the real impacts from it”, he said.Private equity has found its way into everything fromfuneral homesto family dental offices. Once they were acquired by private equity firms, beloved chains such asJoAnn Fabricsand Toys “R” Us facedbankruptcies, and many name brands taken over by the industry have degraded in quality.“When people say private equity, they don’t just mean the exact technical term,” said Hojung Kim, whoseAugust Instagram poston how private equity is changing veterinary care got a million views in just two days. The term has come to represent “leveraged buyouts, hard cost-cutting in order to ruthlessly profit-maximize and saddling the business with debt in order to self-enrich”.Struck by the response, Kim, co-founder of anaffordable LSAT prep business, started a series on other industries changed by private equity and builtGrass, an app that helps users find independent American businesses.“We hit a nerve. A lot of people were being affected by this rampant rise in costs and wanted to know what was behind it,” Kim said. “As it happens, private equity has changed a lot of industry landscapes.”TikTok and Instagram are awash in pro-business content too, of course, as companies overall have spent$37bnon influencer marketing in 2025, one advertising trade group estimates, and private equity companies are even buying up influencer tools like Uscreen.But the private equity criticism continues to grow. Journalist Pablo Torre and comedian Stavros Halkias have gotten hundreds of thousands of views on a YouTube video railing about Blackstone’stakeover of Jersey Mike’s Subsand financial investors in sports teams.“If they fucking destroy the Lakers, guys with Kobe [Bryant] back tattoos are going to start the proletariat revolution,” Halkiassaid on Torre’s podcast, going off news that the Los Angeles basketball team wasacquired byBob Iger and Josh Kushner for $12.5bn in August. “The closest we’re getting to class consciousness is fast food and sports teams.”Natalka Burian, owner of Elsa, a bar in Brooklyn, is among the food industry experts who are chronicling private equity’s takeover of restaurants and bakeries.They can pay outrageous rents and snatch up the best locations, she said, which drives out businesses like her own.“That’s money that should be going to local businesses,” Burian said. “I think there’s something about this blandness that takes away from our communities.”Explore more on these topicsPrivate equityConsumedInstagramTikTokSocial mediaDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: China agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark deal  | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs
Content: BYD cars being loaded on its cargo ship at Nantong Port in Jiangsu Province of China.Photograph: Xu Congjun/VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBYD cars being loaded on its cargo ship at Nantong Port in Jiangsu Province of China.Photograph: Xu Congjun/VCG/Getty ImagesAutomotive industryChina agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark dealBrussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobsLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentFri 9 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations withChinasince June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EV – but it’s too long for UK parking spacesRead more“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.China has beenflooding Europe with cars, including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs.Šefčovič said the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building in every member state in Europe with “literally thousands of job losses” at risk because of the flood of cheap imports from China across many sectors including chemicals and textiles.He said EU leaders were “clearly expecting very fast action” from the European Commission and the Chinese recognised that.“I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” he said.“This ‌is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told ‌reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold ​talks with his Chinese counterpart.Earlier this week senior EU officials said they were heading to Beijing to seek whatthey called a “proof of concept”or pilot scheme with one sector which they hoped could then be expanded to other areas under pressure from Chinese competition.Šefčovič said he put “so much emphasis” on the negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop” a trade war once it was declared.As part of a 16-point agreement, Beijing and Brussels will continue negotiating on cars, export restrictions on rare earths and access to China for more food and drink from the EU.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChina said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” for hybrid cars suggesting one method of curbing sales would be to set higher minimum price tags for Chinese cars sold in Europe.The EU commissioner will brief EU diplomats in Brussels on Sunday ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday.A statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce said China is “willing … to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”.It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”.While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryEuropean UnionChinaEuropeElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thieves make off with €5m haul from prestigious Italian winery | Italy | The Guardian
description: Gang breaks into cellar of Marchesi Antinori in Cortona and loads two trucks with 30,000 bottles before getaway
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Gang breaks into cellar of Marchesi Antinori in Cortona and loads two trucks with 30,000 bottles before getaway
Content: The estate’s chief executive, Renzo Cotarella, seen here with the Marchese Piero Antinori, said the gang was ‘very prepared’.Photograph: Agenzia Sintesi/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe estate’s chief executive, Renzo Cotarella, seen here with the Marchese Piero Antinori, said the gang was ‘very prepared’.Photograph: Agenzia Sintesi/AlamyItalyThieves make off with €5m haul from prestigious Italian wineryGang breaks into cellar of Marchesi Antinori in Cortona and loads two trucks with 30,000 bottles before getawayAngela Giuffridain RomeFri 9 Oct 2026 07.57 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of bottles of wine worth €5m (£4.2m) have been stolen from a prestigious winery in Tuscany in what is thought to be the biggest heist of its kind inItaly.A gang of at least seven masked individuals broke into the cellar of Marchesi Antinori, a family-owned winery dating back to the late 1300s, in Cortona after shutting off the alarms and surveillance cameras before using company forklifts to load two large trucks with 30,000 bottles of wine and making off.Among the bottles targeted were those most prized by wine collectors and consumers, including Solaia, Guado al Tasso and Tignanello, notable as one of the first red wines in the Tuscany region to be produced without white grapes. All the stolen bottles, ranging in price between €120 and €400 a bottle, are from the firm’s 2023 vintage.The theft occurred on Saturday as the company, based in the hilltop town of Cortona, prepared for a major shipment to buyers abroad. The robbery was discovered only when staff arrived for work on Monday morning.“The gang was very prepared,” Renzo Cotarella, chief executive of Marchesi Antinori, toldCorriere della Sera. “A theft of this scale and value has never happened before in Italy.”View image in fullscreenMarchesi Antinori is a world leading brand in the wine industry.Photograph: Agenzia Sintesi/AlamyHe said he had “great confidence” that investigators would trace the stolen wine, which included 3,000 bottles, some of them magnum-sized, of Barolo Ginestra.“Two trucks full of merchandise can’t just disappear into thin air,” he added. “The Tuscan roads are full of cameras. Perhaps with a bit of luck we’ll be able to recover at least some of the bottles.”There have been several thefts at wineries in Italy in recent months, including one in Alba in the northern Piedmont region in mid-September.But Cotarella, who suspects the same gang could have been involved, never imagined a theft of such scale would happen to his company. Unfortunately, its insurance policy does not cover the robbery of wine at such huge value.“We had always considered the possibility of having a few cases of wine being stolen during their transportation, but certainly not that two trucks manage to enter the cellar and make off with such a huge haul,” he told Corriere.Such large wine robberies were usually meticulously prepared and would probably be carried out by those with an intimate knowledge of wine themselves, Corriere suggested, with the target destination possibly collectors, bars or restaurants. However, a sudden increase in the supply of such wines could raise suspicion.As the investigators continue their search, Cotarella said the company, which was established in 1385, has warned customers to be wary of any offers of its wine outside official channels.Explore more on these topicsItalyWineFood & drink industryEuropenewsShareReuse this content
