title: Double moves Andrew Balding clear of Aidan O’Brien in Flat trainers’ race | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: Andrew Balding’s late run at a first success in the Flat trainers’ championship gained extra momentum as wins at Newmarket and York carried him further clear of Aidan O’Brien
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Andrew Balding’s late run at a first success in the Flat trainers’ championship gained extra momentum as wins at Newmarket and York carried him further clear of Aidan O’Brien
Content: Never So Brave (left, yellow cap), ridden by Oisin Murphy, wins the Challenge Stakes at Newmarket, ahead of stable companion Flora of Bermuda.Photograph: Alan Crowhurst/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNever So Brave (left, yellow cap), ridden by Oisin Murphy, wins the Challenge Stakes at Newmarket, ahead of stable companion Flora of Bermuda.Photograph: Alan Crowhurst/Getty ImagesHorse racingDouble moves Andrew Balding clear of Aidan O’Brien in Flat trainers’ raceWinners at Newmarket and York lift Balding’s spiritsNever So Brave wins Challenge Stakes at NewmarketGreg Woodat NewmarketFri 9 Oct 2026 12.26 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 18.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndrew Balding’s late run at a first success in the Flat trainers’ championship gained extra momentum as an across-the-cards double, including a 1-2 in the Group Two Challenge Stakes, carried him further clear of Aidan O’Brien before a potentially pivotal afternoon on Champions Day at Ascot next weekend.Balding was still around £700,000 adrift of O’Brien, the defending champion, at the end of August but has made steady progress since and moved into the lead for the first time when Blue Bolt won the Group One Sun Chariot Stakes at Newmarket last weekend.Daryz makes history with back-to-back Arc de Triomphe triumphsRead moreNever So Brave’s defeat of his stable companion, Flora Of Bermuda, in the Challenge Stakes was worth a total of £129,000, less than half an hour after Balding’s juvenile Nakila Sun had made all in the British EBF Final at York, which was worth £51,000 to the winner.O’Brien then had to settle for second place in the Group One Fillies’ Mile here, as his runner Haven was overhauled inside the final furlong by the odds-on favourite, Musical Times, with Balding’s runners, Forbidden Fire and Scommessa Sicura, picking up minor place money in third and fifth.“I’ve been at the sales all week, but I’d imagine the team at home are pretty pumped for it,” Balding said after his Challenge Stakes success. “If we’re still the same after Champions Day then I’ll start to get excited, but I wouldn’t dare say it will be.”O’Brien has more than a dozen entries on Champions Day at Ascot next weekend, although Jan Brueghel, at 6-4 for the Long Distance Cup, is currently his only favourite on the afternoon. Constitution River, the winner of the French Derby and Eclipse earlier in the season, is a 4-1 chance for the Queen Elizabeth II Stakes and around 10-1 for the Champion Stakes, while Gstaad, the Irish 2,000 Guineas winner, is also quoted for both of the card’s most valuable events.View image in fullscreenAndrew Balding has moved further clear of Aidan O’Brien in the race for the Flat trainers’ championship after making steady progress since August.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAPaddy Power quotes O’Brien at 2-7 (from 1-4) to win the title race after Friday’s action, while Balding is a 5-2 chance (from 11-4).Musical Times, meanwhile, is around 5-2 for next year’s 1,000 Guineas after overcoming significant traffic problems in the Fillies’ Mile. Charlie Appleby’s filly remains unbeaten after three starts and showed a high-class turn of foot to run down Haven after William Buick finally found some daylight a furlong out.“After two furlongs, we just had to hold our breath a little bit, but William was on the class filly in the race and he knew it himself,” Appleby said. “He was just trying to find those gaps and when he did she quickened up smartly.”High Fibre food for thought in CesarewitchJames Owen has established himself as a top-15 trainer on the Flat and over jumps in recent seasons, thanks not least to his habit of coaxing major improvement from other trainers’ castoffs, and his dual-purpose geldingHigh Fibre(3.40) is a fascinating contender for the Cesarewitch Handicap at Newmarket on Saturday.The seven-year-old has already picked up decent handicap prizes both over hurdles and on the Flat in his four starts since joining Owen from Harry Fry. A recent close second at York suggests he remains on a fair mark and Silvestre de Sousa, already a three-times winner of this race, is drawn in stall one for a race in which – despite the extreme title: Rui Pinto to remain under witness protection after U-turn by Portuguese authorities | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The CPES will now allow Pinto to challenge original decision, with the Manchester City whistleblower to receive risk assessment reports
Author: Miguel Dantas
Headline: The CPES will now allow Pinto to challenge original decision, with the Manchester City whistleblower to receive risk assessment reports
Content: Portuguese authorities are expected to reconsider the ending of Rui Pinto’s witness protection.Photograph: Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPortuguese authorities are expected to reconsider the ending of Rui Pinto’s witness protection.Photograph: Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty ImagesSoccerRui Pinto to remain under witness protection after U-turn by Portuguese authoritiesCPES will now allow Pinto to challenge original decisionWhistleblower to receive risk assessment reportsMiguel Dantasin PortoFri 9 Oct 2026 10.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 15.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRui Pinto will remain under witness protection for the time being after Portuguese authorities suspended the decision to end it. The special security programmes commission (CPES) acknowledged he should have been given an opportunity to present his case before the decision was taken. The Manchester City whistleblower can now challenge the withdrawal of his protection, with the commission expected to reconsider the matter.In a statement signed by the Ministry of Justice, the CPES was said to have recognised that Pinto had not been adequately informed of the grounds for terminating the programme or given the opportunity to exercise his right to challenge the decision.Maresca refuses to confirm he will stay at Manchester City if club lose appealRead moreThe protection was due to end on Saturday. The commission will provide Pinto with the risk assessment reports that it says indicated a low threat to his safety. The relevant meeting took place on 9 July. On 30 September, the day Pinto was informed his protected-witness status was coming to an end, an independent commission’sguilty verdict against City, which had been confirmed 24 hours earlier, was dominating headlines around the world.He has 10 working days to review the documentation underpinning the decision and respond to its reasoning and conclusions. The prospect of losing his protection had prompted Pinto to launch a fundraising campaign to help secure his financial future. He has voiced fears for his safety after receiving credible death threats and being assaulted in Lisbon last April.Pinto expressed satisfaction with the decision by Portugal’s minister of justice, Rita Alarcão Júdice, to overturn the CPES ruling. In a statement published on social media, the whistleblower said the commission’s initial decision had clearly violated the law and amounted to a “manifest abuse of power”.Although he believes the minister’s decision has restored legality, Pinto says he has lost confidence in the commission’s members, arguing that their conduct undermines the principles of impartiality, legality and trust that are essential to the functioning of a witness protection programme.Pinto’s protected-witness status dates to April 2020, when Portugal’s judicial police (PJ) placed him under protection after he agreed to give investigators access to millions of files obtained from football clubs, companies linked to the Angolan businesswoman Isabel dos Santos and other entities suspected of criminal activity. Dos Santosdenies corruption allegations.His disclosures have informed investigations by judicial, tax and sporting authorities across Europe, including the Premier League’s inquiry into City. Pinto’s lawyers argue the authorities must consider his cooperation with the justice system and the risks associated with his revelations before withdrawing his protection.Growing scrutiny appears to have prompted the authorities to reconsider their position. Pinto remains willing to cooperate with British authorities investigating City and other matters arising from his disclosures. He also handed millions of documents to investigators in France, which can now be shared with other countries, including the UK.Explore more on these topicsFootballPortugalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Maresca refuses to confirm he will stay at Manchester City if club lose appeal | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Enzo Maresca, who takes Manchester City to Liverpool on Sunday, would not get drawn on his future and said: ‘It’s fair to respect the process’
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Enzo Maresca, who takes Manchester City to Liverpool on Sunday, would not get drawn on his future and said: ‘It’s fair to respect the process’
Content: Enzo Maresca was giving his first press conference since the guilty verdicts against Manchester City.Photograph: Andy Hampson/PAView image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca was giving his first press conference since the guilty verdicts against Manchester City.Photograph: Andy Hampson/PAManchester CityMaresca refuses to confirm he will stay at Manchester City if club lose appealManager says: ‘It’s fair to respect the process’League leaders play Liverpool at Anfield on SundayJamie JacksonFri 9 Oct 2026 07.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 17.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnzo Maresca refused to confirm he will remain as Manchester City manager should the club lose their appeal against beingfound guilty of the vast majorityof 115 charges related to breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules.Maresca was speaking publicly for the first time since the verdict that has thrown English football into turmoil. City continue to deny any wrongdoing and their appeal is expected to be heard before Christmas, with a verdict due in the new year.Maresca believes City players ‘don’t care about the noise’ as Haaland calls for unityRead moreIn May 2022, Pep Guardiola said he would leave the club if he discovered the club’s hierarchy had not told him the truth about their financial dealings. “I said to them: ‘If you lie to me, the day after I am not here. I will be out and I will not be your friend any more.’” Maresca was asked if he shared the same position as his predecessor.“I would like to speak about this situation when we’re going to win the appeal,” the 46-year-old said. “It’s no sense to speak about anything because I don’t have many pieces of information. I trust the club because I trust the people and this is also the reason why I joined the club. There is not another club in the world where I would like to be. I’m very happy to be [here], I’m very proud.”The manager was asked if his trust may change should the appeal be lost. “But it’s the same. I don’t know. We are predicting the future. Again, I’m worried about tomorrow, in two days, in three days,” he said. “I don’t know what’s happening in the future. The only thing I can say is that I think it’s fair, from my point of view, from all of us, to respect the process. The process, verdict. There is an appeal ongoing. We see what’s happening.”One sanction that might be levied against City is expulsion from the Premier League. Guardiola joked that he would manage City in League One or even the National League. Maresca refused to be drawn on that scenario. “I won the Championship with Leicester[in 2023-24]. So in case we [are in] League One, we’re going to see. We are thinking about something that we don’t know,” he said.Maresca also denied that the many honours City have won under the current ownership are now tainted. “Absolutely not,” he said. “The last time I was here was in thetreble season[2022-23, as assistant manager] and I know the effort from the players, the club, the manager. I know the effort that the club put to achieve that kind of target so I don’t have any doubt about that.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGlasner urges quick end to Manchester City saga and fears damage to Premier LeagueRead moreCity lead the Premier League having taken maximum points from their opening five games and travel to Liverpool on Sunday. Maresca has no concern that the uncertainty regarding the club’s future will affect them at Anfield. “We understand the seriousness of the situation. I’m not saying that we don’t understand that,” he said. “The players understand. But it’s our duty, our job, to try to control the noise. Also, the manager and the players are focused on winning games, not on something different.“It is nice – at this moment, we are top of the league. So the players have all the reasons to be happy and excited. It will be a tough game for sure. But the most important thing is that we continue to do the right things. We are on the same page with the players, the owner, the CEO, the sport director and the fans.”Maresca was asked if referring to the guilty verdict as “noise” was dismissive of the anger felt towards City from sections of the wider football community. “I understand the reason why most of you are here,” he said. “But the only thing I can say is that is something that I already said, that there is a process ongoing.”Maresca said Erling Haaland was fit after the striker asked to come off last weekend with Norway.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityEnzo MarescanewsShareReuse this content

title: Phoebe Litchfield powers Australia to crushing ODI victory over Bangladesh | Australia women's cricket team | The Guardian
description: Opener smashes 77 off 75 balls to chase down meagre 166, as Annabel Sutherland takes 4-30 and hits 26 not out
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Opener smashes 77 off 75 balls to chase down meagre 166, as Annabel Sutherland takes 4-30 and hits 26 not out
Content: Phoebe Litchfield during her match-winning innings of 77 against Bangladesh at Allan Border Field.Photograph: Darren England/EPAView image in fullscreenPhoebe Litchfield during her match-winning innings of 77 against Bangladesh at Allan Border Field.Photograph: Darren England/EPAAustralia women's cricket teamPhoebe Litchfield powers Australia to crushing ODI victory over BangladeshOpener smashes 77 off 75 balls to chase down meagre 166Annabel Sutherland takes 4-30 and hits 26 not outAustralian Associated PressFri 9 Oct 2026 06.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Phoebe Litchfield masterclass ensured Australia remain undefeated in 22 ODIs at Allan Border Field after fast bowler Megan Schutt joined an elite club of great bowlers.Litchfield’s 77 off 57 deliveries ensured Australia polished off the meagre 166 all out set by Bangladesh in just 25.4 overs for the loss of three wickets.Litchfield combined ramps, glides, clips, exquisite drives, lofted pitching wedges, reverse hockey thumps and thunderous wallops in another opening knock that confirmed she is unique in world cricket and an absolute joy to watch.The left-hander was unstoppable in racing to her 12th ODI half-century.Allrounder Annabel Sutherland, player of the match, finished the chase with 26 not out after earlier taking four wickets.“It is a while since we have been out there in the yellow so it was nice to start like that,” Sutherland said.“It was nice to use the wicket and I felt like it was holding a bit.“It was pretty good to watch (Litchfield), just the way she can score all around the ground and the exquisite way she plays spin is something everyone in the group looks at.”Australia pace bowler Schutt earlier snared her 150th ODI wicket in a probing opening spell to put the hosts on top.Stand-in captain Tahlia McGrath invited the visitors to have first use of the surface and Schutt struck with the first ball of the innings, a vicious lifter that had opener Fargana Hoque edging to slip.A Schutt inswinger trapped Sarmin Sultana (four) in front and from that moment the bowlers kept a vice-like grip on the run rate and picked up steady wickets to dismiss Bangladesh with the fourth ball of the final over.The wicket of Sultana was the milestone 150th for Schutt. Only legendary speed demon Cathryn Fitzpatrick (180) and current allrounnder Ellyse Perry (166) have more wickets for Australia in the format.Schutt finished with 2-19 from her 10 overs with medium pacer Sutherland (4-30) proving a handful when she hit the pitch hard.Spinners Ashleigh Gardner, Georgia Wareham and Alana King bowled with class.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe visitors had several cameos but nothing substantial. No.3 Sharmin Akhter made a classy and breezy 24, captain Nigar Sultana (29 off 86 balls) was brave but stodgy.Veteran allrounder Ritu Moni (45 off 63) showcased her experience and nous and was the best of a mediocre bunch.Schutt has relished playing at AB Field throughout her career, where she now has 20 wickets.The quick was initially left out of the ODI side in February against India before a quad injury to Kim Garth opened the door for a recall.Schutt took 5-19 at AB Field on that occasion to provide a timely reminder of her talents.McGrath, usually a vice-captain, has been elevated to lead due to injury to regular skipper Sophie Molineux and rotated her bowlers with panache.The opener of three ODIs at the same venue, Friday’s clash is the first match of the summer on home soil for Australia’s victorious T20 World Cup side since lifting the trophy in July.Explore more on these topicsAustralia women's cricket teamBangladesh women's cricket teamWomen's cricketCricketAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mike Ditka, legendary Chicago Bears head coach, dies aged 86 | NFL | The Guardian
description: The Hall of Famer who led the 1985 Bears to the Super Bowl title was one of two people in NFL history to win league titles as a player, assistant and head coach
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Hall of Famer who led the 1985 Bears to the Super Bowl title was one of two people in NFL history to win league titles as a player, assistant and head coach
Content: Mike Ditka led the Chicago Bears to their lone Super Bowl championship in the 1985 season.Photograph: Phil Sandlin/AP/PA PhotosView image in fullscreenMike Ditka led the Chicago Bears to their lone Super Bowl championship in the 1985 season.Photograph: Phil Sandlin/AP/PA PhotosNFLMike Ditka, legendary Chicago Bears head coach, dies aged 86Hall of Famer led 1985 Bears to Super Bowl titleCoach was known for tough, gruff demeanorThe Super Bowl Shuffle to SNL: a life in picturesAssociated PressFri 9 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMike Ditka, who won NFL titles as a player and coach with theChicago Bears, has died at 86, his family announced Friday.“It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka,” the family said. “While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears’ Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever.”Mike Ditka: a life in picturesRead moreNicknamed “Iron Mike” as a player, Ditka helped revolutionize the tight end position, then moved to the sidelines and took over as Chicago’s coach. His 1985 Bears team featured one of football’s most dominant defenses ever. It also had enough outsized personalities to record a rap video,The Super Bowl Shuffle, and back up their boasting in the championship game three months later.After retiring as a coach, Ditka became a restaurateur, pitchman and TV personality, as well as an advocate for improved medical and retirement benefits for former players.Ditka was tough and gruff, the quintessential Chicago Bear nicknamed “Da Coach”. He did everything from order off the menu to knock defensive backs on their butts with a growl, and his adopted home townreveledin every minute. He was enshrined in the College and Pro Football Halls of Fame, and the Bears said during a ceremony in 2013 that his “No 89” jersey will be the last one retired by the team.He was born in Carnegie, Pennsylvania, the son of a welder who changed the family name from Dyczko. He grew up in nearby Aliquippa, close to the coal-mining and steel-manufacturing plants that dotted the western part of the state, a big, talented, three-sport athlete and All-American at Pitt whose bruising style made his first nickname, “Iron Mike” a good fit.View image in fullscreenMike Ditka was a standout tight end for the Chicago Bears as a player before returning to the franchise as a coach.Photograph: James Drake/Getty ImagesSelected fifth overall by flinty Chicago owner George Halas in the 1961 draft, Ditka went on to Rookie of the Year honors, multiple Pro Bowl trips and the 1963NFLchampionship. He left Chicago in 1966, playing briefly for Philadelphia and Dallas. He moved to the sideline in 1973 as an assistant to the revered Tom Landry and stayed with the Cowboys for eight seasons, before returning to a hero’s welcome in Chicago as head coach in 1982.Ditka’s return to the Bears lasted 10 tumultuous years, including five straight NFC Central titles, the Super Bowl win, a DUI conviction, a heart attack, a long-running feud with defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan and a new nickname – “Da Coach.”The public beefs with Ryan mirrored the behind-the-scenes battles Ditka waged trying to contain a team bristling with outsized personalities.“It was more than a team,” Ditka once said. “It was a team of characters that had character that played for a crazy man, who let him be crazy and had fun doing it and don’t apologize for it ever. I wouldn’t want to be one of these suits walking around on the sideline today. I have no desire to be that. I was what I was and they were what they were and, damn, it was fun.”It wasn’t until two dozen players recorded The Super Bowl Shuffle – an audacious rap-styled video released three months ahead of the 1986 title game – that the rest of the football world wondered whether Ditka was losing his grip. His players never did.“We call him ‘Sybil’ after that girl in the movie,” quarterback Jim McMahon once explained. “You know, the one that had all those personalities. Mike will be calm one minute, then throw a clipboard the next. People don’t understand that, but we do.”View image in fullscreenMike Ditka coached the Bears from 1982 to 1992.Photograph: Focus On Sport/Getty ImagesThe Bears demolished the New England Patriots 46-10 in the Super Bowl, but Ditka often said he regretted having McMahon and defensive tackle William “The Refrigerator” Perry run for touchdowns instead of Walter Payton, Chicago’s loyal and longsuffering running back.Ryan departed for a head coaching job in Philadelphia soon after. While the Bears continued to be a contender for most of the next five years, a 5-11 season prompted Ditka’s departure in 1992.After a five-year absence, he returned to coaching with the New Orleans Saints, but failed to revive the franchise. After a miserable 1999 season ended with a 3-13 record- his worst as either a player or coach – he left the sidelines for good.Ditkaland dispatches: why Chicago should rethink its 80s nostalgiaRead moreHis face and demeanor were so familiar by then that a second act became an easy segue. Ditka began building a stable of restaurants and appeared as himself in TV sitcoms from Cheers to Third Rock from the Sun, as well as shows such as LA Law and Saturday Night Live.He also stayed close to the game as an NFL analyst and game-day show personality at ESPN. Ditka’s high-profile status also made him an effective advocate to secure improved health and retirement benefits for former players.His name also circulated for years in Illinois political circles. Though he never ran for office, Ditka described himself asa staunch conservativeand was mentioned several times as a possible Republican candidate, including a congressional race against then state representative Barack Obama for the US Senate.Explore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsChicago BearsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our age | Movies | The Guardian
description: Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning shows how public opinion has changed around billionaire CEOs since The Social Network’s release
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning shows how public opinion has changed around billionaire CEOs since The Social Network’s release
Content: A straitjacketed simmer … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: SonyView image in fullscreenA straitjacketed simmer … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: SonyMoviesThe new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our ageJeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning shows how public opinion has changed around billionaire CEOs since The Social Network’s releaseDan MilmoGlobal technology editorFri 9 Oct 2026 07.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen The Social Network came out, Mark Zuckerberg organised a staff viewing of a film hedescribed as “fun”.A group corporate outing to the sequel is unlikely.The Social Network hardly portrayed the Facebook founder and his company in a hagiographical light (Zuckerberg laterdescribed the film as “hurtful”), but there was at least an element of the plucky upstart to the rise of Zuckerberg as he takes Facebook to 500 million users and a valuation of $25bn (ridiculously small numbers now – Meta has 3.6 billion users and is worth $1.8tn).By the end of that film, though, a steely CEO is emerging and his company is on the brink of global hegemony. The Social Reckoning picks up from there, with a clear perspective that both the founder and his company – as well as the industry they represent – are corporate villains now.This is set to be underlined by the release of theOpenAIdrama, Artificial, where its CEO, Sam Altman, is reportedly given a deeply unflattering portrayal. Elon Musk completes the villainous trilogy by appearing as himself – aside from the odd deployment of an AI avatar – in Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary, Musk, about the world’s first trillionaire.Tech is the obvious thread joining these films, but another is the scathing portrayal of the company leaders in them. Film villains used to be hoodlums, ex-deep state operatives, people with posh British accents. Tech execs are the new Darth Vader.View image in fullscreenDeeply unflattering … Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonThis is underlined by the casting ofJeremy Strong, who looks a touch on the old side to be playing 2019-2021 era Zuckerberg (the Meta CEO was in his mid-30s at the time of the film’s events whereas Strong is 47), but is embedded in our minds as the tortured Roy family scion Kendall in Succession.Strong also brings a straitjacketed simmer to the role here, one that breaks slightly at the end as he backtracks on being a “free speech absolutist” under intolerable pressure. It is the most human Zuckerberg moment in the entire film.Peter Bradshawdescribes Strong’s performanceas a “very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet”. It is much less sympathetic than Jesse Eisenberg’s in The Social Network and is a sort of corporeal representation of Meta as the monolithic, corporate bad guy.Elements of the portrayal chime with some former Meta employees, including a whistleblower, Arturo Béjar,who describes it as “accurate”. Another former employee tells the Guardian that Zuckerberg was “unemotional” in meetings (perhaps what you’d expect from a $1.8tn company CEO, admittedly). Well, Strong’s performance certainly is that.There had already been a turning point in public perception of Facebook beforethe Haugen leaks, with theCambridge Analyticascandal, which raised questions about the privacy of account holders’ data and how it is used.Haugen’s revelations in 2021 compounded this disquiet. By the time of the2022 inquest for British teenager Molly Russell, who took her own life after watching harmful content on Instagram, regulation of social media around the world was inevitable.The tone of The Social Reckoning and Strong’s performance reflect this shift. In the UK, screenings of the film are carrying an advert for the online safety charity established by Molly’s family,in which her father says: “‘Instagram helped kill my daughter”.Responding to Russell,Metasays it has worked to improve the safety of its platforms.The regulatory, legal and political backlash against social media – as well as the release of The Social Reckoning – reflects a lack of trust in such statements.Strong’s Zuckerberg says in the film that “the debate is over”. If it is, The Social Reckoning portrays a world where Meta is on the wrong side of it.Explore more on these topicsFilmMetaMark ZuckerbergOpenAIJeremy StrongSocial mediaDigital mediaShareReuse this content

title: ‘This is not an anti-tech town’: backlash to datacenter in city once home to IBM | Datacenters – US | The Guardian
description: Fight in East Fishkill, New York, part of a growing divide over whether AI benefits outweigh enormous downsides
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Fight in East Fishkill, New York, part of a growing divide over whether AI benefits outweigh enormous downsides
Content: Residents protest against a proposed datacenter in East Fishkill in June.Photograph: Food & Water WatchView image in fullscreenResidents protest against a proposed datacenter in East Fishkill in June.Photograph: Food & Water WatchDatacenters – US‘This is not an anti-tech town’: backlash to datacenter in city once home to IBMFight in East Fishkill, New York, part of a growing divide over whether AI benefits outweigh enormous downsidesMarina DunbarFri 9 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor decades, East Fishkill helped build New York’s tech industry.The hamlet, located 70 miles north of New York City, was home to a 460-acre campus where IBM researched and manufactured semiconductor chips for nearly 50 years.So when the news broke in early 2026 that a real estate developer, Treetop Companies, was exploring plans for what could become one of the largest artificial intelligence (AI) datacenters in the country, a roughly 1-gigawatt campus spanning more than 1m sq ft across about 143 acres, it seemed the town would welcome a new phase in its technological evolution.Instead, a furious backlash erupted before even a single permit application was filed with the municipal government. Residents began attending town board meetings, organizing rallies and advocating for a temporary ban.Even before any plans for the facility were drawn up, East Fishkill’s existing zoning laws did not allow for the construction of large datacenters. The town issueda three-year moratoriumon them anyway, a sign of the extreme ire against datacenters.The temporary ban, adopted unanimously in late June, forbids the town from considering new datacenters larger than 20 megawatts until July of 2029, while officials study their potential impacts on water resources and local ecosystems. The development company at the center of the controversy has appealed the measure.“I just think that we’re at this moment where things are happening very quickly, we need to get our ducks in a row and think about the various ways in which datacenters and new energy usage will affect our long-term community cohesiveness, environmental quality, and character,” said East Fishkill resident and professor Tanya Radford.The fight unfolding in East Fishkill is a single piece of agrowing divide. Both rural towns and communities that once eagerly welcomed hi-tech development are increasingly questioning whether AI infrastructure adds enough local benefit to justify its enormous appetite for electricity, water and land.“This is not an anti-tech town,” said Radford. “I’m an educator. I use technology.”The proposalThe saga began after Treetop Developmentpurchased propertyin East Fishkill, initially pursuing approvals for a warehouse development. Residents later discovered that the company, through local property owner Donovan Drive Holdings, hadentered the queueto have a project approved that would use approximately 1,000 megawatts of electrical service, an amount more consistent with a large-scale AI datacenter than a warehouse.This request for approval was not submitted to the town of East Fishkill. Rather, it was submitted to New York Independent System Operator (NYISO)’s interconnection queue. NYISO is an independent organization responsible for managing New York’s high-voltage power grid, meaning whenever a company wants to build a big new project, it must formally ask NYISO for permission to connect to the grid.For those that call East Fishkill home, the NYISO filing quickly raised concerns.The proposed datacenter would consumemore electricitythan the entire city of Buffalo, which has about 275,000 people. East Fishkill is home to just 30,000.View image in fullscreenNew York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, with the US members of Congress Alexandria-Ocasio Cortez and Pat Ryan in East Fishkill this week.Photograph: Susan Watts/Office of Governor Kathy Hochul“Residents have been speaking out against it to stop any application from coming into the town for the datacenter,” said Melissa Hoffmann, an East Fishkill resident and organizer with a local chapter of Food & Water Watch, an environmental advocacy non-profit.But because no formal application had been filed with East Fishkill, town officials repeatedly stressed that there was nothing before the planning board to review or reject.“There is no application before the Town. There has never been an application for a datacenter,” the East Fishkill supervisor Nick D’Alessandrowroteon Facebook in June. D’Alessandro later took down the post. His office did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.He stressed that standalone datacenters were “not even listed as a permissible use” under the town’s zoning laws. Nonetheless, in June the board banned their construction for three years “to give our community certainty and allow time for further study and discussion”.Hoffmann said months of public pressure ultimately convinced the town board to extend what had initially been discussed as a seven-month pause into a three-year moratorium.Tech townEast Fishkill has often been described as an “innovation hub”, making opposition to the datacenter proposal remarkable precisely because the town has not been hostile towards new technology.International Business Machines Corporation, better known as IBM,transformedthe town during the latter half of the 20th century into one of the nation’s leading semiconductor manufacturing centers, employing thousands of workers and laying the foundation for what is now iPark 84, home to mixed-use commercial and residential facilities.Former IBM facilities remain a defining part of the local economy, and iPark continues to house technology companies. One tenant is currently seeking to expand anexisting datacenterby approximately 150 megawatts, far smaller than the facility proposed by Treetop.Residents have insisted that their opposition is not meant to hinder forward-looking tech, but is directed at the unprecedented scale of emerging AI infrastructure.“The pushback is really to the size,” resident Fran Caracappa, acandidatefor county legislature, said. “The Treetop center would be 1,000 megawatts. People do not want to pay higher electricity rates because of a larger datacenter coming in and putting pressure on the grid.”Residents have also questioned whether the supposed economic benefits justify the costs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHoffmann worried that the datacenter would “provide very few jobs”. Caracappa similarly expressed doubt that temporary construction jobs would lead to lasting employment for locals.“It’s not going to provide work to keep people here like the previous tech businesses did,” Caracappa said. “So what’s the benefit to the town?”Cozy hamlet rejects developmentThe town’s skepticism toward a huge industrial project is also informed by the consequences of its past.IBM’s manufacturing operations helped establish the region’s tech-industrial identity, but groundwater contamination associated with semiconductor production leftlasting scars. Several polluted Superfund sitesremain in the area.In addition to groundwater protection, residents have raised concerns about noise, diesel backup generators, property values, wetlands and the area’s rural character.View image in fullscreenPeople call on Governor Kathy Hochul to sign the Data Center Act in East Fishkill in June.Photograph: Eric Weltman/Food & Water WatchRadford, whose home sits near the Appalachian trail, said that the serene, woodsy landscape that currently surrounds the proposed site is one of the reasons she moved there.“My neighbors and I agree that additional development in the area could only negatively impact the quality of life here,” she said.Barely two weeks after the East Fishkill moratorium passed, New York became the first US state to enact a moratorium on new datacenters when Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order mandating a one-year statewide pause on so-called hyperscale datacenters.New York becomes first state to impose one-year pause on new AI datacentersRead moreDonald Trump, an ally to tech billionaires and AI investors,respondedwith rage. He called the move “a terrible decision” on his Truth Social platform and accused Hochul of implementing the ban for purely political reasons.“One of the biggest Driving Forces in the Future for Jobs, are Data Centers. They are big, strong, bold, and Money Machines for the State in which they are built,” Trump wrote. Later in the summer, he called towns rejecting datacenters “backwards and poor”.Datacenter developer appealsLike Trump, Treetop did not take kindly to East Fishkill’s three-year ban. In a 17-page objection letter submitted to the town board and reviewed by the Guardian, attorneys for the company argued the three-year moratorium unlawfully targets the company’s property and effectively amounts to a permanent prohibition rather than a “legitimate temporary planning measure”.In the letter, the company said it spent years and significant resources advancing development plans for the site, including environmental reviews, wetlands investigations, traffic studies and utility coordination.Town officials have maintained that no datacenter application has ever been submitted and that the moratorium provides time to evaluate whether existing zoning properly addresses an entirely new class of industrial development.East Fishkill residents are claiming victory.“People are winning,” Hoffmann said. “Communities that fight these datacenters are winning.”Explore more on these topicsDatacenters – USDatacentresNew YorknewsShareReuse this content

title: Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts | Palantir | The Guardian
description: Former Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Former Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns
Content: Tom Watson at the Labour party conference in Liverpool last month.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTom Watson at the Labour party conference in Liverpool last month.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesPalantirPalantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contractsFormer Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdownsJamie GriersonFri 9 Oct 2026 03.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Watson, the former Labour deputy leader who recently joined Palantir, has warned against “mob rule” when it comes to awarding public contracts.Lord Watson, now a senior vice-president at the US tech corporation, said UK ministers could get themselves “in a lot of trouble” as he was questioned about concerns raised about the government working with his new employer.Palantir was co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel and has providedAI-powered software to the Israeli military and the White House’s ICE immigration crackdown, leading to a public and political backlash against its deepening involvement in British public services.The prime minister,Andy Burnham, is under significant pressure from Labour MPs and unions to ditch Palantir from government contracts, including a £330m software deal with the NHS.The company is also fighting Sadiq Khan in court over theLondon mayor’s block on a £50m contractto use its AI in Metropolitan police investigations. It is seeking to win more public sector work in the UK, where it already has an annualturnoverof £427m.Watson told the BBC podcast Political Thinking with Nick Robinson: “One of the things I’d say to my former colleagues is: do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices? Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one.”He added: “I think we are very targeted by the people that are targeting Israeli companies. We’re not an Israeli company, but because of our work in Israel we found ourselves in the middle of the row of the Gaza protests.”Watson told the podcast he would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns if the situation arose, saying: “We don’t actually work in that sector, but yes, of course we would.”He calledPalantir“the most interesting company on the planet” as he announced his new role last month. The company said his job would be, in part, to “deepen the social and economic value its work creates through better British public services, jobs and skills”.Watson was a defence minister and a minister for digital engagement in Gordon Brown’s government. Since stepping down from parliament in 2019, he has been an adviser to the gambling and music industries and, since 2024, he has been a part-time adviser to Palantir.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPalantir said Watson had taken a leave of absence from the House of Lords and had relinquished his parliamentary pass while he worked for the company inLondon.The Labour MP Chi Onwurah, who chairs the science, innovation and technology committee, which has raised concerns about Palantir, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “Tom is not the first politician to be blinded by tech hype. The key issue is we can’t be so dependent on one company. It’s a US company, subject to US legislation regarding access to our data.”Explore more on these topicsPalantirTom WatsonPublic services policyNHSMetropolitan policeSadiq KhanAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI projected to bring in $20bn less in revenue than expected | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Questions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled before
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Questions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled before
Content: Forecasts of annual revenues by leading AI players are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for the tech, which is attracting huge investment.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APView image in fullscreenForecasts of annual revenues by leading AI players are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for the tech, which is attracting huge investment.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APOpenAIOpenAI projected to bring in $20bn less in revenue than expectedQuestions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled beforeBusiness live – latest updatesMark SweneyFri 9 Oct 2026 04.06 EDTFirst published on Fri 9 Oct 2026 04.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI.The ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September.However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported.Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rivalAnthropic, the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment.OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn.News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%.The discrepancy arose from attempts by OpenAI investors to provide a more direct comparison with how projected revenue is measured by Anthropic, which hit $65bn in forecast revenue by the end of July.Anthropic includes the revenue from sales via cloud partners, such as Amazon’s AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI does not.Last month, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said that the company wouldnot float on the stock market this year as had been expected, citing safety concerns over AI.Altman’s decision followed cases of AI agentsgoing rogueto hack external systems and AI ​safety researchersquittingtheir companies concerned about the technology’s risks.Democrat and Republican politicians are calling for new rules to govern AI systems, after two researchers from Anthropic warned that the lightning pace of development of AI without safeguards could lead to theextinction of the human race.Anthropic is expected to push ahead with plans for an initial public offering (IPO) as soon as next month.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpenAI’s most recent fundraising was in March when it closed a $122bn round of finance ata valuation of $852bn.Two months later Anthropic announced it had raised $65bn,valuing the company at $965bn.On Friday, it emerged that Masayoshi Son, the founder of Japanese investment company SoftBank, is seeking to raise up to $100bn from Gulf states as he scales up his already mammoth investments in AI.SoftBank has aggressively pivoted towards AI, including making a $65bn investment in OpenAI, and discussions have been held with Gulf investors including the United Arab Emirates, the Financial Times reported.Last month, SoftBank raised $11.1bn in the largest high-yield corporate bond sale globally on record, paying investors yields as high as 9.75%, to fund its bets on AI and semiconductor assets.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIChatGPTAI (artificial intelligence)Technology sectorAnthropicComputingAnnual resultsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic bans users from ‘needless abusive or cruel behavior’ towards Claude | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: A spokesperson for the tech company did not specify what kind of behavior would be considered abusive
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: A spokesperson for the tech company did not specify what kind of behavior would be considered abusive
Content: Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, at a a press briefing with Donald Trump on 29 September 2026 in Washington DC.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, at a a press briefing with Donald Trump on 29 September 2026 in Washington DC.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesAnthropicAnthropic bans users from ‘needless abusive or cruel behavior’ towards ClaudeA spokesperson for the tech company did not specify what kind of behavior would be considered abusiveUwa Ede-OsifoThu 8 Oct 2026 21.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropic hasbarred usersfrom exhibiting “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its models, as the company’s leaders continue to ponder machine consciousness.The Vergefirstreported the change in policy.A spokesperson forAnthropic, which is behind the AI chatbot Claude, did not immediately respond to an inquiry about what could be considered “abusive or cruel”.In an online user policy, the San Francisco-based company noted that its ban would not apply to common user frustrations, model testing or “dark creative themes”.Anthropic’s usage policy previously contained restrictions on abusive conduct.The company’s large language models have the ability to end a conversation if a user is being persistently harmful. When that feature rolled out last August, the company framed it as a safeguard for AI’s welfare.“We remain highly uncertain about the potential moral status of Claude and other LLMs, now or in the future. However, we take the issue seriously, and alongside our research program we’re working to identify and implement low-cost interventions to mitigate risks to model welfare, in case such welfare is possible. Allowing models to end or exit potentially distressing interactions is one such intervention,” according to its website.The notion of AI systems being conscious has been highly polarizing in and outside the tech world.Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, hassaidhe cannot rule out the possibility.Meanwhile, Sam Altman, CEO of rival OpenAI, has appeared averse to the idea.“I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue,” he wrote in an X post, days after the New York Timesreportedon Anthropic leaders’ extensive conversations with religious scholars.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)Dario AmodeiConsciousnessChatbotsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Firmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre company | Datacentres - Australia | The Guardian
description: The $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997
Author: Jonathan Barrett
Headline: The $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997
Content: Tim Rosenfield (left) and Oliver Curtis (right), who together with Curtis’s former brother-in-law Jonathan Levee are the trio behind Firmus, which shelved its IPO plans on Friday.Photograph: Firmus TechnologiesView image in fullscreenTim Rosenfield (left) and Oliver Curtis (right), who together with Curtis’s former brother-in-law Jonathan Levee are the trio behind Firmus, which shelved its IPO plans on Friday.Photograph: Firmus TechnologiesDatacentres - AustraliaFirmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre companyThe $11-a-share offer would have been the biggest debut on the stock market since the telecommunication giant in 1997Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJonathan BarrettandJosh TaylorFri 9 Oct 2026 00.37 EDTFirst published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirmus Technologies has scrapped what was set to be Australia’s biggest company listing in decades after investor demand for its much-hyped AI datacentre business failed to materialise.A Firmus spokesperson said the board decided that proceeding with the offer was no longer in the best interests of the company and its shareholders.“Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options,” the spokesperson said on Friday morning.Australia is building a lot of new homes. But is the datacentre boom holding us back? | Greg JerichoRead more“We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress.”Firmus, with an anticipated $44bn valuation, was expected to be the biggest ASX listing since Telstra in 1997.But it faced mounting scepticism over its huge valuation, and forecast earnings, for a company in its startup phase with just two, small operational sites.Backed by chip maker Nvidia and Wall Street firms Blackstone, Jane Street and Coatue, Firmus’s backers believed they could raise billions of dollars by selling shares in a public float with the help of five brokers.Thelack of demandmeans Firmus will need to raise money from private investors to fund its plans to build liquid-cooled “AI factories” in Australia and across Asia.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailFrantic discussionsThe polished Firmus pitch started to unravel midweek after it became clear the company’s bankers had vastly overestimated demand in their bid to raise $7bn from investors ahead of listing on the ASX on 23 October.This prompted discussions about a heavy reduction in the company’s proposed $11-a-share initial public offering, according to one investment manager briefed on the matter.The company ultimately decided to withdraw its application to list on the ASX altogether.Guardian Australia previously reported growing concern that early Firmus investors were going touse retail investors buying into the float as their “exit strategy”, leaving small investors exposed if the excitement dissipated.The datacentre company’s troubles have already rattled other parts of the market, with shares in Firmus investor Maas Group plunging more than 20% on Thursday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe anticipated financial worth of the founders – Oliver Curtis, his cousin Tim Rosenfield, and Curtis’s former brother-in-law Jonathan Levee – will also be greatly reduced.‘Diverging’ mission blamed for CDC splitVeteran datacentre firm CDC this week ended what was touted as a $73bn deal with Firmus named Project Southgate, which was aimed at building sovereign, renewable-powered AI infrastructure and which claimed Nvidia as its first customer.On Friday, appearing at the federal parliament’s joint standing committee on AI, CDC’s chief strategy officer, Dr Jack Dan, said the arrangements began when Firmus’s focus was “a lot more on Australia and creating sovereign AI capability in Australia.”“Their business model has then since evolved and probably the most blunt way of putting it is we have a very clear business model and a very clear mission for our company,” he said. “And when things start diverging significantly from that, we continue to follow our core mission.”The deal was first announced in October last year.Dan said Firmus had a “very different approach to developing datacentres” and CDC is “very much about critical infrastructure, very significant resilience … essentially 100% availability.”“That comes with a certain degree of assurance, a certain degree of rigor and a certain degree of process, which probably was or could have been construed as being a little bit too heavy for a more commercial type development.”Earlier in the hearing, Dan observed that CDC had been around for nearly 20 years, and until last year, “no one really cared who CDC datacentres was” but now datacentres were front and centre of the national conversation.Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - AustraliaBusinessAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

Content: Illustration: Cynthia KittlerGuardian journalism is independent. Sign up hereGuardian writersFri 9 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Filter is turning two! To celebrate, we asked our contributors for their favourite products from the past year, and rounded up the team’s picks too.From handbag-sized umbrellas and stylish yet practical wellies to reading lights and luxurious duvets, these are the products that stood out.The Filter products we love the mostBrush with greatnessView image in fullscreenRevamp Straight & Go cordless hot brush£89.99 at Currys£90 at ArgosOne of the best tools I’ve tested this year is Revamp’s Straight & Go cordless for my review of thebest hot brushes. It’s my hot brush of choice when I’m away from home (and at home: it’s cordless so I can use it in the bathroom without trailing cables all over the hallway).Lise SmithCream of the cropView image in fullscreenIlliyoon ceramide ato concentrate cream, 75ml£9.99 at Boots£9.99 at AmazonThe best product I’ve bought on another writer’s recommendation is the Illiyoon ceramide ato concentrate cream, whichSarah Matthewswrote about in herbest facial moisturisers roundup. It’s rich but gentle and leaves my rather dry skin soft, smooth and plump.LSScreen saverView image in fullscreenBrick£44.75 at BrickI wrote about Brick, a device that helps reduce screen time,for myphone addiction piece. I didn’t view myself as having a problem,but after finding that Brick really improved my wellbeing, I became the first person in history for whom admitting you have a problem is the last step on the road to recovery.Alan MartinA pizza the actionView image in fullscreenGozney Arc Lite£349.99 at Gozney£349.99 at John LewisI’m continuing to cook with the Gozney Arc Lite, which I reviewed for our guide to thebest pizza ovens, and starting to relax more and enjoy it. Slowly, my hand-stretched bases are getting better, though I think I would still be laughed out of any self-respecting pizzeria: “Don’t quit the day job.”Rachel OgdenA good foundationView image in fullscreenSaie the Base Brush£26 at Cult Beauty£26 at SephoraI trust all beauty recommendations from my beloved colleagueSali Hughesimplicitly, so after reading herguide to makeup brushes, I thought it was perhaps time I stopped slapping foundation on by hand and invested in this Saie brush. It makes foundation sit more lightly on your skin and makes blending at the neck and hairline foolproof.Jess Cartner-MorleyTub thumpingView image in fullscreenTown & Country square flexi-tub, 25l£10.95 at Tooled Up£13.93 at AmazonFor my rundown ofitems that make camping with kids easier, I tested a pair of square flexi-tubs during a trip with my six-year-old. They were a godsend then – helping keep everything organised and tidy – but they’ve since found a place in home life as indispensable declutterers. Kids’ toys everywhere? Throw them in the flexi-tub. Doing some DIY? Tools in the tub! Too many tubs? Stack them! You get the picture.Matt CollinsBest foot forwardView image in fullscreenBarbourBedewellington bootsMen’s£55 at John Lewis£79.95 at BarbourWomen’sFrom £55 at Frasers£79.95 at BarbourIn the past I’ve opted for more fashion-led wellies, but these days I use them more for dog walking than festivals. So I tookDanielle Wilkins’ recommendation in her roundup of thebest welliesand bought her top pick of Barbour boots. With a classic look and excellent grip (even across muddy fields), I get to balance style and practicality.Sabine WieselRain checkView image in fullscreenDavek mini umbrella£65 at DavekWhen I needed an umbrella this year, I turned toPete Wise’sumbrella test. I’m terrible for not carrying a brolly and getting caught out by rain, so I wanted something small I could leave in my handbag. I picked the Davek Mini. It has saved my veggie bacon many times already and its lifetime guarantee is reassuring.Caramel QuinWalk this wayView image in fullscreenUrevo SpaceWalk 5L walking pad£399.99 at Urevo£349.99 at AmazonHaving tested lots ofwalking pads and under-desk treadmillsfor the Filter, I have become quite attached to the Urevo SpaceWalk 5L model (a review for which is on the way). I walk on it most days in an attempt to rack up at least 10,000 steps. It’s an easy way to burn extra calories when I’d otherwise be glued to my desktop, and I’ve found this model exceptionally quiet, while the automatic incline is great for varying the terrain without lifting a finger.Leon PoultneyLight my fireView image in fullscreenPrimus Lite Plus stoveFrom £98.99 at Mountain Warehouse£130 at PrimusI tested the Primus Lite Plus for our guide tobest camping stoves. I recently took it on a three-day trek in the Lake District and found it simple to use and clean, and great for boiling water.Sian LewisCashmere crushView image in fullscreenMicro bandana£55 at Rise&FallJess Cartner-Morleyalsoinspired meto buy a jazzy cashmere bandana from Rise&Fall.SLUnder coverView image in fullscreenPanda the Cloud duvet, double£129.95 at Panda£129.95 at AmazonMy Panda duvet from my test of thebest duvetshas been a real bedding upgrade. When you go from a cheap polyester duvet (which was perfectly fine, I thought) to this cloud-like breathable bamboo hug, there’s no going back. I always look forward to wrapping myself in it at night. I now have two versions – thewinter 10.5-togone I tested for best duvets, and the4.5-tog summer version.Jane HoskynFace valueView image in fullscreenBeauty of Joseon relief sun rice + Probiotics SPF50+, 50ml£15.50 at Cult Beauty£11.62 at AmazonI bought a double pack ofBeauty of Joseon’s Relief Sun Rice + Probiotics SPF50+, which not only took the top spot in Sarah Matthews’best face SPFguide but was also raved about by Sali Hughes in herhero skincare 2025 roundup. I’ve got fair skin, so I need a good daily SPF, ideally one I can slap on without looking like I’ve fallen face-first into my cereal, but my skin is also greasy and spotty, so the light texture of this is such a lovely relief after the thick sun creams I’ve been used to.JHFry highView image in fullscreenNinja Double Stack XL SL400UK air fryer£269 at John Lewis£269.99 at NinjaI’ve been tempted to buy an air fryer for ages but didn’t think I had the counter space. It also produces the crispest, most delicious jacket potato skin I’ve ever had.Lily Smith, researcherLeaf it to meView image in fullscreenStihl SHA 56garden vacuum£231.79 at Farol MowersThe Stihl SHA 56 leaf blower and garden vacuum, which I tested for our guide to thebest leaf blowers and vacuums, has been an absolute hit in my garden this year, not just for collecting leaves but for doing any of the work I’d normally use a broom for. Its added superpower of collecting whatever it’s been blowing about at the end of the job is the icing on the cake.Andy ShawHands downView image in fullscreenE45 repairing hand cream, 50ml£6.60 at Sainsbury’s£5.65 at AmazonI’ve taken up pottery this year, and my hands have paid the price. There’s nothing like handling wet clay to extract all the moisture from your skin. So, as soon as I’m done wiping down my station and labelling my wonky creations, I’m in need of urgent relief. I opted for the E45 repairing hand cream fromSarah Matthews’best hand cream guidefor two reasons: it’s cheap enough to share around the studio, and (as promised) it has a thick, nourishing texture. Sarah described it as a “refreshing drink of water for the hands”, and I couldn’t agree more – my mitts absolutely slurp the stuff up.Millie Fender, commissioning editorCase closedView image in fullscreenJuly packing cellsskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The July set did a particularly good job of preserving the crispness of shirts and trousers during a chaotic cross-country journey this summer.Pete WiseGlow getterView image in fullscreenCeraVe skin renewing vitamin C serum, 30ml£22.50 at Lookfantastic£22.50 at BootsI bought the CeraVe vitamin C serum onDanielle Wilkins’recommendation. I was astounded when, after a week of using it, people started commenting on how “glowy” my face looked. I’m hoping it keeps me looking alive all the way through the grey winter months!Zoë PhillimoreTake a seatView image in fullscreenThunderX3 Solo 360 gaming chair£169.99 at OverclockersWe were switching my son’s and daughter’s rooms over and we needed extra incentive for him (Iggy) to accept the deal – he was moving into the smaller bedroom – and this chair from ourbest gaming chairsguide swung it. Iggy now has his own “gaming nook” (doubling up as my workspace), and the chair is saving my working-from-home slouching.Alex Jones, picture editorMiles betterView image in fullscreenSaucony Endorphin Azura running shoesMen’sFrom £96.89 at Cotswold OutdoorFrom £112 at SauconyWomen’sFrom £97.89 at Runners Need£112 at SauconyI’ve logged thousands of miles this year searching for thebest running shoes. One of the standout all-rounders that can cope with almost anything is the Saucony Endorphin Azura. Go fast, go slow. No trouble. The perfect suitcase shoe at a pretty competitive price.Kieran AlgerDress rehearsalView image in fullscreenNobody’s Childfloral starlight midi dress£51 at Nobody’s ChildThis isn’t so much something I’ve bought as something I’ve bought into. The vast majority of the clothing I’ve bought this year has been secondhand, thanks toJane Hoskyn’smoney-saving tips. My favourite find is along cream dress (with pockets!) from Nobody’s Child, which I snagged for £15, down from a usual £85.Sarah MatthewsDry runView image in fullscreenVonHaus Smart dehumidifier with laundry mode£144.99 at VonHaus£144.99 at ArgosAfter readingCaramel Quin’s roundup of thebest dehumidifiers, I was convinced the budget VonHaus Smart dehumidifier was exactly what our damp house was crying out for. Not only is it incredibly satisfying to see so much water sucked out of the air, but it’s also become my new favourite (and fastest) way to dry laundry.Ella Jinadu, audience editorLight readingView image in fullscreenGritin rechargeable book light£13.95 at Fruugo£8.59 at AmazonMy partner and I each have a clip-on reading light, recommended in our guide to theeveryday items that could improve your life, and can fully vouch for how the disturbance-free glow has transformed our reading routines – both at bedtime and in the dark early mornings. They also came in handy on a recent camping trip when the wind made it impossible to sleep.EJCool customerView image in fullscreenGreenPan Frost ice-cream maker and slushie machine£399 at Debenhams£399.90 at BootsI love a kitchen gadget and became obsessed with the GreenPan soft-serve and slushie maker while I was testing it forbest ice-cream makers. While I enjoyed the ice-cream, I loved making frozen cocktails even more – it was a real crowd-pleaser at parties too.Danielle AmatoSpirited awayView image in fullscreenJo Vodka101 the Purist, 70cl£48.95 at Master of Malt£50 at John LewisView image in fullscreenChopinpotato vodka, 70cl£37.38 at Master of Malt£39.75 at the Whisky ExchangeWhen I am tasked with testing a specific category, it ends up reigniting my love and interest in it. So, sincetesting vodka, I’m still fully into mixing myself ice-cold martinis (dry, with a twist, please) and variations on the theme. The top vodkas I’m still reaching for are the Jo Vodka and the Chopin, though I also made a fab lychee martini recently usingSapling raspberry.Joanne GouldBlooming lovelyView image in fullscreenScilly FlowersFrom £17 at Scilly FlowersI’m also a new customer of Scilly Flowers after readingZoë Phillimore’s piece on thebest flower delivery services. I like that it tends to do arrangements of just one type of flower, which I find elegant, and it has varieties you don’t usually find with online florists; plus it can be amazing value.
