title: The best sunrise alarm clocks in the UK, tried and tested for gentler mornings | Sleep | The Guardian
description: Our reviewer sheds some light on the best dawn simulation alarms, from Lumie and Philips to Dreamegg
Author: Pete Wise
Headline: Our reviewer sheds some light on the best dawn simulation alarms, from Lumie and Philips to Dreamegg
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSleepReviewThe best sunrise alarm clocks in the UK, tried and tested for gentler morningsOur reviewer sheds some light on the best dawn simulation alarms, from Lumie and Philips to DreameggThe best eye masks to help you sleep betterPete WiseFri 9 Oct 2026 05.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo wake each day in darkness is a plight you wouldn’t wish on your worst enemy, yet that’s what many of us do routinely throughout winter. Getting up in the dark decouples our life from our circadian rhythm (our body clock), with bodily processes such as cognition and metabolism put to work before they’re fully prepped.Thank heavens, then, for sunrise alarm clocks. These “dawn simulation” devices glow with gradually intensifying brightness as your wake-up time approaches, kickstarting your circadian rhythm before you get out of bed. For many users, this results in a happier, healthier start to the day.Sunrise alarm clocks can differ vastly – for instance, only some are bright enough to be medically certified as light-therapy devices forSad(seasonal affective disorder) and other disorders. We’ve indicated the two alarms that have this certification in their specs below.I tested 10 wake-up lights from Lumie, Beurer, Philips, Dreamegg, Blueair and Lexon to find out which would make the most difference to my mornings, and these are the eight I recommend. As a lifelong reluctant riser, I’ve found the experience of testing these devices a gamechanger – in fact, I’m now using one daily. Perhaps mornings aren’t so bad, after all …At a glanceBest sunrise alarm clock overallLumieBodyclock Glow 150£118.96 at AmazonBest budget sunrise alarmLumieSunrise Alarm£39.99 at AmazonBest sunrise alarm clock for heavy sleepersLumieBodyclock Spark 100£98.46 at HealfBest sunrise alarm for late-night readingPhilipsSmartSleep£181.99 at AmazonBest mini sunrise alarm clockLexonMina Sunrise£79.90 at John LewisBest sunrise alarm clock for couplesBeurerWake-up Light WL50£57.56 at John LewisWhy you should trust meMornings, eh? I’ve often felt lousy first thing, after waking up to a minutes-long medley of smartphone alarms.When, at last, I drag myself out of bed, I frequently spend the day reviewing all kinds of gadgets, from Sad lamps to electric heaters. It’s a freelance job I’ve been privileged to do since 2017 – and as we tumbled dimly into 2025, the Filter gave me one of my most quietly life-improving assignments yet: reviewing sunrise alarm clocks. I tested three additional models in winter 2025/26, and one of these has emerged as my favourite of all.The extent to which these gadgets have improved my mornings has surprised me – although it was greater in some cases than others. Frankly, I’d like other groggy wakers to feel the same benefit, and my reviews are written and ranked with this in mind.Some brands did not want the sunrise alarm clocks I sourced for testing back, so those will be donated for fundraising toCat Action Trust 1977, a small national charity dedicated to the welfare of feral cats.How I testedView image in fullscreenEach sunrise alarm clock, including the Beurer Wake-up Light WL50 (pictured), was tested over at least two nights.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianThe only proper way to test a sunrise alarm clock is by using it to wake up each morning – so that’s what I did.I used each model for at least two nights, testing out multiple light and alarm sound settings, and assessing the quality of wake-up for each device. I considered the brightness of each alarm, how close the glow felt to real sunlight, and the audio quality. Above all, I reflected on how lively and refreshed I felt after waking up with each one.Many sunrise alarm clocks also have a sundown function, so I used this where available too. I also tried using each sunrise alarm clock as a reading light, to help me finish the day – as well as start it – smartphone-free.Some sunrise alarm clocks go even further, with additional features such as app operability, multiple alarm profiles and mood lighting. To ensure a thorough review of each sunrise alarm clock, I played around with every possible customisation option and functionality.The best sunrise alarm clocks in 2026View image in fullscreenThe Lumie Bodyclock Glow 150, the Blueair Mini Restful sunrise clock air purifier and the Lexon Mina Sunrise.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianBest sunrise alarm clock overall:Lumie Bodyclock Glow 150LumieBodyclock Glow 150from£118.96£119 at Argos£118.96 at AmazonWhat we loveSuperior sunrise simulation; pleasant alarm tonesWhat we don’t loveIt’s relatively expensiveView image in fullscreen£119 at Argos£118.96 at AmazonLumie is the brand that pioneered consumer-grade sunrise alarm clocks in the early 1990s, and that pedigree still shines through.Equipped with a comprehensive set of wake-up sounds and medical-grade sunrise simulation, the Bodyclock Glow 150 is the best sunrise alarm clock of the many I’ve tested. It comes at a premium price, but could pay dividends for your sleep cycle.Why we love itThe sunrise effect is among the most convincing I’ve experienced, rivalling the less fully featured (but slightly cheaper) Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100, which is reviewed below. It feels like waking to daylight, or emerging into a clearing after walking through dense woodland.I found this model easy to control and configure via the five buttons surrounding the digital display. All of the personalisations that really matter are available, including sunrise light intensity and duration.Crucially, there’s a great selection of alarm tones to choose between – not always the case with Lumie models – ranging from the wonderfully gentle to the brusquely rousing. I preferred “tropical birds” and “waves” to “beep” or “steam train”, although I enjoyed imagining a train enthusiast waking contentedly to the latter.It’s a shame that …there’s only one colour available: black (with a white lamp). This will suit some bedroom design schemes better than others.Certification:UK MDR 2002 and EU MDR 2017/745 medical classificationModes:sunrise alarm, sunset, bedside lightFootprint:W19 x D12cmFeatures:light-sensitive auto-dimming displayBrightness settings:fiveSunrise duration:20, 30 or 45 minutesLumieBodyclock Glow 150from£118.96£119 at Argos£118.96 at AmazonWhat we loveSuperior sunrise simulation; pleasant alarm tonesWhat we don’t loveIt’s relatively expensiveRead our fullLumie Bodyclock Glow 150 sunrise alarm clock reviewBest budget sunrise alarm:Lumie Sunrise AlarmLumieSunrise Alarmfrom£39.99£49 at John Lewis£39.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value, with good sunrise simulation and soundsWhat we don’t loveLess bright than swankier Lumie modelsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£49 at John Lewis£39.99 at AmazonImagine telling one of your ancestors that you were awoken this morning by your lamp, which was purring at you. I’m not pulling your leg, you might say, it’s all thanks to the Lumie Sunrise’s “kittens purring” alarm tone, which sits sweetly alongside four other natural sounds, including goats bleating and birdsong.Why we love itIn all seriousness, this is an excellent sunrise alarm clock, and it comes at a standout price. Its sunrise light subtly brightens during the minutes leading up to your chosen alarm time, producing a lovely awakening that really did remind me of natural light.I found it easy enough to set the Sunrise Alarm’s time and alarm, although pressing some of the buttons can be fiddly. Do keep the instruction manual handy, as there are lots of options and buttons to get your head around.It’s a shame that …it lacks a little bedside table appeal. But having said that, this sunrise alarm clock has incredible performance for the price.Certification:noneModes:sunrise alarm, sunset, mood, bedside lightFootprint:W17 x D9cmFeatures:mood lighting (six colours)Brightness settings:10Sunrise duration:30 minutesLumieSunrise Alarmfrom£39.99£49 at John Lewis£39.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value, with good sunrise simulation and soundsWhat we don’t loveLess bright than swankier Lumie modelsBest sunrise alarm clock for heavy sleepers:Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100LumieBodyclock Spark 100from£98.46£98.46 at Healf£98.96 at AmazonWhat we loveOutstanding sunrise simulationWhat we don’t loveLack of gentler alarm soundsView image in fullscreen£98.46 at Healf£98.96 at AmazonI woke up feeling great when I used the medical-grade Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100, which bathes the room in gradually intensifying, sun-like light for a set period before the alarm goes off.Why we love itThe device is supposed to realistically imitate the lightening shades of a sunrise – and it does so more convincingly than any other brand’s sunrise alarm clock. Depending on your chosen light intensity setting, it can get very bright.The Spark 100 also has a sunset feature that graduates through the same red, orange and white light colours used with the sunrise function, but in reverse order. After the sunset cycle, the light can either switch off entirely or remain in a gentle night-light mode, whichever you choose.Besides performing brilliantly as a wake-up light and sunset simulator, the Spark 100 is simply a nicely designed, well-made thing. I appreciated its soft-edged yet robust construction and handy features such as the cable organisation in the base. It’s a pleasure to have on the bedside table.It’s a shame that …the alarm tone sounds piercing at the higher three of its five volume levels. I found myself settling for a 2/5 – though very heavy sleepers may prefer (or even relish) the louder options.Certification:UK MDR 2002 and EU MDR 2017/745 medical classificationModes:sunrise alarm, sunrise, sunset, bedside lightFootprint:W19 x D12cmFeatures:tap to snooze, auto-dimming display, adjustable sunrise/sunset duration, adjustable digital display brightnessBrightness settings:fiveSunrise duration:30 minutesLumieBodyclock Spark 100from£98.46£98.46 at Healf£98.96 at AmazonWhat we loveOutstanding sunrise simulationWhat we don’t loveLack of gentler alarm soundsBest sunrise alarm for late-night reading:Philips SmartSleepPhilipsSmartSleepfrom£181.99£183.99 at Philips£181.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSolid design and good sunrise simulationWhat we don’t loveOne of the most expensive optionsView image in fullscreen£183.99 at Philips£181.99 at AmazonThis lamp soon felt like part of the furniture on my bedside table. In typical Philips fashion, it’s a good-quality, dependable product, with a solid middle-of-the-road design that won’t look out of place in many bedrooms.Why we love itSetup is slick – I was able to set my alarm time, sound and brightness by following the simple prompts on the device’s display, without having to consult the manual. Subsequently tweaking your alarm(s) takes practice, but you’ll master all the controls you need after a few days.The SmartSleep’s wake-up capabilities are impressive, combining brilliant light with a diverse choice of alarm sounds. It also has FM radio and 3.5mm auxiliary audio input options for the user who has tired of Alpine and gong bath soundscapes. There’s a 5V USB charging outlet at the rear of the lamp, too, which could free up a valuable bedside power socket.I loved using this model as a reading light, as well as a sunrise alarm. Even when a bright setting is selected, the light seems relatively mellow and restful, which helped me get to sleep after reading pulpy detective novels late at night. The light can be deactivated with a press.It’s a shame that …it costs such a lot. The SmartSleep has a hefty price to match its impressive performance.Certification:noneModes:sunrise alarm, sleep mode with sunset simulation, bedside lightFootprint:W22 x D12cmFeatures:FM radio, Aux audio input, “RelaxBreathe” breathing exercises, adjustable sunrise duration, snooze, up to two wake-up profiles (with separate alarms)Brightness settings:25Sunrise duration:20, 25, 30, 35 or 40 minutesPhilipsSmartSleepfrom£181.99£183.99 at Philips£181.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSolid design and good sunrise simulationWhat we don’t loveOne of the most expensive optionsBest mini sunrise alarm clock:Lexon Mina SunriseLexonMina Sunrisefrom£77.94£79.90 at John Lewis£77.94 at AmazonWhat we loveCute, chic designWhat we don’t loveAwkward controlsView image in fullscreen£79.90 at John Lewis£77.94 at AmazonMy only general gripe with sunrise alarm clocks is that many of them are an aesthetic downgrade on a conventional bedside lamp – but this charming mini model from French brand Lexon is a stylish exception.Why we love itThe obvious draw here is the design, which comprises a cute, mushroom-shaped light and colourful metal base with a wraparound digital display. It fits very neatly on to a small or well-utilised bedside table.The sunrise light function roused me gently before the alarm tone (also gently rousing) sounded, and I got up feeling alert. Even though this isn’t a very bright light, it evidently did the trick, and it was suitable for bedtime reading, too.You can choose from five alarm tones, all of which sound pleasantly full and rich. These include birdsong and water sounds, as well as some loud, piercing alarms that will suit particularly heavy sleepers. Beautifully finished and stoutly made, the Mina Sunrise is a cut above the rest in terms of build quality.It’s a shame that …the control buttons are on the base, and can’t be seen in the dark without a secondary light source such as a smartphone torch. You’d struggle to adjust the settings in the middle of the night.Certification:noneModes:sunrise alarm, sunset, bedside lightFootprint:W11 x D11cmFeatures:mood lighting (nine colours), snooze, cordless operationBrightness settings:fiveSunrise duration:30 minutesLexonMina Sunrisefrom£77.94£79.90 at John Lewis£77.94 at AmazonWhat we loveCute, chic designWhat we don’t loveAwkward controlsBest sunrise alarm clock for couples:Beurer Wake-up Light WL 50BeurerWake-up Light WL50from£54.99£57.56 at John Lewis£54.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s packed with featuresWhat we don’t loveNot all the features are usefulView image in fullscreen£57.56 at John Lewis£54.99 at AmazonThanks to its capability to save two alarms for different times (each with its own sound and light settings), the Beurer WL 50 is a great choice for couples who get up at different times. That’s a rare feature in any sunrise alarm clock – let alone in such a reasonably priced model.Why we love itThe sunrise mode itself is gentle yet effective, and it’s easy to activate the device as a reading light with a simple, groggy tap. I really liked the alarm sounds you get with the WL 50 too – which is just as well, as there are only two.Perhaps that narrow choice of alarm tones sounds a little stingy, but it seems less so when you explore the WL 50’s alternative audio options. It doubles up as an FM radio, with space to save up to 30 station presets, which you can listen to throughout the day or use as a livelier alternative to an alarm tone. Bluetooth connectivity and an AUX input expand your listening options further.Curiously, this sunrise alarm clock can be unplugged (when fully charged) and used on the go for up to three hours. It’s hard to imagine a situation wherein this would be useful, but I appreciate the gesture.It’s a shame that …the sound quality isn’t great (but it’s good enough for the half-awake).Certification:noneModes:sunrise alarm, sunset simulation, bedside light, radio/speakerFootprint:W11 x D11cmFeatures:FM radio, AUX audio input, Bluetooth audio, portable use (up to three hours), LED mood lightBrightness settings:adjustableSunrise duration:10, 20 or 30 minutesBeurerWake-up Light WL50from£54.99£57.56 at John Lewis£54.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s packed with featuresWhat we don’t loveNot all the features are usefulThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘A beautifully designed alarm clock’: the Dreamegg Sunrise 1.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianBlueair Mini Restful sunrise clock air purifierBlueairMini Restful sunrise clock air purifierfrom£169£169 at Blueair£169 at AmazonWhat we loveInnovative sunrise and air purification comboWhat we don’t loveToo bulky for the bedside tableView image in fullscreen£169 at Blueair£169 at AmazonBest for:an air-purifying sunrise alarm clockMost of us spend around a third of our time in bed, so a sunrise alarm clock that also purifies your bedroom air seems like a good idea. This model, the Blueair Mini Restful, is heralded as the world’s first.By sunrise alarm clock standards, it isn’t really mini. I found myself resting it on the floor, where I could see the digital display on the top, rather than putting it on my bedside table.The sunrise function proved effective, waking me reliably with warm, increasingly bright light before the alarm sounded. As for the purification, the Mini Restful certainly made my air feel fresher after a windowsill-sanding session had kicked up untold volumes of dust. The fan works exceptionally quietly, although I still preferred to run it only during the daytime (this can be automated via the Blueair app’s schedule feature).It didn’t make the final cut because …the sunrise alarm feature is only accessible via the Blueair app, and I feel that users should have the option to activate it manually. With that said, the app is a pleasure to use.Certification:none;modes:night light, sunrise alarm;footprint:W17 x D17cm;features:air purification, app control, alarm schedule;brightness settings:scale of 0-100%;sunrise duration:15-30 minutesBlueairMini Restful sunrise clock air purifierfrom£169£169 at Blueair£169 at AmazonWhat we loveInnovative sunrise and air purification comboWhat we don’t loveToo bulky for the bedside tableDreamegg Sunrise 1DreameggSunrise 1from£62.99£62.99 at Dreamegg£69.99 at AmazonWhat we loveNicely pairs a textured front with mellow lightingWhat we don’t loveRelatively dim lightView image in fullscreen£62.99 at Dreamegg£69.99 at AmazonBest for:soothing sleep soundsThis compact, great-looking device offers something different, with a selection of 29 ambient sounds that can be used as white noise to help you fall asleep. There are also five options for rousing you in the morning, including birdsong, a campfire crackling and, my favourite, waves breaking on a shore. For me, perhaps the only issue with this approach was that the sounds did a better job of putting me to sleep than they did of waking me up.The Sunrise 1 is a beautifully designed alarm clock, with a softly textured front and foolproof dimmer controls on either side to adjust the light level and digital display brightness. Reluctant risers will be pleased to note there’s a prominent snooze button at the top of the device – though, personally, I’ve rarely felt the need to use this feature while testing sunrise alarm clocks.It didn’t make the final cut because …its light is a little too dim for my taste.Certification:none;modes:sunrise alarm, white noise/sleep sounds, bedside light;footprint:W15 x D7.3cm;features:sleep sound timer, nine light colours, five wake-up sounds;brightness settings:adjustable;sunrise duration:Up to 60 minutesDreameggSunrise 1from£62.99£62.99 at Dreamegg£69.99 at AmazonWhat we loveNicely pairs a textured front with mellow lightingWhat we don’t loveRelatively dim lightWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenSunrise alarm clocks that are classified as medical devices, such as the Lumie Bodyclock Glow 150, may be better suited for users seeking a therapeutic effect.Are sunrise alarm clocks a fad?A cursory glance at Google Trends search data – or perhaps at your chosen social media platform – will tell you that interest in sunrise alarm clocks has grown sharply in recent years. You may wonder: is this overdue recognition for a useful technology, or is it a murkier wellness trend to file alongsidemouth tapingand stuffing onion slices into socks?While there hasn’t been a great deal of academic research into sunrise alarm clocks, some studies suggest they may benefit our sleep health. For instance, researchers from Ohio University found thattrial participants had significantly better sleep scoresand lower perceived stress and burnout after spending two weeks waking with a sunrise alarm clock while also avoiding smartphone use in bed.The ultimate test of whether sunrise alarm clocks are a fad will be time. I’m still using mine, as I approach a third winter.Do sunrise alarm clocks help with Sad?Sad bright-light therapy involves the use of intense light (in the region of 10,000 lux) to mimic the effects of bright sunlight. Sunrise alarm clocks tend to be far less bright than the average Sad lamp. With that said, light exposure around dawn and in the early morning can influence our circadian rhythms, so even a relatively dim sunrise alarm may still have benefits.If you’ve been diagnosed with seasonal affective disorder and are looking for a light-therapy device, it’s best to ask your GP which product to use and how to get the most benefit. Sunrise alarm clocks that are classified as medical devices (indicated in the specs each product above) are more likely to suit users seeking a therapeutic effect than models with no medical certifications.Why does it benefit us to wake with the sun?Getting up in the dark can feel awful, which makes a lot of sense because light helps our bodies wake up properly.Humans are diurnal, which means we’ve evolved to be more wakeful, energetic and capable of chasing mammoths over vast distances during daytime. When the brain recognises increasing light at dawn, it sends signals around other regions of the brain and to other organs to calibrate bodily processes including temperature regulation, hormone secretion and metabolism. And when darkness falls, the brain prepares us for sleep – a helpful effect that many of us compromise by looking at bright smartphone or laptop screens.These processes follow roughly 24-hour cycles known as our circadian rhythms. The term is derived from the Latin wordscirca(approximately) anddiem(day), meaning around a day.So, the sun is the original and best alarm clock – activating our minds and bodies with light, rather than startling us awake with sound. Think of your sunrise alarm as a plucky stand-in to rely upon during the star’s shorter winter shifts.Do sunrise alarm clocks work for heavy sleepers?Some users find the light from their sunrise alarm clock more rousing than others do. If you’re a heavy sleeper, there’s a heightened chance that the artificial sunrise will not wake you (although it might still help you feel more alert on waking).How you configure your sunrise alarm clock makes a difference. We all sleep more deeply during certain periods of our sleep cycle – and this includes particularly heavy sleepers. So, by setting your sunrise alarm clock to do a relatively long dawn simulation cycle (30 minutes is an option on several models), you give the gradually increasing light more time to rouse you. You’ll often have a choice between multiple light intensity settings, too, so select the brightest one available.If you’re worried about waking up on time, all of the sunrise alarm clocks featured in this guide can conclude their sunrise cycle with an audio alarm tone. So, they could serve perfectly well as a wake-up alarm, even if they don’t successfully start rousing you before the beep. To be on the safe side, I’d recommend choosing a louder model, such as the Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100.For more:The best mattresses to help you sleep betterHow to create the perfect bed: seven things our sleep expert swears byThe best sleep aids: 13 of the most-hyped remediesPete Wise is ajournalistwith more than a decade’s experience covering everything from global development and social causes to technology and music. He has written extensively on sleep-related topics, including Sad lamps,intermittent fasting, and the effects of caffeine consumption on sleep. title: End Of Abyss review – a creepy dollhouse take on Resident Evil and The Thing | Games | The Guardian
description: This fetchingly presented horror game brings style and scares, but overextends itself with repetition
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This fetchingly presented horror game brings style and scares, but overextends itself with repetition
Content: Your little bobble-headed hero … End of Abyss video game screenshot.Photograph: Section 9/Epic Games PublishingView image in fullscreenYour little bobble-headed hero … End of Abyss video game screenshot.Photograph: Section 9/Epic Games PublishingGamesReviewEnd Of Abyss review – a creepy dollhouse take on Resident Evil and The ThingPlayStation 5 (version played), Xbox, PC; Epic Games PublishingThis fetchingly presented horror game brings style and scares, but overextends itself with repetitionAlex SpencerFri 9 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsmall band of soldiers enters an abandoned facility, where puckered flesh sprouts from cold steel. It’s a promising but familiar start to a sci-fi horror story, with heavy overtones of Alien and The Thing. Neither of those, though, were so … dinky.End of Abyss’s facility is presented as a kind of a model-village recreation of The Thing’s Outpost 31 that you peer into from above. Your little bobble-headed hero takes up a tiny fraction of the screen, with most of the remainder drenched in foggy darkness, or even blanked out entirely. This is a world of Usborne-style cutaways, where anything outside the walls is total blackness.This combination of cute and eerie immediately marks End of Abyss as part of the Scandi-chiaroscuro style pioneered by Limbo and Inside (from Playdead, in Copenhagen) and Little Nightmares (from Malmö-based Tarsier Studios, where the founders of End of Abyss developer Section 9 cut their teeth). Those games, though, were all puzzle-platformers. End of Abyss is a survival-horror game in the mould of PS1-era Resident Evil, which took a similarly zoomed-out approach, using fixed, CCTV-reminiscent camera angles. It’s a great way of controlling each scene’s composition for maximum aesthetic value – and, of course, to set up scares.View image in fullscreenDrenched in darkness … End of Abyss.Photograph: Section 9/Epic Games PublishingEnd of Abyss delights in lovingly decorated dioramas, with bodies and viscera laid outjust so, illuminated by the flickering light of a CRT screen and some orange-glowing item (a valuable key or weapon upgrade) dangling just out of reach. As you’re studying these details, trying to figure out how you might reach that desirable object, at the edge of your vision a monster will peel itself from the darkness and attack before you can consciously register its presence.What follows is a dance of backpedalling and firing your pistol, praying that it’s loaded with enough ammo to finish off the advancing assailant before it can catch up to you. Or, worse, your retreat carries you into another nest of monsters. These are foundational thrills of the genre, and End of Abyss keeps them intact as it shrinks them down to dollhouse size. They might be scarier still, in fact, because manually aiming a gun from a top-down perspective can be fiddly, and End of Abyss’s control scheme is so confounding (who puts reload on the right thumbstick?) that you’re fighting muscle memory as much as the monsters.On top of this survival-horror foundation, though, End of Abyss layers elements of Dark Souls, Metroid and Hollow Knight – and here it overextends. This facility is big and complex enough for you to get lost in, filled with doors that only open from the other side and seemingly separate zones that join up in unexpected ways. These can be some of video games’ finest pleasures, when done right, but they make for an uncomfortable fit in a game that relies on a character so slow-moving that they can be threatened by a shambling zombie.View image in fullscreenStriking gloomy style … End of Abyss.Photograph: Section 9/Epic Games PublishingThat striking gloomy style, meanwhile, is something of an achilles heel when you’re trying to tell one room from another. It’s not helped by a pause-screen map that struggles to convey the interlocking territory, and, at the time of playing, is prone to getting confused over questions as fundamental as which doors are locked.This leads to a lot of unnecessary backtracking and, with every repeat visit, those carefully staged scenes lose some of their sheen. A composition that had you gawping the first time can’t hope to maintain that effect on the dozenth visit, while the shadow-peeling scares turn out to run on the clockwork logic of a fairground ghost train. Reaching the final boss after 12 hours, with much of the map still greyed out and other stretches tromped over endlessly, I’m left feeling exhausted, with little inclination to explore the other half of the game that (according to the completion percentage) remains unseen. Contrary to its fetchingly diminutive presentation, End of Abyss might be just too big for its own good.End of Abyss is out now; £22.69Explore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Stop talking about the US ‘Jewish vote’. It’s not that simple | Judith Levine | The Guardian
description: Political parties vie for Jewish support based on false assumptions that boil down to one issue: Israel
Author: Judith Levine
Headline: Political parties vie for Jewish support based on false assumptions that boil down to one issue: Israel
Content: ‘Everybody wants the Jewish vote. As if there were one.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Everybody wants the Jewish vote. As if there were one.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionUS politicsStop talking about the US ‘Jewish vote’. It’s not that simpleJudith LevinePolitical parties vie for Jewish support based on false assumptions about a single issue: IsraelFri 9 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTShareEverybody wants the Jewish vote. As if there were one.Jews areeducated, generally liberal. Although they comprise only about 2% of the electorate, they vote in high numbers, overwhelmingly for Democrats. In2024,79% chose Kamala Harris. They are also assumed to be steadfast friends of Israel, no matter what it does. Republicans, waging a fake war on antisemitism while courting white supremacists, consider Jews increasingly up for grabs.Democrats need to win. Here’s the message our research says worksRead moreNationally, Jewish Americans are concentrated in a few bright blue spots. A2020map from the Jewish Electorate Institute showed a third of Jews living in 20 congressional districts – out of 435 – most of them in New York, New Jersey, California and (purple) Florida. Of these, only one sent a Republican to Washington.Today, it’s two. Florida’s 21st district switched parties only after falling victim toredistrictingin 2022. The other outlier has elected the pro-Israel, anti-immigration RepublicanChris Smithevery term since 1981. Why? The mapmakers’ explanation: New Jersey fourth district includes Lakewood, where half the residents are ultra-Orthodox – scrupulously, ceaselessly observant. Unsurprisingly, among white voters, regular religious service attendance is abig predictorof conservatism.In other words, in Lakewood,Orthodoxmay be more salient thatJewish.In fact, if pro-Israel candidates are looking for votes, evenJewishis no longer salient. WhiteEvangelical Christiansare more firmly supportive of Israel than American Jews. The US is home to the largest population of Christian Zionists in the world, numbering more than 30 million, a third of whom belong toChristians United for Israel, the largest Zionist organization is the US.The Bible belt churches these people attendpreachthat the founding of Israel in 1948 was part of God’s plan to bring about the End Times, and the ongoing hostilities in the Middle East are the mayhem and destruction preceding the second coming of Christ (when nonbelievers – including Jews – willdrown in the Lake of Fire).While the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac)spendsfar more on political campaigns, Christians United for Israel is busy mobilizing its millions tograssroots action.Meanwhile, aminority of American Jewsnow call themselves Zionists. A late-2025Washington Postpoll found that six in 10 believed Israel was committing war crimes in Gaza; four in 10 said the assault was genocide. And aside from the fiercest partisans, for many young Jews, Israeljust isn’t that important.The Gaza war figured large in the 2024 presidential elections, as the civilian death toll mounted and the Biden-Harris administration stood unwaveringly beside Israel. Now, even as the killing spreads to the West Bank and southern Lebanon, US voters are moving on.Affordabilityis the winning buzzword this cycle,at least for Democrats. Almost no one is thinking aboutforeign policy.What about abortion? Climate change? Voting rights? The press, the pundits, and the mainstream party strategists keep behaving as if every Jew cares about Israel – and all Jews care about is Israel – and a candidate must be pro-Zionist or lose the elusive Jewish vote.We saw this during the campaign of the New York mayor,Zohran Mamdani. Forthright support for Palestinian self-determination had long been central to his politics, and to his appeal to progressives. But Mamdani was running for mayor, not president. His brilliant stroke was affordability – a theme that is easily understandable, widely relatable, and capable of making socialist solutions sound reasonable.Nevertheless, from the moment he appeared, the press, from the New York Timesop-ed pagetocollege newspapersto theinternational Jewish press, made the election a referendum on Israel – and, more perniciously, on Islam.Mamdani’s Democratic primary opponent, former governorAndrew Cuomo, attacked him with flagrant Islamophobia, conflating his critique of Israel with antisemitism and signalling that his faith was a danger to Jews.They tried to smear him as an antisemite – but Mayor Zohran Mamdani walks in a rich Jewish tradition | Molly CrabappleRead moreThe fearmongering did not defeat Mamdani.In the end,only a thirdof Jews voted for him; in Hasidic neighborhoods, 90% went for Cuomo. But progressive Jewish organizations including Jewish Voice for Peace and Jews for Racial and Economic Justice endorsed him. He won inalmost everyracial and class demographic and pulled inthree-quarters of voters under 30.What’s the lesson here? The youth vote – plus the Black vote, the Hispanic vote, the working-class vote, etc – plus good ideas and a great campaign put Mamdani over the top. Furthermore, an analysis byGood Authorityconcludes that no position on Israel, pro or con, is driving Jews out of the Democratic party.Now Abdul El-Sayed, the Muslim Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, is shlepping the burden of this vaguely defined, perpetually disgruntled “Jewish vote”. After narrowly winning the primary, heapologizedto members of the Jewish community for a statement he made after a Lebanese-born naturalized citizen rammed his truck into a large synagogue, injuring a guard.The apology came after El-Sayed clumsily linked the man’santisemitismto Israeli violence in Lebanon, saying: “Hurt people hurt people.” It was an inoffensive adage among, say, prison abolitionists. But to some Jews, it sounded as if El-Sayed felt more sympathy for the perpetrator than for his targeted victims.The Republicans have taken advantage of these fissures, attacking El-Sayed with a combination of Islamophobia and the usual hypocritical condemnations of antisemitism. At their midterm “convention”, El-Sayed’s opponent Mike Rogersclaimed,falsely, that the Democrat had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. And while El-Sayed definitively distanced himself from the leftwing Israel criticHasan Piker– a Twitch streamer the press began to cover obsessively – speaker after speaker hammered on the connection between the two men.These tactics appear to be falling flat. A recentNew York Times/Siena pollfound that most Michiganders have never heard of Piker. The poll found that El-Sayed leads his opponent by 39 points among voters 44 and younger, who are far more critical of Israel’s policies than their elders. That generational split is alsopronouncedamong Jews.El-Sayed has theendorsementsof JVP and IfNotNow, an organization that attracts many young Jews who are painfully rejecting their parents’ Zionism, as well as Vermont’s Jewish senator, Bernie Sanders. While Rogers has been collecting pledges of votes from Jewish Michiganders, more than 600 “Michigan Jews for Democracy”, including elected officials and rabbis, havesigned a letter in support of El-Sayed.Recently, Mamdanirepeatedhis condemnation of Benjamin Netanyahu as a war criminal who should be arrested in advance of the Israeli prime minister’s visit to New York to address the UN. That revived Zionist fury toward the mayor, but Jews both supportive and critical of Israel – and Mamdani – held noisyrallies.The reason for Mamdani to keep trying to speak to both sides is not to win the mythical Jewish vote. It is to make common cause with people who don’t want Israel swept into the sea but also cannot abide a Jewish ethnostate whose survival depends on occupation and apartheid.That said, if El-Sayed were the Islamist Jew-hater his enemies claim he is, it should be obvious to a lot more Jews. If it were obvious to a lot more Jews, Aipac would not havehad to pour $32m– unsuccessfully – into Stevens’ campaign orcontemplate pouringmore into supporting Rogers in the general election.And of course, the “Arab American” or “Muslim vote” isno more unanimousthan the hypothetical Jewish vote.To be frank, the whole discourse stinks. It boils down to “support the Muslim” or “support the Jew”, as if this were some ancient racial animosity – natural enemies “fighting”, as Trumpsaidof the Palestinians and Israeli Jews, “for a thousand years”.Not only is this contention untrue. Such thinking obviates politics, the effort to understand a problem and convince others that your solution is best. It is not good for the Jews – or for anyone. And it is deadly for a secular, pluralistic democracy.Judith Levine is a frequent contributor to the Guardian. title: AI and the climate crisis pose existential risks. The law offers a way to reduce them | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: Liability lawsuits have held tobacco, oil and pharma companies to account in the past. AI investors won’t ignore this threat
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: Liability lawsuits have held tobacco, oil and pharma companies to account in the past. AI investors won’t ignore this threat
Content: ‘Liability law is hardly an easy or perfect fix, but it’s an important start.’Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Liability law is hardly an easy or perfect fix, but it’s an important start.’Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)AI and the climate crisis pose existential risks. The law offers a way to reduce themRobert ReichLiability lawsuits have held tobacco, oil and pharma companies to account in the past. AI investors won’t ignore this threatFri 9 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTShareThe most basic function of government is to protect people from harm. Two growing phenomena – the climate crisis and AI – pose escalating risks ofextraordinaryharm.The climate crisis is already causing floods, wildfires, drought and record heat. AI agents are already escaping super-secure environments to hack into systems they’re supposed to avoid.Yet Donald Trump and his Republican enablers, backed by big money from big oil and big AI, refuse to do a thing about either risk. In many ways, they’re worsening both.But there’s another way to reduce these risks: through liability law.I have no more faith in the supreme court than you do, but I was struck by the responses of at least half the justices who will be considering an important case that opened the supreme court’s new term, Suncor v Boulder.The case was brought by several Colorado localities against Suncor and ExxonMobil – one of about three dozen filed around the country in which cities and states are demanding that big oil reimburse them for the escalating costs of climate disasters brought on by the burning of fossil fuels.On Monday, at least four justices (Samuel Alito has recused himself) expressed skepticism about big oil’s argument that the Clean Air Act explicitly prevents such lawsuits against polluters. “It’s like, wow, like, where is the text for that? Where’s the support for that? Where’s the precedent for that? Where’s the anything for that?” asked Justice Elena Kagan.Chief Justice John Roberts drew parallels between Boulder’s claim and prior lawsuits against the tobacco and opioid industries in which states and localities won significant damages. “I’m not quite sure what makes this situation different from all those other ones where we’ve allowed them to proceed in state court,” said Roberts.In 1998, the leading US tobacco companies agreed to pay $206bn to cover public health costs and smoking-related expenses. When translated into current dollars, this is more than $423bn.And recall the $20bn paid by BP in 2010 to cover environmental and economic damage to the Gulf coast after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. Or the $7.4bn paid by the Sackler family and Purdue Pharma to resolve liability for the opioid crisis.Such liability lawsuits – the last resort when the public is harmed by corporate malfeasance or nonfeasance – are also relevant to the risks posed by AI.If AI agents escape super-secure environments to release dangerous toxins, or destroy critical water, electricity, transportation, or health infrastructure, AI companies and the tech giants behind them could be on the hook fortens if not hundreds of billions of dollarsin payments to those who are harmed.No way major investors in AI – or the insurance companies backstopping AI – are going to ignore this potential liability. The current dollar value of the tobacco settlement – as I said, $423bn – is comparable to what the tech giants spent on AI chips, servers, and datacenters last year.This gigantic financial risk will weigh on the values of AI companies and the tech companies unless or until they become far more serious about protecting the public against such harms.I expect political demands from the AI industry to limit such liability through federal laws that set caps on it and that establish industry-funded “trust funds” to pay for big liability judgments. A sane Congress (we may yet have one) wouldn’t agree without specific industry steps to dramatically increase safety.In all likelihood, the AI industry will also seek government regulations it could use as partial defenses against such massive liability, just as pharmaceutical companies use certification by the Food and Drug Administration that their drugs are safe and effective to defend against lawsuits claiming their drugs cause harm.The big AI investors and insurers will force this issue. More than200 cases already in the courtsinvolve cyber-liability and AI-related product liability. Follow the money. Insurers are already demanding more effective means of controlling AI risks, and big investors are demanding better means of limiting them.Both the climate crisis and AI pose existential risks to human life on this planet. Liability law is hardly an easy or perfect fix, but it’s an important start.The fact that liability for the climate crisis is already in the supreme court and that four justices seem sympathetic suggests how significant a role liability can play as an incentive for both fossil fuel and AI giants – and their insurers and major investors – to clean up their acts.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionClimate crisisLaw (US)commentShareReuse this content

title: Christa Pike’s botched execution is a reminder of the horror of the death penalty | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: Lethal injection was a way for us to deny the reality of capital punishment. Pike’s experience shows us what it is
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: Lethal injection was a way for us to deny the reality of capital punishment. Pike’s experience shows us what it is
Content: ‘We should be angry, too. In our name, a woman was tortured.’Photograph: Dipti Vaidya/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters ConnectView image in fullscreen‘We should be angry, too. In our name, a woman was tortured.’Photograph: Dipti Vaidya/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters ConnectOpinionChrista PikeChrista Pike’s botched execution is a reminder of the horror of the death penaltyMoira DoneganLethal injection was a way for us to deny the reality of capital punishment. Pike’s experience shows us what it isFri 9 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTShareChrista Pike had asked to be hanged. In the weeks before her botched execution by lethal injection on 30 September, in which she survived two lethal doses of barbiturate pentobarbital and had to be hospitalized, Pike and her legal team had challenged Tennessee’s execution protocol.The state’s lethal injection regimen had failed before. In May,Tony Carrutherswas also sent to Tennessee’s death chamber, only to leave alive after prison officials struggled to find a vein.In Pike’s case, her lawyers argued, the lethal injection protocol was likely to fail again.She also had vein issues, they said; if she was subjected to an ordeal like Carruthers’, in which prison officials punctured their prone prisoner more than a dozen times over the course of an hour in an attempt to administer the drug, Pike’s history of trauma, which is lengthy and acute, would serve to make the experience unconstitutionally torturous.Pentobarbital, the drug that was set to be used to kill Pike, also risked a needlessly painful death.“The drug supposedly burns very bad,” Pike said in a taped interview just weeks before her scheduled execution. “And so that sounds scary to me because they used the word Draino in speaking about this drug, and the thought of suffocating and drowning on my own bodily fluid and blood isn’t very appealing to me.”It was to avoid this ordeal that Pike requested to be hanged by the neck until dead instead. Her request was denied. From the execution chamber during Tennessee’s failed attempt to kill her, witnesses said that they could hear Pike complaining about a burning pain in her arm, which felt, she said, like it was about to burst.After nearly a week of being unconscious and intubated at a Nashville hospital after her failed execution attempt, Pike is nowawakeand talking. Her arms are severely injured from her execution attempt and not fully usable, but she’s still shackled to her hospital bed anyway. She still remains “foggy” from the effects of the state-administered overdose, and it’s unclear whether she will recover full cognitive function as doctors assess the state of her brain damage.But she remembers the moments when Tennessee tried and failed to kill her. She is reportedly very angry.We should be angry, too. In our name, a woman was tortured.In many death penalty cases, there are real questions about the factuality of a condemned person’s guilt or the fairness of their trial and appeals process.That is less true in Pike’s case: there is no factual doubt that in 1995, when she was 18, Pike, now 50, lured her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer into a wooded area, and with an accomplice, Pike’s 17-year-old boyfriend, tortured her for about half an hour before finally killing her by smashing her skull in with a piece of concrete. Slemmer’s mother has been a particularly vocal advocate for Pike’s execution, and is reportedly furious that her daughter’s killer has survived.The wishes of victims and their families should be crucial to what our understanding of justice means. No one knows better the meaning and significance of violence than the people who it is inflicted on.But it is also true that Pike’s criminal trial did not take into account factors in her life that might have explanatory, if not mitigating, power – such as the reality that she committed murder at the end of a childhood that had been marked by horrific, repeated, and severe sexual and physical violence.And it is true, too, that when we assess what justice looks like, we must ask not only what would be most meaningful and satisfying for victims but also what best reflects our values and meets our obligations as a state. By that metric, the death penalty has always failed. It does not mete out justice so much as lower the collective community to the level of its worst perpetrators.Lethal injection used to be a way for us to deny this. The protocol was developed in the US and first adopted for executions in the late 1970s. It was meant to replace older methods of state killing, such as gas chambers, electric chairs and firing squads, offering what was positioned as a more dignified and civilized, and supposedly less painful, way of murdering a human being.What lethal injection did instead was medicalize the death penalty’s brutality, allowing its proponents a kind of polite denial of what the punishment actually is.Pike shows us what it really is. It is violent, brutal and cruel. It is painful, no matter how much medical science is used to deny or obscure this; it is superfluous and contrary to the needs of justice, and it degrades those who engage in it.For a long time, I thought of the death penalty as dangerously final, opening up the possibility of innocent people irretrievably lost, of mistakes that can’t be taken back. And it is true that this happens: America has executed innocent people.But Pike’s experience shows us that this is not the end of execution’s horror. There is something worse.Tennessee has issued a temporary moratorium on executions, and the governor has called for a review of what went wrong in Pike’s execution. But he should know what went wrong: the problems with the lethal injection protocol, as well as with the death penalty more broadly, were not mysteries even before the state of Tennessee failed to kill Pike.It is still possible that Pike will have to fight not to be sent back to the execution chamber again. And this is another harm of the death penalty: the repetitiveness of its injustice, the way it keeps us from learning from our mistakes.Rarely do we get a second chance to do right by someone like Pike. The state of Tennessee should not get a second chance to try to kill her.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsChrista PikeOpinionCapital punishment (US news)Capital punishment (World news)TennesseecommentShareReuse this content

title: Execution TV? Pete Hegseth has taken the once ‘greatest democracy’ to a horrific new low | Paul Daley | The Guardian
description: A proposal to livestream the killing of Nidal Hasan by firing squad opens a window ever wider to the Trump administration’s complete moral vacuity
Author: Paul Daley
Headline: A proposal to livestream the killing of Nidal Hasan by firing squad opens a window ever wider to the Trump administration’s complete moral vacuity
Content: ‘The world has become inured to Donald Trump’s monstrous narcissism and maladministration,’ writes Paul DaleyPhotograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The world has become inured to Donald Trump’s monstrous narcissism and maladministration,’ writes Paul DaleyPhotograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionTrump administrationExecution TV? Pete Hegseth has taken the once ‘greatest democracy’ to a horrific new lowPaul DaleyA proposal to livestream the killing of Nidal Hasan by firing squad opens a window ever wider to the Trump administration’s complete moral vacuityThu 8 Oct 2026 21.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 01.43 EDTShareMore fool me! Here I was thinking nothing that America’sTrump administrationcould do or say, no matter how politically and morally bankrupt, no matter how venal or violent, was capable of shocking me any longer.Then I woke to today’s news that one of the Trump cabinet’s bigger boofheads – the uber Christian nationalist, crusader-fantasist and “secretary of war”Pete Hegsethhad announced that America wouldhave a public firing squad executionof murderer Nidal Hasan.Reckless global militarisation including athreat at the UN to annihilate Iran, a litany ofsexual misconduct allegationsagainst the commander in chief, claims of blatantpresidential corruption… they have all ceased to surprise and shock us, so inured has the world become to Donald Trump’s monstrous narcissism and maladministration.But now we have execution TV. Tune in to the livestream on Thursday 3 December to watch a military firing squad shoot the life out of Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at a US army base in 2009.Pentagon says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamedRead moreState-sanctioned killing as entertainment! Yes, the world’s supposedly greatest (or formerly greatest) democracy has arrived at an horrific new moral nadir.The fact that America remains Australia and the west’s most relied-upon and trusted ally despite the global wrecking ball the second Trump administration has proved to be, was already cause for deep concern.But being so closely allied to a country that now wants to turn the execution of a human being – no matter what their crimes – into a live entertainment event, promises to redefine depravity.Given that American statescontinue to execute so manyconvicted criminals, where might the United States ultimately draw the line? No doubt the ilk of Hegseth in American society – and elsewhere – will count down the days until they can tune in to the live coverage of Hasan’s execution in droves. Might the audience cry out for more – for livestream cameras in the death chambers across theland of the free?How would this populist administration respond? If you think it’s a fanciful question, consider how far American governance and presidential values have slid in the moral murk in the past two years alone.Meanwhile, it’s hard to contemplate a more audacious appeal to American society’s darker angels than this looming entertainment event.But there we are. We have arrived.Pass the popcorn, Don and Pete!It would be heartening today to hear political leaders the world over condemn Hegseth and Trump’s planned introduction of Ghoul TV.But let’s please start in Australia, where federal governments have for a long time opposed capital punishment – let alone turning it into a public spectacle. Will the prime minister and his senior ministers stand up and condemn without qualification this depraved plan for America to livestream an execution? What about the leaders of other political parties here,some of whomhave, after all, supported capital punishment?We’re waiting.Meanwhile, how much further into the moral quagmire must America wallow beforeAustralia rethinksits craven military dependence on Washington – not least via the reckless shackling of our strategic reliance to the US via the $368bn (and counting)Aukus submarine deal?Announcing America’s decision to turn killing into a form of entertainment, Hegseth said: “It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”America’s defense department later confirmed the execution would be livestreamed.This represents a significant lurch in the US from civilisation towards savagery.You can’t choose your family. But you can choose your friends and allies. And you can also tell them firmly when they’ve careened off the ethical rails.Actions speak louder than words.And this planned livestreamed execution says it all about what is happening in America today, opening the window ever wider on the Trump administration’s moral vacuity and its paucity of human decency.Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionPete HegsethUS politicsUS militaryCapital punishmentAustralian foreign policyDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham is lucky – Polanski, Farage and Badenoch all seem determined to help him  | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: Everywhere the PM turns, he finds generous adversaries. They have made his early days in No 10 so much easier, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: Everywhere the PM turns, he finds generous adversaries. They have made his early days in No 10 so much easier, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Andy Burnham after his meeting with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, in Berlin on Thursday.Photograph: Sean Gallup/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham after his meeting with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, in Berlin on Thursday.Photograph: Sean Gallup/ReutersOpinionAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham is lucky – Polanski, Farage and Badenoch all seem determined to help himJonathan FreedlandEverywhere the PM turns, he finds generous adversaries. They have made his early days in No 10 so much easierFri 9 Oct 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 13.38 EDTShareIdon’t know where Andy Burnham found his magic lamp, but I hope he’s taking good care of it. In the early hours of Friday morning, the genie that’s looked so kindly on him these past few months granted him yet another wish, with abyelection winin Holborn and St Pancras. It was just the latest gift for a prime minister for whom things keep going right – and who is especially blessed in his choice of opponents.Let’s start with that win in London, where Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali defeated the Green party leader, Zack Polanski. It’s easy to miss how rare such a victory is. As the veteran psephologist Peter Kellner pointed out, this was a win that “defied history”. If the past half-century were any guide, Labour should have lost, thanks to a “truly dreadful record” defending its own seats when in government and facing a byelection challenge from the left or centre-left, the likes of the Greens or the Lib Dems. The average swing against Labour in such contests had been 24%. “On those figures,” wrote Kellner, “Polanski should have won at a canter.” But he lost.That reinforces the case Burnham made for why he should replace the previous Holborn and St Pancras MP, one Keir Starmer, asLabourleader: namely, that he was uniquely placed to defeat challenges from both left and right. This latest win over the Greens, coupled with his own success in Makerfield in June, is early vindication of that argument.Burnham can claim much credit for the London result: it’s his leftward shift that has persuaded many progressive voters that they don’t need to vote Green to get what they want and that they should give Labour another chance. But Burnham really ought to share the credit with Polanski himself, who has proved a most generous adversary.Yes, Polanski brought an initial surge in energy, enthusiasm and membership to the Greens. But under him the party has steadily dismantled the moral halo it once enjoyed as the UK’s foremost advocate for the planet, reshaping itself into something darker. Thanks to Sunday’s conference vote branding Zionism as racism, which Polanski ducked, the party now demands the destruction of a state founded,and still regardedby most Jews, as an essential refuge, one whose creation was approved by a UN vote. “Destruction” is not metaphorical, by the way. The motion passed says that the change it seeks – a Palestinian state replacing, rather than existing alongside, Israel – must be secured “by all available means”,a phrase clarifiedin an accompanying booklet produced by the motion’s proposers to include “armed struggle”. Meaning, violence.Thus have the Greens allowed themselves to becometoxified by the kind of cranksand bigots whose manias crowd out anyone who dares hold a moderate or nuanced view, including many longtime, dedicated local activists. A moment like this calls for leadership, but all the Greens have is a quack hypnotherapist who once earned a living promising to make women’s breasts larger and who, when faced with a difficult decision, ran away. (Now, after the event, Polanski says he would not havevoted for the Zionism resolution.) Instead of a leader, the Greens arestuck with a charlatan and a coward.No wonder former leader Caroline Lucas could not say yes,when asked by Newsnight, whether Polanski should stay in his post. Burnham himself would have no such hesitation: the PM might even be quietly pleased that Polanski performed just well enough in Thursday’s byelection to fend off an immediate challenge. The longer Polanski leads the Greens, the better for Labour.Meanwhile, Burnham’s other opponents seem similarly determined to do him a favour. Of course, there will be stormier times ahead, but the party conference season now concluded was like a warm, extended summer for the prime minister.Reform UK, for so long Labour’s strongest challenger in the polls, saw its moment in the sun clouded byeve-of-conference revelationsthat two senior aides to Nigel Farage had been caught on film apparently discussing how they might get around UK electoral law to take a £500,000 donation from a US benefactor. In politics, the scandals that bite hardest are those that confirm suspicions the voters already harbour. In this case, three in four Britonstold YouGovback in July that they regarded Farage as sleazy, with 56% describing him as “very sleazy”.The party’s leading lights tried to make assorted policy announcements, but the only debate that really cut through was the one started by Suella Braverman, with her eccentric and exclusivist insistence that certain minorities, even those born in England into families rooted in the country for several generations, are not truly English – a definition that would exclude Rishi Sunak and a good portion of the England football team. Farage’s army of would-be mavericks and rebels looks increasingly like arabble of crooks and spivsand – as if to prove the Greens have no monopoly on the demographic – cranks and bigots.All this has created an opening for the Conservatives to reclaim their place as the dominant party of the right – but here, too, the genie has smiled on Burnham. True, Kemi Badenoch continues to enjoy higher ratings than her party, but that isn’t saying much. True, too, that she has, belatedly, woken up to the fact that victory will not come solely from trying to out-Reform Reform – people will always vote for the real thing – and that she has to appeal to that vast swathe of Middle England seats lost in 2024 to the Lib Dems.Her conference pitch – promising toabolish inheritance taxon even the most expensive homes, and to extendfree childcare to those earning over £100,000– might conceivably appeal to some of those high earners. But it draws a dividing line with Labour that Burnham could only have dreamed of. Now the Tories have made plain that, in an age of stretched resources, their priority is to help some of the richest people in the land. That is a battle Burnham will be itching to fight.As for the Lib Dems, the PM will be only too happy to see them muddling along, an inoffensive receptacle for Tory-sceptic voters in parts of the country that would never go to Labour. Though Burnham wants to eat into their vote too, promising that he will, in the next term, deliver on two of their signature issues: Europe and electoral reform.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe did that in a speech that was the highlight of the conference season, one that showed a politician who understands the importance of making arguments – and is comfortable making them. After Starmer, who was the opposite in both respects, listening to Burnham was like “gulping down oxygen”, one cabinet minister told me.And yet, everyone at Labour’s top table knows that the weather will change soon enough. The government, and everyone else, is paying too much to borrow money. At some point, the welfare budget will have to be cut: Labour MPs may be applauding now, but they will be less cheerful when asked to vote for reduced benefits, especially as they face re-selection contests in their local parties, a process that gets under way as soon as January.There’s a hole in defence spending to fill, the full sweep of public services crying out for cash, a US president apparently bent on driving up global oil prices and therefore inflation, and a civil service machine that ministers privately curse as bloated and ineffective. What’s more, the period we’re in right now – the middle of the parliament – is when governments should be focused entirely on delivery, driving through their agenda. Instead, vital time has been spent on the transition from one PM to another – time Labour will not get back.For now, Burnham is lucky in his opponents, whose choices hurt them and help him. But the skies will eventuallydarken and, when they do, the prime minister will reach once again for that magic lamp – hoping against hope that it still works.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
