title: The fight over using super for housing has deep roots in Australian politics. But would it actually work? | Emily Millane | The Guardian
description: Ultimately, the debate is a battle for power over Australians’ savings pool of $4.8tn dating back to the scheme’s inception
Author: Emily Millane
Headline: Ultimately, the debate is a battle for power over Australians’ savings pool of $4.8tn dating back to the scheme’s inception
Content: Compulsory superannuation was legislated in 1992 by the Keating Labor government and was opposed by the Liberal party.Composite: Getty Images/Fairfax MediaView image in fullscreenCompulsory superannuation was legislated in 1992 by the Keating Labor government and was opposed by the Liberal party.Composite: Getty Images/Fairfax MediaPast/PresentSuperannuationThe fight over using super for housing has deep roots in Australian politics. But would it actually work?Emily MillaneUltimately, the debate is a battle for power over Australians’ savings pool of $4.8tn dating back to the scheme’s inceptionPast/Presentis a column which places current events in historical contextFri 9 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 20.44 EDTShareShould you be able to take money out of your super to pay for housing?One Nationhas recently suggested you should.Liberal senator Andrew Bragghas also revived the idea. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, tells us the Coalition and One Nation are “coming after super” and want to “vandalise” the retirement savings scheme. He also predicts the next federal election will be a referendum on super.In the midst of a national cost of living crisis and housing shortage, it would seem reasonable to ask about the balance between how much money we are saving for retirement and how much money we have to use now. It would also seem uncontroversial to discuss whether altering that balance will assist with cost-of-living pressures or add to them.The idea of using super for housing is hotly contested.Why is this the case? The answer resides in the history of Australia’s private retirement saving system, the battles over its design and, ultimately, for power over a $4.8tn savings pool.The national system of compulsory superannuation was legislated in 1992 by the Keating Labor government. Paul Keating and former ACTU secretary Bill Kelty are regarded as the founders of the system and continue to be active voices in the debate more than 30 years after superannuation was introduced.Greg Jericho on One Nation’s superannuation ‘sugar hit’ - podcastRead moreThe 1992 legislation grew out of industrial campaigns by trade unions for a “right” to superannuation. Before the superannuation reforms, most workers received only the government age pension in retirement. Those who also had superannuation were limited to some white-collar workers and government employees, and mostly to men.As Kelty put it in an interview with me for my book, “before superannuation, when you got the sack, you got nothing”. When super was introduced, Kelty recalled there was a sense that “never again can you leave workers in a position where they’ve got nothing.”For these reasons theLabor partyand the broader labour movement regard themselves as proprietors and custodians of superannuation as a social justice measure.The Liberal party originally opposed universal superannuation for ideological and political reasons. Forcing workers to hand over a portion of their wages was anathema to a party of free enterprise. Hence the reminder today by people like Liberal MP Tim Wilson that superannuation is“your money”, compulsorily acquired by government mandate. There was – and still remains – a deep suspicion within the Coalition about the links between industry superannuation funds, the unions and Labor.In the late 1980s, then shadow treasurer John Howard characterised the industrial precursor to the superannuation legislation as the “Keating/Kelty accord”, creating a “union slush fund which would be controlled by union bosses”. He later labelled national superannuation legislation as “nothing short of parliamentary confiscation of the assets of employers”.In 1906 Australia’s high court backed ethnic cleansing. That historical wrong and error of law must be put right | Peter Prince and (Waskam) Emelda DavisRead moreAfter theSuperannuationGuarantee was legislated, the Liberal party would come to accept that superannuation was here to stay, but it sought to refashion the policy in their philosophical mould.In 2005, Howard and then treasurer Peter Costello introduced choice-of-fund legislation. The choice changes meant that employees would no longer be defaulted into a superannuation fund because of their industrial award or agreement but instead have the option of choosing where their savings went. This was an effort to divert savings away from industry superannuation funds with union ties and an attempt to open superannuation to the private market.There have been earlier proposals by theLiberal partyto use super for housing, too. Indeed, as some have pointed out, there already exists a means to use superannuation for a first home deposit. The Turnbull government introduced the First Home Super Saver Scheme in 2017, allowing individuals to make up to $15,000 in voluntary superannuation contributions per year, to a maximum of $30,000 in total, which could be withdrawn to help fund a first home deposit.Labor opposed the scheme, with then shadow treasurer Chris Bowencharacterising itas a “fundamental undermining of Australia’s superannuation system” and one that will “make housing affordability worse, not better, by pushing up demand and overinflating prices”. Keating described the earlier proposal for the scheme as “not responsible enough even to be considered a thought bubble”.TheMorrison governmentwent to the 2022 election with the Super Home Buyer policy, under which first home buyers would be able to use 40% of their super, up to $50,000, towards buying a home.These same arguments have been used to advance the current proposals by politicians as well as superannuation interest groups who have their own links to different actors in the system. Some groups have ties to not-for-profit and industry funds, which have equal representatives of employers and employees on their boards. Others have members from the for-profit retail sector.Super Members Council (SMC) was created after a merger of two former peak bodies, including Industry Super Australia, with its famous “compare the pair” ads.SMC foundthat the Morrison government’s Covid-19 early release scheme saw about 725,000 Australians effectively wipe out their superannuation accounts. This was a measure legislated in the early days of the pandemic to allow people to access ‘their own money’ when many lost their incomes. It was only afterwards that the jobkeeper reforms took place.Recently,Senator Braggreignited the super-for-housing debate in an address to the retail fund-aligned Financial Services Council. He pointed out that Keating himself floated the idea of using up to $10,000 for housing in 1993.Australia has had housing crises before: what can we learn from them? | Anne O’BrienRead moreHousing is an unofficial pillar of the retirement system. Those who rent in retirement, especially single people, are more likely to be living in poverty. There are other measures to address this issue, namely the tax and transfer system or potentiallyboosting commonwealth rent assistance to retirees.Superannuation is a complex system that many find hard to understand, especially with so many actors who have a dog in the fight over how the savings pool should be used.Super was created to address a genuine social problem: ensuring Australians could retire with more than the age pension and avoid poverty in old age. But housing is also a social problem, and for many younger Australians, the prospect of ever owning a home is becoming increasingly remote. Considering the history of superannuation and the scale of Australia’s housing crisis helps us understand why proposals such as using super for housing have arisen and why the debate over their merits is ongoing.Emily Millane is a lawyer, policy analyst and researcher. She is a member of the Australian Historical Association. Her book,Super: The Policy History of Australia’s Retirement Savings Scheme, is out on Tuesday through Melbourne University PublishingExplore more on these topicsSuperannuationPast/PresentAustralian economyLiberal partyLabor partyAustralian politicsHousingcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Nobody is listening to us’: on the school protest frontline, I heard why France’s students feel disowned | Alexander Hurst | The Guardian
description: Fixing the broken education system will be just the start. The biggest challenge for an aloof political class is to finally pay attention to an abandoned generation, says Guardian Europe columnist Alexander Hurst
Author: Alexander Hurst
Headline: Fixing the broken education system will be just the start. The biggest challenge for an aloof political class is to finally pay attention to an abandoned generation, says Guardian Europe columnist Alexander Hurst
Content: Student protesters in Place de la République, Paris, on Monday.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAView image in fullscreenStudent protesters in Place de la République, Paris, on Monday.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAOpinionFrance‘Nobody is listening to us’: on the school protest frontline, I heard why France’s students feel disownedAlexander HurstFixing the broken education system will be just the start. The biggest challenge for an aloof political class is to finally pay attention to an abandoned generationFri 9 Oct 2026 07.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTShareWhen adolescents protest that the government is failing to uphold their right to an education, and the government’s response is to send in riot police, the government has lost the plot. People outsideFrancemay have spent the past week watching the student protests in Paris and other cities, and thought, “Well, France has a long tradition of insurrection” or, “That’s just the French being French.”But the situation that has provoked the high-schoolwalkouts and teenage angeris most likely not one they would immediately associate with the France of their imaginations. In place of its lost plot, the French government has a collection of anecdotes and statistics that it should be ashamed of: 27th place in the most recent OECDeducation rankings, schools with ceilings collapsing and rats in classrooms and, in a school in Bagnolet,no drinkable water; an increase in the average number of students per class from 27 in 2010 toover 30 today; half of primary and high schoolsmissing teachers at the start of the school year– many of them with no substitutes or replacements.Julie, a 34-year-old teacher who joined the demonstrations, told me that staff shortages were the fault of “low salaries and poor treatment.” She has to commute for an hour and 45 minuteseach waybetween Paris and the school on the city’s outskirts where she accepted a post last year after switching careers. All for €2100 (£1,780) a month, plus some overtime pay. Teachers’ salaries in France are only56% of what they are in Germany– even as over €200bn inpublic subsidiesfinds its way annually to businesses.So it could easily have been a teacher-led revolt – instead, the high-schoolers themselves cracked first.They paid a high price for refusing to accept a failing education system: a 16-year-old has lost the use of an eye, a 15-year-old has lost a hand, a 14-year-old has a broken jaw – all from police munitions. Hundreds morehave been injuredin some way. In total, 4,400 people, the vast majority minors, have been arrested in a little over a week,almost halfthe number of arrests made during the months ofgilets jauneschaos. It might be incoherent that protesting students shoot fireworks at high school buildings, while at the same time denouncing the poor facilities they have to study in. But the far greater incoherence belongs to a government that has disinvested in its youth, and has chosen to answer bin fires with police charges.“Sure some people were burning trash cans,” Fatoumata Sylla Wague, a 17-year-old in her final year at the Lycée Paul Éluard in Seine-Saint-Denis, where pupils were among the first to set up blockades outside their campus, told me. “But trash cans can’t feel anything.” She and her fellow students, on the other hand, certainly felt the teargas that the police launched in response.Despite “unlivable” temperatures in the school buildings, extreme heat and extreme cold, walls covered in mould, electricity cuts and often not enough tables or chairs for everyone, Fatoumata would rather have been in class than out braving the riot police. But she wants to teach history some day and felt compelled, in a moment in history, comparable to May 1968, to take part. “If I’m fighting for our rights today, it’s because I really want to teach, but in good conditions. And so this is for the next generation of students and teachers.”View image in fullscreenStudents gather during a blockade at the Lycee Paul-Eluard high school in the northern Paris suburb of Saint-DenisPhotograph: Luc Auffret/Anadolu/Getty ImagesI can’t imagine how hard it must be to be a teenager in general today. In 2021 The Lancetfound that75% of French 16-25-year-olds exhibited signs of eco-anxiety, telling researchers they were “frightened” about the future. In France and beyond, students and young workersactively dislike AIand feel pessimistic about the future it portends. As for Fatoumata, she worries about the rise of far-right political movements, both in France and elsewhere.For years, successive French governments have dealt with problems in some of France’s most troubled urban areas by unleashing heavy-handed policing that all too frequently targets young people with random checks that can be personally degrading. Centralised policymaking has also produced a national education system that often sends its least experienced teachers to these same areas, while granting more senior teachers priority in requesting transfers to other, less difficult, schools.A future far-right government, the kind Fatoumata says she worries about, would almost certainly ramp up these kinds of tensions. Already, in response to the protests, rightwing politicians have called for harsher sentences andmore law and order.But this is not a problem that will be solved with more police and more batons, any more than it already has been.Because none of it signals a government that truly wants to listen – it signals that society at large does not really claim these places, or these teenagers, as its own.On n’est pas mal éduqué, on n’est pas écouté(“We’re not poorly educated, we’re just not being listened to”), read one sign I saw brandished at Paris’s Place de la République on Tuesday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionResponding to the crisis is going to require some tangible acts, such as upgrading dilapidated facilities. Arnaud Richards, 50, head of student services at Iqbal Masih middle school in Saint-Denis, offered me the example of how thoughtful architecture can have more impact than one might expect. The technical high school he previously worked in – Gabriel Péri, in an extremely poor area –reopened in 2022 after a total reconstruction, which, according to Richards, led to a calmer climate for both students and teachers. “Having the school itself be a beautiful place made the community feel more respected,” he told me. That in turn “created a calmer environment” for both students and staff.But a real answer doesn’t stop with better facilities. Showing up to cut ribbons on new construction, or renovations, isn’t enough. During Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power, his government has, on any number of issues, successively failed to listen in a way that makes people feel deeply seen and heard.As Fatoumata said: “Honestly, I don’t think the government cares, they just want to shut us up with false promises. We know nothing will change, because the government doesn’t listen to us.” Of all the things going wrong for France at the moment, this underlying lack of a feeling of “togetherness”, the feeling that nobody is really listening, is going to be the most difficult to deal with.Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. title: Heathrow’s third runway is a bottomless money pit. Stop it now | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: It won’t promote growth, will take decades and will swallow up billions of taxpayers’ money, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: It won’t promote growth, will take decades and will swallow up billions of taxpayers’ money, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: ‘Heathrow and HS2 are plagued by extravagant planning horizons and consultancy-driven budgets in which each contractor has a vested interest in cost inflation.’Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Heathrow and HS2 are plagued by extravagant planning horizons and consultancy-driven budgets in which each contractor has a vested interest in cost inflation.’Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty ImagesOpinionHeathrow third runwayHeathrow’s third runway is a bottomless money pit. Stop it nowSimon JenkinsIt won’t promote growth, will take decades and will swallow up billions of taxpayers’ money. The only winner will be the airport’s ownersFri 9 Oct 2026 06.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 06.47 EDTShareInfrastructure sends politicians berserk. Propose more money for the health service or reopening youth clubs and frowns break out all round. Can we afford it? But shout infrastructure and cheers go up. The word suggests glamour, chest-beating and “growth”. Reason flies out of the window.The saga of Heathrow’sthird runwaybeggars belief. Aforeign-owned private companywants to make more money out of its cramped west London investment. The airlinesare scepticaland passengers will have to paysurcharges higherthan any in Europe. Meanwhile fields lie empty round its rival, Gatwick, and capacity atLondon’s third airport, Stansted, is underused.The third runway is a nightmare. The official price tag is now a staggering £49bn but the overall budget for Heathrow’s expansion and operating expenditure couldsoar beyond £100bn. An unknown proportion of this willfall on the taxpayer. Theproposal has been debated for 20 yearsand the opening constantly postponed. A date of 2035 has now become 2039. I would not take bets on 2045.Sixty years ago, the British government agreed it was totally inappropriate for crowded and polluted Heathrow to expand in densely populated westLondon. Nor could an expanded Gatwick meet demand. The debate was over where to locate a new third airport. Sites in the Thames estuary and at Cublington and Stansted were researched. Stansted won. It already had an RAF base and it would service the expected growth in demand from London’s growing eastern reaches. Stansted opened in 1991.The Tories privatised London’s airports. This turned what should have been a planned expansion into a battleground of feuding rivals. Each airport became a matter not of orderly growth but of quick profits, self-serving airline slots and a shifting army of amateur officials. Commissions came and went, in the grip of overpaid lobbyists. A Heathrow runway proposed by businessman Surinder Arora within the existing airport curtilage wasbrushed aside as insufficiently bold. As for Stansted, it was taken over by Manchester airport and is now hardly mentioned as an alternative to a third runway.Airport public relations endlessly suggests it is about “business” and therefore relevant to “growth”, as if it were part of Andy Burnham’s re-industrialisation of Britain. Heathrow claims its new runway willcreate 100,000 jobs. Butfewer than 15%of air travellers claim to be “on business”, and whatever happened tovideo conferencingreducing the need for intensive business air travel? As for Heathrow’s claim to be Britain’s leading cargo airport – “a quarter of all UK trade by value” – that is based, ludicrously, on thevalue of the gold ingotsthat form roughly 60% of the goods it transports. What banks shifting bullion has to do with growth is unclear.Heathrow now has eerie echoes of HS2. Even its upper cost limit of £100bn is much the same. Both are plagued by extravagant planning horizons and consultancy-driven budgets in which each contractor has a vested interest in cost inflation. A third similar project is Hinkley Point nuclear power station, its cost currently rising through £50bn. Both the railway and the power station have beensavaged by the National Audit Office. These projects are widely considered political white elephants and years from completion. Few dare say so. Meanwhile we should note that a new general hospital costs £1bn, aswould rebuilding 50 secondary schools.Stupefying sums are here being channelled into London and the south of England. That they have been born of the age of Boris Johnson’s “levelling up” and Burnham’s tilt to the north is bizarre. This week, conference politicians have cited budgets with endless savings: half a million off student exchanges here, a billion off quangos there. Yet no one mentioned thatevery yearfor the next decade John Healey’s Treasury willblow about £7bnjust to relieve overcrowding on trains from London to Birmingham. This is almost70% of his total rail investment.The fact is that big infrastructure is monumental and sexy. No one boasts about building a care home, rather a fancy train or a nuclear power plant. One ofParkinson’s lawsstates that, while tiny items of corporate spending are debated for hours, big ones go through on the nod. They are too big to check and easy to promote.It is absurd for the government to spend the next two decades upheaving Heathrow and tearing apart the M4 corridor for the profit of a band of foreign investors, when a simple alternative lies in growing Gatwick and Stansted. This whole debate is about tourism, and tourists can surely suffer the mild inconvenience of using the other two venues, as was intended half a century ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe rest of us – politicians not least – should realise that this is serious money. There are serious uses to which it should be put.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsHeathrow third runwayOpinionHeathrow airportAir transportInfrastructureTransportLondonAirline industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: A promising future now looks perilous for election loser Zack Polanski. He sowed, now he reaps | John Harris | The Guardian
description: There was a real chance of a Green byelection win in Holborn and St Pancras. He made bad decisions and cost his party dear, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: There was a real chance of a Green byelection win in Holborn and St Pancras. He made bad decisions and cost his party dear, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Zack Polanski, left, watches on as Sagal Abdi-Wali speaks, following her victory in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in the early hours of 9 October 2026.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenZack Polanski, left, watches on as Sagal Abdi-Wali speaks, following her victory in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in the early hours of 9 October 2026.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockOpinionGreen partyA promising future now looks perilous for election loser Zack Polanski. He sowed, now he reapsJohn HarrisThere was a real chance of a Green byelection win in Holborn and St Pancras. He made bad decisions and cost his party dearFri 9 Oct 2026 03.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.08 EDTShareAs ever, among all the noise triggered by Labourholding the seat of Holborn and St Pancras, the most plain-spokenand undeniable analysiswas provided by that sage and national treasure John Curtice, of Strathclyde University. The result, he said, echoed national opinion polls and reflected two undeniable facts: that the Greens are in need of a period of contrition and reflection, and Labour ought to be slightly less than ecstatic.Andy Burnham’s party, with a majority of 3,364, he said, showed they “are in a much better position than they were six months ago, but still not as popular as they were in 2025”. The Greens, meanwhile, remain “a more significant player than historically they have ever been”, but have lost much of the ground they gained during Zack Polanski’s first year as leader, when the serial failures of the local MP – one Keir Starmer – provided him and his party with such a glorious succession of political opportunities.Do not forget: the Greens’success earlier this year in Gorton and Dentonplayed a massive part in Starmer eventually leaving the political stage, and the man he barred from being the Labour candidate snatching his job. But now? Publicly, Polanski seems largely unrepentant aboutthe “Zionism is racism”motion passed at his party conference, and confident he can resume where he left off. But his party’s claim that it tripled its previous vote share in the seat is very specious indeed: as the pollster Peter Kellnerputs it, “the leftwing vote two years ago was divided between the Greens’ 10.4% and an independent, Andrew Feinstein’s, 18.9%. Together, they won 29.3%.” The true increase in the leftwing anti-Labour vote, therefore, is only 3.5 percentage points, and Polanski has thus taken such a significant blow that his experience of the next few weeks and months could be very choppy indeed.Over the last week, I spent two days in the constituency, filming another episode of the Guardian’sAnywhere But Westminster video series, and got a deep sense that our politics remains in a state of unpredictable flux. So many people and the conversations we had come to mind. The young people of colour in the pinched neighbourhood of Somers Town – the urban village right next to Euston station – who were all voting Green, and talked of Gaza and the impossibility of living in our capital. The woman in upmarket Primrose Hill who told us she no longer told people she was Jewish for fear of instant uproar and upbraiding about Israel, a country she had last visited 15 long years ago. But most of all, a 24-year-old trainee teacher called Tom, who reluctantly still lives with his parents, and has no idea how he is going to hold down a job in his home city. He had once been an enthusiastic Green member and activist, he told me, and had every intention of voting for them, untilthe Zionism motionsuggested a party perfectly happy to inflame the UK’s sense of division and polarisation. He decided to switch to Labour.The searing summer should have provided the Greens with another boost, and a real chance of another byelection win. But now? Polanski –who endorsed the ideathat Zionism is a form of racism eight days before his party’s conference began – looks not just morally questionable, but distinctly weak: one central bit of symbolism in this whole affair, let us not forget, was his absence from the Zionism debate and vote at his party conference.And so to a geographical jump to a few other parts of the country. As I may have written once or twice in the past, I live in Frome, in Somerset: a 25,000-population settlement whose affinity with the Greens has been deepening for the last decade or so. They provide four of the six councillors who represent the town on our new unitary council. The rurality and climate-fear in the villages that surround us chimes with Ellie Chowns’s seeminglyout-of-the-blue election two years agoas the Green MP for North Herefordshire andAdrian Ramsay’s successin the East Anglian seat of Waveney Valley. But there are also elements of the maverick, future-facing attitudes that waft down into our neck of the woods from Bristol Central, the seat held since 2024 byCarla Denyer, the former Green party co-leader. I think I know what was holding those two elements together, and partly powering the Greens’ resurgence: a mixture of radical, empathetic social democracy and urgency about the fate of the planet that also seems to have taken root in some of England’s suburbs.With the possible exception of Bristol, if you wanted to completely wreck the Greens’ successes in all those places, you would bin that approach and accelerate exactly what Polanski has facilitated: not just a politics of no-surrender and provocation, but the entry into the partyof embittered former Jeremy Corbyn supportersand assorted ultra-leftists, bringing with them a flimsy, pious gesture politics.The party’s former leaderCaroline Lucasand the longstandingGreen activist Rupert Readare about to publish a mini-manifesto titledClimate Popularism: a guide to “breaking the grip of rightwing populism through a new politics of crisis resilience”, to be formally launched on 15 October. Written before the antisemitism meltdown, it rather minces its words about Polanski’s project, but makes it pretty clear why things have now gone wrong. “Some observers have wondered whether this new eco-populism has at times been a little tooquietabout the ‘eco’ part,” Lucas and Read write. “On the doorstep, at least, this may be an understandable strategy … [But] as recent heatwaves have made abundantly clear, the salience of climate impacts will make adaptation concerns a doorstep issue before long.”Lucas and Read make the case for “centrally funded, locally appropriate action to adapt neighbourhoods, infrastructure and ways of life, to prepare for the broad, cascading impacts of human-triggered climate change”. They propose a domestic retrofit programme that would entail a lot of “secure green jobs”. They also write, very perceptively, about an “exhausted majority” tired of our shrill politics, and suggest the “depolarisation” of the climate issue in the face of plain facts – which sounds like the direct opposite of how Polanski operates. There is talk of a politics of “courage, hope, love of place” – and, crucially, a decisive turn into the use of citizens’ assemblies. This is the kind of turn the Greens should undoubtedly take – but even if they do, they will now be starting in a deeply troubled and weakened state.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham, meanwhile, still has no end of work to do. For what it’s worth, many of us have long believed that the substantial presence in British politics of a radical party free of Labour’s pussyfooting around the climate crisis and the harsh realities of inequality was an absolute necessity, and the Greens’ fitful growth was nothing but a good thing. Now, by contrast, as the fallout from Polanski’s sudden crash only deepens, they have a massive amount of self-questioning and reinvention to do. Whether they will even have the inclination is another question entirely.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsGreen partyOpinionHolborn and St Pancras byelectionZack PolanskiByelectionscommentShareReuse this content

title: You have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents. So what went wrong? | Devi Sridhar | The Guardian
description: Some change in our lifestyles and environments over a generation has caused this increased risk. What, exactly, is a mystery, says chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Devi Sridhar
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: Some change in our lifestyles and environments over a generation has caused this increased risk. What, exactly, is a mystery, says chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Devi Sridhar
Content: A patient undergoing a CT scan.Photograph: JohnnyGreig/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA patient undergoing a CT scan.Photograph: JohnnyGreig/Getty ImagesOpinionCancerYou have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents. So what went wrong?Devi SridharSome change in our lifestyles and environments over a generation has caused this increased risk. What, exactly, is a mysteryProf Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghFri 9 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTShareIn the field of global health, we often talk about each generation living longer and healthier lives than their parents. We’ve seen this in the gains in life expectancy, the sharp decrease in child mortality and in the near elimination of many vaccine-preventable diseases. But since the turn of the century this progress has stalled, and in some cases several health metrics have gone backwards.Take cancer, which was long thought to be a disease linked to old age. While most cancers do indeed still occur in elderly people, a new report highlights that a number of cancersare increasing in people who are under 50, often referred to as “early onset cancer”. The report, undertaken by the World Cancer Research Fund, looked at data from 12 different cancer types in England, the US and the Netherlands over the past 20 years. What they found isn’t pretty.While there were slight variations among the three countries, larger patterns are clear. Among women who are under 50 in England, breast, bowel, uterine, kidney, liver, pancreatic and stomach cancershave increased. For men under 50 in England, there were increases in bowel, kidney, liver, pancreatic and prostate cancers. This is the opposite of what we would hope to achieve in public health – and no, it isn’t only because we have better diagnostic tools, or are doing more testing. While this explains some of the increase, it doesn’t account for it all. The data indicates that younger generations are experiencing a higher incidence of some cancers than previous generations at the same age. Put more simply: you have a higher chance of cancer at a younger age than your parents.Scientists are now working to unpick what has changed between generations that might be driving this uptick, especially trying to find things people may have been exposed to during childhood or adolescence in the 1990s that they wouldn’t have been in the 1950s.Here are some potential explanations: what we eat has changed significantly over the past 50 years, with the rise in ultra-processed and fast foods as well as sugary drinks. We also are more sedentary as a population. These changes are linked to rising levels of excess weight and obesity. Body fat, especially around the vital organs and waist, is a risk factor for chronic inflammation, insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction, all of which are linked to higher cancer incidence. Globally, obesity rates havemore than doubledamong adults and quadrupled among adolescents since 1990. Data collected in 2024 found that about 66% of adults in England were eitheroverweight or living with obesity.Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research findsRead moreBut diet, physical activity and excess body weight doesn’t fully explain the rise of certain cancers – such as breast cancer – in young people. Studies have shown that for women before menopause, a higher BMI is, in fact,linked to a slightly lower risk of cancer(which is in contrast to older women, where a higher BMI significantly increases risk of developing breast cancer.) Going further, scientists are looking at the health impact of sustained exposure to environmental toxins like air and water pollution, chemicals and plastics that have become widespread and almost impossible to avoid over the past 50 years.It has been scientifically challenging to identify one toxin that explains the global increase in cancers.Cancercan develop long after exposure to a toxic chemical, and over our lives we encounter a range of chemicals and pollutants. Saying which one, or whether it was during childhood, in utero, or adulthood, is difficult to pin down.On the positive side, one area that we have made progress with in young people is lung cancer, largely driven by anti-smoking campaigns and widespread awareness of the links between smoking and lung cancer. So not everything is getting worse.None of the continuing research into risk factors for early onset cancer should mean attaching blame to patients. One of the first human impulses when getting a diagnosis is to think “what caused this?”, and even further, “what have I done?” – and this isn’t helpful. In addition, scientists estimate that only 40% of cancers at a population level are because of an “individually modifiable” behaviour like smoking, alcohol consumption, diet, physical activity, or weight. The other 60% is a mix of ageing, genetic susceptibility, infection, possible environmental factors, and sometimes just bad luck.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith the research and investment continuing into scientific research, we will eventually learn what’s driving the rise in cancer in younger people. But for now, that mystery is still to be uncovered.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghExplore more on these topicsCancerOpinionYoung peopleHealthObesityCancer researchMedical researchcommentShareReuse this content

title: British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents | Gordon Brown | The Guardian
description: We have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policy, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Author: Gordon Brown
Headline: We have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policy, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Content: Andy Burnham and Mark Rutte inspecting a robotic dog at RAL Space, the UK's national space laboratory, at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus, Didcot, 16 September 2026.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA Pool/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Mark Rutte inspecting a robotic dog at RAL Space, the UK's national space laboratory, at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus, Didcot, 16 September 2026.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA Pool/APOpinionScienceBritish households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talentsGordon BrownWe have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policyGordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010Fri 9 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.53 EDTShareThe coming 10 years are almost certain to be the decade that sees the greatest scientific breakthroughs in a century. The question is whether advances now under way in AI, quantum computing and biology can address cancer, find ways to treat or prevent dementia, and overcome thegrowing resistanceto antibiotics. Can we find sustainable ways to address our energy needs and protect the environment at the same time? Can AI transform the way we deliver education, health and social care to the benefit of millions, as well as advance modern manufacturing strength? And what role can Britain’s inventors, investors and industrialists play in developing these transformative technologies?While the US and China are the world’s obvious innovation powerhouses, the UK also has enormous assets, as the Innovation Nation Conference in Manchester addressed by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will hear today. We are home tofour of the world’stop 10 universities and 16 of the top 100, five of which are in Europe’s top 10 for spin-outs, startups based on intellectual property produced through a university’s research. With less than 1% of the world’s population, theUK produces6% of the world’s research papers, nearly 9% of citations and 12% of the most highly cited research.Our research expertise is one of the many reasons we have been at the forefront of recent inventions:from AlphaFold, which predicts how proteins behave, to viral-vector vaccine technology and AI that detects cancer as reliably as radiologists. Britain already sits at the intersection of AI, quantum computing and synthetic biology. The question then is: why, having led the first Industrial Revolution, should the UK not be the world’s great innovation nation once again?We know the public have an entrepreneurial spirit, and back this vision. New polling for this week’s conference finds that75% of peopleagree that innovation is essential for creating UK economic growth.But it is disappointing thatonly 36%of the British publicbelieves the country is a world leader in science. It is time for innovation to move to the forefront of government policy and the10-year planthe government is preparing. If we were to raise Britain to Swedish or Japanese levels of innovation intensity we would, over time, leave every household £5,000 better off (according to my calculations), and increase our national income by £150bn a year as higher investment in research and development feeds through into productivity. And a jobs plan on the scale thatOur Scottish Futurehas proposed for Scotland would mean about 3m new jobs across the UK.We can identify the major hurdles to overcome. While the UK is good at startups and spin-outs, we are slow to turn startups into scale-ups, and even slower to turn scale-ups into global success stories. Per head of population, the US has double the number of $1bn companies and nearly three times as many $10bn-plus companies than the UK. And even when we do scale up at home, three-quarters of venture capital investment comes from overseas.Turning this around will require a government to keep tackling the bottlenecks that are inevitably created from innovation. Speakers from future-facing companies at today’s conference will set out the steps that we need to consider. These will range from making sure firms can access the money they need to grow from UK investors, to new incentives for investors, to public-private partnerships – as happens in Germany, France and Italy – capitalised by theBritish Business Bankand thenational wealth fund. Competition policy must favour new entrants against vested interests and be aligned with a favourable tax regime, such as through research and development credits that favour companies of all sizes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money | Chris Stokel-WalkerRead moreResearchfor the conferencehas identified 127 innovative clusters covering every region and nation of the UK, many of which will succeed if we are willing to give long-term support to the infrastructure, skills training and research and development support from UK Research and Innovationthey need to grow. In order to harness this potential, more power needs to be devolved to enable mayors and regional authorities to act locally while ensuring access to global markets.Britain does not lack genius or great assets. Every nation, including ours, must do more to find its “lost Einsteins” – the young people in lower-income areas who have the talent but not yet the opportunity to show their creative genius. What we need now is to create a chain of hope that connects all people to intellectual discovery and deployment, to startups and scale-ups, and to global leadership – all aligned around a shared national purpose.Sixty-four years ago, John F Kennedy declared that the US would lead a nationwide effort to be first on the moon. But the space initiative was not his first choice. He had wanted a national project that everybody could feel part of, and revealed he would have preferred to have chosen a project on Earth – if he could have found one with the same power to inspire a national mission that the whole population could enthusiastically embrace.Today, we can choose to be the innovation nation. “This generation does not intend to founder in the backwash of the coming age,” said Kennedy of the US. And this generation of Britons has no intention of being left behind as the age of AIaccelerates. Today’s event, spearheaded by the prime minister in Manchester – itself a city of innovation – will send a message that we mean to be in the global vanguard; not because, as Kennedy said, it is easy to do, but even though it is hard. For the challenge now is to do more than invent the future. We must invest in it, manufacture it and, wherever possible, own it here in Britain.Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010Explore more on these topicsScienceOpinionTechnology sectorTechnology policyUniversitiesAI (artificial intelligence)Medical researchcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Old-timey fascism was kept secret. Now you don’t have to hide it’: Martin McDonagh, John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell on Wild Horse Nine | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: McDonagh’s latest film has Malkovich and Rockwell shooting the breeze as CIA agents in 1973 on Easter Island. They discuss grandchildren, swimming with turtles and who shot JFK
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: McDonagh’s latest film has Malkovich and Rockwell shooting the breeze as CIA agents in 1973 on Easter Island. They discuss grandchildren, swimming with turtles and who shot JFK
Content: I now pronounce you … Sam Rockwell, John Malkovich and Martin McDonagh.Photograph: Giulia ParmigianiView image in fullscreenI now pronounce you … Sam Rockwell, John Malkovich and Martin McDonagh.Photograph: Giulia ParmigianiVenice film festivalInterview‘Old-timey fascism was kept secret. Now you don’t have to hide it’: Martin McDonagh, John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell on Wild Horse NineXan BrooksMcDonagh’s latest film has Malkovich and Rockwell shooting the breeze as CIA agents in 1973 on Easter Island. They discuss grandchildren, swimming with turtles and who shot JFKFri 9 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Earmuffs!” says Sam Rockwell, pausing his gushing tribute mid-flow and turning to faceJohn Malkovichon the couch. Rockwell loves Malkovich and has been discussing his work at some length. Malkovich, he says, is charismatic and dangerous, half masculine, half feminine; a unique combination and the perfect sparring partner. He’s one of the world’s finest actors and annoyingly modest to boot. “Earmuffs!” says Rockwell and pivots back towards me. “He hates hearing all this. That’s why I keep saying ‘earmuffs’.”Malkovich frowns. “I don’t mind it,” he says.“Hates it,” says Rockwell. “He truly hates all this stuff.”In Martin McDonagh’sWild Horse Nine, Malkovich and Rockwell play bickering CIA agents who may also be the best of friends. Chris and Lee are fresh from plotting the 1973 coup in Chile and are spinning their wheels on Rapa Nui, amid the crashing waves and the moai statues. They’ve seen too much and sinned too greatly and now Chris has cancer, which is hardly helping his mood. So he takes Lee aside and asks for one last big favour.Ahead of the film’s premiere, the production team commandeer suites at an opulent Venice hotel and hand out hats and T-shirts to each new arrival. The lobby becomes a sea of merch. The harried concierge has to raise his voice to be heard. He says: “Second floor for the Six White Horses press interviews.”McDonagh makes films that are playful and volatile, spring-loaded with violence and spiced with absurdist black comedy. Wild Horse Nine nods to In Bruges andThe Banshees of Inisherinwith its odd-couple antics and explosive side notes. But its mood is more mournful, death-haunted, with one eye on the past. McDonagh – once the upstart enfant terrible of London theatre – is now a silver-haired 56-year-old who comes at life from a different angle. “I’m getting older,” he says. “Maybe this is my first old-man movie.”On sitting down to script Wild Horse Nine, the film-maker wrote GUILT and REGRET at the top of page one, as though setting his course with a compass and sextant. His film opens in Santiago before relocating to the South Pacific. From there it homes in on Malkovich’s CIA veteran, a leaky repository of cold war horror with his memories of the Bay of Pigs and Dealey Plaza. Chris is likely dying and wants to go out with a bang. He claims that he knows who killed JFK and is about to spill the beans.View image in fullscreenIn focus … Sam Rockwell as Lee and John Malkovich as Chris in Wild Horse Nine.Photograph: Diego Araya Corvalán/Searchlight PicturesThe Kennedy assassination is the God particle of conspiracy theories. It marked the loss of US innocence, or the start of the rot of disinformation and fake news. McDonagh knows the official version and remains breezily unconvinced. “I definitely think there was something going on,” he says. “I’m definitely a believer in the conspiracy. Exactly what that was, we’ll never really know. Was Lee Harvey Oswald involved? More than likely. Was he the lone gunman? I don’t believe that for a second.”Martin McDonagh says CIA has ‘done awful things all around the world’Read moreHe’s made several pictures with Woody Harrelson. Wasn’t Harrelson’s father once rumoured to have been involved in the killing? McDonagh sits up and mimes zipping his lip. “I know nothing,” he says.Wild Horse Nine was never intended as a comment on the present-day United States. Except that history has a tendency to repeat and the shoot coincided with Donald Trump’s strike on Venezuela. Operations like that used to be more covert, conducted via proxies, whereas now they seem brazen, the equivalent of a smash-and-grab raid. “But I don’t think Trump is the worst president that we’ve had,” he says. “I don’t even think he’s the worst in the past 60-years. Nixon was more of a fascist pig. George W Bush probably killed more people than Trump. And then if you look at Vietnam, there’s Johnson. The difference is that with old-timey fascism, you at least had to keep it secret. These days you don’t have to hide it any more. Is that more fucked? Or is it more honest?”McDonagh sits behind one closed door; Rockwell and Malkovich behind another. On-screen or off, the two actors have different energies, different speeds, so that the interview feels like a private performance: the Energizer Bunny versus the all-seeing Sphinx. One of these men has left his sunglasses on the floor. Inevitably it is Rockwell, who is altogether more bouncy and heedless. “My Guccis,” he cries. “Oh man, I would have stepped on those.”View image in fullscreenOn location … the director Martin McDonagh with John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell in Rapa Nui.Photograph: Diego Araya Corvalán/Searchlight PicturesRockwell won an Oscar for playing the bumptious small-town deputy in McDonagh’sThree Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri. Malkovich may well follow suit thanks to Wild Horse Nine, which goes on to receive a rapturous 13-minute ovation at the premiere. The 72-year-old is on fabulously flavourful form as Chris, a tragicomic monster who is simultaneously melting down and seeing the light, lashing out and making amends. The character plays to the actor’s natural strengths, mining his innate theatricality and enigmatic air. But he explains that the role required some heavy lifting as well. Endless rehearsals and hours of line-readings, he says. “Sam and I did each scene at least a thousand times.”A thousand? Malkovich is so self-contained and unblinking, it’s hard to know when he’s joking.Rockwell chips in. “Yeah, about a thousand times. We ran it on the weekends. John’s a workhorse.”“You are, too,” Malkovich says. It’s good to have a co-star to rehearse with, he adds, although every good actor has their own way of working. Clint Eastwood, for instance, prefers to hit the ground running. “You have to be a slick talker to get more than two takes out of Clint. You have to be pretty convincing, because he doesn’t take that lightly. As I know from experience.”They were on Rapa Nui for six weeks, which helped with the process. “I have two granddaughters, so it was a long time away from them,” he says. “I don’t like being away from my grandchildren. But it’s a great place to shoot because there’s nothing else to do. You can swim with the turtles but that’s about it. Your work days are long. You’re always prepping for tomorrow. If it weren’t for a movie, I’d probably go nuts.”Rockwell enjoyed it. “We had a great time,” he says. “Every night we had a little Chile wine and some rum. And there was a drink made with sugarcane, what the hell was it called? They put an egg-white in it.”You can handle the truth! Why cinema suddenly loves conspiracy theoriesRead moreHis partner, the actor Leslie Bibb, has materialised in the doorway. “Pisco sour,” she says.“Pisco sour!” He’s delighted to see her and glad of the intel. Bibb has swung by to check when Rockwell breaks for lunch. He introduces her to me and indicates Malkovich on the couch. “But you can’t miss John,” he says. “Look at him, he’s beautiful.”Marooned on his island, Chris plans to write his memoirs and come clean. His bosses are terrified he’ll mention “the Dallas parts” of his story. Some secrets, they feel, must be taken to the grave.Malkovich has played heroes and villains. He’s been Tom Ripley, Biff Loman and the Vicomte de Valmont. But his career has been long and he’s covered this particular topic before. In 1994, he adapted and directed a stage version of Libra, Don DeLillo’s novel about Lee Harvey Oswald. He studied the Zapruder footage of JFK’s final moments and wandered down several conspiracy rabbit holes. The Warren Commission’s findings, he concluded, were either flawed or a lie. And if that makes him a crank, he’s hardly in the minority.“Well, I think 60% of the American public don’t believe it,” he says. “Could the official story be true? Yeah, I guess. So could Keebler elves. The government tells us all kinds of things. Some of them may be true but not the majority of them, that’s my experience.”View image in fullscreenHeading for trouble? John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyI’ve read that he hasn’t voted since the 1972 presidential election, when the liberal George McGovern lost in a landslide to Nixon. He nods; this is true. “I’m not a believer,” he says.Not a believer in what? Democracy? Malkovich shrugs. “In the whole thing, really. As they say in France: ‘Je ne pratique pas’, I’m not practising. I remember the night McGovern lost. I was talking to my father on the phone and I said: ‘Well, I’m done.’ He said: ‘My God, John, you can’t be done.’ I was 19 years old but that was it, I was done. I concentrate on what I can make and leave it at that.”What about Rockwell? Is he still practising? “Yeah, well, I vote,” he says glumly. “I vote with faint hope. Hoping Obama will come back.”The publicist sticks her head around the door. She reports that lunch is almost ready, which means that we’ve reached the last question. Rockwell perks up. “No pressure,” he says.Let’s finish with death. That’s where the whole film is leading. Chris has decided he wants to die on Rapa Nui. Then he changes his mind and opts for Venice instead. Assuming that a death can be scripted like a film, where in the world would be the ideal place to bow out?Malkovich thinks for a moment. “Probably on stage,” he says. “About 15 years ago I toured with a new opera based on Casanova’s memoirs. It started with Casanova chasing a chambermaid around the stage, as he was known to do, and then he has a heart attack. The play stops and people come out with a stretcher and then everyone breaks into song. Before the performance, I always made sure to tell all my friends: ‘It’s just the beginning of the play. I fake a heart attack. Don’t pay any attention.’ But forgot to tell my then-agent and I don’t think she has ever forgiven me.”A few nights after that, he made the exact same mistake. “I have a friend, Barbara Sturm, who is a knee doctor in Düsseldorf. She came to see me and I suddenly realised I hadn’t warned her either. So I tried to text from the dressing room but of course she already had her phone switched off, being a well-mannered person. And so blah-blah-blah, the whole thing happened again.”The production was pure chaos, but it was also rather funny. Every night he’d fake a coronary and see the panic sweep through the audience like wildfire. “As many as 20 people would run up to the stage. You’d have the doctors and a stretcher and then everybody starts singing.”Rockwell is laughing. “That’s good acting,” he says.“Well no, it’s terrible,” says Malkovich. “But still, it wouldn’t be the worst way to go.”Wild Horse Nine is released in the US, UK and Ireland on 6 November and in Australia on 5 NovemberExplore more on these topicsVenice film festivalMartin McDonaghSam RockwellJohn MalkovichJohn F KennedyFestivalsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It gave me a superpower – question everything’: ​as punk turns 50, bands from China to Greenland explain how it fires up their lives | Punk | The Guardian
description: Whether on the frontline in Ukraine or skate parks in Soweto, the genre is still a vital outlet for disaffected people everywhere. Here, musicians explain how they rage against the machine
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: Whether on the frontline in Ukraine or skate parks in Soweto, the genre is still a vital outlet for disaffected people everywhere. Here, musicians explain how they rage against the machine
Content: (Clockwise from top left)Beton, Twenty One Children, Taqbir and Depustūtes.Composite: Jess Clark/The Guardian; Getty Images; Katrīna Līva Dalbiņa; Alejandra Núñez; Assante Chiweshe; Ruslan Bulgakov; Valeriia Nekhvodiuk; Yulia SachulView image in fullscreen(Clockwise from top left)Beton, Twenty One Children, Taqbir and Depustūtes.Composite: Jess Clark/The Guardian; Getty Images; Katrīna Līva Dalbiņa; Alejandra Núñez; Assante Chiweshe; Ruslan Bulgakov; Valeriia Nekhvodiuk; Yulia SachulPunk‘It gave me a superpower – question everything’: ​as punk turns 50, bands from China to Greenland explain how it fires up their livesWhether on the frontline in Ukraine or skate parks in Soweto, the genre is still a vital outlet for disaffected people everywhere. Here, musicians explain how they rage against the machineAs told toDave SimpsonFri 9 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 08.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine: ‘I was lucky not to die. I had guitars with me on the frontline’Andriy Zholob,vocalist/guitarist,Beton:When MTV arrived inUkraine, I heard Nirvana, the Offspring, Bad Brains, Social Distortion and thrash metal, and realised that all this started from punk rock. Our drummer and I were in a ska-punk band first, but when our vocalist became pregnant we started Beton in 2017 and played lots of festivals.Everything changed with the invasion. In 2022, I started military service as a surgeon on the frontline. We were attacked many times and on at least four occasions I was lucky not to die. I had guitars with me on the frontline and every evening we’d play just to relax. At one point, my commander gave me eight days off to record a battle song for our brigade and Beton did a cover of the Clash’s London Calling – Kyiv Calling – to raise money for the Ukrainian resistance. I wanted to use punk rock to stand against evil.Watch the video for Kyiv Calling by Beton.I finished my service two years ago, quit medicine and now work with veterans, many of whom come to our gigs. There are guys and girls with prosthetics, slam dancing, singing along and everything. It’s a real moment of punk rock unity. We play two or three shows every month, but I like to spend time in the mountains. Although I play punk rock, sometimes I need silence.Morocco and Spain: ‘People would tell me: you love Satan’Nao, vocalist, Taqbir:In the Muslim community ofMorocco, where I come from, the punk look is not accepted. For a long time, I had to perform anonymously, with my face covered, in case people recognised me and wanted to hurt me. Being a punk is not for the faint-hearted. Even in Spain, where I live now, I felt isolated as an immigrant and as a woman who did crazy things to my hair. People would tell me: “You love Satan.”View image in fullscreen‘Being a punk is not for the faint-hearted’ … Taqbir.Photograph: Alejandra NúñezI heard Crass when I was 13. They were the first band I heard where I recognised myself in the lyrics, because I felt oppressed by religion. Then through chatting with friends online, I discovered more. I’d go to shows in Madrid, take off my hijab and wear makeup. It was a double life that meant I finally felt free to be myself, but for a long time punk cost me my relationship with my family.Being in Taqbir really helped. I was very angry, so fronting the band was like a cure for this rage. People seem to connect with the rawness. We’ve played in north Africa and the UK and my dream is to be able one day to play in Morocco.Punkhas helped me see that things don’t have to be black and white: people can be punk and Muslim and gay. Although there’s anger, our message is positive. If you’re feeling oppressed or that you cannot be yourself in this society, Taqbir are for you.South Africa: ‘Being from Soweto automatically makes you political’Abdula Skink, vocalist, Twenty One Children:A lot of kids in Johannesburg got into punk because there were no jobs or infrastructure for us. I grew up in a hip-hop house, but found bands such as Suicidal Tendencies and Black Flag through video games and older friends who skated. Punk just flicked all these switches in my head. Our guitarist, Thula, used to play in TCIYF, the first all-black punk band inSouth Africa. When we started our band in 2023, I was an assistant teacher for 21 autistic kids, so that became our name. I was also 21, so it felt like a lucky number.Being from Soweto automatically makes you political. All the great revolutionaries – Hugh Masekela, Nobel prize winners, Desmond Tutu and so on – came from here. Our motto is: if something isn’t true, we won’t sing about it. Our song Scab is about a time I was stopped by police because I was skating through a historically Afrikaans/white area. I had green hair and the policeman was like: “You’re on drugs.” He ripped my Suicidal Tendencies T-shirt, dropped my laptop from my bag on the street and tried to take my skateboard. I wasn’t doing anything illegal. They were just fucking with me. Mostly, we try to make a difference in our communities. Thula built the first DIY skate park in Soweto; we’ve done charity shows for orphanages and such. For us, punk is not so much a livelihood but a way of life.India: ‘We were bombarded with threatening messages’Aditya Naik, vocalist/guitarist, Punkon Toast:I grew up listening to Bad Religion, NOFX, the Sex Pistols and the Clash and saw a satirical commentary about our times, so I started the band when I was 17 so I could talk about what was happening around us. InIndia, you see cruelty or injustice on every corner, so we don’t relate to mainstream music, which ignores this.View image in fullscreen‘There’s a lot of oppression of artists’ … Punk on Toast.Photograph: Courtesy of Punk on ToastAt the moment, there’s a lot of oppression of artists. After our song Modified talked about what the right wing are trying to do with us, we were bombarded with threatening messages online. People went through all our profiles, trying to find our phone numbers, where we live, our employers. It felt like being molested. Although we’ve had coverage in Rolling Stone India, the punk scene mostly flies under the radar, but that means we’re freer to sing about what we want.We took part in the recentCockroach protests in Mumbai, which alerted people to how things are and got everybody out on the street. Before that, India felt like a small elite club where everyone else is the “cockroaches”, so it was like seeing a phoenix: hope. The punk scene is growing, with our friends Pacifist and Emergency Trigger and bands such as the Light Years Explode and the Riot Peddlers. It’s more about documenting our times and standing for what’s right rather than selling lots of records, but punk rock gave me the greatest superpower: question everything.Brazil: ‘Under a military dictatorship, there were kids brave enough to play with passion and fury’Henrike Baliu, vocalist,Blind PigsandArmada:When the original UK punk explosion happened in 1977, my dad was a naval engineer stationed in Southampton. He saw the Boomtown Rats performing Lookin’ After No 1 on Top of the Pops and told the guy in the record shop: “Give me everything you’ve got” – which meant the Sex Pistols, Generation X and so on.Listen to São Paulo City by Armada.Years later, when I was 12, I played some of my dad’s records to my friends and they told me about the punk scene inBrazil. Bands such as Ratos de Porão, Inocentes and Cólera sang about life under a military dictatorship, which Brazil was in the 80s. People were disappearing or being murdered, so it blows my mind that under a dictatorship with virtually zero news, poverty and police brutality there were kids with spiky hair brave enough to wear fake leather jackets and play with passion and fury. Those bands were pioneers who paved the way for us.Blind Pigs were probably the biggest punk band in Brazil over the last 30 years, but now I’m focused on Armada. We are bilingual and sing in Portuguese and English. When we recorded our English language album, Tales of Treason, the country was going through another crazy time politically and the right wing were on the rise again. With the music, I wanted to warn people to learn from history: “Dudes, you don’t want that again.”Latvia: ‘On stage I let out all my anger’View image in fullscreen‘On stage, I let out all my anger’ … Evisa Petrovska of Depustūtes.Photograph: Katrīna Līva DalbiņaEvisaPetrovska, vocalist, Depustūtes:In high school, I didn’t really like pop, so I got into metal, but I felt it was missing lyrical depth, so punk really resonated. Ramones and the Sex Pistols sang about the same stuff that made me mad or frustrated. The Dead Kennedys’ political commentary really connected and then I discovered riot grrrl. As I got older, I realised there was a punk scene here in Riga and a whole community of people like me.There’s so much going on in the world – I’ll never run out of topics and writing and singing in the band never gets boring. On stage, I let out all my anger. Whether I’m running or crawling on the floor, it’s just pure emotion. Singing in Latvian makes it easier to sing about local politics. Lately, we’ve been addressing how people who actually benefit society aren’t getting paid as well as those who aren’t, but I sing about societal norms and stereotyping.Our song Mrs Pieklājība (Mrs Polite) starts, in a mocking way: “I love listening to men and being obedient.” It was inspired by people telling me “you should smile more” or “women don’t dress like that”. There’s always been at least two women in the band, but most people are really supportive. I love inspiring other girls’ lives. A lot of them come up after shows and say: “That was so inspiring. I wish I could speak as freely as you.”China: ‘Our albums were confiscated and our work was taken offline’Wu Wei, vocalist, SMZB: Wuhan and Beijing were the first cities inChinato have punk music. I founded the first punk band in Wuhan in 1996 after falling in love with tapes that my friends sent me from the US – initially the Sex Pistols, the Clash, Ramones and then bands with other styles, such as US Bombs, Suicide Machine and Rancid. Through punk, I finally found a way to express myself. Although the scene is still quite small, we were one of the first bands to go on national tours, which influenced the development of punk in other cities. We sing about the environment we operate in: political aspects and things I’ve witnessed in daily life under the system in China.Watch the video for Ten Thousand Ways to Rebel by SMZB.A few years ago, the authorities prohibited us from performing. Some albums were confiscated, our work was taken offline and our record company was forced to terminate our contract. Despite this, our audiences have a wide age span and range from other punks and bands to art workers, students and ordinary wage-earners. Punk has brought me so many things, from running the bar Wuhan Prison to my personal life. I’ve now settled in the UK with my family, but frequently return to Wuhan for rehearsals and recording. SMZB just released a bilingual album, When the Party Is Over, for our 30th anniversary. Punk has given me my life.Greenland: ‘I’m 38, a father, still have my piercings and still consider myself a punk’Jenseeraq Olsen, vocalist/guitarist, Uummat:We have a running joke with Iceland that they are green and we are ice, so most people live on the coast. I was in Denmark for a festival recently and realised that there were more people there – 70,000 – than the entire Greenlandic population. Punk is very much a minority interest here, but I was always rebellious when I was young and didn’t like the mainstream pop my friends were into.‘I knew it was over for us’: the bands who got left behind when punk explodedRead moreAfter I saw an advert for Blink-182’s Enema of the State album after the movie American Pie, I realised they were the band I’d been searching for. I was teased for having multicoloured hair and ripped clothes, but Blink were a big influence on Uummat, which means “heart”. We were different from other bands in Greenland and people connected with it: we’ve played to 2,000 people.I’ve never really written political songs, butTrump’s threat to annex Greenlandhas made a lot of people emotional, stressed and nervous, which I’m sure will come out in the music. I’m 38, a father and manage a youth centre now, but Blink resonate as much as they did when I was 15. I still have my piercings and I still consider myself a punk. Meanwhile, my 11-year-old son listens to the same music and plays guitar like me. He thinks labels like “punk” are for adults, but he likes the word, so he’ll probably follow in my footsteps.Twenty One Childrentour the UK and Europe from 9-31 October.
