title: End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland review – Murakami’s marvel brilliantly brought to life | Theatre | The Guardian
description: With a dual narrative set in Tokyo and a world of dreams, Philippe Decouflé’s epic production is as bewitching as its balletic unicorns
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: With a dual narrative set in Tokyo and a world of dreams, Philippe Decouflé’s epic production is as bewitching as its balletic unicorns
Content: Beautiful but dangerous … Kiita Komagine and Misato Morita in End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBeautiful but dangerous … Kiita Komagine and Misato Morita in End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewEnd of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland review – Murakami’s marvel brilliantly brought to lifeBarbican theatre, LondonWith a dual narrative set in Tokyo and a world of dreams, Philippe Decouflé’s epic production is as bewitching as its balletic unicornsArifa AkbarFri 9 Oct 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow to stage Haruki Murakami’s epic, dual-narrative novel without leaving the audience in a muddle? Director-choreographer Philippe Decouflé goes big, filling the enormous Barbican stage with a kaleidoscope of dream worlds for Ako Takahashi’s adaptation. It could have become a scramble of stories and inquiries into memory, technological advances in society and the imagination. Instead, it is turned into one long immaculate coup de théâtre.There are two versions of the protagonist, Watashi(Tatsuya Fujiwara) – oneisin Tokyo, the other in a world comprising dreams. The city is noirish while the latter is beautiful but dangerous, with a complicated storyline involving the sundering of humans from their shadows, a walled city, roaming animals and a professor (Narushi Ikeda) who collects their skulls to channel past experiences through sound.View image in fullscreenRabbit hole of wonderlands … Miu Tomita plays Woman in Pink and Tatsuya Fujiwara is Watashi.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe professor’s 17-year-old granddaughter (Miu Tomita) accompanies Watashi in Tokyo and appears like a kitsch version of the prophetess who goes with Aeneas into the underworld. Watashi seeks escape, so he can be reunited with his shadow (Shuntaro Miyao), but is drawn to this strange world too and has a romance with a librarian (Misato Morita).Initially, it spirals into a rabbit hole of wonderlands, with kooky humour and references to western canonical and pop culture, as is Murakami’s way, from ancient myth to Lewis Carroll’s Alice and Luis Buñuel’s Un Chien Andalou. A playful set, designed by K Ishihara, shows its own theatrical construction with cheeky playfulness.View image in fullscreenNoirish … one version of Watashi is in Tokyo.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe visual pyrotechnics suck you in, from big projections to the speed, flow and agility of dancing that gestures at anime. They bring forth Murakami’s many creatures, from underground “murks”, with porcupine spikes, who flip and cartwheel, to a herd of balletic unicorns.Decouflé’s choreography is unsurpassable in its elastic grace and athleticism without seeming circus-like. The aesthetics on the whole are so ravishing that it doesn’t matter if the story is not easy to grasp in the first half. At least not for some because, while Murakami fans will know that the unity of the story is to come, initiates to his work may be left punch-drunk and befuddled by the onslaught of worlds and images.View image in fullscreenMurakami’s creatures include unicorns.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianIt becomes clear after the interval that this is controlled and deliberate confusion, reflecting Watashi’s state of mind. The dance becomes imbued with feeling as Murakami’s world reveals its underlying themes of loneliness, grief, the fear of disappearing and of death.Franz & Marie review – Woyzeck folk musical finds heart amid the horrorRead moreBut the story of lost shadows, representing the “true” self, bears bigger socio-political echoes that feel contemporary, and even prescient (the book was published in 1985). This world looks like Neo’s in The Matrix, and its technology chimes with ideas in Naomi Klein’s book,Doppelganger: A Trip into the Mirror World. The sinister side of the perfectionism that this dream society has cultivated could be a comment on postwar Japan, or on our world of AI, real and fake selves, code and machine-constructed subjectivity.At almost three hours, it leaves you with the sense that you have been dreaming, collectively, about a world of dead animals, lost shadows and unfeeling humans, but also of unicorns, impossible beauty and an ocean-like imagination. It is both of our world, and other.AtBarbican theatre, Londonuntil 11 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreHaruki MurakamireviewsShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for Richard Thompson | Richard Thompson | The Guardian
description: Ahead of new album Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the British folk music legend will join us to answer your questions
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Ahead of new album Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the British folk music legend will join us to answer your questions
Content: Richard Thompson pictured in 2026.Photograph: Paul ClampinView image in fullscreenRichard Thompson pictured in 2026.Photograph: Paul ClampinFilm & Music reader interviewRichard ThompsonPost your questions for Richard ThompsonAhead of new album Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the British folk music legend will join us to answer your questionsBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 9 Oct 2026 08.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom Fairport Convention to his musical partnership with then-wife Linda and on to solo albums that still trouble the UK charts,Richard Thompsonis an undisputed icon of British folk music – and ahead of his latest release, entitled Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, he’s joining us to answer your questions.Now 77, Thompson’s career began in his teens when he formed Fairport Convention and struck out into writing new material rather than covers and folk standards: in so doing, albums such as 1969’s Liege and Lief became part of the British folk canon themselves.A “gut decision” prompted him to go solo, though he soon formed a duo with his wife, Linda, who he had married in 1972, putting out albums such as I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight and Pour Down Like Silver. Thompson converted to Islam, specifically Sufism, and spent time away from music before returning in the late 1970s and, after splitting with Linda, based himself in the US with his new partner.Drawing from global cultures and the fringes of rock music as well as various folk forms backed by astoundingly accomplished guitar playing has meant that Thompson has created a radically cosmopolitan body of work. He’s collaborated with everyone from Werner Herzog to David Byrne and Harry Shearer, and even attempted to synthesise an entire millennium of music in his show 1000 Years of Popular Music (encompassing Sumer is Icumen In to Oops! I Did It Again).He’s now recorded his 20th solo studio album, Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, full of picaresque characters and storytelling, in instinctive songs recorded often in just a couple of takes.Ahead of its release on 16 October, he’ll answer your questions on the new album and anything else in his career. Post them in the comments below before 10am BST on Monday 12 October, and we’ll publish his answers in the following Friday’s edition of the Film & Music section, as well as online.Explore more on these topicsRichard ThompsonFilm & Music reader interviewFolk musiccalloutShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve hit my midlife sexpot era!’ Romola Garai on marital misery, cheating … and sex scenes in cars | Television | The Guardian
description: Layby hookups are all in a day’s work for Romola Garai in her steamy new drama Adultery. She talks faking orgasms, keeping secrets – and making audiences pass out
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: Layby hookups are all in a day’s work for Romola Garai in her steamy new drama Adultery. She talks faking orgasms, keeping secrets – and making audiences pass out
Content: Tryst issues … Romola Garai in Adultery.Photograph: Nick Eagle/ITVView image in fullscreenTryst issues … Romola Garai in Adultery.Photograph: Nick Eagle/ITVTelevisionInterview‘I’ve hit my midlife sexpot era!’ Romola Garai on marital misery, cheating … and sex scenes in carsMichael HoganLayby hookups are all in a day’s work for Romola Garai in her steamy new drama Adultery. She talks faking orgasms, keeping secrets – and making audiences pass outFri 9 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a raging storm in the Peak District last winter, a blue Toyota Yaris was parked in a remote roadside spot with a sex scene being filmed inside it. “It can pose challenges, depending on the size of the car,” chucklesRomola Garai. “Me and Dominic [Cooper] got in this hatchback and asked: ‘How far do these seats go back?’ Soon there was a gale blowing outside. We were in the car, ready to shoot, but outside the entire film crew were being buffeted by high winds. They said: ‘You guys stay in there, don’t get out!’ while all the lights were getting blown away.”What did the co-stars do while the camera crew battled the elements? “What actors always do in these situations – have a long, gossipy conversation about people in the industry. While everyone else was trying to save the show, we were sitting in the car, like: ‘Well, I’ve heard he’s a total nightmare!’”The in-car tryst is a pivotal moment in new drama Adultery, created by Bafta-winning writer Danny Brocklehurst (Shameless, Fool Me Once, Brassic). The six-parter is billed as a “steamy, scandalous romance” about a whirlwind fling that threatens to unravel two families. Personal trainer Beth (Garai) and GP Tom (Cooper), both married, are thrown together when their teenage children start dating. Insatiably drawn to one another, the pair embark on an intense illicit affair.Can they keep it secret? Will the guilt get too much? Might they even leave their respective spouses? There are shades of Doctor Foster, Cold Feet and The Affair as the story unfolds. The 44-year-old actor – who helpfully explains that her name is pronounced “Romola with the emphasis on ‘Rom’, not ‘ola’, andGary as in Neville or Barlow” – admits the premise gave her pause.View image in fullscreenContents may be hot … Dominic Cooper and Romola Garai in Adultery.Photograph: Thomas Wood/ITV“I picked up a script about a cheating wife, written by a man, with a little bit of hesitation,” she admits. “In our cultural imagination, unfaithful women haven’t always been well served and can often be a projection of male insecurity – from Eve onwards. But some of my favourite books, like Madame Bovary, are so much more than that. Happily, Danny’s scripts were brilliant. They go into the complex area of marital disappointment. Beth’s dissatisfaction isn’t based on anything big. Her husband is a good guy but she’s had to suppress herself. By the time Beth realises she’s given up too much for her marriage, it’s too late. When you have an extreme physical connection with someone else, growing in the fertile ground of marital disappointment, disaster ensues.”Garai immediately connected to the character of Beth. “I just knew her. There are so many versions of that woman in my life. Somebody who’s exhausted from doing all the right things. Ferrying the kids around, washing the team’s football kit, contributing financially to the home in two different jobs. She’s part of the sandwich generation and she’s overwhelmed. I was like: hard-relate. No acting required. She’s also had to give up her own business. I know so many women who had high-powered jobs which went on the back-burner in service of the family. It gave them meaning in their life and value in society. Losing that can be destructive. Resentment sits inside you like a little gremlin.”Extramarital liaisons take place in cars, kitchens and toilets – not to mention the storeroom of a city farm. “I’ll never look at a city farm the same way,” says Garai. “As a mother of two [she’s married to actor-director Sam Hoare and they have two children, aged 10 and 13], I’ve spent many a day at those places but certainly never had anything like that happen. I just had a juice box and bought a squirrel keyring.”Sex scenes have transformed since Garai started out. “They never used to be properly directed,” she says. “It was a case of ‘Do what you want. As long as she gets her tits out, it doesn’t matter.’ Which was awful for 90% of people and great for 10% of people. It’s so much better now with intimacy coordinators. There are respectful, technical conversations. You’re doing it like a stunt, basically, with the equivalent of a fight director telling everyone exactly what to do. You have a very strong line of communication with someone whose responsibility, apart from getting the footage, is to ensure you feel comfortable. It’s a shame it had to get so bad before change came.”Humour helps, too. “Sex scenes are still weird and a bit embarrassing. Physical intimacy with another person releases all sorts of chemicals. Your body is responding and your brain sometimes doesn’t know how to process that. So it’s useful to have a scene partner you can laugh with. It releases the tension.”View image in fullscreen‘I just knew her. There are so many versions of that woman in my life’ … Romola Garai on Adultery.Photograph: PRGarai gets a Meg Ryan moment as the camera lingers on her orgasmic face. “Our intimacy director asked: ‘What’s the storytelling here?’ And I was like: ‘Well, I think she comes.’ Beth is sexually unfulfilled in her marriage. It was important to see her get the specific thing she’s lacking in her life: sexual pleasure.” She laughs. “All it’s missing is a woman in a diner saying: ‘I’ll have what she’s having.’ Hopefully the audience will fill in that gap!”She realises adultery is a hot-button topic. “I’ve already had some pretty punchy conversations, just by telling people what the show’s about. At the hairdresser’s or school gates, I’ll say it’s two ordinary married people who have an affair and people are angry already. Cheating is an issue that’s affected or wounded everyone.” Will there be whispering in the street? “Hope so,” she grins. “I have such a boring life, I love the idea of causing scandalous chat. Maybe I’ll become a figurehead for adulterers. Women might come up and say: ‘Now you understand why I was serially unfaithful to Jasper!’ I’ll be like: ‘I really don’t! Poor Jasper!’”Adultery doesn’t flinch from the fallout from the affair. “It doesn’t pull its punches,” says Garai. “I’m like a prefect on set and thought it was important to show the impact on their spouses and children.” How is she a prefect? “You know in Celebrity Traitors where Professor Hannah Fry says she’s dripping with prefect energy? I’ve got a similar vibe, albeit for less academic reasons. I like to talk about the moral aspects of scenes more than other actors. I don’t mean that as a boast. It’s probably deeply annoying. I bet Danny would be delighted if he never saw my face looming at him again!”She also points out the double standard of how men and women are judged for affairs: “Women get called ‘whores’. There’s no slur word for sexual incontinence in men. You’d never call a dude a ‘home-wrecker’ either.” Even the show’s title caused misunderstandings. “People would ask my kids: ‘Where’s Mummy? She’s not been around for ages.’ They’d reply, ‘She in Manchester doing Adultery. She’s busy with Adultery.”Could Garai’s husband and Cooper’s partner, Gemma Chan, start looking at them askance? “I knew you’d ask that!” she says. “Thankfully not, because there’s nothing more helpful for the stresses and strains of a marriage in midlife than doing a show like this. It really makes you discuss the pitfalls. I hope it provokes conversations between couples at home. Beth and Tom are both the hands-on parent. They’re the carers. But it’s them that have the forbidden relationship. They’re good people doing something bad.”Garai had to master a Manchester accent for the part. “That was terrifying,” she says. “I tried to stay in it on set, which makes everyone call you a twat. People took the piss but I went through fire to make it as accurate as I could. When the show airs, I’ll stay away from Mancunians because I’m sure they’ll tell me exactly what they think!”View image in fullscreenDangerous waters … Beth (Romola Garai) and Tom (Dominic Cooper).Photograph: Thomas Wood/ITVEqually challenging was leading a zumba class. “What got me through the embarrassment was the sense of a woman who loves being in her body. Beth relishes being sweaty and having that endorphin release. It relates to her quest for passion. There’s a well-spring of physical energy within her which needs to be run off. She wants to feel alive and feel joy.” She also croons loudly along to the car stereo. “That was another moment with heavy cringe factor. I figured that Beth married too young. Singing and dancing shows her longing for lost youth. For freedom, for fun, for sex. But belting out Rhythm Is a Dancer without a backing track? God! Dominic and I were both like: ‘Let’s never speak of this again.’”Much of Adultery’s intrigue is played out via technology. Sexy selfies are sent, phone-tracking apps are deployed, Insta accounts are stalked. Teens are regularly told off for being glued to their devices. “Of course, it’s all bullshit,” says Garai. “Kids would be perfectly within their rights to say: ‘No, fuck off, older people. You’re all on email for work, you’re meeting people on Hinge, you’ve got Ring doorbells for your parcels.’ The show attacks that hypocrisy. Technology is ingrained in all their lives. Personally, I’m a complete technophobe with very mixed feelings about social media but it’s a huge part of modern relationships.”Garai was among the 80-plus women who accused Harvey Weinstein of sexual misconduct in 2017, allegations that sparked the #MeToo movement. Has enough progress been made? “It’s much harder for women to get sexually assaulted at work now, which can only be a good thing. Social media played a huge role. It gave women the power to push back against systemic abuse. They could call it out anonymously and en masse. I’m happy but also sad it wouldn’t have happened without social media. The tech itself is something I’m still conflicted about.”Garai has been a reliably excellent presence on stage and screen for two decades. Her TV breakthrough came in 2011 when she was Bafta-nominated for playing a polymath sex worker in The Crimson Petal and the White. She got a Golden Globe nod the following year for period newsroom drama The Hour. Other TV roles include Emma, Born to Kill, The Miniaturist, Just Act Normal, Scoop, Betrayal and Vigil. Such roles have been punctuated by acclaimed theatre work.She won an Olivier award last year for her blistering performance in the stage adaptation of Annie Ernaux’s memoir The Years. Garai was actually nominated twice, for her back-to-back performances in The Years and Giant, the play about the antisemitism row that engulfed Roald Dahl. This double honour led to the strange sight of Garai competing with herself, simultaneously appearing in two closeups as the winner was announced. “That was so surreal,” she smiles. When her Giant co-star John Lithgow collected the best actor gong, he began his acceptance speech with “Romola, I think I’m going to faint!” – a reference to The Years’ graphic backstreet abortion scene, which infamously made theatregoers pass out.“It was so intense,” says Garai. “It didn’t totally blindside me because the piece was originally staged at the National Theatre in Holland and the director warned me that people had fainted. I was like: ‘That won’t happen here. We’re British, we’re not fainters! We do Coriolanus and Sarah Kane plays. I’ve been in shows where people’s hands have been chopped off.’ But the first time I said the word ‘foetus’, it was bang, bang, bang. People were just hitting the deck. It happened almost every night. Out of 53 performances, I’d say it happened 51 times. Extraordinary. I doubt I’ll experience anything like that again as an actor.”With Adultery, she’s about to shock a whole new audience. “I’m hoping I’ll get lots more cheating wife roles,” she says. “I was in my nun era, playing a lot of buttoned-up characters. A sort of a professional cross lady. Now I’m hoping to be a sexy untrustworthy wife. Entering my midlife sexpot era. That would be great.”Adultery starts this October on ITV1 and ITVX.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionRomola GaraiDramafeaturesShareReuse this content

consentMasterpiece of the weekAn Angel in Red With a Lute by Giovanni Ambrogio de Predis, c1495–1499View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Album/AlamyLeonardo da Vinci is said to have been sent to the court of Milan by Lorenzo de’ Medici to play on a bizarre stringed instrument of his own invention. His drawings do include inventions for novel musical devices. This painting is closely influenced by Leonardo: not only does it imitate his shadowed, dreamy style but it was originally part of the same altarpiece in Milan as his National Gallery masterpiece The Virgin of the Rocks. Leonardo, De Predis and every other Renaissance artist associated music with the mathematics of Pythagoras and the harmony of the universe: the angel here is playing, could we but hear it, such heavenly music. But it is the lute that suggests a very direct influence by Leonardo. The precise and detailed, entrancing way that De Predis depicts its nine strings and the angel’s highly realistic fingering echo Leonardo’s fascination with machinery and technology – in this case the sweet machinery of music. Painted under the hypnotic sway of the Tuscan polymath who was Milan’s court artist, this painting holds you charmed and soothed by the sound of silence.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in touchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsLondon listingsScotland and Ireland listingsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m lovingly making fun of everyone I’ve ever met’: on the set of Leo Reich’s gen Z sitcom | TV comedy | The Guardian
description: The comedy wunderkind shot to fame with his show Literally, Who Cares?! and a role in Lena Dunham’s Too Much. Now he’s bringing his take on self-involved zoomers to the TV screen. Just don’t call him the voice of a generation
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: The comedy wunderkind shot to fame with his show Literally, Who Cares?! and a role in Lena Dunham’s Too Much. Now he’s bringing his take on self-involved zoomers to the TV screen. Just don’t call him the voice of a generation
Content: Squat goals … Leo Reich.Photograph: Raphael Neal/Channel 4View image in fullscreenSquat goals … Leo Reich.Photograph: Raphael Neal/Channel 4TV comedy‘I’m lovingly making fun of everyone I’ve ever met’: on the set of Leo Reich’s gen Z sitcomThe comedy wunderkind shot to fame with his show Literally, Who Cares?! and a role in Lena Dunham’s Too Much. Now he’s bringing his take on self-involved zoomers to the TV screen. Just don’t call him the voice of a generationRachel AroestiFri 9 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeo Reich’s new Channel 4 sitcom is “Girls meets Peep Show. That’s always my favourite part of pitching anything: choose two really good things and say it’s a mix of those!” says the comedian with a slight smirk. Still, it’s a fair summary: It Gets Worse is a bracingly candid, occasionally provocative hangout comedy about twentysomethings floundering professionally and personally in the big city that comes accompanied by a strong stench of British bleakness (see: the title, for a start). Yet it does fail to flag one key aspect. While Girls and Peep Show covered the travails of millennials and gen X respectively, It Gets Worse is happening now – making it the UK’s first true gen Z sitcom.Or not. “I’m sceptical of the idea that generations have any real unifying features across the board, so I don’t want it to be like: this is a gen Z sitcom!” says the 28-year-old. In fact, it soon becomes clear that It Gets Worse is deliberately USP-less. We first meet Reich’s Ethan – “a middle-class loser gay guy” – and his pals Sam and Abi as they’re packing up their London flatshare, having been forced out because of a rent hike. But this isn’t the start of a meditation on the cost of living crisis – or anything else. “The point isn’t there’s some big concept where everyone’s a superhero, it’s: these are some people dot dot dot.” When I ask how closely the final show resembles his original idea, Reich looks askance. “The idea, I would say, was quite broad …”I’d wager that the real idea – the main idea, the only idea – was to give a sitcom (any sitcom) to Reich, who since the pandemic has established himself as the future of comedy with remarkable ease. Following a stint in Footlights at Cambridge and a lockdown that birthed a few cleverly mordant TikToks (“for us, there were no rules! Apart from obviously don’t go outside,” he quips in one clip captioned “telling my kids about my wild 20s”), Reich took his debut standup show to the Edinburgh fringe in 2022. Literally, Who Cares?! saw him pose as a heightened parody of a stereotypical zoomer: “a deliriously self-involved, fragmentarily informed, habitually self-pitying, comprehensively cynical member of Generation Z”, as a celebratory New Yorker profile put it the following year. (A British reviewer likened his character to a 21st-century Rick from The Young Ones.) Reich performed his ingenious script, which merged pastiche with drolly accurate observations about the modern world, looking like a pre-Raphaelite club kid: dramatic eye shadow, short shorts, mop of curls. It was an immediate hit, and swiftly picked up for a HBO special – unheard of for a fledgling British comedian. No wonder he’s been given carte blanche to bring his sensibility to TV.View image in fullscreenFlat broke … Reich with Olive Gray (left) and Emily Fairn.Photograph: Jack BarnesIt’s an autumn day when I visit the set of It Gets Worse in south-east London, where a former spice warehouse is doubling as the squat Sam has moved into. Reich is in this scene – an awkward sex party – but still finds time to swing by the monitors to see how things are looking and – I quickly realise from the script in my hand – ad lib half of Ethan’s ludicrous small talk (there’s nothing on the page about Tutankhamun or the idea that as a society “we need to get back to the land”).Afterwards, in a liminal space upstairs, Reich is vaping and sipping a canned coffee. He encourages improvisation: the show “is about mess and people being fucking stupid and delusional, so I think it suits a level of roughness … thank God!” Yet as a longtime standup fanatic (as a teenager he’d make his mum take him to the now defunct alternative north London comedy club the Invisible Dot; his heroes included Simon Amstell and James Acaster), he remains serious about the art of comedy. He describes his on-set role as “a sort of joke warden”, who steps in when “the rhythm’s a little bit out” in his castmates’ delivery. I notice one particular line about a party guest – “Leon’s cousin from Tring” – is non-negotiable in terms of both syntax and cadence.double quotation markThis is a very specific time to be looking down the barrel of the rest of your lifeReich may shrug off any voice of a generation label, but It Gets Worse does feel distinctly of the moment. That’s partly thanks to the protagonists: “a campy gay guy, uptight northern girl and mixed-race artist” have typically been restricted to “side character” status on screen in the past, he says. But it also has a lot to do with that depressing title. While gen Z isn’t a monolith, its members do all have something significant in common: they are coming of age during the permacrisis, the omnipresent financial, political and ecological precarity that is making the future feel hopeless for many. “Trying to say this without being cringe, but it’s a very specific time to be looking down the barrel of the rest of your life,” says Reich. “All of these traditional institutions like marriage and climbing the career ladder don’t really exist, or if they do exist you can’t trust them. There’s a vague sense of massive anxiety.”Reich is, presumably, not feeling the fear to quite the same degree. Since his breakthrough he has appeared in Lena Dunham’s Netflix comeback Too Much (she returns the favour here by playing Abi’s boss, one of a host of big-name cameos including Andrew Scott and Zadie Smith) and now, obviously, has his own sitcom. But that doesn’t mean he can’t identify with his characters. It Gets Worse isn’t an issue-led drama but an attempt “to recreate a mood or feeling of helplessness, which isn’t about success in a brutal material way. It’s an existential feeling of being lost and stupid and not knowing what to do.”In the show, all three leads have “radically different responses to the broader existential anxiety”, says Reich. Ethan sees himself as “a charming clown” whose philosophy is “fuck it, let’s just have a laugh, live in the moment so you don’t have to plan your future”. He is easily the luckiest of the trio – his living situation is solved when he moves back in with his London-based mum (a sublimely irritable Vicki Pepperdine) – but far from aspirational. There’s an arch Fleabagian nihilism to his humiliating sexual experiences (including one with a therapist played by Scott), which dovetails with the sense that Ethan is “being fucked by life but kind of enjoying it”, says Reich, who tends to think of sex as inherently hilarious (“it’s such an insane thing to do!”).Meanwhile, Abi, played by Emily Fairn (The Responder, House of Guinness), takes the good girl route, chasing the hallmarks of an Instagrammable lifestyle via industrious perfectionism. Sam (Olive Gray) is a tutor and wannabe writer who pursues the same meaning and control by building her “own kind of life and rejecting social norms”, says Reich. Her cynicism has also led to a kind of radical independence. “I think,” says Gray, “that she’s the type of person who believes no one owes anyone anything and everyone is responsible for themselves – to her own detriment and the detriment of the people around her, unfortunately.”Unlike many messy millennial dramedies, It Gets Worse clearly aims to replace myopia with multiplicity. Fairn appreciated the show’s acknowledgment of class dynamics, like how “Ethan makes fun of Abi for working so hard, but that’s how she affords her rent”. She was encouraged to keep her native Liverpool accent and channel her own experiences as a “working-class northerner” into Abi, who leans into or plays down her accent depending on the situation – and occasionally slips in some scouse slang. (It was Fairn’s suggestion for Abi to call Sam a “jarg writer. Leo was like: I don’t even need to know what that means, that sounds hilarious!”)Even so, Ethan is quite obviously the comic engine. Like Reich himself, he is winningly self-deprecating, disarmingly frank, hyper-articulate and endlessly amusing company. There is naturally some crossover between him and Reich’s chronically narcissistic persona in Literally, Who Cares?! (he’s another “quite irritating gay guy because I can’t really do anything else”), but Ethan is aware of his own ridiculousness and can laugh at himself. And whereas the standup show was a precision-tooled piece of satire, It Gets Worse is a heartfelt paean to friendship and, in a weird way, a bit of “wish fulfilment” for its creator: he’s never lived in a grotty flat with friends, moving straight from his parents’ home to his own place.Leo Reich review – uproarious Gen-Z narcissist blazes throughRead moreThat said, any sentimentality is countered by a fierce joke rate, plus Reich’s aversion to cosy earnestness: he is still trying to send up his peers, just in a slightly more subtle way. “Sometimes I want to be made fun of by TV and I think the point of this is really lovingly making fun of everyone I’ve ever met.” Despite the real difficulties faced by gen Z, this is ultimately a show about “people who don’t have really, really serious problems complaining all the time”. For that reason, he’s anticipating at least some intergenerational pushback. “I don’t know if everyone’s always in the mood to hear a fine 27-year-old going: actually, being kind of scared of the future is really hard! It’s like: well, it’s not!”It Gets Worse begins 22 October on Channel 4 in the UK and Binge in Australia on 23 October.Explore more on these topicsTV comedyComedyTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Infinite genius’: Yiyun Li on Anne Carson | Nobel prize in literature | The Guardian
description: When her sons died, the Book of Goose author turned to Grief Lessons, Carson’s translation of four plays by Euripides. She reflects on the ‘life sustaining’ work of an extraordinary writer
Author: Yiyun Li
Headline: When her sons died, the Book of Goose author turned to Grief Lessons, Carson’s translation of four plays by Euripides. She reflects on the ‘life sustaining’ work of an extraordinary writer
Content: ‘She does not subjugate or manipulate her words. She lets them be’ … Anne Carson.Photograph: TT News Agency/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreen‘She does not subjugate or manipulate her words. She lets them be’ … Anne Carson.Photograph: TT News Agency/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Nobel prize in literature‘Infinite genius’: Yiyun Li on Anne CarsonWhen her sons died the Book of Goose author turned to Grief Lessons, Carson’s translation of four plays by Euripides. She reflects on the ‘life sustaining’ work of an extraordinary writerWhere to start with: Anne Carson‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Anne CarsonYiyun LiFri 9 Oct 2026 07.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is preposterous to agree to write a short piece on Anne Carson’s work. The task is impossible, akin to that of solving the mathematical problem of dividing zero by zero. If one had the power to solve it, perhaps one would have some confidence in attempting to write about Anne Carson’s work. Attempting, I say, not succeeding. In attempting to do so, I shall emphasise that all words fall short in extreme situations, which not only include unfathomable losses (of children, in my case) but also include articulating anything about Anne Carson’s work.One could start with Carson’s words. “Words, if you let them, will do what they want to do and what they have to do.” (Autobiography of Red) But to let the words exist in their own desires and yearnings and frustrations and confusions, to let the words scream with inarticulable pain or tell a riddle with a twinkling smile or make love to one another – how many of us have achieved that kind of mastery of words? But, oh no, mastery is the wrong word here. Only the minor and the greedy and the power-thirsty writers want to be the masters of the words. Carson does not subjugate or manipulate her words. She lets them be; and lets herself be led by the words – hers, and the ancients’ translated into unforgettable English by her.And what extraordinary words they are! Say, let’s suppose every person in the world could be viewed as a formation of some words – a poem, a story, a play, a novel, an earnest and muddle-minded op-ed, a loud slogan, or a much repeated and tired cliche, or, simply, a line of ellipses, or some white space (if we include words in this game, we must also include punctuations and silences).In a gathering of a vast number of word formations, those written byAnne Carsonwould surely be easily recognisable. The fact that they exist at all is a miracle, because many rules have been bent or broken to make them possible. Nevertheless, they are not anarchists or revolutionaries. They are both mortal and immortal because they know their priorities (“Love is not conditional. / Living is very conditional.”– The Beauty of the Husband). They are compelling because they are compelled (“I know / you find me extreme / in my grief. / I bear it hard. / But I tell you I have no choice. / It compels. I act because it compels” – Elektra, translated by Carson). They, beings unto themselves, are defiant (“That which is known, attained, possessed, cannot be an object of desire.” – Eros, the Bittersweet). Their concerns are vast and undefinable; one blunders if one uses words like philosophical or metaphysical, tragical or dramatic.For those who were less fortunate, written by a lesser mind, there is no worry because any encounter with Anne Carson’s creations expands, deepens, mystifies and clarifies our minds; a paragraph from her is enough for a long meandering in a less visited landscape, a line is enough for one to understand oneself better.I teach Anne Carson from time to time, but to say one can teach Anne Carson is also preposterous. One hands her work to the next generation, trusting that there are bound to be kindred spirits among them. I have done this for the past 20 years, and like to watch the first encounter of young, inquisitive minds with Anne Carson. Some of them, like me, will remain her lifelong readers. Some will find her work the only words to read in life’s extremities.This morning, when the news came out that Anne Carson is the newest Nobel Laureate, I immediately moved all of Anne Carson’s books from my bookcase to my desk, intending to spend a morning with them. Then I realised that the most important book of hers for me – Grief Lessons, her translation of four Euripides plays – was missing. It was likely misplaced because I taught it in a recent semester. After our older son Vincent died in 2017, I spent a winter reading that book. Then I read it again after our younger son James died. To say Carson’s words are life-sustaining is an understatement. What is infinity divided by infinity? Or, infinity subtracted by infinity? Or, zero multiplied by infinity? Reading Carson gives one the perspective and the courage to live in an often inexplicable life.It is joyful news to see Anne Carson recognised with the Nobel prize. Sometimes there comes the good news that is rightandjust. But that is only as simple as knowing one plus one makes two. The recognition underlines the infiniteness of Anne Carson’s genius, but to get a better sense of that genius, one only needs to turn to any page of any one of her books.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Gromit finally gets a voice … and it’s Martin Freeman | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: After 37 years, the staunchly silent dog will speak for the first time in the audiobook of his autobiography – and it turns out he sounds like a hobbit
Author: Alexi Duggins
Headline: After 37 years, the staunchly silent dog will speak for the first time in the audiobook of his autobiography – and it turns out he sounds like a hobbit
Content: ‘Who could possibly be the voice of a character everyone feels they know, but nobody’s actually heard?’Photograph: PRView image in fullscreen‘Who could possibly be the voice of a character everyone feels they know, but nobody’s actually heard?’Photograph: PRTelevision & radioGromit finally gets a voice … and it’s Martin FreemanAfter 37 years, the staunchly silent dog will speak for the first time in the audiobook of his autobiography – and it turns out he sounds like a hobbitAlexi DugginsFri 9 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe has been on screen for 37 years, but he has never uttered a word. Now, Gromit will speak for the first time – with the voice of the Hobbit starMartin Freeman.The claymation dog, who has partnered with his eccentric inventor-owner Wallace in a series of Oscar-winning films including The Wrong Trousers, A Close Shave and Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit, is releasing an autobiography this month – including an audiobook edition.“When you create a character who has no voice and whose facial expressions are everything, what do you do when your publisher reminds you there’ll be an audiobook?” said Nick Park, the animator and film-maker who created the series. “Who could possibly be the voice of a character everyone feels they know, but nobody’s actually heard?View image in fullscreen‘He’s reading Gromit’s story as Gromit put it’ … Martin Freeman.“The more I thought about it, the more I realised Martin Freeman was the obvious choice, really. I was genuinely thrilled and honoured when he said yes.”Freeman previously honed the role of put-upon sidekick in his Bafta- and Emmy-winning turn as Dr John Watson toBenedict Cumberbatch’s unpredictable detective in Sherlock. It should stand him in good stead to voice Gromit – who has had to put up with Wallace variously falling in love with a serial killer, welcoming in a hardened criminal penguin as a lodger, and inventing a hackable robot gnome that spawned an army of evil garden decorations.Freeman won’t be taking too much creative licence with the character, however. “Martin is not doing a Gromit ‘voice’ as such,” said Park. “He’s reading Gromit’s story as Gromit put it: his inner thoughts, his candid insights and endless witticisms, bringing to them his usual colour, thoughtfulness and wry humour.”View image in fullscreenThe book is not the only spin-off of the franchise in the works.Larger Than Life, an immersive, behind-the-scenes experience projected across four 11-metre walls, will open on 14 October at the Lightroom in King’s Cross, London.Grand: The Autobiography of Gromit, as told to Nick Park, will be published on 22 October.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioAudiobooksTelevisionWallace & GromitAnimation on TVMartin FreemannewsShareReuse this content

title: Lightsaber Darth Vader used in ‘I am your father’ Star Wars duel up for auction | Star Wars | The Guardian
description: Saber is expected to fetch at least $1m and is one of more than two dozen props that will be up for sale
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Saber is expected to fetch at least $1m and is one of more than two dozen props that will be up for sale
Content: A scene from the 1980 film The Empire Strikes Back.Photograph: Lucasfilm/Fox/Kobal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA scene from the 1980 film The Empire Strikes Back.Photograph: Lucasfilm/Fox/Kobal/ShutterstockStar WarsLightsaber Darth Vader used in ‘I am your father’ Star Wars duel up for auctionSaber is expected to fetch at least $1m and is one of more than two dozen props that will be up for saleAssociated PressFri 9 Oct 2026 09.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 13.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA lightsaber used by Darth Vader in theStar Warsduel where he tells Luke Skywalker “I am your father” is going up for sale at Heritage Auctions next month.The Vader saber, also used in Return of the Jedi, is expected to fetch at least $1m. It is one of more than two dozen lightsaber props that will be up for sale at the auction that spans Star Wars Episodes I through IX and other films and TV shows from the universe George Lucas created.View image in fullscreenA lightsaber used by the character Darth Vader in the film The Empire Strikes Back.Photograph: Heritage Auctions/APOthers include dueling lightsabers wielded by Ewan McGregor’s Obi-Wan Kenobi and Hayden Christensen’s Anakin Skywalker in Revenge of the Sith that are expected to go for at least $10,000 apiece.In July, a lightsaber with Luke Skywalker’s severed hand from The Empire Strikes Back sold for $3.75m at auction, the highest price ever fetched for a prop used in a Star Wars film according to the auction house.An EE-3 carbine blaster wielded by Boba Fett throughout The Empire Strikes Back is estimated to bring in more than $100,000.Also included are a Yoda puppet hand used by Frank Oz in the character’s original appearance in The Empire Strikes Back, C-3PO actor Anthony Daniels’ signed, personal third-draft screenplay for the original 1977 Star Wars and a TIE Fighter pilot helmet from Rogue One: A Star Wars Story.Explore more on these topicsStar WarsStar Wars: The Empire Strikes BackCollectingScience fiction and fantasy filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Please, sir, can I have a walk? Dickens biographer finds likely inspiration for Oliver Twist | Charles Dickens | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Theresa Musgrove unearths newspaper archives showing one Alice Shepherd was severely punished in 1836 for similarly innocent request
Author: Dalya Alberge
Headline: Exclusive: Theresa Musgrove unearths newspaper archives showing one Alice Shepherd was severely punished in 1836 for similarly innocent request
Content: Mark Lester in the title role of the 1968 musical OLIVER!Photograph: Cinetext Bildarchiv/Romulus/AllstarView image in fullscreenMark Lester in the title role of the 1968 musical OLIVER!Photograph: Cinetext Bildarchiv/Romulus/AllstarCharles DickensPlease, sir, can I have a walk? Dickens biographer finds likely inspiration for Oliver TwistExclusive: Theresa Musgrove unearths newspaper archives showing one Alice Shepherd was severely punished in 1836 for similarly innocent requestDalya AlbergeFri 9 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCould a consumptive young woman called Alice Shepherd have been the inspiration for Oliver Twist? That is a question now being posed by a historian, who has discovered parallels between the brutality suffered by a real-life pauper incarcerated in one of Victorian London’s notorious workhouses and Charles Dickens’s fictional orphan.In researching a new book on Dickens, Theresa Musgrove unearthed 1836 newspaper reports on Alice Shepherd, who endured starvation and solitary confinement within a workhouse in Hendon, after a magistrate ruled she was to be punished for daring to ask for permission to take a walk.In his classic novel, which was published in monthly instalments from 1837 to 1839, Dickens wrote that nine-year-old Oliver was hauled up before a magistrate and imprisoned in a “dark and solitary room” for having the temerity to ask for a second helping of gruel, with the poignant words: “Please, sir, I want some more.”The starving child was locked up for week. Dickens wrote: “Oliver was the victim of a systematic course of treachery and deception.”View image in fullscreenAn illustration by James Mahoney from The Adventures of Oliver Twist, Chapman and Hall edition, 1838. Original caption: ‘Stop thief; Oliver is pursued by an angry crowd.’Photograph: Bridgeman/Getty ImagesNewspaper reports record that Alice Shepherd was put in a “straightjacket”, having been “in a state of great agitation”. A Rev Theodore Williams, in his capacity as a magistrate and chair of the local board of guardians responsible for overseeing the conduct of Hendon’s old workhouse, recommended a punishment for her “disgusting conduct”.She was put in solitary confinement for 24 hours, and starved on a diet of bread and water until the next meeting of the board – which met once a fortnight.Another local magistrate, also one of the workhouse’s guardians of the board, tried in vain to defend her, arguing that such “a thin spare woman apparently suffering from consumption … [was the] last person … to whom such a punishment should have been inflicted”.Musgrove told the Guardian: “When you read the report of her punishment, it is almost, word for word, like a description of Oliver Twist when he is punished after asking for more.”She said: “The reaction to Oliver Twist’s ‘impertinence’ in asking for more food is perhaps an echo of Alice’s daring to ask to go out for a walk: a reasonable request met by fury by those whose job it was to enforce the unremitting authority of the board of guardians, by whose mercy the undeserving poor were granted the means of a life of such bleak subsistence.”Her research features in her new book, titledCharles Dickens and his Hidden Family History, which is published this week by Pen & Sword Books.She writes: “Both Oliver and Alice were subjected to solitary confinement, and yet, as we learn, the parish boy’s punishment was to be considered not so bad because he was allowed out into the stone yard to wash under the pump, just as Reverend Williams pointed out … that the room appropriated for the solitary confinement and starvation of Alice Shepherd ‘looked upon the yard where all the other paupers were, and therefore, was not a very severe punishment’.“In mid-January, within weeks of this story being reported, Dickens was writing to his publisher Bentley that he had ‘hit upon a capital notion for myself, and one which will bring Cruikshank out’. In other words, the creation of Oliver Twist had begun, and indeed the first chapters would be published in February 1837, illustrated by the starkly graphic work of George Cruikshank.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe notes that Dickens was familiar with Hendon, in the present-day London borough of Barnet: “Hendon and Barnet are mentioned, for example, in Oliver Twist … but also there are other references in his letters and journalism that reveal a knowledge of Hendon and a fondness for the area, which was within walking or riding distance of the city itself, a quiet landscape of villages and farmland.“In the later stages of Oliver Twist, after his brutal killing of Nancy, Bill Sikes goes on the run … After sleeping rough, Sikes heads off towards Hendon, but the people there seem suspicious of him and he goes back to the Heath.”Oliver Twist exposed the brutality of poverty in Victorian Britain. Dickens became a tireless campaigner for social reform, having been scarred by his own childhood experiences after his father was incarcerated in a debtors’ prison and, aged about 12, he was sent to work in a blacking factory.Leon Litvack, a leading Dickens expert and professor of Victorian studies at Queen’s University Belfast, said it was “perfectly feasible” that Dickens was inspired by Alice Shepherd, as newspaper reports were among “an amalgam of influences that sparked his imagination, distilled into a coherent narrative”, particularly early in his career.He added: “Dickens was a journalist before he was a novelist, so he was well aware of the power of sensation. He was fascinated by the workhouse and aware of what was appearing in the press about particular abuses.”Explore more on these topicsCharles DickensHistorynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Me and the lads would not survive a day in here’: inside TV’s utterly stunning, Bafta-winning prison drama | Television | The Guardian
description: The third series of Jimmy McGovern’s breathtaking series Time stars David Tennant – and might just be its best ever. We go behind the scenes
Author: Gabriel Tate
Headline: The third series of Jimmy McGovern’s breathtaking series Time stars David Tennant – and might just be its best ever. We go behind the scenes
Content: ‘It’s no way to bring up kids, is it?’ … David Tennant as Bailey and Ollie McNulty as Peter in Time.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/PAView image in fullscreen‘It’s no way to bring up kids, is it?’ … David Tennant as Bailey and Ollie McNulty as Peter in Time.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/PATelevision‘Me and the lads would not survive a day in here’: inside TV’s utterly stunning, Bafta-winning prison dramaThe third series of Jimmy McGovern’s breathtaking series Time stars David Tennant – and might just be its best ever. We go behind the scenesGabriel TateFri 9 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Idon’t think you would find a young offender institution (YOI) in which stories like these haven’t happened. Seventeen years of age, loads of energy, hormones, bravado – you know they’ll kick off. It must be an absolute nightmare.”Yes, Jimmy McGovern has gone back to prison again. After two series of Time, which toldstories from men’sandwomen’s institutions, he has turned his attention to perhaps the most distressing ones of all. Set in a YOI, it’s full of tales of bad decisions, directionless rage and lost potential at the most vulnerable of ages. If this third series is, as he suggests, the last, it is quite the curtain call.I have come to Downpatrick, just outside Belfast, to look around the fictional institution of HMP Alderwick. We are in a former school whose strip-lit spaces are doubling as the prison’s gated corridors, reception area, visiting rooms, staff room and a chapel that is firmly in the realm of functional rather than celestial. Other scenes were shot in the former HMP Belfast (now called Crumlin Road Gaol) and HMP Hydebank Wood, an active young offender centre, but the school locations are quite grim enough.Alderwick’s teenage prisoners include James (Louis McCartney), estranged from his parents after an apparently unforgivable act, Peter (Ollie McNulty), one of five on remand for the killing of an innocent man and Christopher (Chukwubuikem Molokwu), whose Kenyan mother hasn’t seen him since he was four and whose stammer (a condition shared with McGovern), combined with her lack of English, make communication between them almost impossible.View image in fullscreen‘Me and the lads were like, we would not survive a day in here’ … Louis McCartney as inmate James in the third series of Jimmy McGovern’s Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyI watch filming while standing next to a coffin and five headstones – a strong hint that all may not end well for everyone – and indeed the scene follows an incident of appalling violence. A small group includingDavid Tennant’s veteran prison officer Bailey is being led in the Lord’s Prayer bySiobhan Finneran’s chaplain Marie-Louise (“I think my face must suggest either religious people or addicts …”), who has been the moral and spiritual heart of all three series even as she is now enduring a deep crisis of faith after the abrupt end of her affair with a Catholic priest.“She’s heartbroken,” Finneran – a “very lapsed” Catholic – tells me in her trailer. “The bishop has sent the priest away and told Marie-Louise she needs to grow up. She can’t understand why he couldn’t have been kinder and more Christian, but she’s determined not to be judgmental herself and to throw herself into being there for these kids. I spoke to a chaplain before series one who told me: ‘You will never be more needed than in that job’, which I’ve never forgotten. A couple of friends who were watching that series rang up and said: ‘I can’t wait for you to knock on the door [in the show], because we can probably have 30 seconds of calm where nobody’s going to try and kill each other.’”Bailey enjoys precious little such respite, but Tennant still leaped at the chance to work with “the guv’nor”. “Jimmy writes very human, inconsistent, believable people, so Bailey makes sense to me. He’s perfectly good at his job. It gives him a routine, but he’s got into a rut until he’s forced to examine where he’s at professionally and, when his wife leaves him, personally: how he’s got there, and how he feels about that.”After 35 years in the service, Tennant says while sitting in the chapel, Bailey is thoroughly disillusioned. “He once had respect and enthusiasm for the job, but it has become very compromised. He feels prisons are now just to hold these boys in place and keep them out of the way, rather than to rehabilitate them in any meaningful way. He talks about how there used to be education, a library, training, and nowadays there’s not enough staff or opportunity, which he finds very difficult.”During a scene later in the afternoon, Bailey is told the young men must remain banged up all day due to staff shortages. “They’ll be raging,” he warns, his frustration and concern palpable for those in a place where self-harm, despair and violence are already commonplace. Once used as last resorts, 23-hour bang-ups and keep-aparts (where groups from particular postcodes are stopped from socialising) are, says McGovern, being deployed with increasing frequency since Covid. “It offered them the perfect excuse to keep these kids cooped up longer, but you’ve got to allow people to associate or nothing will improve. It’s no way to bring up kids, is it?”View image in fullscreen‘Jimmy writes very human, inconsistent, believable people’ … Tennant and McCartney in Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyFor young men, to be bottled up to stew over grievances real or imagined, the effects are predictably disastrous. Filming in a real prison hammered this home.“I’d never really considered why people might be in jail, or that idea of not judging a book by its cover,” says Molokwu, one of a number of the young cast for whom this is, remarkably, their first acting job. “I realised that me and Christopher have something in common, coming from countries with less opportunities – Kenya for him, Nigeria for me – and moving to a country with more. The difference is that I’m blessed with a healthy lifestyle and a loving family, but he’s still a good-hearted kid, just vulnerable because of growing up in care with a stammer, someone who hasn’t had the opportunity to learn how to make the best decision in a bad situation.”McCartney, the exception among the debutants as a Tony nominee (forStranger Things: the First Shadow), was also profoundly affected by the role. “I’d get in this freezing cell, they’d lock the door, and you’d think: yeah, simple enough, I’ll do that. But the scene is three minutes long, so you’re sitting on your bed, tray in front of you, hearing muffled voices. Then there are pictures of James’s family, a dog, some trips that he’s taken … You’re just sitting there like you’re strapped in some electric chair, seeing all of your mistakes. It’s so important to remember these guys are kids who, maybe a month ago, might have been having a family dinner. It made it so real. Me and the other lads were like, we would not survive a day in here.”“We were in a young offender institution and got shown into a young man’s room,” says McGovern. “He must have been 17 or 18, recently given a life sentence for murder. He was sat on his bed, every flicker crushed out of him, devastated. What changed the dynamic for a second was that I got down to his eye level. He wasn’t expecting that, because he’s used to officers standing and talking down to him. I asked him: ‘What’s it like here?’ Then he looked around like, am I able to answer this question?, seeing officers, and said: ‘Well, it’s all right …’ It was a strange conversation, but it moved me immensely.”View image in fullscreen‘She’s determined not to be judgmental’ …Tennant with Finneran in Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyMcGovern has spent his writing life getting down to look people in the eye; the results have a rawness, honesty and empathy that few writers can match, frequently fuelled by a righteous anger that surfaces when I mention prisons losing out in the intensifying competition for investment from an ever-shrinking public purse. “And yet we always find resources for war,” he says. “Why can’t we find it for prisons?”That debate is further compromised by the relative ease of arguing for putting money into, say, schools or the NHS instead. “Yes, prisoners have made their own beds and deserve to be there,” sighs Tennant. “That’s the thinking, isn’t it? But if we aspire to be a civilised society, then we aspire to help the most damaged member of that society. Our responsibility is to make sure we’re not just locking people away so we don’t have to look at them, but to help them find a better future. That applies especially to these young men because there’s more potential for a life lived well. We’re all trying our best and we all make mistakes, so that vulnerability combined with that possibility is heartbreaking.”The indefatigable McGovern remains unbowed by the further deterioration ofthe Prison Servicesince the first series of Time in 2021; after all, his Bafta-winning 1996 drama Hillsborough rekindled a campaign for justice and helped shift the focus of culpability from fans to police. Thirty years later, the so-called Hillsborough law designed to prevent institutional cover-ups is finally heading for the statute books, so McGovern is used to the long game.“But I wouldn’t do this unless I loved doing it,” he says. “I hopeAndy Burnham, who I know through the Hillsborough campaign [and whointroduced the bill in 2017], will bring about the changes we need in the prison system. But the real problem with society is that we find a wonderful principle, like justice or Christian faith or solidarity, and establish an institution around it. Then the institution becomes beautiful and we start to defend it at the expense of the very principle that founded it. So, inside a YOI, we can’t tell the truth because it will get us and the institution into trouble, so let’s not. It’s a major problem which ought to be addressed … but it never will be.”In the meantime, he will keep on telling stories that bring us all down to eye level, daring us to look away.Time is on BBC One on 11 OctoberThis article was amended on 9 October 2026. It has been 30 years since the television film Hillsborough, not 20 as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionDavid TennantPrisons and probationUK criminal justicefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: things get nasty in War’s blockbuster divorce | Television | The Guardian
description: One of the lawyers is a mole in Sienna Miller and Dominic West’s soapy drama. Plus: the Lionesses shoot for the World Cup. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: One of the lawyers is a mole in Sienna Miller and Dominic West’s soapy drama. Plus: the Lionesses shoot for the World Cup. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Love is a battlefield … Dominic West in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesView image in fullscreenLove is a battlefield … Dominic West in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: things get nasty in War’s blockbuster divorceOne of the lawyers is a mole in Sienna Miller and Dominic West’s soapy drama. Plus: the Lionesses shoot for the World Cup. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Graeme Virtue,Ali CatterallandSimon WardellFri 9 Oct 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWar9pm, Sky AtlanticThe naughty divorce drama – made even juicier by its casting of two huge stars, Sienna Miller and Dominic West, whose own eventful relationships have been under the press spotlight – picks up after actor Carla is served on the red carpet (inspired by a representative for Jason Sudeikis handing Olivia Wilde custody papers on stage). Things look even worse for her as eager junior solicitor Johnny starts his first day on her legal team – as a mole for her husband’s side.Hollie RichardsonGardeners’ World8pm, BBC TwoMonty Don guides us into autumn in his last series of the well-loved gardening show. Pruning roses, planting spring cabbages and storing apples are all on the week’s to-do list. Elsewhere, Rachel de Thame learns about wild flowers that help wildlife, and Toby Buckland has some handy budget gardening hacks.HRThe Walking Dead: Dead City9pm, Sky OneRoad trip! With medical supplies running low, Maggie and dishy surgeon Luis strike out from zombified New York to try to locate a suspiciously well-stocked trader. But back at base, there are ominous rumblings when astute community leader Renata tries to domesticate bat-swinging badass Negan.Graeme VirtuePlay for Today: Closing Time9.05pm, Channel 5“See anything you like?” kebab shop worker Mo (Antonio Aakeel) asks Ellora Torchia’s lawyer Laila. She does: him. Pity she is on her hen night, and he’s an illegal migrant. Is she prepared to take the ensuing affair to another level? And what bigger dangers might they be inviting, professionally and personally? A gut-punch drama from Mina Barber.Ali CatterallThe Graham Norton Show10.40pm, BBC OneA few months ago, Alexander Skarsgård and Olivia Colman caused quite a stir with a horny trailer for their new film Wicker – leading to many a “husband material” meme. Now, they’re telling Graham what fans can expect. Plus, John Malkovich chats about his dark new comedy Wild Horse Nine and there’s music from Orville Peck.HRGetting It Back: The Story of Cymande10.40pm, BBC FourView image in fullscreenThe way they were: Cymande, circa 1970.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesCult London collective Cymande were funk pioneers from the Windrush generation who found themselves marginalised in the racially charged UK of the 70s. But years after disbanding, their cosmic grooves inspired hip-hop hits in the US. This affecting film charts the group’s origins, afterlife and resurgence.GVFilm choiceOasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger(Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace, 2026),Disney+With more sold-out dates next year, 90s rock blokes Oasis are sustaining the pomp and circumstance they generated with their 2025 reunion, the subject of this entertaining film. The two directors, with writer Steven Knight, document the tour from tense rehearsals to the warm glow of US acclaim – and, more interestingly, the thawing of relations between Liam and Noel Gallagher after 15 years of silence. The brothers’ contrasting styles are endlessly fascinating: Liam, with his “big boy pants” on, is cocky and sharply witty, while a nervous Noel seems surprised at how well it’s all going. The hatchet-burying takes a while but there’s always a singalong hit to catch while you wait.Simon WardellLonglegs(Osgood Perkins, 2024),10pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenUnsettling … Maika Monroe in Longlegs.Photograph: APThis is a film in which every shot is creepy. Whether it’s a weird angle, shadowy lighting or just some pale yellow walls (as seen in Backrooms), there’s an ever-present dread that something bad is going to happen – and it very often does. Osgood Perkins’ nerve-shredding horror follows a series of crimes in which fathers murder their families, then kill themselves. Left at each scene is a letter in code, signed “Longlegs”. Maika Monroe’s intuitive FBI agent Lee takes the case and becomes increasingly haunted by it, while Nicolas Cage gives a suitably out-there cameo as her nemesis.SWLive sportWomen’s international football:Greece v England,5pm, ITV1Leah Williamson returns to captain England in the first leg of their World Cup qualifying play-off semi-final in Heraklion.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mao’s Last Dancer Li Cunxin on his long-awaited follow-up: ‘I don’t think my publisher expected it to take 14 years!’ | Australian books | The Guardian
description: As The Lucky Son picks up where Cunxin’s 2003 memoir left off, the renowned Chinese Australian ballet dancer reflects on sacrifices made by his wife, his years at a stockbroker, and his success leading the Queensland Ballet
Author: Tim Byrne
Headline: As The Lucky Son picks up where Cunxin’s 2003 memoir left off, the renowned Chinese Australian ballet dancer reflects on sacrifices made by his wife, his years at a stockbroker, and his success leading the Queensland Ballet
Content: Ballet dancer Li Cunxin’s new memoir, The Lucky Son, is the sequel to the internationally successful Mao’s Last Dancer.Photograph: David Kelly/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBallet dancer Li Cunxin’s new memoir, The Lucky Son, is the sequel to the internationally successful Mao’s Last Dancer.Photograph: David Kelly/The GuardianAustralian booksInterviewMao’s Last Dancer Li Cunxin on his long-awaited follow-up: ‘I don’t think my publisher expected it to take 14 years!’Tim ByrneAs The Lucky Son picks up where Cunxin’s 2003 memoir left off, the renowned Chinese Australian ballet dancer reflects on sacrifices made by his wife, his years at a stockbroker, and his success leading the Queensland BalletGet our weekend culture and lifestyle emailFri 9 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 20.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome people live such extraordinary lives that a single autobiography simply won’t suffice. Li Cunxin has now written two. The renowned ballet dancer and former artistic director ofQueenslandBallet had hoped he was finished writing his story after the phenomenal international success of his 2003 memoir, Mao’s Last Dancer. But life had other plans.“Actually, I had signed a contract with Penguin Random House for a follow-up,” Cunxin says, from his home in Brisbane. “It was going to be about the lives of my brothers and friends in China, and the ways the country has changed over time. But then I was offered the job at QueenslandBalletand I had to dedicate all my time to that. I don’t think they were expecting [the sequel] to take 14 years!”double quotation markOne of the things my mother taught me was to keep moving forward at all timesLi CunxinHis second memoir, The Lucky Son, takes up precisely where Mao’s Last Dancer left off: as Cunxin and his ballet dancer wife Mary fly to their new lives at Houston Ballet under the directorship of Ben Stevenson. That outline of the proposed book onChinacan be glimpsed under the surface of this one, like a palimpsest; Cunxin’s six brothers’ lives are sketched, and a fascinating portrait of a country lifting itself from abject poverty to world superpower emerges.View image in fullscreenLi Cunxin and Mary McKendry in Ben Stevenson’s Sleeping Beauty in 1988.Photograph: Houston Ballet“One of the things my mother taught me was to keep moving forward at all times,” Cunxin says. “Don’t think about the past, just concentrate on what is ahead.” That grit kept her children alive and was instrumental in shaping Cunxin’s dogged, highly ambitious personality.Determination runs in the family. Mary was a deeply respected dancer herself, a career she sacrificed when she and Cunxin discovered their daughter Sophie was born profoundly deaf. “We were so fearful that Sophie would miss out on so much,” Cunxin says. “Music and dance and all the magical things.”Mary immediately left the world of ballet (she would return years later as ballet mistress at Queensland Ballet) to teach Sophie to talk. “Mary was incredible,” Cunxin recalls. “She gave everything to the task.”One one hand, it was a complete success. Sophie was fitted with a bionic ear (then known as a cochlear implant) and thrived; she embraced dance, had a successful education and excelled in the workplace. Cunxin and Mary assumed they’d done all that was needed.View image in fullscreen‘To be a leader of any kind takes vision. I had a very strong vision for Queensland Ballet.’Photograph: David Kelly/The GuardianBut then in 2015, Sophie sent an email to her parents that shocked and devastated them. Sophie expressed frustration at her parents for wanting their daughter to hear; she felt she’d come halfway to meet their world, but they had not met hers. They had not even bothered to learn sign language. Her “deafness was her birthright”, Cunxin writes in the book. Now, he says, Sophie “is a kind of ambassador between the hearing and deaf communities”. And he and Mary have begun learning Auslan.Cunxin’s dance career was so exemplary – moving from the BeijingDanceAcademy to Houston Ballet, and then to principal artist at Australian Ballet – he could have been forgiven for hanging up his pointe shoes and walking into a lucrative position in a stockbroking firm. Indeed, that’s exactly what he did. An unsuccessful tilt at the artistic directorship of Australian Ballet (the role eventually went to David McAllister) utterly crushed him, and it seemed for a few years he would never return to the world of professional ballet.Of course, that wasn’t how it panned out: despite being burned by that failure, Cunxin reluctantly put his name in the hat when Queensland Ballet were looking for their next artistic director. That tenacity and resolve was once more poured into the theatre.“To be a leader of any kind takes vision,” Cunxin says. “I had a very strong vision for Queensland Ballet. But you also have to be a good communicator, because you need to inspire others to join in your vision.” And you need to apply yourself, which wasn’t such an issue for someone trained at Beijing Dance Academy, with its brutal rehearsal regime and exacting standards.One of the delights of The Lucky Son is the way it tracks some of our favourite characters from Mao’s Last Dancer, including The Bandit, Cunxin’s bestie at the Beijing Dance Academy; his gorgeous instructor Teacher Xiao; and his astonishing mum and dad, Niang and Dia. There are echoes in the events too: Stevenson’s trip to Queensland to watch his protégé mount Cinderella recalls the unforgettable moment in Mao’s Last Dancer when his parents leave China for the first time to see their son dance and the audience gives them a standing ovation.View image in fullscreenCunxin at the Thomas Dixon Centre, home of the Queensland Ballet.Photograph: David Kelly/The GuardianCentral to Cunxin’s success at Queensland Ballet – where he oversaw a massive improvement in standards and built a stunning new home for the company, the Thomas Dixon Centre – were the lessons he learned from his time away from ballet, when he was a stockbroker: “I learned so much from the business world – when we had to approach donors for money, I could speak their language.” Relationships with Elisabeth Murdoch and the Ian Potter Foundation came in handy, and he and Mary also contributed some money of their own. It’s now a world-class organisation.Looking back on his life now, Cunxin feels an overwhelming sense of “gratitude, for the opportunities I was given and the people and artists who shaped me”. The Lucky Son concludes on stage – hardly surprising, given so many of the key moments in Cunxin’s life have been there – but this time it is in Switzerland, where he was awarded ballet’s most prestigious award, the Prix de Lausanne, in 2025.Best Australian books out in October: Magda Szubanski, delicious recipes and a picture book ‘masterpiece’Read moreAfter a few years of serious health issues (Mary is a cancer survivor and Cunxin has a major heart condition), the couple are increasingly happy to chill. “Our health has forced us to slow down,” he says with the emphasis on forced, as if there were no way they would slow down on purpose. “I worked very hard for two years on this book – it’s been all-consuming. So yes, I am enjoying taking things a little slower.”Is he confident that ballet will survive the coming AI tsunami, given how hard the art form is to perfect and how much time and effort is required? “I am worried, but I do think ballet is special,” he says. “When people come to see ballet, they are blown away by the artistry, the physicality and the music. I think it’s more important than ever to connect people.”The Lucky Son by Li Cunxinis out now (Penguin, $36.99)Explore more on these topicsAustralian booksBalletAutobiography and memoirDanceChinaQueenslandinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: AK Blakemore: ‘The Goldfinch by Donna Tartt was extremely silly and bad’ | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The poet and author on F Scott Fitzgerald’s perfect novel, losing faith in Ernest Hemingway – and the recent debut that blew her away
Author: AK Blakemore
Headline: The poet and author on F Scott Fitzgerald’s perfect novel, losing faith in Ernest Hemingway – and the recent debut that blew her away
Content: ‘I often find myself revisiting Virginia Woolf’s Orlando’ … AK Blakemore.Photograph: Alice ZooView image in fullscreen‘I often find myself revisiting Virginia Woolf’s Orlando’ … AK Blakemore.Photograph: Alice ZooThe books of my lifeFictionAK Blakemore: ‘The Goldfinch by Donna Tartt was extremely silly and bad’The poet and author on F Scott Fitzgerald’s perfect novel, losing faith in Ernest Hemingway – and the recent debut that blew her awayAK BlakemoreFri 9 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryLynley Dodd’s Hairy Maclary from Donaldson’s Dairy – where an assortment of differently shaped dogs go on a walk – wormed its way into my subconscious when I was very young. The great dane (Hercules Morse, as big as a horse), the dalmatian (Bottomley Potts, covered in spots), the dachshund (Schnitzel Von Krumm with a very low tum) … I could probably still recite most of it from memory.My favourite book growing upI had a lot of picture books illustrated by the great Korky Paul, and remember being obsessed – even as quite a young child – with the intricate grotesquerie of it all. He’s probably best known these days for illustrating the Winnie the Witch books, but my favourite was The Rascally Cake by Jeanne Willis, in which a rotund, green-haired man called Rufus Skumskins O’Parsley makes a cake out of disgusting things (rotten eggs, spider legs, garden snails and so on), only for the cake to come to life and attempt to eathim. Probably more than a little bit of Skumskins found its way into the protagonist of my second novel, The Glutton.The book that changed me as a teenagerI studied F Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby for my English GCSE and it entirely reshaped my brain. I still think it’s about as near to perfect as it’s possible for a novel to be. All the stupid loveliness and yearning in the world, distilled down into image after image, with a core of white-hot rage, at the way extreme wealth enables – necessitates, really – extreme cruelty. There’s functional alcoholism, and then there’s whatever Fitzgerald was doing in 1923. Everyone should read it.The writer who changed my mindI had a baby in May, and in the first weeks post-partum I read Of Woman Born: Motherhood as Experience and Institution, by the poet and activist Adrienne Rich, while my son was napping on my belly.It made me realise that I’d wrongly – though, perhaps, understandably – held on to this notion that mothering would necessarily mean setting aside the work of the imagination, and a narrowing of my horizons, creatively. But Rich writes so thrillingly of parenthood as a politically radicalising and artistically activating experience. Rich’s work has made me excited for the years to come as a writer, as well as a mother. I wish I’d read her a long, long time ago.The book that made me want to be a writerPortrait of My Lover As a Horse by Selima Hill.I bought it with a book voucher in Foyles on Charing Cross Road, when I was about 14. I’d never heard of Hill, but I picked it up based on the strangeness of the title and cover. All of Hill’s poetry collections, as published by Bloodaxe, have this naive, under-designed quality to them. I read the whole collection front-to-back on the train home, and then again back-to-front.
