By the next day I was trying to emulate Hill’s guileless, cryptic style in my own – far less masterly – little poems. That was basically my apprenticeship as a poet.Theauthor I came back toJane Austen. Until my mid-20s I subscribed to that surprisingly common, reductive view of her as the author exclusively of novels about rich people having dinner at each other’s houses. But now I’m a rich person (in global terms, at least – I mean, I have Chanel foundation and a mortgage) who likes having dinner at other people’s houses, I’m like,this rules.The book I rereadI often find myself revisiting bits of Virginia Woolf’s Orlando. In case you aren’t aware of it, it’s about a gender-swapping and functionally immortal Elizabethan nobleman who spends several languid centuries falling in and out of love and eventually achieving something like self-knowledge. Such a totally exhilarating, audaciously fun bit of work from an author who was – bless her – a bit of a Debbie Downer overall.The book I could never read againThe Sun Also Rises. I was worryingly into Ernest Hemingway, for a teenage girl, whereas now I think he’s a bit of a pillock.The book I discovered later in lifeI’m 35 so I flatter myself nothing I could say really counts, but: I thought I’d use my maternity leave to finally give some Donna Tartt a go. I staggered through The Goldfinch and thought it was extremely silly and bad.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe book I am currently readingI just finishedWhat Am I, a Deer?by Polly Barton, and I was totally blown away by it. It’s about how we have fun and what we find funny, how we choose our friends and construct our pet fantasies, and I loved it, and I love how Barton’s brain works. She thinks so profoundly about the minutiae of modern life and modern social dynamics and I somehow found myself feeling strangely optimistic about the world and the eccentricities of the people in it. A banger.Doom Painting by AK Blakemore is published by Granta. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFictionThe books of my lifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Is death necessary?’: why Peter Greenaway’s assisted dying drama is stuck in post-production hell | Movies | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Three years after filming began on the contentious Lucca Mortis, starring Dustin Hoffman, the British director is still in dispute with producers over which version to release, and a battle over rights rumbles on
Author: Geoffrey Macnab
Headline: Exclusive: Three years after filming began on the contentious Lucca Mortis, starring Dustin Hoffman, the British director is still in dispute with producers over which version to release, and a battle over rights rumbles on
Content: Peter Greenaway pictured in Madrid, Spain, in 2015.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeter Greenaway pictured in Madrid, Spain, in 2015.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesMovies‘Is death necessary?’: why Peter Greenaway’s assisted dying drama is stuck in post-production hellExclusive:Three years after filming began on the contentious Lucca Mortis, starring Dustin Hoffman, the British director is still in dispute with producers over which version to release, and a battle over rights rumbles onGeoffrey MacnabFri 9 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeter Greenaway’s new movie was supposed to mark a glorious swansong for him and his lead actor Dustin Hoffman, the Oscar-winning star of The Graduate and Tootsie. Both men were in their 80s when shooting began in Lucca, Tuscany, in late 2023. Neither knew the storms ahead or that this was going to turn into arguably the most troublesome project in Greenaway’s career.Turn the clock back to 2023 and Greenaway, who has been based in the Netherlands for the last 20 years, could hardly conceal his excitement during a Q&A at International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA) in the huge art deco Tuschinski theatre in Amsterdam in November 2023, after receiving a lifetime achievement award from the festival. He told the audience that he would be flying toItalythe next morning “and that, all being well, we will start shooting seriously in the next couple of days”.The film was then called Lucca Mortis, and Greenaway explained that it explored death. He said he had already made “quite a number of films” about sex (“Eros”) “but the other thing was Thanatos (death). There are, and have been, some extremely good films made about old age. I am thinking of [Ingmar] Bergman’s Wild Strawberries, for example, but not that many.”View image in fullscreenDustin Hoffman at the premiere of Twiggy in Los Angeles last week.Photograph: Variety/Getty Images“Our film is really about notions of death and it asks the rather absurd and ridiculous question – is death necessary? The popular media is absolutely covered now in considerations about assisted death, about euthanasia, about the legitimacy of suicide. I believe that we must take death more seriously.”Greenaway’s pitch was that Lucca Mortis isn’t a horror picture “full of coffins and skulls and macabre activities”. Instead, it a drama about a New York writer contemplating his mortality; a man who wants to round off his life in the neatest, most elegant way possible. Jacob Zucchine (Hoffman) was adopted as a kid and eventually grew up in the US. He returns to Lucca in Tuscany in search of his Italian roots. The film is set around the time of 9/11. Like New York, Lucca is dominated by looming towers and these inspire the author to write stories but also to feel that death is stalking him.Ominously, Lucca Mortis encountered difficulties right from the outset. In late 2023, the director and his crew arrived in Lucca but the lead actors weren’t yet there. Dozens of trucks filled with technical gear turned up from Rome: sets were built and the crew sat waiting for several weeks for work to begin – but it never did and they were eventually sent home. It appeared that the production had already hit cashflow problems.View image in fullscreenAnne Bancroft and Dustin Hoffman in The Graduate from 1967.Photograph: Cinetext Bildarchiv/Lawrence Turman\embassy/AllstarSuch a delay, though, is not unusual in film production. It is often a mad scramble to complete the financing for an ambitious independently funded film such as this. Production finally got under way in early 2024 – and this time with actors.The trade press reported that Lucca Mortis had a €15m (£12m) budgetand that it would use 25 locations in Lucca. The city threw itself behind the movie. Many of the locals were involved andthe Tuscan press reporteda carnivalesque atmosphere during shooting akin to that on a Fellini movie, with the Livorno-based publication Il Tirreno saying: “For a few months, Lucca became an open-air film set, with the citizens acting as unwitting extras and the historic centre crisscrossed by cameras, dolly shots and familiar faces.”However, the charm soon wore off as constant delays ate up large chunks of the budget. Produced by Facing East (whose previous credits include Robbie Williams biopic Better Man and Liam Neeson thriller, In The Land of Saints and Sinners) the budget for the film came mainly from private financiers Jumpy Cow Pictures in Switzerland. There was extra support through Italian and Dutch tax rebates.When most of the shooting was completed, Greenaway and Saskia Boddeke (his Dutch wife and creative partner) set to work with their team. A first draft assembly of the film was delivered in late 2024 and was reportedly warmly received. However, it was at this point that tensions threatened to reach breaking point. Sources close to Greenaway have said that the director’s contract gave him final cut, but that the producers subsequently decided to make their own, more “commercial” cut without the director’s involvement. Their position was that they were entitled to intervene because the film had gone over budget. Facing East has not responded to requests for comment.View image in fullscreenAlan Howard, Richard Bohringer, Helen Mirren and Michael Gambon in Peter Greenaway’s 1989 film The Cook, The Thief, His Wife & Her Lover.Photograph: Palace Pictures/Sportsphoto/AllstarThe net result is that there are two different versions of the film in circulation, neither of them fully completed (although the producers’ cut is said to be more advanced). There is also an ongoing row about who controls the rights to the movie – which is now stuck firmly in limbo.And the citizens of Lucca are not happy. Three years on from the start of production, there is still no sign of the movie made in their back yard and which they embraced with so much enthusiasm and affection. Lucca councillor Remo Santini commented earlier this week: “We’re disappointed because, as a municipality, we’ve spent time and energy making this film. We even had a sneak preview of it, months ago, and it really made a great impression on us. Yet, despite filming having wrapped over two years ago, all is quiet. Unfortunately, this stalemate isn’t our fault.”The city says it has made repeated requests to the production and the director for explanations about what has happened to the movie, “and no one has contacted us since”. This, then, clearly wasn’t a smooth or happy shoot. Even the title is proving contentious. Partly because the city of Lucca isn’t keen to be associated with death, the film is now called Tower Stories.The irony is that those who have seen the two cuts say they are not that different. Whichever way the film is edited, it is still based on the same dense and digressive Greenaway screenplay, which takes the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein’s gnomic observation “death is not an event in life; we do not live to experience death” as its starting point. Some have talked admiringly of the picture’s visual splendour, lush musical score, operatic set-pieces and narrative intricacy. Hoffman is said to give a very poignant performance as the elderly writer, a character who appears to be partially based on Greenaway himself.“It’s a great legacy for Greenaway and not only for him, but for Dustin – a great performance. It’s a movie that needs to be finished and needs to be released,” one frustrated member of the production crew told me last week.View image in fullscreenGreenway’s The Draughtsman’s Contract from 1982.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyThere is, though, something quixotic about the very idea of Lucca Mortis. Greenaway is the grand old visionary of British cinema. He has dozens of credits to his name, shorts, features and documentaries, all with his firm authorial imprint. Whether he is dealing with cannibalism (The Cook, The Thief, His Wife & Her Lover), Shakespeare (Prospero’s Books) or garden design (The Draughtsman’s Contract), his approach remains the same: magical realism, obtuse ideas, puns, and plenty of visual flamboyance.This could be Greenaway’s final feature, but whether it will be seen in the way he intended is now in serious doubt. The longer it is stuck in postproduction purgatory, the less chance that its director, 84, and its star, who turned 89 in August, will be fit and able enough to promote it properly. There are also obvious questions over whether distributors and festivals will accept a Greenaway film over which the director hasn’t had the final say.The talk is now of trying to protect the “dignity” of Lucca Mortis. For that to happen, everyone involved will need to accept what surely should have been obvious from the outset, namely that when you commission Peter Greenaway to make a film, that’s exactly what you are going to get – a Peter Greenaway film – and you risk disaster if you try to turn it into something else.Explore more on these topicsFilmPeter GreenawayDustin HoffmanItalyEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our age | Movies | The Guardian
description: Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning shows how public opinion has changed around billionaire CEOs since The Social Network’s release
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning shows how public opinion has changed around billionaire CEOs since The Social Network’s release
Content: A straitjacketed simmer … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: SonyView image in fullscreenA straitjacketed simmer … Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: SonyMoviesThe new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our ageJeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning shows how public opinion has changed around billionaire CEOs since The Social Network’s releaseDan MilmoGlobal technology editorFri 9 Oct 2026 07.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen The Social Network came out, Mark Zuckerberg organised a staff viewing of a film hedescribed as “fun”.A group corporate outing to the sequel is unlikely.The Social Network hardly portrayed the Facebook founder and his company in a hagiographical light (Zuckerberg laterdescribed the film as “hurtful”), but there was at least an element of the plucky upstart to the rise of Zuckerberg as he takes Facebook to 500 million users and a valuation of $25bn (ridiculously small numbers now – Meta has 3.6 billion users and is worth $1.8tn).By the end of that film, though, a steely CEO is emerging and his company is on the brink of global hegemony. The Social Reckoning picks up from there, with a clear perspective that both the founder and his company – as well as the industry they represent – are corporate villains now.This is set to be underlined by the release of theOpenAIdrama, Artificial, where its CEO, Sam Altman, is reportedly given a deeply unflattering portrayal. Elon Musk completes the villainous trilogy by appearing as himself – aside from the odd deployment of an AI avatar – in Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary, Musk, about the world’s first trillionaire.Tech is the obvious thread joining these films, but another is the scathing portrayal of the company leaders in them. Film villains used to be hoodlums, ex-deep state operatives, people with posh British accents. Tech execs are the new Darth Vader.View image in fullscreenDeeply unflattering … Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonThis is underlined by the casting ofJeremy Strong, who looks a touch on the old side to be playing 2019-2021 era Zuckerberg (the Meta CEO was in his mid-30s at the time of the film’s events whereas Strong is 47), but is embedded in our minds as the tortured Roy family scion Kendall in Succession.Strong also brings a straitjacketed simmer to the role here, one that breaks slightly at the end as he backtracks on being a “free speech absolutist” under intolerable pressure. It is the most human Zuckerberg moment in the entire film.Peter Bradshawdescribes Strong’s performanceas a “very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet”. It is much less sympathetic than Jesse Eisenberg’s in The Social Network and is a sort of corporeal representation of Meta as the monolithic, corporate bad guy.Elements of the portrayal chime with some former Meta employees, including a whistleblower, Arturo Béjar,who describes it as “accurate”. Another former employee tells the Guardian that Zuckerberg was “unemotional” in meetings (perhaps what you’d expect from a $1.8tn company CEO, admittedly). Well, Strong’s performance certainly is that.There had already been a turning point in public perception of Facebook beforethe Haugen leaks, with theCambridge Analyticascandal, which raised questions about the privacy of account holders’ data and how it is used.Haugen’s revelations in 2021 compounded this disquiet. By the time of the2022 inquest for British teenager Molly Russell, who took her own life after watching harmful content on Instagram, regulation of social media around the world was inevitable.The tone of The Social Reckoning and Strong’s performance reflect this shift. In the UK, screenings of the film are carrying an advert for the online safety charity established by Molly’s family,in which her father says: “‘Instagram helped kill my daughter”.Responding to Russell,Metasays it has worked to improve the safety of its platforms.The regulatory, legal and political backlash against social media – as well as the release of The Social Reckoning – reflects a lack of trust in such statements.Strong’s Zuckerberg says in the film that “the debate is over”. If it is, The Social Reckoning portrays a world where Meta is on the wrong side of it.Explore more on these topicsFilmMetaMark ZuckerbergOpenAIJeremy StrongSocial mediaDigital mediaShareReuse this content

title: Branford Marsalis Quartet and Dianne Reeves: Dedicated to You review – eloquent Coltrane tribute | Jazz | The Guardian
description: This elegant contemporary reinvention of 1963 album John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman pairs Marsalis’s post-bop sax with Reeves’ agile vocals, to time-stopping effect
Author: John Fordham
Headline: This elegant contemporary reinvention of 1963 album John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman pairs Marsalis’s post-bop sax with Reeves’ agile vocals, to time-stopping effect
Content: We say it’s wonderful … Branford Marsalis and Dianne Reeves.Photograph: Courtesy of Shervin LainezView image in fullscreenWe say it’s wonderful … Branford Marsalis and Dianne Reeves.Photograph: Courtesy of Shervin LainezJazz album of the monthJazzReviewBranford Marsalis Quartet and Dianne Reeves: Dedicated to You review – eloquent Coltrane tribute(Blue Note)This elegant contemporary reinvention of 1963 album John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman pairs Marsalis’s post-bop sax with Reeves’ agile vocals, to time-stopping effectJohn FordhamFri 9 Oct 2026 04.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early 1960s, the Impulse! label tried to steer its star saxophonist John Coltrane away from increasingly uncompromising and experimental music that it feared might be scaring its customers. Label boss Bob Thiele suggested a more palatable all-ballads album with a little-known African American supper-club singer called Johnny Hartman, whose warm, Bing Crosby-like baritone but bracing absence of schmaltz had already impressed Frank Sinatra and Tony Bennett. Coltrane and Hartman hit it off perfectly, and the 1963 album, John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman, was an unexpected mini masterpiece of restraint, flawless timbral expressiveness, and mutual understanding.View image in fullscreenBranford Marsalis and Dianne Reeves: Dedicated to You album coverInvited by Blue Note Records in Coltrane’s centenary year to curate his own tribute, post-bop sax luminary Branford Marsalis made that album the template for Dedicated to You – done as contemporary reinventions, not mere cover versions. Marsalis invited Dianne Reeves, a vastly experienced jazz singer with a Sarah Vaughan-like mix of flawless intonation and agile spontaneity, to take the vocal role. “Listening to all the great singers coming up”, Reeves has said, “I learned that they stood in the band, not in front of the band. They saw themselves as co-creators of the sound.”Marsalis’s tenor murmurs and twists behind Reeves’ juggling of nostalgia and hope on Autumn Serenade, and the title track makes time stand still in its cherishing of every word and sound. Lush Life’s famous small-hours ruminating on life’s mistakes is reinvented in Reeves’ almost defiant resignation and the sleepy languor of the tenor sax and piano, while her slyly taunting stretch of the syllables of “won-der-ful” unerringly nails the love-is-fab irony of They Say It’s Wonderful.Marsalis adds Trane instrumentals from the same period here, including the exhilaratingly beboppish soprano feature Big Nick, a hurtling Charlie Parkeresque genuflection on the uptempo 26-2, plus three bonus tracks engagingly balancing the vocal and jazz-instrumental eloquence of this fine album.Also out this monthThe prodigiously eclectic German pianistMichael Wollnyreleases the solo-piano set Eine Winterreise (ACT), a rumination on the Schubert song cycle that the pianist typically recasts as “a meditation on walking – on moving forward without having any reliable guidance, without a fixed destination”. Wollny relishes abstract sound, improv, and jazz phrasing, but his idiomatic range is profound. Alongside Schubert’s themes, Kate Bush’s Snowflake gets a glisteningly awestruck treatment here, as does Björk’s Aurora, as Wollny continues – unintentionally – to reinforce his stature as a piano visionary in the league of Jarrett, Hancock or Mehldau. London harpist/vocalistTara Mintonunveils a sensitive interweaving of Latin American rhythmic ideas and Spanish and English lyrics on her distinctive autobiographical set The Devil Invites You to Dance (Adhyâropa Records), while pianist/composerMyra Melford’s Fire and Water Quintet, including guitarist Mary Halvorson and cellist Tomeka Reid, delivers Sure Grand Out (RogueArt), her compelling third exploration of sonic parallels for the physicality, animation and grace of painter Cy Twombly’s work.Explore more on these topicsJazzJazz album of the monthalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Jess Williamson: A Mile South of Heaven review – alt-country singer’s love-hate affair with LA | Music | The Guardian
description: Following 2023 breakout Time Ain’t Accidental, the best songs here are when Williamson strips back country music, rebuilding it as something familiar yet different
Author: Aimee Cliff
Headline: Following 2023 breakout Time Ain’t Accidental, the best songs here are when Williamson strips back country music, rebuilding it as something familiar yet different
Content: Nostalgic … Jess Williamson.Photograph: Courtesy of  Jackie Lee YoungView image in fullscreenNostalgic … Jess Williamson.Photograph: Courtesy of  Jackie Lee YoungMusicReviewJess Williamson: A Mile South of Heaven review – alt-country singer’s love-hate affair with LA(New West)Following 2023 breakout Time Ain’t Accidental, the best songs here are when Williamson strips back country music, rebuilding it as something familiar yet differentAimee CliffFri 9 Oct 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn her essay Goodbye to All That,Joan Didion writes that she left New York City when “the golden rhythm was broken”. Texas-born alt-country singer Jess Williamson borrows the title for the aching opening track of her sixth solo album, on which she contemplates whether she has had enough of Los Angeles. But while Didion was looking back on leaving the city of her youth behind, Williamson is still in LA, wrestling with competing desires to stay or flee.View image in fullscreenJess Williamson: A Mile South of Heaven.Photograph: Courtesy of  Jackie Lee YoungThis tumultuous love-me, love-me-not is set to Williamson’s most traditional soundscapes to date: “Deep in the woods I feel the hum of the city,” she sings on Hum of the City in her strongest Texas drawl over mournful strings and twiddling banjo. Gone are the iPhone-programmed drums that made her 2023 breakout Time Ain’t Accidental so appealingly offbeat, and while the Americana flourishes give weight to Williamson’s nostalgia for her native Dallas, at times they make the album stodgier and less imaginative than her previous record.A Mile South of Heaven’s most intriguing moments come when she strips country music back to its bare essentials, rebuilding it as something that looks uncannily similar yet different. Take the sparse climate anxiety meditation Tracking the Tropics, backed by eerie Mellotron, with even the hand claps sounding sinister. Or album closer The Gem and Mineral Show, in which Williamson recalls sipping champagne with a pop star, and chills with a visceral, unadorned ending as she sings of the loneliness of being a perpetual tourist. On this record, homesickness is a constant no matter where you go, and every note is packed with yearning.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: End Of Abyss review – a creepy dollhouse take on Resident Evil and The Thing | Games | The Guardian
description: This fetchingly presented horror game brings style and scares, but overextends itself with repetition
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This fetchingly presented horror game brings style and scares, but overextends itself with repetition
Content: Your little bobble-headed hero … End of Abyss video game screenshot.Photograph: Section 9/Epic Games PublishingView image in fullscreenYour little bobble-headed hero … End of Abyss video game screenshot.Photograph: Section 9/Epic Games PublishingGamesReviewEnd Of Abyss review – a creepy dollhouse take on Resident Evil and The ThingPlayStation 5 (version played), Xbox, PC; Epic Games PublishingThis fetchingly presented horror game brings style and scares, but overextends itself with repetitionAlex SpencerFri 9 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsmall band of soldiers enters an abandoned facility, where puckered flesh sprouts from cold steel. It’s a promising but familiar start to a sci-fi horror story, with heavy overtones of Alien and The Thing. Neither of those, though, were so … dinky.End of Abyss’s facility is presented as a kind of a model-village recreation of The Thing’s Outpost 31 that you peer into from above. Your little bobble-headed hero takes up a tiny fraction of the screen, with most of the remainder drenched in foggy darkness, or even blanked out entirely. This is a world of Usborne-style cutaways, where anything outside the walls is total blackness.This combination of cute and eerie immediately marks End of Abyss as part of the Scandi-chiaroscuro style pioneered by Limbo and Inside (from Playdead, in Copenhagen) and Little Nightmares (from Malmö-based Tarsier Studios, where the founders of End of Abyss developer Section 9 cut their teeth). Those games, though, were all puzzle-platformers. End of Abyss is a survival-horror game in the mould of PS1-era Resident Evil, which took a similarly zoomed-out approach, using fixed, CCTV-reminiscent camera angles. It’s a great way of controlling each scene’s composition for maximum aesthetic value – and, of course, to set up scares.View image in fullscreenDrenched in darkness … End of Abyss.Photograph: Section 9/Epic Games PublishingEnd of Abyss delights in lovingly decorated dioramas, with bodies and viscera laid outjust so, illuminated by the flickering light of a CRT screen and some orange-glowing item (a valuable key or weapon upgrade) dangling just out of reach. As you’re studying these details, trying to figure out how you might reach that desirable object, at the edge of your vision a monster will peel itself from the darkness and attack before you can consciously register its presence.What follows is a dance of backpedalling and firing your pistol, praying that it’s loaded with enough ammo to finish off the advancing assailant before it can catch up to you. Or, worse, your retreat carries you into another nest of monsters. These are foundational thrills of the genre, and End of Abyss keeps them intact as it shrinks them down to dollhouse size. They might be scarier still, in fact, because manually aiming a gun from a top-down perspective can be fiddly, and End of Abyss’s control scheme is so confounding (who puts reload on the right thumbstick?) that you’re fighting muscle memory as much as the monsters.On top of this survival-horror foundation, though, End of Abyss layers elements of Dark Souls, Metroid and Hollow Knight – and here it overextends. This facility is big and complex enough for you to get lost in, filled with doors that only open from the other side and seemingly separate zones that join up in unexpected ways. These can be some of video games’ finest pleasures, when done right, but they make for an uncomfortable fit in a game that relies on a character so slow-moving that they can be threatened by a shambling zombie.View image in fullscreenStriking gloomy style … End of Abyss.Photograph: Section 9/Epic Games PublishingThat striking gloomy style, meanwhile, is something of an achilles heel when you’re trying to tell one room from another. It’s not helped by a pause-screen map that struggles to convey the interlocking territory, and, at the time of playing, is prone to getting confused over questions as fundamental as which doors are locked.This leads to a lot of unnecessary backtracking and, with every repeat visit, those carefully staged scenes lose some of their sheen. A composition that had you gawping the first time can’t hope to maintain that effect on the dozenth visit, while the shadow-peeling scares turn out to run on the clockwork logic of a fairground ghost train. Reaching the final boss after 12 hours, with much of the map still greyed out and other stretches tromped over endlessly, I’m left feeling exhausted, with little inclination to explore the other half of the game that (according to the completion percentage) remains unseen. Contrary to its fetchingly diminutive presentation, End of Abyss might be just too big for its own good.End of Abyss is out now; £22.69Explore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5reviewsShareReuse this content

title: I hitchhiked from Sydney to Perth, and found comfort in the company of strangers | Adventure travel | The Guardian
description: The lost practice of hitchhiking is a subculture, an art, and a way of travel that satisfies wanderlust like no other trip. Plus, it costs nothing
Author: Aston Brown
Headline: The lost practice of hitchhiking is a subculture, an art, and a way of travel that satisfies wanderlust like no other trip. Plus, it costs nothing
Content: ‘I smile, stretch out my arm and raise my thumb’: Aston Brown hitchhikes west in Australia, attempting to travel from Sydney to Perth.Photograph: Em JensenView image in fullscreen‘I smile, stretch out my arm and raise my thumb’: Aston Brown hitchhikes west in Australia, attempting to travel from Sydney to Perth.Photograph: Em JensenAdventure travelI hitchhiked from Sydney to Perth, and found comfort in the company of strangersThe lost practice of hitchhiking is a subculture, an art, and a way of travel that satisfies wanderlust like no other trip. Plus, it costs nothingGet our weekend culture and lifestyle emailAston BrownFri 9 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 20.20 EDTShareI’m alone, hunched over by a dusty road junction, and feeling the bite of the morning sun. I’ve already been waiting here, on the outskirts of Esperance on the south coast of Western Australia, for more than three hours. Another wave of traffic approaches. I smile, stretch out my arm and raise my thumb.Most drivers who pass wave or give me a thumbs up. One gives me the finger. There isn’t much traffic. Someone tosses a water bottle out their window at me.Just as I start to catastrophise in the dust, a four-wheel-drive quietly pulls off the road and comes to a stop behind me. I hoist my backpack around my shoulder, run over and jump in the passenger seat, thanking the driver profusely.One of my stranger interests is hitchhiking. I’m drawn to the idea of abandoning control and finding comfort in a stranger’s company. It’s a subculture, an art, and a way of travel that satisfies wanderlust like no other trip. Plus, it costs nothing.Once a popular way to travel in the 70s and 80s, these days it’s pretty rare to see a hitchhiker on the side of Australian roads. For starters, its reputation was overwhelmingly tarnished by its association withserial killer Ivan Milat, who murdered several hitchhikers in the early 90s. Australia is also one of the few countries in the world that make it legally fraught to hitchhike, with laws explicitly naming hitchhiking as an offence, though legislation differs between state and territories.View image in fullscreenDehydration while waiting for a lift is a concern for hitchhikers.Photograph: Aston BrownAccording toHitchwiki(Wikipedia for hitchhiking), most jurisdictions essentially prohibit a pedestrian from standing on or moving on to a road to hitchhike, though the wording and what legally constitutes “the road” varies. However, in the ACT hitchhiking is legal in most circumstances and Tasmania removed any reference to hitchhiking from its road rules in 2019.But safety and legal baggage aside, there are some signs hitching is making a comeback. Online resources such as the hitchhiker community Hitchwiki and its offshoot,Trustroots, which has more than 120,000 members, are steadily growing. And according to the University of Western Australia’s Dr Fang Liu, who studies adventure tourism,social media accounts sharing extreme ways of travellingare demystifying and normalising hitchhiking.View image in fullscreenHitching is making a comeback as social media influencers normalise hitchhiking.Photograph: Aston Brown“Young international travellersare seeing people online and think, ‘Oh, I can do that too,’ but they may be unprepared and unaware of the risks,” she says.“In a lot of places there’s no [phone] signal and you might have to wait hours for someone to stop. By then you’ve probably already dehydrated. Social media doesn’t convey that.”Confessions of an 82-year-old hitchhikerRead moreInside strangers’ carsI introduce myself to my latest ride. The driver is Doug Hilton, the boss of Australia’s national science agency, CSIRO. His job will make for good conversational fodder, but more importantly, he’s driving 500km west to Albany, his car has air conditioning, and the dusty intersection is in the rear-vision mirror.I’ve hitchhiked in Australia a few times before, once up Tasmania’s east coast and across Flinders Island on the Bass Strait, and another time from Canberra to Sydney. But never as far and never as ambitious as this latest leg – the plan is to go all the way from Sydney to Perth, mostly inside strangers’ cars.It’s the final leg of my journey and things have taken a fortunate turn.View image in fullscreen‘You’re the first hitchhiker I’ve seen in decades,’ Mike tells Aston Brown as they drive through South Australia.Photograph: Aston Brown‘Here we feel so safe’Five days earlier I’m fresh and clean-shaven, standing outside Broken Hill in outback New South Wales. I wait just five minutes before an SUV with a bull bar doubles back and offers me a ride.Inside is Miranda and her two children, originally from Zimbabwe. The car is crammed with pillows and baggage, but they find room for me. While I ram my backpack into the boot, Miranda’s teenage daughter moves to the backseat, squishing in beside her younger brother and an Esky packed with yoghurt cups and juice boxes.The family immigrated to the US a few years ago, but because of gun violence and immigration crackdowns decided to leave. “I never would have picked up someone there, but here we feel so safe,” Miranda says, the desert rushing by.View image in fullscreenMiranda with her two children in South Australia after giving Aston Brown a lift from Broken Hill, NSW.Photograph: Aston BrownThey now live in the regional Queensland town of Chinchilla, where Miranda says they’ve been embraced by the community. “We are so happy here,” she says. “Every day I thank God for where we have ended up.” From the backseat, her daughter says she wants to study medicine when she finishes high school.After four hours of meandering conversations between long silences, we part ways somewhere in rural South Australia. They’re headed to Adelaide to visit a family friend and make the most of school holidays. I’m going west.‘Milat changed things’Soon I’m racing through rolling hills of green oats and yellow canola flowers draped in golden afternoon light. Hulking wind turbines spin on the hilltops. Mike, 67, is in the driver’s seat of his Toyota troop carrier. He spends his retirement restoring century-old farm tractors and is headed to Cowell to pick up some engine parts. He says by sundown we’ll be in Jamestown, a small town with a pleasant campground by the river.“You’re the first hitchhiker I’ve seen in decades,” he says. “Milat probably changed things.”View image in fullscreenCanola fields whiz past in South Australia.Photograph: Aston BrownIvan Milat was convicted of the murder of five female and two male backpackers between 1989 and 1992 in NSW, several of whom had been hitchhiking. It’salleged he’s responsible for dozens more unsolved murders or disappearances.There’s no denying the act of hitchhiking is inherently risky. But I am a white male. Whatever the risks I face, they are not the samedangersa woman or female-presenting person can encounter hitchhiking alone. Hitchwikioffers specific safety advicefor female hitchers, but maintains “you have a right to be respected and it is not true that while hitchhiking you expose yourself to a risk at your own wish”. They also point out that women willusually spend less time waitingto be picked up.View image in fullscreenMike in front of his vehicle in Jamestown, South Australia.Photograph: Aston BrownOn my journey I follow the general rule of thumb when it comes to hitching safely: I stand well off the road, in places with good visibility, with enough room for cars to pull over, and slow-moving traffic. I stick to footpaths where I can.When a car does pull over I give the driver a once-over and follow my gut. If I feel uncomfortable or unsafe, I know I’m under no obligation to get in the car. Though that’s a hypothetical. Every experience I’ve had has been positive so far.View image in fullscreenThe wide open road in South Australia.Photograph: Aston BrownOver beer and dinner at the Jamestown pub, I learn about Mike’s extended family and how proud he is of his overachieving daughter. The next morning I tag along with him further west, snaking up a mountain pass before plunging into a treeless and barren plain below. Across the Spencer Gulf, grey and faint in the distance, is the Whyalla steelworks. Last monthmore than 500 of the plant’s employees lost their jobs.“People are feeling pissed off – there’s only bad news now and the major parties have no solutions,” Mike says. Talking about politics is a staple of the journey, though in a stranger’s car I prefer to do most of the listening. “Still, we are a lucky country, it’s just a lot of us don’t realise how lucky,” Mike says. An hour later we part ways.‘Middle of everything’By midday I meet Neil, a 79-year-old widower on the final leg of a four-month road trip across the continent. Neil, who lives in Geraldton in Western Australia, has stopped in his ute. His first joke is about hitchhiking.“A hitchhiker gets into a car,” Neil tells me. “He says to the driver, ‘You’re fairly brave picking up a hitchhiker these days. For all you know, I could be a mass murderer.’“The driver turns to him and says, ‘Well, what are the chances of us both being axe murderers?’”View image in fullscreenNeil provides a running commentary as they drive through South Australia.Photograph: Aston BrownAs we get comfortable, Neil’s running commentary begins. There’s a “ripper” wheat crop over there and another a few kilometres later, much the same. Over there is a slag heap from an abandoned iron ore mine. But where are all the sheep? And what could that truck be hauling?I learn about his life, too. Marrying at 21, raising a family, working 96-hour weeks driving trucks and saving prudently. We talk about relationships, love and getting to the “pointy end”. His motto is: “If you never go, you never never know.”At dusk we pull off the Eyre Highway at a truckstop and Neil disappears into his camper trailer for the night. I pitch my tent beside it. The ground is gravel and my sleep is restless. In the morning we set off at dawn and I doze off in the passenger seat.View image in fullscreenRain falls on the Nullarbor Plain along the Eyre Highway in Western Australia.Photograph: Aston BrownBy the time I wake the sun is high and the landscape has transformed, thickets of silver saltbush and red dirt as far as the eye can see. We’ve reached the Nullarbor, a vast arid plain stretching 1,200km across southern Australia. “Middle of nowhere,” I say. “Nah mate, middle of everything,” Neil replies, road trains swooshing by endlessly.Towing his camper, Neil sticks to about 80km/h for safety and fuel efficiency, so it’s slow going. In the afternoon we drive down the 90 Mile Straight, the longest straight road in the southern hemisphere, and that night, under a gibbous moon, we share a dark beer, dinner and a Magnum mini vanilla ice-cream by the fire, all courtesy of Neil.View image in fullscreenThe 90 Mile Straight on the Nullarbor Plain in Western Australia.Photograph: Aston BrownThree days and 1,900km since we met, Neil pulls up outside a campground in Esperance. We take a selfie and exchange a warm handshake. I know it’s probably the last time I’ll see him.A birding detourI don’t know it yet, but Doug from the CSIRO, 62, will be the last driver to pick me up before I hit Perth.I bookend my journey by talking to Doug about his passion for moths, his dream of inventing a way to eradicateferal cats, and the benefits of therapy to his mental health. Among other scientific pursuits, he’s on his way to Albany to meet with two Menang Indigenous elders who co-authored a paper with him about moths in the region, including three newly discovered species of primitive jaw moths.In the afternoon I take up his invitation to join him bird watching by the ocean. We park at a headland, Doug grabs a Nikon Z9 with a huge telephoto lens out of the boot, and we start walking through thick coastal scrub. At sunset we witness a brown blur scurry across a dirt track. Doug misses the photo but is nonetheless ecstatic and wraps his arm around me in joy.View image in fullscreenThe Nullarbor Plain.Photograph: Aston BrownApparently we’ve just seen one of Australia’s rarest birds, the noisy scrubbird, presumed extinct until it was rediscovered in 1961. The significance of the sighting is lost on me but Doug assures me I’ve just hit the peak of my bird-watching career. I didn’t know I’d started it.We pull into Albany at dark and Doug drops me off at a hostel. It reeks of marijuana and there’s no hot water but I’m just happy to be sleeping on a thick mattress. When I wake up it’s miserable outside so I make the call to take the bus for the final six hours of the route to Perth. I’m comfortable, but it’s decidedly dull as the sprawling suburbs of the world’s most isolated capital city start rolling by. I’ve spent 4,360km travelling across the most isolated inhabited continent on Earth, yet for all the distance, I’ve rarely felt alone.

title: Cocktail of the week: All Roads’ daiquiri – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: A touch of homemade scotch bonnet jam turns up the heat in this classic concoction
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A touch of homemade scotch bonnet jam turns up the heat in this classic concoction
Content: ‘As good for crisp autumn evenings as it is on a sunny day’: the All Roads daiquiri.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreen‘As good for crisp autumn evenings as it is on a sunny day’: the All Roads daiquiri.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: All Roads’ daiquiri – recipeA touch of homemade scotch bonnet jam turns up the heat in this classic concoctionMalika Green and Paschelle BrownFri 9 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOur daiquiri sums up whatAll Roadsis all about: familiar flavours with a little twist. Pineapple, rum and lime are a classic combination, and the addition of scotch bonnet jam brings a subtle warmth that makes this just as good for those first crisp autumn evenings as it is on a sunny day.All Roads daiquiriServes1For the pineapple and scotch bonnet jam75g fresh pineapple, roughly chopped30g caster sugar1small slicescotch bonnet chilli, or more to taste, or 1 pinch chilli flakesFor the drink10ml overproof white rum– we useWray & Nephew45ml white rum– we useHavana Club 3-Year-Old25ml fresh lime juice30g pineapple and scotch bonnet jam(see above and method)First make the jam. Put the pineapple and caster sugar in a saucepan and cook over a low heat until the fruit begins to soften. Blend smooth – we use a stick blender – then add the scotch bonnet to taste and keep cooking gently for 20-25 minutes, stirring regularly, until the jam thickens and turns lightly golden. Take off the heat, leave to cool completely, then lift out and discard the chilli (if using chilli flakes, leave them in). Decant into a small jar or container and keep in the fridge until needed.To build the drink, put everything in a cocktail shaker filled with ice, shake hard until well chilled, then double strain into a chilled coupe.Malika Green and Paschelle Brown,All Roads, London SW9Explore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodCaribbean food and drinkHerbs and spicesFruitrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for toffee apple Basque cheesecake | Food | The Guardian
description: Crisp surface, creamy centre, spicy, sticky topping – my go-to dessert
Author: Benjamina Ebuehi
Headline: Crisp surface, creamy centre, spicy, sticky topping – my go-to dessert
Content: Benjamina Ebuehi’s toffee apple Basque cheesecake.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.View image in fullscreenBenjamina Ebuehi’s toffee apple Basque cheesecake.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.The sweet spotFoodBenjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for toffee apple Basque cheesecakeA crisp surface and creamy core are the traits of this cheesecake with no base, here topped with spiced and sliced apples and a sticky, caramel sauceBenjamina EbuehiFri 9 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 05.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy go-to cheesecake these days is a burnt Basque. It’s so good it doesn’t even need a biscuit base, which might be the very reason some people aren’t fans. But Basque cheesecakes are rarely too sweet, because the burnt top provides just enough bitterness to balance things out and the insides stay ridiculously creamy. If I can give you one tip, though, it’s to make sure you take it out of the oven while it’s still really wobbly, to get the best set. An overbaked Basque is no fun at all.Toffee apple Basque cheesecakeI’ve given this an easy autumn spin with a generous topping of lightly spiced toffee apple slices.Prep5 minCook1 hr 10 minChillOvernightServes12750g cream cheese220g caster sugar1½ tsp vanilla bean paste4 large eggs, plus 1 egg yolk300ml double cream1 tsp fine sea salt20g plain flourFor the toffee apples3 eating apples60g butter80g dark brown sugar½ tsp ground cinnamon120ml double creamHeat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/465F/gas 9. Scrunch up two large sheets of baking paper, then smooth them out into the corners of a deep 20cm cake tin.Put the cream cheese, sugar and vanilla in a large bowl or stand mixer, and beat briefly until smooth. Add the eggs one at a time, followed by the extra yolk, making sure you don’t beat at high speed to avoid incorporating too much air. Stir in the cream and salt.Scoop about an eighth of the batter into a smaller bowl and sift the flour on top. Mix well to ensure there are no lumps, then scrape it back into the main mixture and stir well to combine.Pour the batter into the prepared tin and bake for 35-40 minutes, until the top is very well browned and the cheesecake still has a huge wobble. (If the top isn’t dark enough, just put it under a hot grill for a couple of minutes.) Leave the cheesecake to cool to room temperature, then chill in the fridge, ideally overnight. The next day, remove the cheesecake from its tin.To make the toffee apples, peel and core the apples, then slice them thickly into eighths. Heat the butter in a wide pan, then toss in the apples, turning to coat, and cook for three to four minutes, until they start to soften around the edges. Add the sugar and cinnamon, stir to combine, then, once the sugar has melted, pour in the cream. Cook briefly until the sauce is smooth, let it simmer for a minute, then take off the heat and stir in a pinch of salt.Let the apples cool, then spoon them and some of the caramel sauce on top of the cheesecake. Serve slices of cheesecake with extra sauce, if you like.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotCakeSpanish food and drinkCheeseFruitAutumn food and drinkEggsrecipesShareReuse this content
